Ibn Jarir reported from al-Ḥasan: When this verse about the property of orphans was revealed, they disliked mixing with them, and the guardian of an orphan separated the orphan's property from his own. They complained of this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best. And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220]. He said: so they mixed with them.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported that ʿUrwah asked ʿAisha about God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the care of her guardian. He shares with her in her property, and he is attracted to her wealth and her beauty. So her guardian wants to marry her without giving her a fair dower, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them the highest of their customary dowers. They were ordered to marry whatever women were lawful to them other than them." And "the people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a ruling after this verse, so God revealed ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾" [al-Nisāʾ 4:127]. ʿAisha said: God's saying in the other verse ﴿And you desire to marry them﴾ is the desire of one of you to avoid his orphan girl when she has little wealth and little beauty. So they were forbidden to marry those whom they desired for her wealth and beauty, from among the other women, except with justice, because of their aversion to them when they had little wealth and beauty.

al-Bukhari reported from ʿAisha: a man had an orphan girl whom he married. She had a palm tree, and he kept her under his control, and she had no share of it of her own. So God revealed ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. I think he said: she was his partner in that palm tree and in his wealth.

This meaning has been related through many chains. Ibn Jarir reported through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: a man would marry with the property of an orphan as much as God willed, so God forbade that. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him: "He limited men to four wives because of the property of orphans." Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr concerning God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾: he said, "A man would marry as many as he wished. So He said: just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women, and He limited them to four."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: they used to marry ten women in the pre-Islamic period, and they used to magnify the status of the orphan. Then, in their religion, they became mindful of the status of orphans and abandoned what they used to do in marriage in the pre-Islamic period. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him concerning the verse: "Just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women when you gather them with you."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported through Muḥammad ibn Abi Mūsā al-Ashʿarī from him: "If you fear adultery, then marry them." He says: just as you feared regarding the property of orphans that you would not be just with it, so fear for yourselves regarding what you do not marry. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported similar from Mujahid. Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Abu Malik concerning ﴿what is good for you﴾: he said, "what is lawful for you." Ibn Jarir reported the same from al-Ḥasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAisha something similar.

al-Shafiʿi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿUmar: "Ghaylān ibn Salamah al-Thaqafī embraced Islam while he had ten wives. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Choose from among them" — and in one wording: "Keep four of them and separate from the rest." This hadith was reported by those mentioned through many chains from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayyah, Ghundar, Zayd ibn Zurayʿ, Saʿīd ibn Abi ʿArūbah, Sufyān al-Thawrī, ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī, al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā and others among the memorizers, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Sālim, from his father, and he mentioned it.

al-Bukhari gave a defect (ʿillah) to this hadith. al-Tirmidhi transmitted from him that he said: "This is a hadith that is not preserved (ghayr maḥfūẓ). The correct version is what was reported from Shuʿayb and others, from al-Zuhri: 'I was told (ḥuddithtu) from Muḥammad ibn Suwayd al-Thaqafī that Ghaylān ibn Salamah...'" and he mentioned it. As for the hadith of al-Zuhri from his father, that a man from Thaqīf divorced his wives, then ʿUmar said to him: "I will stone your grave as the grave of Abū Righāl was stoned."

Maʿmar reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal (with a missing companion in the chain), and Mālik also reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal. Abū Zurʿah said: "And this is more authentic." ʿUqayl reported it from al-Zuhri: "It reached us from ʿUthmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Abi Suwayd." Abū Ḥātim said: "This is an error; it is only al-Zuhri who conveyed to us from ʿUthmān ibn Abi Suwayd." Aḥmad, however, judged it to be of the sound transmitters, and said: "Ismāʿīl and Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Maʿmar narrated to us from al-Zuhri." Abū Jaʿfar said in his narration: "Ibn Shihāb informed us from Sālim from his father that Ghaylān..." and he mentioned it. It has also been reported through other routes than Maʿmar and al-Zuhri: al-Bayhaqi reported it from Ayyūb, from Nāfiʿ and Sālim, from Ibn ʿUmar, that Ghaylān... and he mentioned it.

Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Majah reported in their Sunan from ʿUmayr al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives, so I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Choose four of them.'" Ibn Kathir said: its chain is good (ḥasan).

al-Shafiʿi reported in his Musnad from Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Dīlī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had five wives, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Keep four and separate from the other.'" Ibn Majah and al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh reported from Qays ibn al-Ḥārith al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives under me. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Choose four of them and release the rest.' So I did." These are corroborating reports (shawāhid) for the first hadith, as al-Bayhaqi said.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 1–4 (part 4 of 4):

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from al-Hakam, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that a slave-owner may not combine more than two women (in marriage) from among those who are owned.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning the verse, who said: "If you fear that you will not be just among four, then three; and if not, then two; and if not, then one. And if you fear that you will not be just even with one, then (marry) what your right hand possesses." 

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' the like of this. He also related from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾, that he said: "In intercourse and in love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, that he said: "The concubines (sarari)."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih related from ʿAʾishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "﴿That is closer to not being unjust﴾ means: that you do not oppress."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father said: This is an erroneous hadith (hadith khata'), and the correct report from ʿAʾishah is that it is a mawquf (companion's) statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿that you not be unjust﴾, that he said: "That you not deviate."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah, who said: "That you not deviate." Then he said: Have you not heard the verse of Abu Talib:

*With a scale of justice that does not cheat a barleycorn,*
*and a balance of truth whose weight is not deficient.*

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, who said: "That you not deviate." Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Razin, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak the like of this. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That is closer to there being fewer whom you must support (ta'ulu)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, who said: "That you not become impoverished."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Salih, who said: "A man, when he married a widow (ayyimah), would take her dowry for himself instead of giving it to her. So Allah forbade them from that, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying "nihlah" (as a gift), that he said: "By nihlah he means the mahr (bridal gift)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAʾishah concerning "nihlah," that she said: "Obligatory."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, that he said: "A specified obligation (fariḍah musammah)." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related the like of this from Qatadah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it﴾, that he said: "It refers to the husbands (lil-azwaj)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrimah concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "Of the dowry."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "If it is without harm or deception, then it is wholesome and pleasant (hanee'an mari'an), as Allah said."

(p-266) It is entirely Madinan (Madani, revealed after the Hijrah). Al-Qurtubi said: Except for one verse, which was revealed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest concerning ʿUthman ibn Talhah al-Hajabi, and it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa': 58], as will come, God willing. Al-Naqqash said: It was also said that it was revealed during the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah. And according to what was mentioned earlier from some of the scholars, that His saying, Exalted is He, "O mankind" wherever it occurs is Makki, this would require that this surah be Makki. ʿAlqamah and others held this view.

Al-Nahhas said: This verse is Makki. Al-Qurtubi said: The correct view is the first, for in Sahih al-Bukhari it is reported from ʿAishah that she said: "Surat an-Nisa' was not revealed except while I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." She meant that he had consummated the marriage with her. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the Prophet ﷺ consummated his marriage with ʿAishah only in Madinah. Whoever examines its rulings knows that it is undoubtedly Madinan.

He said: As for the one who said that "O mankind" is Makki wherever it occurs, this is not correct, for al-Baqarah is Madinan and in it "O mankind" occurs in two places. Ibn al-Durays in his Fada'il, al-Nahhas in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Surat an-Nisa' was revealed in Madinah." In its chain is al-ʿAwfi, who is weak. Likewise Ibn Mardawayh reported it from ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from Qatadah.

Something has also been transmitted concerning the virtue of this surah: al-Hakim in his Mustadrak reported from ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud who said: "Indeed, in Surat an-Nisa' there are five verses which would not please me if I had the world and all that is in it in exchange: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ [an-Nisa': 40], the verse ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ [an-Nisa': 31], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [an-Nisa': 48], the verse, ﴿And if they, when they wronged themselves﴾ [an-Nisa': 64]." Then he said: This is a sound chain, if ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud heard from his father, but this has been disputed.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported it from Ma'mar from a man, from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "Five verses of an-Nisa' are dearer to me than the whole world: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 35], ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 30], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 48], ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 110], ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 152]." Ibn Jarir also reported it.

Then it was narrated through the route of Salih al-Murri from Qatadah from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Eight verses were revealed in Surat an-Nisa', which are better for this Ummah than what the sun rises upon and sets upon," and he mentioned what Ibn Mas'ud mentioned, and added ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 26], ﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 27], ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 28].

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAishah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever takes the seven, he is a rabbi (a learned scholar)."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab reported from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been given in place of the Torah the seven long (surahs), and the al-Mi'in: every surah that reaches a hundred verses or more; and the al-Mathani: every surah less than the al-Mi'in and more than the al-Mufassal." Abu Ya'la, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab reported from Anas who said: "One night the Messenger of Allah ﷺ felt something, and in the morning it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the effect of an ailment is clearly upon you.' He said: 'As for me, I am, as you see, by the praise of Allah, well. I have recited the seven long (surahs).'"

Ahmad reported from Hudhayfah who said: "I stood with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he recited the seven long (surahs) in seven rak'ahs." ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported from some of the family of the Prophet ﷺ "that the Prophet ﷺ recited the seven long (surahs) in one rak'ah."

Al-Hakim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Ask me about Surat an-Nisa', for I recited the Qur'an while I was young." Al-Hakim said: Sound according to the condition of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it. Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf reported from him: "Whoever recites Surat an-Nisa' and knows what is veiled from what is not veiled, knows the obligatory shares of inheritance."

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

By "mankind" is meant the human beings present at the time of the address, and it includes those who will exist later, by an external proof, which is the consensus (ijma') that they are obligated with what those present are obligated with. Or it is by taghlib (predominance), where those present are given precedence over those not yet existing, just as the males were given precedence over the females in His saying: "Fear your Lord," because that is specific to the masculine plural form. The "single soul" here means Adam.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited (wahidin) without the ta' marbuta, in observance of the meaning. The feminine is by consideration of the wording, and the masculine by consideration of the meaning.

His saying: ﴿and created from it its mate﴾. It was said: It is coordinated with an implied element indicated by the speech; that is: He created you from a single soul which He created first, and created from it its mate. It was also said: It is coordinated with "He created you," so the second verb falls together with the first within the scope of the relative clause (sila).

The meaning: and He created from that soul, which is a designation for Adam, its mate, who is Eve. The meanings of taqwa (God-consciousness), Rabb (Lord), zawj (mate), and bath (dispersing) have already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The pronoun in His saying "from them" refers back to Adam and Eve, who are expressed by "soul" and "mate."

His saying: ﴿many﴾ is a descriptive word emphasizing what the plural form implies, since it is one of the plurals of multitude. It was also said that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; that is, a many dispersing. His saying: ﴿and women﴾, meaning many women, and the explicit mention of the adjective was omitted by relying on the first descriptive word.

His saying: (p-267) ﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾. The people of Kufa recited with the second ta' omitted, and its original form is tatasa'alun, lightened because of the coming together of two identical letters. The people of Madinah, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir recited with the ta' assimilated into the sin, and the meaning is: some of you ask others by Allah and the womb (kinship), for they used to link the two together in asking and in appeal, saying: "I ask you by Allah and the womb, and I implore you by Allah and the womb." Al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, al-Aʿmash, and Hamzah recited ﴿wal-arhami﴾ in the genitive (al-arhami).

The rest recited in the accusative. The grammarians differed in explaining the recitation in the genitive. The Basrans said: It is a solecism (lahn); the recitation with it is not permissible. The Kufans said: It is an ugly recitation (qira'ah qabihah). Sibawayh, explaining this ugliness, said: The pronoun in the genitive is like tanwin, and tanwin is not coordinated upon.

Al-Zajjaj and a group said that it is ugly to coordinate an apparent noun upon a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the genitive particle, like His saying: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. Sibawayh permitted this in poetic necessity, and recited:

"Today you have come near to satirizing us and praising us, so go away; what is with you and with the days is no marvel."

And a similar saying of another:

"Our swords are hung on the like of pillars, and between them and the Kaʿb is an open expanse."

Coordinating "al-Kaʿb" upon the pronoun in "baynihā."

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi related that al-Mubarrad said: "If I prayed behind an imam who recites ﴿wat-taqaw Allaha alladhi tasa'aluna bihi wal-arhami﴾ in the genitive, I would take my sandals and leave." Imam Abu Nasr al-Qushayri refuted what those who disparaged the genitive recitation said, and said: Such speech is rejected by the scholars of religion, because the recitations which the imams of the reciters recited were established from the Prophet ﷺ by tawatur (mass transmission). It is not hidden from you that the claim of tawatur is false, as knows whoever knows the chains of transmission they narrated with them. But one should argue for its permissibility by its occurrence in the poetry of the Arabs, as has preceded, and as in the saying of someone:

"Sufficient for you, and al-Dahhak, is a keen-edged sword."

And the saying of another:

"And the horizons of heaven desired it, but found for it no place to ascend in them, nor a place of rest on the earth."

And the saying of another:

"There is no in it and in the affairs from destruction."

And the saying of another:

"I charge against the host, not knowing whether my death was in it or in something else."

So "siwaha" is in the genitive position coordinated upon the pronoun in "fīhā." From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have made for you therein means of living, and [also for] those whom you do not provide for﴾ [al-Hijr: 20].

As for the accusative recitation, its meaning is clear and manifest, for it coordinates the womb upon the noble Name; that is: Fear Allah and fear the wombs, so do not sever them, for they are among what Allah has commanded to be joined. It was said: It is coordinated upon the place (mahall) of the preposition and its object in His saying "by Him," as when you say: "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr"; that is: Fear Allah by whom you ask one another, and you ask one another by the wombs.

The first is better. ʿAbdullah ibn Yazid recited "wal-arhamu" in the nominative, as a subject with an implied predicate; that is: and the wombs—join them, or and the wombs are deserving of being joined. It was also said that the nominative is by incitement (al-ighra') according to those who raise by it, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed a people among them are ʿUmayr and Ashba' ʿUmayr, and among them is al-Saffah."

"They are indeed worthy of meeting, when the man of valor calls: 'The weapons! The weapons!'"

"Al-arham" is a name for all relatives without distinction between the forbidden (mahram) and others. There is no disagreement about this among the people of the Shariʿah nor among the people of the language.

Abu Hanifah and some of the Zaydiyyah (a Shi'i group) specified the womb as the forbidden relatives in preventing the retraction of a gift, although they agree that its meaning is more general, and there is no basis for this specification. Al-Qurtubi said: The community (millah) agreed that maintaining ties of kinship is obligatory and that severing them is forbidden, end of quote. Numerous sound hadiths have been reported with this.

Al-Raqib: the observer, and it is an intensive form. It is said: "raqibtu arqubu ruqbatan wa rukbanan" when you wait.

His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. It is addressed to the guardians and the executors. Al-iya' is giving. The orphan (yatim) is one who has no father. The Shariʿah has specified it as one who has not reached puberty.

The explanation of its meaning was already fully discussed in al-Baqarah. The name "orphan" was applied to them at the time of giving them their property, although they are not given it except after the removal of the name of orphanhood by reaching maturity, as a metaphor, considering what they were before. It is also possible that "orphans" is meant in its literal sense, and "giving" means what the guardians and executors hand to them of sustenance and clothing, not the handing over of all of it. This verse is qualified by another verse, which is His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, then hand over to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. So mere removal of orphanhood by reaching puberty does not justify handing over their property to them until maturity of judgment is perceived in them.

His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. It is a prohibition for them against doing the practice of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) concerning the property of orphans, for they used to take the good from the property of orphans and replace it with the inferior from their own property, and they saw no harm in that. It was also said: The meaning is: Do not eat the property of orphans, which is forbidden and bad, and leave the good of your own property.

It was also said: The meaning is: Do not hasten to eat the bad of their property and leave waiting for the lawful provision from Allah. The first is better, for substituting one thing for another in the language means taking it in its place, and likewise exchanging it, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever substitutes disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], and His saying: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

And as for *al-tabdil* (substitution), it is sometimes used in this sense, as in His words: ﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens﴾, and sometimes in the reverse sense, as in your saying, "I substituted the ring for the silver," when you melt it and make it into a ring. al-Azhari stated this explicitly.

His words: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾. A group of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) held that what is forbidden in this verse is mixing, so the verb is taken to include the meaning of joining. That is: do not consume their property joined to your property. Then this was abrogated (*naskh*) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. It was also said that *ila* (to) here means *ma'a* (with), as in His words: ﴿Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52].

The first view is the better. *Al-huub* means sin. It is said: "al-rajul yahuubu huuban," meaning he sinned. Its root meaning is driving away camels, so sin was called *huub* because one is driven away from it. *Al-hawbah* means need. *Al-huub* also means loneliness (*al-wahshah*). It has three dialects: a *dammah* on the *ha'* (*hubb*), which is the reading of the majority; a *fathah* on the *ha'* (*habb*), which is the reading of al-Hasan, and al-Akhfash said it is the dialect of Tamim; and a third, *al-haab*.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *haaban* as a verbal noun, like *qala qalaan*. *Al-tahawwub* means grieving, and from it is the verse of Tufayl:

*So taste as we have tasted, his enemy being restrained,*
*By rage in our livers and by grief.*

His words: ﴿a great [sin]. And if you fear that you will not act justly regarding orphans, then marry﴾. The connection of the answer (*jaza'*) to the condition (*shart*) is that a man would be guardian of an orphan girl and wish to marry her, but he would not be just to her regarding her dowry; that is, he would not be fair in it and give her what others give to their wives. So Allah forbade them to marry them unless they were just to them and gave them the highest amount of dowry that is due to them. They were commanded to marry from other women who were lawful to them. This is the cause of the revelation of the verse, as will come. So it is a prohibition specific to this case.

A group of the early scholars (*salaf*) said: this verse abrogates what existed in the Jahiliyyah and at the beginning of Islam, that a man could marry as many free women as he wished. So He restricted them to four by this verse. The connection of the answer to the condition is that if they feared not acting justly regarding orphans, then likewise they should fear not acting justly regarding women, because they used to be scrupulous regarding orphans but not regarding women. Fear can relate to opposites, for what is feared may be known or may be merely suspected. For this reason the imams differed about its meaning in the verse. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "*khiftum*" means "you were certain." Others said: "*khiftum*" means "you suspected."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is what the skilled scholars (*hudhdhaq*) chose, and that it is on its usual meaning of suspicion, not certainty. The meaning is: whoever suspects that he will fall short in justice toward the orphan girl, let him leave her and marry another.

al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read *tuqsitu* with a *fathah* on the *ta'* from *qasata*, meaning he acted unjustly. On this reading the *la'* (not) is taken as extra, as if he said: "and if you fear that you will act unjustly."

al-Zajjaj reported that *aqsata* is used in the sense of *qasata*, whereas the known usage among the lexicographers is that *aqsata* means "he was just" and *qasata* means "he was unjust."

The *ma* in His words *ma taaba* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). The word *ma* was used in place of *man*, because the two may replace one another, and each may stand in place of the other, as in His words: ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 2], and ﴿Among them are those who walk on their bellies, and among them are those who walk on two legs, and among them are those who walk on four﴾ [al-Nur: 45].

The Basrans said: *ma* is used for attributes just as it is used for non-rational things. One says *ma 'indaka* ("what is with you"), and the answer is "graceful" or "generous." So the meaning is: marry the good women, that is, the lawful ones, and what Allah has forbidden is not good. It was also said that *ma* here is temporal (*mudiyyah*), meaning: as long as you are inclined to marriage. Ibn 'Atiyyah considered this weak.

al-Farra' said: *ma* here is verbal (*masdariyyah*). al-Nahhas said: this is very far-fetched.

Ibn Abi Ablah read *fankihu man taaba*. The people of knowledge are agreed that this condition mentioned in the verse has no implicit opposite meaning (*mafhum*), and that it is permissible for one who does not fear being unjust regarding orphans to marry more than one wife. The *min* in His words *min al-nisa'* is either explanatory (*bayaniyyah*) or partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), because what is intended is other than orphans.

His words: ﴿two, three, or four﴾ are in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for *ma*, as Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said. It was also said they are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). These words are not declined because of "*'adl*" (a form of indirect meaning) and descriptiveness, as is explained in the science of grammar. The original is: "marry what is good for you of women, two by two, three by three, and four by four."

The verse has been used as evidence for the prohibition of more than four wives. They explained this by saying that it is an address to the entire community, and that each one who marries may choose whatever number of this count he wishes, just as one says to a group: "Divide this money," which is a thousand dirhams, or "this money that is in the bag," as "two by two, three by three, and four by four."

This is accepted when the thing divided has had its total mentioned or its place specified. But if it is unrestricted, as when one says "divide the dirhams," meaning what they have earned, then the meaning is not like this. The verse belongs to the other category, not to the first.

Moreover, if someone said to a group dividing a large specific amount of property, "Divide it two, three, and four," and they divided part of it among themselves two dirhams each, part three each, and part four each, this would be the Arabic meaning. And it is known that if someone says, "The people came to me two by two, and they were a hundred thousand," the meaning is that they came to him in pairs. Likewise with "The people came three by three, four by four." The address to the whole is in the position of an address to each individual, as in His words: ﴿Kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and ﴿Establish prayer, give zakah﴾, and similar. So His words: ﴿marry what is good for you of women, two, three, or four﴾ mean: let each one of you marry what is good for him of women, two by two, three by three, and four by four. This is what the Arabic language requires. So the verse indicates the opposite of what they used it to prove. This is supported by His words at the end of the verse: ﴿But if you fear you will not be just, then one only﴾, for although it is an address to all, it is in the position of an address to each individual.

So it is better to derive the prohibition of exceeding four from the Sunnah rather than from the Qur'an. As for the argument of those who used the verse to permit marrying nine, based on the conjunctive *waw*, it is as if they said: "marry the total of this number mentioned." This is ignorance of the Arabic meaning. If He had said, "marry two, three, and four," this statement would have had some basis. But with the use of the form of distribution (*'adl*), it does not. Allah, glorified is He, used the conjunctive *waw* rather than *aw* (or), because *aw* would imply that only one of the mentioned numbers is permitted and not others, and that is not the intended meaning of the Qur'anic wording.

al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *thulutha wa rubu'a* without an *alif*.

His words: ﴿But if you fear you will not be just, then one only﴾: marry one only, as His words ﴿marry what is good﴾ indicate. It was also said the implied phrase is: "then keep to one" or "then choose one."

The first is better. The meaning is: if you fear you will not be just among the wives in distribution and similar matters, then marry one only. This prohibits more than one for whoever fears that. It was read in the nominative, as a subject (*mubtada'*) with an omitted predicate.

al-Kisa'i said: that is, "one is sufficient." It was also said the implied phrase is: "one, in which there is sufficiency." And "one" in the reading of the nominative may be the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, "the sufficient one is one."

His words: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ are coordinated with "one" (*wahidah*); that is, marry one, or marry what your right hands possess of slave-girls, however many they are, as the relative pronoun indicates.

What is meant is marrying them by way of ownership, not by way of marriage contract. This is evidence that slave-women have no right to equal distribution, as shown by making them a counterpart of "one" in the security from not being just. The attribution of ownership to the right hand is because the right hand is the one that directly handles the receiving and giving of wealth and other matters commonly attributed to a person. From this is the verse:

*When a banner is raised for glory,*
*'Arabah receives it with the right hand.*

His words: ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾. That is: that is closer to your not transgressing (*ta'ulu*), meaning not being unjust. It comes from *'ala al-rajul ya'ulu*, meaning he inclined and acted unjustly. From this is the saying: "'ala al-sahm 'an al-hadaf," the arrow deviated from the target; and "'ala al-mizan" when the scale tilted. From it is the saying: "They followed the Messenger of Allah, but they cast aside the Messenger's word and deviated in the scales." From it is also the verse of Abu Talib:

*By a scale of truth that does not cheat a grain,*
*Having a witness of itself that is not deviating.*

From it also:

*We are three, and three camels,*
*Surely time has burdened the dependents.*

The meaning is: if you fear injustice among the wives, then what you have been commanded is nearer to not being unjust. It is also said: "'ala al-rajul ya'ilu," meaning he became poor and became dependent. From this is His words: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. From it is the verse of the poet:

*The poor man does not know when his wealth will come,*
*And the rich man does not know when he will become poor.*

al-Shafi'i said: "*an la ta'ulu*" means "that your dependents do not increase." al-Tha'labi said: no one else said this. It is said "a'ala yu'ilu" only when a man's dependents increase.

Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that *'ala* comes in seven meanings: first, *'ala* means *mala*, he inclined. Second, *zada*, he increased. Third, *jara*, he was unjust. Fourth, *iftaqara*, he became poor. Fifth, *athqala*, he became burdened. Sixth, *qama bi-mu'unat al-'iyal*, he took responsibility for the expenses of dependents, from which is the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Begin with those whom you support." Seventh, *'ala*, meaning *ghalaba*, he overcame, from which is "'ila sabri," my patience was overcome. He said: it is said "a'ala al-rajul," meaning his dependents increased.

As for *'ala* in the sense of "his dependents increased," this is not sound. al-Tha'labi's denial of what al-Shafi'i said, and likewise Ibn al-'Arabi's denial of it, is answered: Zayd ibn Aslam and Jabir ibn Zayd preceded al-Shafi'i in saying it. They are two of the imams of the Muslims, and they would not interpret the Qur'an with something that has no basis in Arabic, nor would they nor al-Shafi'i do so.

al-Daraqutni recorded this from them in his *Sunan*. al-Qurtubi related it from al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Umar al-Duri, and Ibn al-A'rabi. Abu Hatim said: al-Shafi'i was more knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs than us, and perhaps this is a dialect.

al-Tha'labi said: our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I asked Abu 'Umar al-Duri about this, and he was an unchallenged imam in the language. He said: "It is the dialect of Himyar," and he recited:

*Death surely seizes every living thing,*
*Without doubt, even if its flock is large and its dependents increase.*

That is, even if its flock and its dependents become numerous. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *an la tu'ilu*. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Zajjaj criticized the interpretation of *'ala* as from *'iyal* (dependents) by saying that Allah, glorified is He, permitted the multiplication of concubines, and in that there is an increase of dependents, so how can it be nearer to their not multiplying? This criticism is not valid, because concubines are merely property that is disposed of by sale; the dependents are the free women who have obligatory rights.

Ibn al-A'rabi related that the Arabs say, "'ala al-rajul," when his dependents increase, and that is sufficient. *'Ala* has also come with meanings other than the seven mentioned by Ibn al-'Arabi, among them: *'ala*, it became intense and severe, related by al-Jawhari; *'ala al-rajul fi al-ard*, when he traveled in the land, related by al-Harawi; and *'ala*, when he was unable, related by al-Ahmar. These are three meanings beyond the seven, and the fourth is *'ala*, his dependents increased. So the total meanings of *'ala* are eleven.

His words: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾. The address is to the husbands, and it was said it is to the guardians. *Sudqat* with a *dammah* on the *dal* is the plural of *sadaqah*, like *thamarah*. al-Akhfash said: the Banu Tamim say *sadaqah*, plural *sadaqat*, and if you wish, you may use a *fathah* or a sukun.

The nihlah (a freely given gift, or obligation) may be read with a kasra or a damma on the nun, and both are attested. Its root sense is giving: nahaltu fulānan means "I gave so-and-so." On this reading it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), since ītāʾ means iʿṭāʾ. It is also said that nihlah means religious obligation (tadayyun), so that the meaning of nihlatan is "as an act of religious devotion." This is the view of al-Zajjaj, and on it the word is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). Qatadah said that nihlah means obligation (farīḍah), and on this reading it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was also said that nihlah means goodwill of the soul (ṭībat al-nafs). Abu ʿUbayd said: "Nihlah is only given with goodwill of the soul."

The meaning of the verse, if the address is to the husbands: give the women whom you have married their dower (mahr), which is theirs by right, as a gift, or as a religious duty from you, or as an obligation upon you, or with goodwill from yourselves. If the address is to the guardians: give the women from among your relatives the dowers that you have received from their husbands.

It is reported that the guardian used to take the dower of his female relative in the pre-Islamic period and give her nothing. This is related from Abu Ṣāliḥ and al-Kalbi. The first reading is preferable, because the pronouns from the beginning of the context refer to the husbands.

The verse is evidence that the dower is obligatory upon husbands toward wives, and this is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi said. He said: The scholars agreed that there is no limit to its amount, but they differed regarding its minimum.

Qatadah read ṣudqātihinna with a damma on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl. Al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Wathhab read both with a damma. The majority read it with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a damma on the dāl.

His saying: ﴿But if they give you any of it willingly, then consume it with enjoyment and ease﴾. The pronoun in minhu refers to the dower, which is the singular of ṣudqāt, or to the mentioned item, which is ṣudqāt, or it has the status of a demonstrative, as if he said "from that." Nafsan is a specification (tamyīz). The companions of Sibawayh said it is accusative by an implied verb and is not a specification; that is, "I mean the soul." The first view is preferable, and the majority held it.

The meaning: if they (the women) give you, O husbands or guardians, any part of the dower willingly, then consume it with enjoyment and ease. In his saying "if they give," there is evidence that what counts for making this lawful for them to you is only goodwill of the soul, not merely the words that come from them which do not establish genuine goodwill. If there appears from them what indicates that their soul is not willing, it is not lawful for the husband or the guardian, even if she has pronounced a gift, a vow, or something similar. How strong is the indication of this verse that words coming from women which by themselves are meant to effect ownership are not taken into account, because of the deficiency of their intellects, the weakness of their understanding, the speed with which they are deceived, and their being drawn to what is demanded of them by the slightest encouragement or intimidation.

His saying ﴿wholesome and agreeable﴾ are two accusatives, being attributes of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "eating that is wholesome and agreeable." Or they stand in place of the verbal noun, or they are circumstantial states. It is said: hannaʾahu al-ṭaʿām wa-l-sharāb yuhannīhi, and marraʾahu and amraʾahu, from hanīʾ and marīʾ. The verb is hanaʾa and maraʾa; that is, it comes without hardship or vexation. It was said: it is the pleasant thing without any spoiling in it. It was said: it is the praiseworthy in its outcome, good for digestion. It was said: it is that which has no sin in it. The intended meaning here is that it is lawful for them and pure, free of impurities. The eating was singled out because it is the main purpose for which wealth is used, although all other uses of it are permissible, like eating.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid concerning his saying ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾: he said, "Adam." ﴿And from it created its mate﴾: he said, "Eve, from the two ribs of Adam," that is, the two short ribs of his sides. Abu al-Shaykh reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbas. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported: Eve was created from the left side of Adam (khalf Adam al-aysar).

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: from the rib of the side (ḍilʿ al-khalf), which is from the lowest of the ribs.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another﴾: he said, "They deal with one another by Him." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from al-Rabīʿ: "You make contracts with one another and make covenants." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid: he said, "He says: I ask you by God and by the ties of kinship." Ibn Jarir reported the same from al-Ḥasan. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: he said, "Fear God, by whom you ask one another, and fear the ties of kinship and maintain them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid concerning ﴿Indeed, God is ever watchful over you﴾: he said, "Preserving." Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: a man from Ghaṭafān had a great deal of wealth belonging to his nephew. When the orphan reached maturity, he demanded his wealth, but his uncle refused him. So he brought him before the Prophet (ﷺ), and ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ was revealed, meaning the guardians. He says: give the orphans their property. ﴿And do not substitute the bad [of your own] for the good [of theirs]﴾: he says: do not exchange the unlawful from the property of the people for the lawful from your property. He says: do not leave your lawful wealth and consume their unlawful wealth.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Īmān reported from Mujahid: he said, "Do not hasten to unlawful provision before the lawful that has been decreed for you comes to you." ﴿And do not consume their property along with your property﴾: he said, "Together with your property, mixing it so that you consume it all." ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (ḥūb)﴾: sin.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse: the people of the pre-Islamic period did not give inheritance to women or to children; the eldest would take it. So his share of the inheritance was good, while what this one takes was bad.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah: "Together with your property." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Ḥasan: When this verse about the property of orphans was revealed, they disliked mixing with them, and the guardian of an orphan separated the orphan's property from his own. They complained of this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best. And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220]. He said: so they mixed with them.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported that ʿUrwah asked ʿAisha about God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the care of her guardian. He shares with her in her property, and he is attracted to her wealth and her beauty. So her guardian wants to marry her without giving her a fair dower, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them the highest of their customary dowers. They were ordered to marry whatever women were lawful to them other than them." And "the people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a ruling after this verse, so God revealed ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾" [al-Nisāʾ 4:127]. ʿAisha said: God's saying in the other verse ﴿And you desire to marry them﴾ is the desire of one of you to avoid his orphan girl when she has little wealth and little beauty. So they were forbidden to marry those whom they desired for her wealth and beauty, from among the other women, except with justice, because of their aversion to them when they had little wealth and beauty.

al-Bukhari reported from ʿAisha: a man had an orphan girl whom he married. She had a palm tree, and he kept her under his control, and she had no share of it of her own. So God revealed ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. I think he said: she was his partner in that palm tree and in his wealth.

This meaning has been related through many chains. Ibn Jarir reported through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: a man would marry with the property of an orphan as much as God willed, so God forbade that. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him: "He limited men to four wives because of the property of orphans." Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr concerning God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾: he said, "A man would marry as many as he wished. So He said: just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women, and He limited them to four."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: they used to marry ten women in the pre-Islamic period, and they used to magnify the status of the orphan. Then, in their religion, they became mindful of the status of orphans and abandoned what they used to do in marriage in the pre-Islamic period. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him concerning the verse: "Just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women when you gather them with you."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported through Muḥammad ibn Abi Mūsā al-Ashʿarī from him: "If you fear adultery, then marry them." He says: just as you feared regarding the property of orphans that you would not be just with it, so fear for yourselves regarding what you do not marry. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported similar from Mujahid. Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Abu Malik concerning ﴿what is good for you﴾: he said, "what is lawful for you." Ibn Jarir reported the same from al-Ḥasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAisha something similar.

al-Shafiʿi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿUmar: "Ghaylān ibn Salamah al-Thaqafī embraced Islam while he had ten wives. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Choose from among them" — and in one wording: "Keep four of them and separate from the rest." This hadith was reported by those mentioned through many chains from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayyah, Ghundar, Zayd ibn Zurayʿ, Saʿīd ibn Abi ʿArūbah, Sufyān al-Thawrī, ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī, al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā and others among the memorizers, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Sālim, from his father, and he mentioned it.

al-Bukhari gave a defect (ʿillah) to this hadith. al-Tirmidhi transmitted from him that he said: "This is a hadith that is not preserved (ghayr maḥfūẓ). The correct version is what was reported from Shuʿayb and others, from al-Zuhri: 'I was told (ḥuddithtu) from Muḥammad ibn Suwayd al-Thaqafī that Ghaylān ibn Salamah...'" and he mentioned it. As for the hadith of al-Zuhri from his father, that a man from Thaqīf divorced his wives, then ʿUmar said to him: "I will stone your grave as the grave of Abū Righāl was stoned."

Maʿmar reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal (with a missing companion in the chain), and Mālik also reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal. Abū Zurʿah said: "And this is more authentic." ʿUqayl reported it from al-Zuhri: "It reached us from ʿUthmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Abi Suwayd." Abū Ḥātim said: "This is an error; it is only al-Zuhri who conveyed to us from ʿUthmān ibn Abi Suwayd." Aḥmad, however, judged it to be of the sound transmitters, and said: "Ismāʿīl and Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Maʿmar narrated to us from al-Zuhri." Abū Jaʿfar said in his narration: "Ibn Shihāb informed us from Sālim from his father that Ghaylān..." and he mentioned it. It has also been reported through other routes than Maʿmar and al-Zuhri: al-Bayhaqi reported it from Ayyūb, from Nāfiʿ and Sālim, from Ibn ʿUmar, that Ghaylān... and he mentioned it.

Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Majah reported in their Sunan from ʿUmayr al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives, so I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Choose four of them.'" Ibn Kathir said: its chain is good (ḥasan).

al-Shafiʿi reported in his Musnad from Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Dīlī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had five wives, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Keep four and separate from the other.'" Ibn Majah and al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh reported from Qays ibn al-Ḥārith al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives under me. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Choose four of them and release the rest.' So I did." These are corroborating reports (shawāhid) for the first hadith, as al-Bayhaqi said.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 1–4 (part 4 of 4):

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from al-Hakam, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that a slave-owner may not combine more than two women (in marriage) from among those who are owned.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning the verse, who said: "If you fear that you will not be just among four, then three; and if not, then two; and if not, then one. And if you fear that you will not be just even with one, then (marry) what your right hand possesses." 

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' the like of this. He also related from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾, that he said: "In intercourse and in love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, that he said: "The concubines (sarari)."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih related from ʿAʾishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "﴿That is closer to not being unjust﴾ means: that you do not oppress."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father said: This is an erroneous hadith (hadith khata'), and the correct report from ʿAʾishah is that it is a mawquf (companion's) statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿that you not be unjust﴾, that he said: "That you not deviate."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah, who said: "That you not deviate." Then he said: Have you not heard the verse of Abu Talib:

*With a scale of justice that does not cheat a barleycorn,*
*and a balance of truth whose weight is not deficient.*

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, who said: "That you not deviate." Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Razin, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak the like of this. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That is closer to there being fewer whom you must support (ta'ulu)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, who said: "That you not become impoverished."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Salih, who said: "A man, when he married a widow (ayyimah), would take her dowry for himself instead of giving it to her. So Allah forbade them from that, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying "nihlah" (as a gift), that he said: "By nihlah he means the mahr (bridal gift)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAʾishah concerning "nihlah," that she said: "Obligatory."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, that he said: "A specified obligation (fariḍah musammah)." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related the like of this from Qatadah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it﴾, that he said: "It refers to the husbands (lil-azwaj)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrimah concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "Of the dowry."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "If it is without harm or deception, then it is wholesome and pleasant (hanee'an mari'an), as Allah said."

(p-266) It is entirely Madinan (Madani, revealed after the Hijrah). Al-Qurtubi said: Except for one verse, which was revealed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest concerning ʿUthman ibn Talhah al-Hajabi, and it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa': 58], as will come, God willing. Al-Naqqash said: It was also said that it was revealed during the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah. And according to what was mentioned earlier from some of the scholars, that His saying, Exalted is He, "O mankind" wherever it occurs is Makki, this would require that this surah be Makki. ʿAlqamah and others held this view.

Al-Nahhas said: This verse is Makki. Al-Qurtubi said: The correct view is the first, for in Sahih al-Bukhari it is reported from ʿAishah that she said: "Surat an-Nisa' was not revealed except while I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." She meant that he had consummated the marriage with her. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the Prophet ﷺ consummated his marriage with ʿAishah only in Madinah. Whoever examines its rulings knows that it is undoubtedly Madinan.

He said: As for the one who said that "O mankind" is Makki wherever it occurs, this is not correct, for al-Baqarah is Madinan and in it "O mankind" occurs in two places. Ibn al-Durays in his Fada'il, al-Nahhas in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Surat an-Nisa' was revealed in Madinah." In its chain is al-ʿAwfi, who is weak. Likewise Ibn Mardawayh reported it from ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from Qatadah.

Something has also been transmitted concerning the virtue of this surah: al-Hakim in his Mustadrak reported from ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud who said: "Indeed, in Surat an-Nisa' there are five verses which would not please me if I had the world and all that is in it in exchange: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ [an-Nisa': 40], the verse ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ [an-Nisa': 31], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [an-Nisa': 48], the verse, ﴿And if they, when they wronged themselves﴾ [an-Nisa': 64]." Then he said: This is a sound chain, if ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud heard from his father, but this has been disputed.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported it from Ma'mar from a man, from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "Five verses of an-Nisa' are dearer to me than the whole world: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 35], ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 30], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 48], ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 110], ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 152]." Ibn Jarir also reported it.

Then it was narrated through the route of Salih al-Murri from Qatadah from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Eight verses were revealed in Surat an-Nisa', which are better for this Ummah than what the sun rises upon and sets upon," and he mentioned what Ibn Mas'ud mentioned, and added ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 26], ﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 27], ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you﴾ the verse [an-Nisa': 28].

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAishah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever takes the seven, he is a rabbi (a learned scholar)."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab reported from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been given in place of the Torah the seven long (surahs), and the al-Mi'in: every surah that reaches a hundred verses or more; and the al-Mathani: every surah less than the al-Mi'in and more than the al-Mufassal." Abu Ya'la, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab reported from Anas who said: "One night the Messenger of Allah ﷺ felt something, and in the morning it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the effect of an ailment is clearly upon you.' He said: 'As for me, I am, as you see, by the praise of Allah, well. I have recited the seven long (surahs).'"

Ahmad reported from Hudhayfah who said: "I stood with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he recited the seven long (surahs) in seven rak'ahs." ʿAbd al-Razzaq reported from some of the family of the Prophet ﷺ "that the Prophet ﷺ recited the seven long (surahs) in one rak'ah."

Al-Hakim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Ask me about Surat an-Nisa', for I recited the Qur'an while I was young." Al-Hakim said: Sound according to the condition of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it. Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf reported from him: "Whoever recites Surat an-Nisa' and knows what is veiled from what is not veiled, knows the obligatory shares of inheritance."

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

By "mankind" is meant the human beings present at the time of the address, and it includes those who will exist later, by an external proof, which is the consensus (ijma') that they are obligated with what those present are obligated with. Or it is by taghlib (predominance), where those present are given precedence over those not yet existing, just as the males were given precedence over the females in His saying: "Fear your Lord," because that is specific to the masculine plural form. The "single soul" here means Adam.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited (wahidin) without the ta' marbuta, in observance of the meaning. The feminine is by consideration of the wording, and the masculine by consideration of the meaning.

His saying: ﴿and created from it its mate﴾. It was said: It is coordinated with an implied element indicated by the speech; that is: He created you from a single soul which He created first, and created from it its mate. It was also said: It is coordinated with "He created you," so the second verb falls together with the first within the scope of the relative clause (sila).

The meaning: and He created from that soul, which is a designation for Adam, its mate, who is Eve. The meanings of taqwa (God-consciousness), Rabb (Lord), zawj (mate), and bath (dispersing) have already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The pronoun in His saying "from them" refers back to Adam and Eve, who are expressed by "soul" and "mate."

His saying: ﴿many﴾ is a descriptive word emphasizing what the plural form implies, since it is one of the plurals of multitude. It was also said that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; that is, a many dispersing. His saying: ﴿and women﴾, meaning many women, and the explicit mention of the adjective was omitted by relying on the first descriptive word.

His saying: (p-267) ﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾. The people of Kufa recited with the second ta' omitted, and its original form is tatasa'alun, lightened because of the coming together of two identical letters. The people of Madinah, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir recited with the ta' assimilated into the sin, and the meaning is: some of you ask others by Allah and the womb (kinship), for they used to link the two together in asking and in appeal, saying: "I ask you by Allah and the womb, and I implore you by Allah and the womb." Al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, al-Aʿmash, and Hamzah recited ﴿wal-arhami﴾ in the genitive (al-arhami).

The rest recited in the accusative. The grammarians differed in explaining the recitation in the genitive. The Basrans said: It is a solecism (lahn); the recitation with it is not permissible. The Kufans said: It is an ugly recitation (qira'ah qabihah). Sibawayh, explaining this ugliness, said: The pronoun in the genitive is like tanwin, and tanwin is not coordinated upon.

Al-Zajjaj and a group said that it is ugly to coordinate an apparent noun upon a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the genitive particle, like His saying: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. Sibawayh permitted this in poetic necessity, and recited:

"Today you have come near to satirizing us and praising us, so go away; what is with you and with the days is no marvel."

And a similar saying of another:

"Our swords are hung on the like of pillars, and between them and the Kaʿb is an open expanse."

Coordinating "al-Kaʿb" upon the pronoun in "baynihā."

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi related that al-Mubarrad said: "If I prayed behind an imam who recites ﴿wat-taqaw Allaha alladhi tasa'aluna bihi wal-arhami﴾ in the genitive, I would take my sandals and leave." Imam Abu Nasr al-Qushayri refuted what those who disparaged the genitive recitation said, and said: Such speech is rejected by the scholars of religion, because the recitations which the imams of the reciters recited were established from the Prophet ﷺ by tawatur (mass transmission). It is not hidden from you that the claim of tawatur is false, as knows whoever knows the chains of transmission they narrated with them. But one should argue for its permissibility by its occurrence in the poetry of the Arabs, as has preceded, and as in the saying of someone:

"Sufficient for you, and al-Dahhak, is a keen-edged sword."

And the saying of another:

"And the horizons of heaven desired it, but found for it no place to ascend in them, nor a place of rest on the earth."

And the saying of another:

"There is no in it and in the affairs from destruction."

And the saying of another:

"I charge against the host, not knowing whether my death was in it or in something else."

So "siwaha" is in the genitive position coordinated upon the pronoun in "fīhā." From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have made for you therein means of living, and [also for] those whom you do not provide for﴾ [al-Hijr: 20].

As for the accusative recitation, its meaning is clear and manifest, for it coordinates the womb upon the noble Name; that is: Fear Allah and fear the wombs, so do not sever them, for they are among what Allah has commanded to be joined. It was said: It is coordinated upon the place (mahall) of the preposition and its object in His saying "by Him," as when you say: "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr"; that is: Fear Allah by whom you ask one another, and you ask one another by the wombs.

The first is better. ʿAbdullah ibn Yazid recited "wal-arhamu" in the nominative, as a subject with an implied predicate; that is: and the wombs—join them, or and the wombs are deserving of being joined. It was also said that the nominative is by incitement (al-ighra') according to those who raise by it, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed a people among them are ʿUmayr and Ashba' ʿUmayr, and among them is al-Saffah."

"They are indeed worthy of meeting, when the man of valor calls: 'The weapons! The weapons!'"

"Al-arham" is a name for all relatives without distinction between the forbidden (mahram) and others. There is no disagreement about this among the people of the Shariʿah nor among the people of the language.

Abu Hanifah and some of the Zaydiyyah (a Shi'i group) specified the womb as the forbidden relatives in preventing the retraction of a gift, although they agree that its meaning is more general, and there is no basis for this specification. Al-Qurtubi said: The community (millah) agreed that maintaining ties of kinship is obligatory and that severing them is forbidden, end of quote. Numerous sound hadiths have been reported with this.

Al-Raqib: the observer, and it is an intensive form. It is said: "raqibtu arqubu ruqbatan wa rukbanan" when you wait.

His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. It is addressed to the guardians and the executors. Al-iya' is giving. The orphan (yatim) is one who has no father. The Shariʿah has specified it as one who has not reached puberty.

The explanation of its meaning was already fully discussed in al-Baqarah. The name "orphan" was applied to them at the time of giving them their property, although they are not given it except after the removal of the name of orphanhood by reaching maturity, as a metaphor, considering what they were before. It is also possible that "orphans" is meant in its literal sense, and "giving" means what the guardians and executors hand to them of sustenance and clothing, not the handing over of all of it. This verse is qualified by another verse, which is His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, then hand over to them their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 6]. So mere removal of orphanhood by reaching puberty does not justify handing over their property to them until maturity of judgment is perceived in them.

His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. It is a prohibition for them against doing the practice of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) concerning the property of orphans, for they used to take the good from the property of orphans and replace it with the inferior from their own property, and they saw no harm in that. It was also said: The meaning is: Do not eat the property of orphans, which is forbidden and bad, and leave the good of your own property.

It was also said: The meaning is: Do not hasten to eat the bad of their property and leave waiting for the lawful provision from Allah. The first is better, for substituting one thing for another in the language means taking it in its place, and likewise exchanging it, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever substitutes disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], and His saying: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

And as for *al-tabdil* (substitution), it is sometimes used in this sense, as in His words: ﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens﴾, and sometimes in the reverse sense, as in your saying, "I substituted the ring for the silver," when you melt it and make it into a ring. al-Azhari stated this explicitly.

His words: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾. A group of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) held that what is forbidden in this verse is mixing, so the verb is taken to include the meaning of joining. That is: do not consume their property joined to your property. Then this was abrogated (*naskh*) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. It was also said that *ila* (to) here means *ma'a* (with), as in His words: ﴿Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52].

The first view is the better. *Al-huub* means sin. It is said: "al-rajul yahuubu huuban," meaning he sinned. Its root meaning is driving away camels, so sin was called *huub* because one is driven away from it. *Al-hawbah* means need. *Al-huub* also means loneliness (*al-wahshah*). It has three dialects: a *dammah* on the *ha'* (*hubb*), which is the reading of the majority; a *fathah* on the *ha'* (*habb*), which is the reading of al-Hasan, and al-Akhfash said it is the dialect of Tamim; and a third, *al-haab*.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *haaban* as a verbal noun, like *qala qalaan*. *Al-tahawwub* means grieving, and from it is the verse of Tufayl:

*So taste as we have tasted, his enemy being restrained,*
*By rage in our livers and by grief.*

His words: ﴿a great [sin]. And if you fear that you will not act justly regarding orphans, then marry﴾. The connection of the answer (*jaza'*) to the condition (*shart*) is that a man would be guardian of an orphan girl and wish to marry her, but he would not be just to her regarding her dowry; that is, he would not be fair in it and give her what others give to their wives. So Allah forbade them to marry them unless they were just to them and gave them the highest amount of dowry that is due to them. They were commanded to marry from other women who were lawful to them. This is the cause of the revelation of the verse, as will come. So it is a prohibition specific to this case.

A group of the early scholars (*salaf*) said: this verse abrogates what existed in the Jahiliyyah and at the beginning of Islam, that a man could marry as many free women as he wished. So He restricted them to four by this verse. The connection of the answer to the condition is that if they feared not acting justly regarding orphans, then likewise they should fear not acting justly regarding women, because they used to be scrupulous regarding orphans but not regarding women. Fear can relate to opposites, for what is feared may be known or may be merely suspected. For this reason the imams differed about its meaning in the verse. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "*khiftum*" means "you were certain." Others said: "*khiftum*" means "you suspected."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is what the skilled scholars (*hudhdhaq*) chose, and that it is on its usual meaning of suspicion, not certainty. The meaning is: whoever suspects that he will fall short in justice toward the orphan girl, let him leave her and marry another.

al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read *tuqsitu* with a *fathah* on the *ta'* from *qasata*, meaning he acted unjustly. On this reading the *la'* (not) is taken as extra, as if he said: "and if you fear that you will act unjustly."

al-Zajjaj reported that *aqsata* is used in the sense of *qasata*, whereas the known usage among the lexicographers is that *aqsata* means "he was just" and *qasata* means "he was unjust."

The *ma* in His words *ma taaba* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). The word *ma* was used in place of *man*, because the two may replace one another, and each may stand in place of the other, as in His words: ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 2], and ﴿Among them are those who walk on their bellies, and among them are those who walk on two legs, and among them are those who walk on four﴾ [al-Nur: 45].

The Basrans said: *ma* is used for attributes just as it is used for non-rational things. One says *ma 'indaka* ("what is with you"), and the answer is "graceful" or "generous." So the meaning is: marry the good women, that is, the lawful ones, and what Allah has forbidden is not good. It was also said that *ma* here is temporal (*mudiyyah*), meaning: as long as you are inclined to marriage. Ibn 'Atiyyah considered this weak.

al-Farra' said: *ma* here is verbal (*masdariyyah*). al-Nahhas said: this is very far-fetched.

Ibn Abi Ablah read *fankihu man taaba*. The people of knowledge are agreed that this condition mentioned in the verse has no implicit opposite meaning (*mafhum*), and that it is permissible for one who does not fear being unjust regarding orphans to marry more than one wife. The *min* in His words *min al-nisa'* is either explanatory (*bayaniyyah*) or partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), because what is intended is other than orphans.

His words: ﴿two, three, or four﴾ are in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for *ma*, as Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said. It was also said they are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). These words are not declined because of "*'adl*" (a form of indirect meaning) and descriptiveness, as is explained in the science of grammar. The original is: "marry what is good for you of women, two by two, three by three, and four by four."

The verse has been used as evidence for the prohibition of more than four wives. They explained this by saying that it is an address to the entire community, and that each one who marries may choose whatever number of this count he wishes, just as one says to a group: "Divide this money," which is a thousand dirhams, or "this money that is in the bag," as "two by two, three by three, and four by four."

This is accepted when the thing divided has had its total mentioned or its place specified. But if it is unrestricted, as when one says "divide the dirhams," meaning what they have earned, then the meaning is not like this. The verse belongs to the other category, not to the first.

Moreover, if someone said to a group dividing a large specific amount of property, "Divide it two, three, and four," and they divided part of it among themselves two dirhams each, part three each, and part four each, this would be the Arabic meaning. And it is known that if someone says, "The people came to me two by two, and they were a hundred thousand," the meaning is that they came to him in pairs. Likewise with "The people came three by three, four by four." The address to the whole is in the position of an address to each individual, as in His words: ﴿Kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and ﴿Establish prayer, give zakah﴾, and similar. So His words: ﴿marry what is good for you of women, two, three, or four﴾ mean: let each one of you marry what is good for him of women, two by two, three by three, and four by four. This is what the Arabic language requires. So the verse indicates the opposite of what they used it to prove. This is supported by His words at the end of the verse: ﴿But if you fear you will not be just, then one only﴾, for although it is an address to all, it is in the position of an address to each individual.

So it is better to derive the prohibition of exceeding four from the Sunnah rather than from the Qur'an. As for the argument of those who used the verse to permit marrying nine, based on the conjunctive *waw*, it is as if they said: "marry the total of this number mentioned." This is ignorance of the Arabic meaning. If He had said, "marry two, three, and four," this statement would have had some basis. But with the use of the form of distribution (*'adl*), it does not. Allah, glorified is He, used the conjunctive *waw* rather than *aw* (or), because *aw* would imply that only one of the mentioned numbers is permitted and not others, and that is not the intended meaning of the Qur'anic wording.

al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *thulutha wa rubu'a* without an *alif*.

His words: ﴿But if you fear you will not be just, then one only﴾: marry one only, as His words ﴿marry what is good﴾ indicate. It was also said the implied phrase is: "then keep to one" or "then choose one."

The first is better. The meaning is: if you fear you will not be just among the wives in distribution and similar matters, then marry one only. This prohibits more than one for whoever fears that. It was read in the nominative, as a subject (*mubtada'*) with an omitted predicate.

al-Kisa'i said: that is, "one is sufficient." It was also said the implied phrase is: "one, in which there is sufficiency." And "one" in the reading of the nominative may be the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, "the sufficient one is one."

His words: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ are coordinated with "one" (*wahidah*); that is, marry one, or marry what your right hands possess of slave-girls, however many they are, as the relative pronoun indicates.

What is meant is marrying them by way of ownership, not by way of marriage contract. This is evidence that slave-women have no right to equal distribution, as shown by making them a counterpart of "one" in the security from not being just. The attribution of ownership to the right hand is because the right hand is the one that directly handles the receiving and giving of wealth and other matters commonly attributed to a person. From this is the verse:

*When a banner is raised for glory,*
*'Arabah receives it with the right hand.*

His words: ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾. That is: that is closer to your not transgressing (*ta'ulu*), meaning not being unjust. It comes from *'ala al-rajul ya'ulu*, meaning he inclined and acted unjustly. From this is the saying: "'ala al-sahm 'an al-hadaf," the arrow deviated from the target; and "'ala al-mizan" when the scale tilted. From it is the saying: "They followed the Messenger of Allah, but they cast aside the Messenger's word and deviated in the scales." From it is also the verse of Abu Talib:

*By a scale of truth that does not cheat a grain,*
*Having a witness of itself that is not deviating.*

From it also:

*We are three, and three camels,*
*Surely time has burdened the dependents.*

The meaning is: if you fear injustice among the wives, then what you have been commanded is nearer to not being unjust.
