It is also said: "'ala al-rajul ya'ilu," meaning he became poor and became dependent. From this is His words: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. From it is the verse of the poet:

*The poor man does not know when his wealth will come,*
*And the rich man does not know when he will become poor.*

al-Shafi'i said: "*an la ta'ulu*" means "that your dependents do not increase." al-Tha'labi said: no one else said this. It is said "a'ala yu'ilu" only when a man's dependents increase.

Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that *'ala* comes in seven meanings: first, *'ala* means *mala*, he inclined. Second, *zada*, he increased. Third, *jara*, he was unjust. Fourth, *iftaqara*, he became poor. Fifth, *athqala*, he became burdened. Sixth, *qama bi-mu'unat al-'iyal*, he took responsibility for the expenses of dependents, from which is the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Begin with those whom you support." Seventh, *'ala*, meaning *ghalaba*, he overcame, from which is "'ila sabri," my patience was overcome. He said: it is said "a'ala al-rajul," meaning his dependents increased.

As for *'ala* in the sense of "his dependents increased," this is not sound. al-Tha'labi's denial of what al-Shafi'i said, and likewise Ibn al-'Arabi's denial of it, is answered: Zayd ibn Aslam and Jabir ibn Zayd preceded al-Shafi'i in saying it. They are two of the imams of the Muslims, and they would not interpret the Qur'an with something that has no basis in Arabic, nor would they nor al-Shafi'i do so.

al-Daraqutni recorded this from them in his *Sunan*. al-Qurtubi related it from al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Umar al-Duri, and Ibn al-A'rabi. Abu Hatim said: al-Shafi'i was more knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs than us, and perhaps this is a dialect.

al-Tha'labi said: our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: I asked Abu 'Umar al-Duri about this, and he was an unchallenged imam in the language. He said: "It is the dialect of Himyar," and he recited:

*Death surely seizes every living thing,*
*Without doubt, even if its flock is large and its dependents increase.*

That is, even if its flock and its dependents become numerous. Talhah ibn Musarrif read *an la tu'ilu*. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Zajjaj criticized the interpretation of *'ala* as from *'iyal* (dependents) by saying that Allah, glorified is He, permitted the multiplication of concubines, and in that there is an increase of dependents, so how can it be nearer to their not multiplying? This criticism is not valid, because concubines are merely property that is disposed of by sale; the dependents are the free women who have obligatory rights.

Ibn al-A'rabi related that the Arabs say, "'ala al-rajul," when his dependents increase, and that is sufficient. *'Ala* has also come with meanings other than the seven mentioned by Ibn al-'Arabi, among them: *'ala*, it became intense and severe, related by al-Jawhari; *'ala al-rajul fi al-ard*, when he traveled in the land, related by al-Harawi; and *'ala*, when he was unable, related by al-Ahmar. These are three meanings beyond the seven, and the fourth is *'ala*, his dependents increased. So the total meanings of *'ala* are eleven.

His words: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾. The address is to the husbands, and it was said it is to the guardians. *Sudqat* with a *dammah* on the *dal* is the plural of *sadaqah*, like *thamarah*. al-Akhfash said: the Banu Tamim say *sadaqah*, plural *sadaqat*, and if you wish, you may use a *fathah* or a sukun.

The nihlah (a freely given gift, or obligation) may be read with a kasra or a damma on the nun, and both are attested. Its root sense is giving: nahaltu fulānan means "I gave so-and-so." On this reading it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), since ītāʾ means iʿṭāʾ. It is also said that nihlah means religious obligation (tadayyun), so that the meaning of nihlatan is "as an act of religious devotion." This is the view of al-Zajjaj, and on it the word is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). Qatadah said that nihlah means obligation (farīḍah), and on this reading it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was also said that nihlah means goodwill of the soul (ṭībat al-nafs). Abu ʿUbayd said: "Nihlah is only given with goodwill of the soul."

The meaning of the verse, if the address is to the husbands: give the women whom you have married their dower (mahr), which is theirs by right, as a gift, or as a religious duty from you, or as an obligation upon you, or with goodwill from yourselves. If the address is to the guardians: give the women from among your relatives the dowers that you have received from their husbands.

It is reported that the guardian used to take the dower of his female relative in the pre-Islamic period and give her nothing. This is related from Abu Ṣāliḥ and al-Kalbi. The first reading is preferable, because the pronouns from the beginning of the context refer to the husbands.

The verse is evidence that the dower is obligatory upon husbands toward wives, and this is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi said. He said: The scholars agreed that there is no limit to its amount, but they differed regarding its minimum.

Qatadah read ṣudqātihinna with a damma on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl. Al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Wathhab read both with a damma. The majority read it with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a damma on the dāl.

His saying: ﴿But if they give you any of it willingly, then consume it with enjoyment and ease﴾. The pronoun in minhu refers to the dower, which is the singular of ṣudqāt, or to the mentioned item, which is ṣudqāt, or it has the status of a demonstrative, as if he said "from that." Nafsan is a specification (tamyīz). The companions of Sibawayh said it is accusative by an implied verb and is not a specification; that is, "I mean the soul." The first view is preferable, and the majority held it.

The meaning: if they (the women) give you, O husbands or guardians, any part of the dower willingly, then consume it with enjoyment and ease. In his saying "if they give," there is evidence that what counts for making this lawful for them to you is only goodwill of the soul, not merely the words that come from them which do not establish genuine goodwill. If there appears from them what indicates that their soul is not willing, it is not lawful for the husband or the guardian, even if she has pronounced a gift, a vow, or something similar. How strong is the indication of this verse that words coming from women which by themselves are meant to effect ownership are not taken into account, because of the deficiency of their intellects, the weakness of their understanding, the speed with which they are deceived, and their being drawn to what is demanded of them by the slightest encouragement or intimidation.

His saying ﴿wholesome and agreeable﴾ are two accusatives, being attributes of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "eating that is wholesome and agreeable." Or they stand in place of the verbal noun, or they are circumstantial states. It is said: hannaʾahu al-ṭaʿām wa-l-sharāb yuhannīhi, and marraʾahu and amraʾahu, from hanīʾ and marīʾ. The verb is hanaʾa and maraʾa; that is, it comes without hardship or vexation. It was said: it is the pleasant thing without any spoiling in it. It was said: it is the praiseworthy in its outcome, good for digestion. It was said: it is that which has no sin in it. The intended meaning here is that it is lawful for them and pure, free of impurities. The eating was singled out because it is the main purpose for which wealth is used, although all other uses of it are permissible, like eating.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid concerning his saying ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾: he said, "Adam." ﴿And from it created its mate﴾: he said, "Eve, from the two ribs of Adam," that is, the two short ribs of his sides. Abu al-Shaykh reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbas. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported: Eve was created from the left side of Adam (khalf Adam al-aysar).

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: from the rib of the side (ḍilʿ al-khalf), which is from the lowest of the ribs.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another﴾: he said, "They deal with one another by Him." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from al-Rabīʿ: "You make contracts with one another and make covenants." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid: he said, "He says: I ask you by God and by the ties of kinship." Ibn Jarir reported the same from al-Ḥasan. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: he said, "Fear God, by whom you ask one another, and fear the ties of kinship and maintain them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Mujahid concerning ﴿Indeed, God is ever watchful over you﴾: he said, "Preserving." Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: a man from Ghaṭafān had a great deal of wealth belonging to his nephew. When the orphan reached maturity, he demanded his wealth, but his uncle refused him. So he brought him before the Prophet (ﷺ), and ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ was revealed, meaning the guardians. He says: give the orphans their property. ﴿And do not substitute the bad [of your own] for the good [of theirs]﴾: he says: do not exchange the unlawful from the property of the people for the lawful from your property. He says: do not leave your lawful wealth and consume their unlawful wealth.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Īmān reported from Mujahid: he said, "Do not hasten to unlawful provision before the lawful that has been decreed for you comes to you." ﴿And do not consume their property along with your property﴾: he said, "Together with your property, mixing it so that you consume it all." ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (ḥūb)﴾: sin.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse: the people of the pre-Islamic period did not give inheritance to women or to children; the eldest would take it. So his share of the inheritance was good, while what this one takes was bad.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah: "Together with your property." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Ḥasan: When this verse about the property of orphans was revealed, they disliked mixing with them, and the guardian of an orphan separated the orphan's property from his own. They complained of this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best. And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220]. He said: so they mixed with them.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported that ʿUrwah asked ʿAisha about God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the care of her guardian. He shares with her in her property, and he is attracted to her wealth and her beauty. So her guardian wants to marry her without giving her a fair dower, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them the highest of their customary dowers. They were ordered to marry whatever women were lawful to them other than them." And "the people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a ruling after this verse, so God revealed ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾" [al-Nisāʾ 4:127]. ʿAisha said: God's saying in the other verse ﴿And you desire to marry them﴾ is the desire of one of you to avoid his orphan girl when she has little wealth and little beauty. So they were forbidden to marry those whom they desired for her wealth and beauty, from among the other women, except with justice, because of their aversion to them when they had little wealth and beauty.

al-Bukhari reported from ʿAisha: a man had an orphan girl whom he married. She had a palm tree, and he kept her under his control, and she had no share of it of her own. So God revealed ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾. I think he said: she was his partner in that palm tree and in his wealth.

This meaning has been related through many chains. Ibn Jarir reported through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: a man would marry with the property of an orphan as much as God willed, so God forbade that. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him: "He limited men to four wives because of the property of orphans." Saʿid ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr concerning God's saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾: he said, "A man would marry as many as he wished. So He said: just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women, and He limited them to four."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse: they used to marry ten women in the pre-Islamic period, and they used to magnify the status of the orphan. Then, in their religion, they became mindful of the status of orphans and abandoned what they used to do in marriage in the pre-Islamic period. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from him concerning the verse: "Just as you fear that you will not be just with orphans, fear that you will not be just with women when you gather them with you."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported through Muḥammad ibn Abi Mūsā al-Ashʿarī from him: "If you fear adultery, then marry them." He says: just as you feared regarding the property of orphans that you would not be just with it, so fear for yourselves regarding what you do not marry. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported similar from Mujahid. Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Abu Malik concerning ﴿what is good for you﴾: he said, "what is lawful for you." Ibn Jarir reported the same from al-Ḥasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAisha something similar.

al-Shafiʿi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿUmar: "Ghaylān ibn Salamah al-Thaqafī embraced Islam while he had ten wives. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Choose from among them" — and in one wording: "Keep four of them and separate from the rest." This hadith was reported by those mentioned through many chains from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayyah, Ghundar, Zayd ibn Zurayʿ, Saʿīd ibn Abi ʿArūbah, Sufyān al-Thawrī, ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī, al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā and others among the memorizers, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Sālim, from his father, and he mentioned it.

al-Bukhari gave a defect (ʿillah) to this hadith. al-Tirmidhi transmitted from him that he said: "This is a hadith that is not preserved (ghayr maḥfūẓ). The correct version is what was reported from Shuʿayb and others, from al-Zuhri: 'I was told (ḥuddithtu) from Muḥammad ibn Suwayd al-Thaqafī that Ghaylān ibn Salamah...'" and he mentioned it. As for the hadith of al-Zuhri from his father, that a man from Thaqīf divorced his wives, then ʿUmar said to him: "I will stone your grave as the grave of Abū Righāl was stoned."

Maʿmar reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal (with a missing companion in the chain), and Mālik also reported it from al-Zuhri as a mursal. Abū Zurʿah said: "And this is more authentic." ʿUqayl reported it from al-Zuhri: "It reached us from ʿUthmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Abi Suwayd." Abū Ḥātim said: "This is an error; it is only al-Zuhri who conveyed to us from ʿUthmān ibn Abi Suwayd." Aḥmad, however, judged it to be of the sound transmitters, and said: "Ismāʿīl and Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Maʿmar narrated to us from al-Zuhri." Abū Jaʿfar said in his narration: "Ibn Shihāb informed us from Sālim from his father that Ghaylān..." and he mentioned it. It has also been reported through other routes than Maʿmar and al-Zuhri: al-Bayhaqi reported it from Ayyūb, from Nāfiʿ and Sālim, from Ibn ʿUmar, that Ghaylān... and he mentioned it.

Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Majah reported in their Sunan from ʿUmayr al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives, so I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Choose four of them.'" Ibn Kathir said: its chain is good (ḥasan).

al-Shafiʿi reported in his Musnad from Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Dīlī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had five wives, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Keep four and separate from the other.'" Ibn Majah and al-Naḥḥās in his Nāsikh reported from Qays ibn al-Ḥārith al-Asadī, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had eight wives under me. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Choose four of them and release the rest.' So I did." These are corroborating reports (shawāhid) for the first hadith, as al-Bayhaqi said.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 1–4 (part 4 of 4):

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from al-Hakam, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that a slave-owner may not combine more than two women (in marriage) from among those who are owned.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning the verse, who said: "If you fear that you will not be just among four, then three; and if not, then two; and if not, then one. And if you fear that you will not be just even with one, then (marry) what your right hand possesses." 

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' the like of this. He also related from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾, that he said: "In intercourse and in love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, that he said: "The concubines (sarari)."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih related from ʿAʾishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "﴿That is closer to not being unjust﴾ means: that you do not oppress."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father said: This is an erroneous hadith (hadith khata'), and the correct report from ʿAʾishah is that it is a mawquf (companion's) statement.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿that you not be unjust﴾, that he said: "That you not deviate."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah, who said: "That you not deviate." Then he said: Have you not heard the verse of Abu Talib:

*With a scale of justice that does not cheat a barleycorn,*
*and a balance of truth whose weight is not deficient.*

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, who said: "That you not deviate." Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Razin, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak the like of this. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That is closer to there being fewer whom you must support (ta'ulu)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, who said: "That you not become impoverished."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Salih, who said: "A man, when he married a widow (ayyimah), would take her dowry for himself instead of giving it to her. So Allah forbade them from that, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying "nihlah" (as a gift), that he said: "By nihlah he means the mahr (bridal gift)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAʾishah concerning "nihlah," that she said: "Obligatory."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, that he said: "A specified obligation (fariḍah musammah)." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related the like of this from Qatadah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it﴾, that he said: "It refers to the husbands (lil-azwaj)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrimah concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "Of the dowry."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And if they willingly give you of it, something of it, (as) a soul﴾, that he said: "If it is without harm or deception, then it is wholesome and pleasant (hanee'an mari'an), as Allah said."

This is a return to the remaining rulings concerning the property of orphans. The command to hand their property over to them has already been given in His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Here, He (glorified is He) makes clear that the one who is foolish (safih) and the one who has not reached maturity may not be given his property.

The meaning of safih linguistically has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. Scholars differed over who these "foolish ones" are. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the orphans, so do not give them your property. Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best of what has been said about the verse. Malik said: they are the young children, so do not give them your property, lest they waste it and you are left with nothing. Mujahid said: they are the women. Al-Nahhas and others said: this view is not correct, since the Arabs say safa'ih or safihat (the feminine plural forms of safih).

They also differed over why the property is attributed to the addressees when it belongs to the foolish. It was said: He attributed it to them because it is in their hands and they are the ones who manage it, as in His saying: ﴿So greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and His saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], meaning: let some of you greet others, and let some of you kill others. It was also said: He attributed it to them because it is of the same kind as their own property, since property was originally made common among creation. It was also said: the intended meaning is the property of the addressees in reality, and this is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah. The intended meaning is the prohibition of handing it over to one who does not manage it well, such as women and children, and one whose understanding is weak and who cannot identify the ways of benefit that improve property, nor avoid the ways of harm that destroy it and carry it away.

His saying: ﴿which Allah has made for you as a means of support (qiyaman)﴾. The first object is omitted, and the sense is: which Allah has made for you. The reading qayyaman is that of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amir; others read qiyaman; and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read qiwaman. Qiyam and qiwam mean that by which one is sustained, as it is said: so-and-so is the qiyam (support) of his household and the qiwam (mainstay) of his house, meaning he is the one who sustains their affairs, that is, sets them right. When the qaf in qiwam was given a kasra, they changed the waw into a ya'. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: qayyaman and qiwaman have the same meaning as qiyaman, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); that is: do not give the foolish your property by which your affairs are set right, so that you stand by it in support. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is that it is sustaining your affairs, and he took it to be a plural.

The Basran grammarians said: qiyaman is the plural of qimah, like dimah and diyam; that is, Allah made it a value (qimah) for things. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this view and said: it is a verbal noun, like qiyam and qiwam.

The meaning is that it is a means of setting the condition right and of its stability. As for those who say that the intended property is their own, according to what the apparent attribution requires, the meaning is clear. As for those who say it is the property of the orphans, the meaning is that it is of the kind by which your livelihood is sustained and your condition is set right among property.

Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read: al-lati (the feminine relative pronoun for the plural) ja'ala. Al-Farra' said: in Arabic usage, the most common form is al-nisa' allati (the women who) and al-amwal allati (the property which), and likewise for non-property (i.e., the feminine plural relative is used for plural non-rational nouns). This was mentioned by al-Nahhas.

His saying: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾, meaning: make provision for them from it, or set an allowance for them. This applies to those whose maintenance and clothing are obligatory upon you, such as wives, children and the like.

As for those who say the property is the property of the orphans, the meaning is: trade with it until you profit, and spend on them from the profits, or set aside for them from their property a provision that they spend on themselves and by which they clothe themselves. This verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of placing restrictions (hajr) on the foolish, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Hanifah said: one who has reached maturity while sensible may not be restricted. The verse has also been cited as evidence for the obligation of maintaining relatives, and the disagreement on this is well known in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿and speak to them a kind word﴾. It was said: pray for them, such as "May Allah bless you, protect you, and provide for you." It was also said: its meaning is to promise them a good promise, such as saying: "If you act rightly, we will hand over your property to you," and a father saying to his son: "My wealth will come to you, and you, God willing, will be its owner," and the like.

The apparent meaning of the verse is whatever satisfies the designation of a good word. In it is guidance to good conduct with family and children, or with orphans in one's care. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in what is authentically reported from him: "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."

His saying: ﴿And test the orphans﴾. Testing (ibtila') means examining (ikhtibar), and its reality has already been discussed. They differed on the meaning of this examination. It was said: it is that the guardian (wasi) considers the character of his orphan, to know his intelligence and good management, and then hands over his property to him when he reaches marriageable age (al-nikah) and he perceives in him rectitude. It was said: the meaning of the examination is that he hands over to him some of his property and orders him to dispose of it until he knows the reality of his condition. It was said: the meaning of the examination is that he returns to him the management of household expenses, so that he knows how he manages, and if it is a girl, he returns to her what the mistress of the house is returned in managing her household. The meaning of reaching marriageable age is reaching puberty (ihtilam), in accordance with His saying: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty﴾ [al-Nur: 59]. Among the signs of puberty are growth of hair and reaching fifteen years of age.

Malik, Abu Hanifah and others said: one who has not experienced wet dreams (ihtilam) is not judged to have reached puberty until seventeen years have passed. These signs apply to both males and females, while females are specifically marked by pregnancy and menstruation.

His saying: ﴿then if you perceive (anastum)﴾, meaning: if you see and notice. From this is His saying: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the mountain﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs say: "Go and istanis (look carefully) whether you see anyone," meaning: look carefully. It was also said: here it means "found" and "knew," that is: if you find and know in them rushd (maturity of judgment). The reading of the majority is rushdan with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin.

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sulami and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read it with a fatha on the ra' and shin. It was said: both are dialectal variants. It was also said: with a damma it is the verbal noun of rashida, and with a fatha it is the verbal noun of rashada. Scholars differed on the meaning of rushd here. It was said: it is soundness in intellect and religion, and it was said: in intellect alone.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi said: the property of an orphan is not handed over to him if his rushd has not been perceived, even if he is an old man. al-Dahhak said: even if he reaches one hundred years.

The majority of scholars hold that rushd cannot occur except after puberty, and that if he does not show rushd after reaching puberty, the restriction is not lifted from him. Abu Hanifah said: one who is free and adult is not restricted, even if he is the most dissolute of people and the most wasteful, and this is also the view of al-Nakha'i and Zufar.

The apparent structure of the Qur'anic text is that their property is not handed over to them except after reaching a limit, which is reaching marriageable age, this limit being restricted by perceiving rushd. Therefore both matters must be combined: their property is not handed over to orphans before puberty even if they are known for rushd, nor after puberty except after rushd has been perceived in them.

The intended rushd is its type, namely that which relates to good management of their property, not squandering it, and placing it in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾. Israf (extravagance) linguistically means excess and exceeding the limit.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: israf and tabdhir (squandering) are the same, and bidar means hastening (mubadarah). The phrase ﴿that they will grow up﴾ is in the accusative position with respect to bidaran, meaning: do not consume the property of orphans in extravagance, and in hastening before they grow up; or: do not consume it for the sake of extravagance and for the sake of hastening; or: do not consume it while being extravagant and hasty for fear of their growing up, and saying: "We will spend the property of orphans on what we desire before they reach maturity, lest they take it out of our hands."

His saying: ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾. He (glorified is He) made clear what is permitted to them from the property of orphans. He commanded the wealthy to abstain and to preserve the child's property and not to take from it, and He permitted the poor to eat in a reasonable manner. (p-273)

Scholars differed on what eating in a reasonable manner (bi-al-ma'ruf) is. Some said: it is a loan if he needs it, and he repays it when Allah makes him prosperous. This was the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abidah al-Salmani, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Awza'i. al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', al-Hasan and Qatadah said: there is no repayment obligation on the poor for what he eats in a reasonable manner, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. This is closer to the Qur'anic text, since the permission to the poor to eat implies that it is allowed to him without a loan.

By reasonable manner is meant what is customary among people. So he does not enrich himself with the property of orphans or excessively indulge in eating, drinking and clothing, nor does he refrain from relieving his hunger and covering his nakedness. The address in this verse is to the guardians of orphans who manage what benefits them, such as the father, the grandfather and their executors (wasi).

Some scholars said: the verse means that if the orphan is wealthy, he is to be given ample provision and his property is to be kept from him; and if he is poor, spending on him is according to what he gains. This view is extremely weak.

His saying: ﴿So when you hand over their property to them, then have witnesses over them﴾, meaning: when the condition for handing over is met and you hand their property to them, then have witnesses against them that they have received it from you, so that accusations are removed from you and you are safe from the consequences of claims they might make. It was said: the prescribed witnessing is for what the guardians spent on them before their rushd. It was also said: it is for the return of what he borrowed to their property. This contains a severe warning. The bi' (in bi-Allah) is superfluous, meaning: Allah suffices.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾: he said: do not intend your property, which Allah has entrusted to you and made your livelihood, and give it to your wife or your daughter, and then be compelled to what is in their hands. Rather, keep your property and manage it, and be the one who spends on them for their clothing, provision and support. He said: His saying "qiwaman" means your sustenance from your livelihood.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him through al-'Awfi regarding the verse: he said: do not give your foolish son authority over your property, and command him to provide for himself from it and clothe himself. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him: he said: they are your sons and women.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Umamah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The foolish women are only those who obey their guardian." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: they are the servants, and they are the devils of mankind. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: they are the women and the children. Ibn Jarir reported from Hadrami: that a man deliberately gave his property to his wife, and she placed it in other than what is right, so Allah said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: they are orphans and women. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah, who said: it is the property of an orphan that is with you; He says: do not give it to him, and spend on him until he reaches maturity.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿and provide for them﴾: he said: spend on them. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning ﴿and speak to them a kind word﴾: he said: they were commanded to say to them a kind word in kindness and good relations.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 5–6 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾, that he said: "A promise you make to them."

And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up﴾, meaning: that you consume the orphan's property hastily before he reaches maturity, and so it will come between him and his property.

Al-Bukhari and others related from 'A'isha, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the guardian of an orphan: ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable﴾, in proportion to his management of it.

Ibn Jarir related from him, who said: "It is a loan (qarḍ)." 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "If he is poor, he takes from the surplus of the milk and from the surplus of the food, without exceeding that, and [he takes] what covers his nakedness of garments. The command to hand their property over to them has already been given in His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Malik said: they are the young children, so do not give them your property, lest they waste it and you are left with nothing. Mujahid said: they are the women. Al-Nahhas and others said: this view is not correct, since the Arabs say safa'ih or safihat (the feminine plural forms of safih).

They also differed over why the property is attributed to the addressees when it belongs to the foolish. It was said: He attributed it to them because it is in their hands and they are the ones who manage it, as in His saying: ﴿So greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and His saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], meaning: let some of you greet others, and let some of you kill others. It was also said: He attributed it to them because it is of the same kind as their own property, since property was originally made common among creation. It was also said: the intended meaning is the property of the addressees in reality, and this is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah. The intended meaning is the prohibition of handing it over to one who does not manage it well, such as women and children, and one whose understanding is weak and who cannot identify the ways of benefit that improve property, nor avoid the ways of harm that destroy it and carry it away.

His saying: ﴿which Allah has made for you as a means of support (qiyaman)﴾. The first object is omitted, and the sense is: which Allah has made for you. The reading qayyaman is that of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amir; others read qiyaman; and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read qiwaman. Qiyam and qiwam mean that by which one is sustained, as it is said: so-and-so is the qiyam (support) of his household and the qiwam (mainstay) of his house, meaning he is the one who sustains their affairs, that is, sets them right. When the qaf in qiwam was given a kasra, they changed the waw into a ya'. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: qayyaman and qiwaman have the same meaning as qiyaman, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); that is: do not give the foolish your property by which your affairs are set right, so that you stand by it in support. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is that it is sustaining your affairs, and he took it to be a plural.

The Basran grammarians said: qiyaman is the plural of qimah, like dimah and diyam; that is, Allah made it a value (qimah) for things. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi rejected this view and said: it is a verbal noun, like qiyam and qiwam.

The meaning is that it is a means of setting the condition right and of its stability. As for those who say that the intended property is their own, according to what the apparent attribution requires, the meaning is clear. As for those who say it is the property of the orphans, the meaning is that it is of the kind by which your livelihood is sustained and your condition is set right among property.

Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read: al-lati (the feminine relative pronoun for the plural) ja'ala. Al-Farra' said: in Arabic usage, the most common form is al-nisa' allati (the women who) and al-amwal allati (the property which), and likewise for non-property (i.e., the feminine plural relative is used for plural non-rational nouns). His saying: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾, meaning: make provision for them from it, or set an allowance for them. This applies to those whose maintenance and clothing are obligatory upon you, such as wives, children and the like.

Abu Hanifah said: one who has reached maturity while sensible may not be restricted. The verse has also been cited as evidence for the obligation of maintaining relatives, and the disagreement on this is well known in its proper places.

It was also said: its meaning is to promise them a good promise, such as saying: "If you act rightly, we will hand over your property to you," and a father saying to his son: "My wealth will come to you, and you, God willing, will be its owner," and the like.

The apparent meaning of the verse is whatever satisfies the designation of a good word. In it is guidance to good conduct with family and children, or with orphans in one's care. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in what is authentically reported from him: "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."

It was said: the meaning of the examination is that he hands over to him some of his property and orders him to dispose of it until he knows the reality of his condition. It was said: the meaning of the examination is that he returns to him the management of household expenses, so that he knows how he manages, and if it is a girl, he returns to her what the mistress of the house is returned in managing her household. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 7–10:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the ruling on the wealth of orphans (yatama), He connected it to the rulings on inheritance (mawarith) and the manner of dividing it among the heirs.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned women separately after mentioning men, and He did not say "for men and women there is a share," to signal their rootedness (asala) in this ruling and to repel what the Jahiliyya (Age of Ignorance) practiced, namely not giving women any inheritance. In mentioning kinship (qaraba) there is an explanation of the reason (illa) for inheritance, together with a generalization to whatever truly falls under the name of kinship without restriction. His saying, ﴿of what little or much of it﴾, is a substitute (badal) for His saying, ﴿of what has been left﴾, with the repetition of the genitive (jarr) case, and the pronoun in His saying "minhu" (of it) refers back to the thing substituted for.

His saying "nasiban" (a share) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) or as an absolute object (masdariyya) or as a specification (ikhtisas). The cause of the revelation of this verse will be mentioned later, if Allah wills. Allah, glorified is He, in these places summarized the measure of the obligatory share, then He revealed His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa: 11], so the inheritance of each individual became clear.

His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives﴾. The intended "relatives" here are other than the heirs, and likewise the orphans and the needy. Allah, glorified is He, legislated that if they attend the division of the estate, they are to be given a provision from it, so those who divide it shall give them something from it.

Some have held that the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) and that the command is for recommendation (nadb). Others have held that it is mansukh (abrogated) by His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa: 11]. The first view is stronger, because what is mentioned in the verse for the relatives who are not heirs is not part of the inheritance itself, so that it could be said it is abrogated by the verses of inheritance; unless you say that the relatives mentioned here are the heirs, in which case there would be a basis for abrogation.

A group said: this giving to non-heir relatives is obligatory, to the extent that the heirs' souls are content with it, and this is the literal meaning of the command, so one does not turn to recommendation except with an indication (qarina). The pronoun in His saying "minhu" refers to the divided property understood from the division, and it was said that it refers to what was left. The "known saying" (qawlun ma'ruf) is the good speech which contains no reproach (manna) regarding what has reached them of the provision, nor any harm (adha).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) related to us about the night of his Night Journey (isra') and said: 'I looked and saw people who had lips like the lips of camels, and there were appointed over them those who took hold of their lips, then placed in their mouths a rock of fire which was thrust into the mouth of one of them until it came out from their lower parts, and they were crying out and shrieking. I said: O Jibril, who are these? He said: These are ﴿those who consume the property of orphans unjustly; they only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blaze﴾.'" Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: "This verse is for the people of polytheism, when they did not give them inheritance and consumed their property."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 7–10:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the ruling on the wealth of orphans (yatama), He connected it to the rulings on inheritance (mawarith) and the manner of dividing it among the heirs.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned women separately after mentioning men, and He did not say "for men and women there is a share," to signal their rootedness (asala) in this ruling and to repel what the Jahiliyya (Age of Ignorance) practiced, namely not giving women any inheritance. In mentioning kinship (qaraba) there is an explanation of the reason (illa) for inheritance, together with a generalization to whatever truly falls under the name of kinship without restriction. His saying, ﴿of what little or much of it﴾, is a substitute (badal) for His saying, ﴿of what has been left﴾, with the repetition of the genitive (jarr) case, and the pronoun in His saying "minhu" (of it) refers back to the thing substituted for.

His saying "nasiban" (a share) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) or as an absolute object (masdariyya) or as a specification (ikhtisas). The cause of the revelation of this verse will be mentioned later, if Allah wills. Allah, glorified is He, in these places summarized the measure of the obligatory share, then He revealed His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa: 11], so the inheritance of each individual became clear.

His saying: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives﴾. The intended "relatives" here are other than the heirs, and likewise the orphans and the needy. Allah, glorified is He, legislated that if they attend the division of the estate, they are to be given a provision from it, so those who divide it shall give them something from it.

Some have held that the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) and that the command is for recommendation (nadb). Others have held that it is mansukh (abrogated) by His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa: 11]. The first view is stronger, because what is mentioned in the verse for the relatives who are not heirs is not part of the inheritance itself, so that it could be said it is abrogated by the verses of inheritance; unless you say that the relatives mentioned here are the heirs, in which case there would be a basis for abrogation.

A group said: this giving to non-heir relatives is obligatory, to the extent that the heirs' souls are content with it, and this is the literal meaning of the command, so one does not turn to recommendation except with an indication (qarina). The pronoun in His saying "minhu" refers to the divided property understood from the division, and it was said that it refers to what was left. The "known saying" (qawlun ma'ruf) is the good speech which contains no reproach (manna) regarding what has reached them of the provision, nor any harm (adha).

His saying: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾ refers, as a number of exegetes have held, to the guardians (awsiya'), and in it there is an admonition to them to deal with the orphans in their care as they would wish their own children to be dealt with after them. Another group said: the intended are all people, who are commanded to fear Allah regarding orphans, whether or not they are in their custody. Others said: the intended are those who attend the dying person at his death; they are commanded to fear Allah and to say to the dying person a right word, guiding him to free himself from the rights of Allah and the rights of the children of Adam, and to bequeath to the things that bring one near to Allah, glorified is He, and to abandon wasteful spending of his property and depriving his heirs, just as they would fear for their own heirs after them if they left them poor and dependent, begging from people. Ibn 'Atiyya said: People are of two kinds; for one of them it is fitting to say at his death what is not fitting for the other. When a man leaves heirs who are independent and wealthy, it is good to recommend bequest, and he is directed to put forward something for himself; and when he leaves heirs who are weak and destitute, it is good to recommend that he leave them and take care for them, for his reward in intending that is like his reward in [giving to] the needy. Al-Qurtubi said: this detailed distinction is sound.

His saying: "law taraku" (if they left) is a relative clause (silat al-mawsul), and the fa' in His saying "falyattaqu" (so let them fear Allah) indicates the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes. The meaning: let those fear whose state is such that, if they were about to leave behind them weak offspring (which is at their dying), they would fear for them loss after them, due to the passing of their protector and earner. Then He commanded them to fear Allah and to speak a right word to the dying or to their children after them, as previously explained.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly﴾ is a new sentence (isti'naf) containing a prohibition against wronging orphans by guardians and trustees. The accusative of His saying "zulman" is either as a masdar, meaning consuming in injustice, or as a circumstantial, meaning being unjust toward them.

His saying: ﴿They consume only fire into their bellies﴾, meaning: that which is a cause for the Fire, expressing the effect by its cause. Similar verses have already been explained. His saying "wa-sayaslawna" (and they will burn) is the reading of 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir with a damma on the ya' in the passive voice. Abu Haywa read it with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the sad, and a shadda on the lam, from the causative (tasliya) with repetition of the action time after time. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya', from salla al-nar, yaslaha (to be burned by the fire); and al-salla is being warmed near the fire or coming into direct contact with it, and from this is the saying of al-Harith ibn 'Abbad:

"I was not among its (the fire's) people — Allah knows it — and indeed I am today burning in its heat."

And al-sa'ir is the blazing ember.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to daughters or to young children until they reached maturity. A man from the Ansar called Aws ibn Thabit died, leaving two daughters and a young son, and his two paternal cousins, who were his agnates, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and took all his inheritance. His wife came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for them both and said: 'Do not touch anything of the inheritance, for something has been revealed to me about which I have been perplexed: that the male and the female have a share.' Then after that came: ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾ [an-Nisa: 127], then came: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ [an-Nisa: 11], so he called for the inheritance, gave the wife the eighth, and divided the remainder, the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrima concerning the verse, who said: "It was revealed concerning Umm Kulthum, daughter of Umm Kahla or Umm Kuhha, and Tha'laba ibn Aws and Suwayd, who were from the Ansar. One of them was her husband and the other was the paternal uncle of her child. She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my husband has died and left me and his daughter, and we were not given inheritance from his property.' The paternal uncle of her child said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she does not ride a horse, nor confront an enemy, and she earns nothing; she is supported by it, and does not earn.' Then the verse was revealed." Al-Bukhari and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And when the division is attended﴾ that he said: "It is definitive (muhkama) and is not abrogated."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Khattab ibn 'Abd Allah concerning this verse that he said: "Abu Musa judged by it." Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "It is obligatory upon the heirs, to the extent that their souls are content with it."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shayba reported from al-Hasan and al-Zuhri, who both said: "It is definitive, to the extent that their souls are content with it." Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Jarir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: (p-275) "He gives them a provision; if there is any shortfall in his property, he apologizes to them, and that is 'a known saying'."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'A'isha that it was not abrogated. Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported that this verse is abrogated by the verse of inheritance. Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab who said: "It is abrogated." Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "If they are adults, they are given a provision; if they are minors, they are apologized to."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported concerning His saying ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them...﴾ that he said: "This concerns a man who attends another man at his death and hears him bequeath a bequest that harms his heirs; so Allah commands the one who hears it to fear Allah, to grant him success and guide him to what is right, and to look after his heirs as he would wish to be done for his heirs if he feared their loss." Similar has been narrated through several chains.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Barza, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "On the Day of Resurrection a people will be raised from their graves with their mouths blazing with fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they?" He said: "Have you not seen that Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾?" Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) related to us about the night of his Night Journey (isra') and said: 'I looked and saw people who had lips like the lips of camels, and there were appointed over them those who took hold of their lips, then placed in their mouths a rock of fire which was thrust into the mouth of one of them until it came out from their lower parts, and they were crying out and shrieking. I said: O Jibril, who are these? He said: These are ﴿those who consume the property of orphans unjustly; they only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blaze﴾.'" Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: "This verse is for the people of polytheism, when they did not give them inheritance and consumed their property."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 11–14 (part 1 of 3):

This is an elaboration of what was stated in summary in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾ [an-Nisa: 7], and it has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of delaying clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) beyond the time of need. This verse is a pillar of the religion, a foundation of its rulings, and a "mother" of verses (umm min ummahat al-ayat), because it comprises what is important of the science of the obligatory shares (ilm al-fara'id, the science of inheritance). This science was among the most noble of the sciences of the Companions, and most of their disputes were concerned with it. After completing the explanation of what the word of God contains of the obligatory shares, I will mention, God willing, some of the virtues of this science.

His words: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾, meaning: concerning the clarification of their inheritance.

The scholars differed on whether the children of children (awlad al-awlad) are included or not. The Shafi'is said: they are included metaphorically (majazan), not literally (haqiqatan). The Hanafis said: the word "children" (awlad) literally includes them when there are no children of the loins (awlad al-sulb). There is no disagreement that the sons' sons are like sons in inheritance when the sons are absent; this disagreement concerns only whether the word "children" denotes their children when the sons are absent. The word "children" includes one of them who is a disbeliever, though he is excluded by the Sunnah; likewise the one who kills intentionally is included, though he is excluded by the Sunnah and consensus (ijma'); and the hermaphrodite (khunha) is included. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that he inherits according to the place from which he urinates. If he urinates from both, then according to whichever came first. If the urine came out from both without one preceding the other, he has half the share of a male and half the share of a female. It was said: he is given the lesser of the two shares, which is the share of a female; this was said by Yahya ibn Adam, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i.

This verse abrogates what existed in the early days of Islam of inheritance through alliance (al-hilf), emigration (al-hijrah), and contract (al-mu'aqadah). The scholars have agreed that if there is with the children someone who has a defined share (fard musamma), he is given it, and what remains of the property goes to the male, equal to the share of two females, based on the established hadith in the Sahihayn and others, in the wording: "Give the obligatory shares to their rightful owners, and whatever remains is for the nearest male relative," unless he is excluded in their presence, such as the uterine brothers (al-ikhwa li-umm). His words: ﴿For the male, the like of the share of two females﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaanifah) explaining the bequest concerning the children, so a pronoun referring back to them must be supposed: "God enjoins you concerning your children: for the male among them is the like of the share of two females."

What is meant is when males and females come together. As for when they are alone: the male has the entire inheritance, the female has half, and two or more females have two-thirds. His words: ﴿If they are women above two, then for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, meaning: if they are the children, the feminine form being in accordance with the predicate, or the daughters, or the offspring are women with no male with them, above two, that is, exceeding two. The phrase "above two" is either a qualifier of "women" or a second predicate of "was" (kana): ﴿then for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, the deceased being implied by the context.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that two-thirds is the obligatory share of three or more daughters. It does not specify an obligatory share for two, and therefore the people of knowledge differed about their share. The majority held that when the two stand apart from sons, they have two-thirds. Ibn Abbas held that their obligatory share is one-half. The majority argued by analogy (qiyas) with the two sisters, for God, Exalted is He, said concerning them: ﴿If they are two, then for them is two-thirds﴾ [an-Nisa: 176], so they joined the two daughters to the two sisters in entitlement to two-thirds, just as they joined sisters exceeding two to daughters in sharing the two-thirds. It was also said that the verse contains what indicates that two daughters have two-thirds, because when one female with her brother has a third, two daughters when alone have two-thirds. This argument was used by Isma'il ibn Ayyash and al-Mubarrad. Al-Nahhas said: This argument is an error in the view of the people of reasoning, because the disagreement concerns two daughters when they stand apart from sons. Moreover, the opponent may say: if he leaves two daughters and a son, the two daughters have one-half; this is evidence that this is their obligatory share. The argument of the majority can be supported by the fact that when God obligated for a single daughter standing alone one-half, by His words: ﴿And if she is one, then for her is one-half﴾, the obligatory share of two daughters standing alone exceeds that of the one; and analogy with the two sisters required restricting the two daughters to two-thirds.

It was said: the word "above" (fawq) is superfluous, and the meaning is: "if they are two women," as in His words: ﴿strike above the necks﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], meaning "the necks." Al-Nahhas and Ibn Atiyyah rejected this and said: it is an error, because adverbs and all nouns are not permitted in the speech of the Arabs to be added without meaning. Ibn Atiyyah said: Moreover, His words ﴿above the necks﴾ are the eloquent form, and "above" is not superfluous; rather it carries a determined meaning, because the blow to the neck must fall above the bones at the joint, not on the brain, as Durayd ibn al-Simmah said: "Lower it below the brain and raise it above the bone; thus I used to strike the necks of heroes," end of quotation. Furthermore, if the word "above" were superfluous, as they claim, it would say: "then for the two of them is two-thirds of what he left," and not "then for them is two-thirds of what he left."

The strongest thing the majority can cite is what Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Jabir, who said: "The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God, these are the two daughters of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', whose father was killed with you at Uhud as a martyr, and their paternal uncle took their property and left them no property, and they cannot be married unless they have property. He said: God will decide in this matter. Then the verse of inheritance was revealed: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾, the verse. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent to their uncle and said: Give the two daughters of Sa'd two-thirds, their mother one-eighth, and what remains is for you." They related it through several chains from Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Aqil, from Jabir. al-Tirmidhi said: It is not known except from his narration.

His words: ﴿And if she is one, then for her is one-half﴾. Nafi' and the people of Madinah read "wahidatun" (one) in the nominative, with "kana" as a complete verb meaning: "if one exists," or "if one comes into being." The rest read it in the accusative. Al-Nahhas said: This is a good reading, meaning: if the one left behind or the one born is a single female.

His words: ﴿And for his parents, to each one of them is the sixth﴾. This means the parents of the deceased, and it is a pronoun referring to something not mentioned, which is permissible because the context implies it. "To each one of them is the sixth" is a substitute (badal) for His words "and for his parents," by repetition of the governing element for emphasis and clarification.

Al-Hasan and Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read "al-sudsu" (the sixth) with a sukun on the dal, and likewise they read al-thuluth (the third) and al-rub' (the quarter) up to al-'ushr (the tenth) with sukun. This is the dialect of Banu Tamim and Rabi'ah. The majority read with a vowel (harakah), a damma, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad for all of them. The meaning of "the two parents" is the father and the mother, and the dual is in the form of the word "father" by way of prevalence (taghlib).

The scholars differed about the grandfather: is he in the position of the father, so that the brothers are excluded by him, or not? Abu Bakr al-Siddiq held that he is in the position of the father, and none of the Companions opposed him during his caliphate. They differed on this after his death. Those who agreed with Abu Bakr's view were: Ibn Abbas, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Aisha, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Hanifah, Abu Thawr and Ishaq. They argued from such words as His saying: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His saying: ﴿O children of Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 26, 27, 31, 35], and His words, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Shoot, O sons of Isma'il." Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Mas'ud held that the grandfather inherits along with the brothers of full or paternal blood, and he does not reduce them from the third; and with the sharers (dhawu al-furud) he does not reduce from the sixth, according to the view of Zayd, Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and al-Shafi'i. It was said: the grandfather shares with the brothers up to the sixth, and he does not reduce it by any amount with the sharers and others; this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla and a group.

The majority held that the grandfather excludes the children of the brothers. Al-Sha'bi related from Ali that he treated the children of brothers in the division (al-qasimah) as brothers. The scholars agreed that the grandfather inherits nothing alongside the father, and they agreed that the grandmother has the sixth when the deceased has no mother, and they agreed that the father does not exclude the maternal grandmother (umm al-umm).

They differed concerning the inheritance of the grandmother when her son is alive. It is related from Zayd ibn Thabit, Uthman and Ali that she does not inherit when her son is alive, and this was the view of Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion. It is related from Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Musa that she inherits alongside him; it is also related from Ali and Uthman, and this was the view of Shurayh, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ubaydullah ibn al-Hasan, Shurayk, Ahmad, Ishaq and Ibn al-Mundhir.

His words: ﴿If he has a child﴾. The word "child" (walad) applies to both male and female. But if the child present is a male alone or with a female among them, the grandfather has only the sixth. If the child present is a female, the grandfather has the sixth as a fixed share and is an agnatic heir (asabah) for what exceeds the sixth. The children of a deceased son are like the children of the deceased. His words: ﴿But if he has no child﴾, meaning: nor a son's child, due to the consensus mentioned before, ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾, alone apart from all other heirs, as the majority held, that the mother does not take a third of the estate except when the deceased has no heir other than the two parents. As for when one of the spouses is with them, the mother has only a third of what remains after the existing spouse's share.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that the mother has a third of the original estate when one of the spouses is present, which entails preferring the mother over the father in the case of a spouse and two parents, with agreement that the father is superior to her when they stand alone apart from one of the spouses. His words: ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is the sixth﴾. The unqualified word "brothers" indicates that there is no difference between brothers of full blood or of one parent.

The people of knowledge have agreed that two brothers stand in the place of three or more in excluding the mother to the sixth, except what is related from Ibn Abbas, that he made two as one in not excluding. They also agreed that two or more sisters are like two brothers in excluding the mother.

His words: ﴿after a bequest he makes, or a debt﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Asim read "yusa" (bequeathed) with a fatha on the sad. The rest read it with a kasra. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the kasra, because the deceased was mentioned before this.

Al-Akhfash said: Confirmation of this is His words: "yusina" and "tusuna." Scholars differed on the reason the bequest is mentioned before the debt, though the debt is by consensus prior to it. It was said: the intent is to place both before the inheritance without intending an order between them. It was said: since the bequest is less binding than the debt, it is mentioned first out of concern for it. It was said: it is mentioned first because it occurs frequently, so it became like a matter binding on every deceased. It was said: it is mentioned first because it is the share of the needy and the poor, while the debt is placed later because it is the share of a creditor who demands it with strength and authority. It was said: since the bequest arises from the deceased himself, it is mentioned first, unlike the debt, which is established and must be paid whether mentioned or not. It was said: it is mentioned first because it resembles inheritance in being taken without return, so it may be hard for the heirs to carry out, unlike the debt, since their souls are at rest about paying it. This bequest is restricted by His words: ﴿without causing harm﴾, as will come, God willing.

**His words, "Your fathers and your sons; you know not which of them is nearer to you in benefit":** It has been said that the predicate of "your fathers and your sons" is omitted, meaning "they are the ones for whom the shares are apportioned." It has also been said that the predicate is his words "you know not," and what follows it, while "nearer" is the predicate. His words "which of them" and "in benefit" are a *tamyiz* (a specifying accusative, which clarifies the ambiguity of the preceding term). The meaning is: you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit, through supplicating for you and giving charity on your behalf, as in the authentic hadith, "or a righteous child who supplicates for him." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "A son may be superior, so that he is allowed to intercede for his father."

Some exegetes said: If the son is of higher rank than his father in the Hereafter, he asks Allah to raise his father up to him; and if the father is of higher rank than his son, he asks Allah to raise his son up to him. It has also been said: the intended benefit is in this world and the Hereafter, as said by Ibn Zayd. It has also been said that the meaning is: you do not know who among your fathers and sons is most beneficial to you, the one who made a bequest and thereby directed you to the reward of the Hereafter by executing his bequest, so that he is nearer to you in benefit, or the one who left no bequest and left you abundant worldly wealth? Sahib al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) strengthened this view, saying: "Because the sentence is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*), and it is proper for a parenthetical clause to emphasise what it interrupts. This is consistent with his words, 'an obligation from Allah,' which is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (*masdar mu'akkid*), since the meaning of 'He enjoins you' is 'He imposes upon you.'" Makki and others said: it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (*hal mu'akkidah*), and its governing element is "He enjoins you."

The first view is preferable. **"Indeed Allah is ever Knowing"** of the distribution of inheritances, **"Wise,"** who ordained their distribution and clarified it to its rightful recipients. Al-Zajjaj said: Knowing of things before He created them, Wise in what He decrees and executes concerning them.

**His words, "And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child":** The address here is to the men. By "child" is meant a child of the loins or a grandchild, based on the consensus we mentioned earlier. **"But if they have a child, then for you is a quarter of what they leave":** This is agreed upon. The scholars did not differ that the husband, in the absence of a child, receives one half, and in the presence of a child, however remote, receives one quarter.

**His words, "after any bequest" etc.:** the discussion of it is as previously stated.

**His words, "And for them is a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child; but if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave":** This share with a child and the share without a child are such that a single wife may take it alone, and more than one wife share it. There is no disagreement on this. The discussion of bequest and debt is as previously stated.

**His words, "And if a man leaves an inheritance as *kalala*":** By "man" is meant the deceased. *Yuwarathu* is in the passive voice, from *waritha* and not *awratha*, and it is the predicate of *kana*. *Kalalatan* is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *yuwarathu*, meaning: "is inherited while being in a state of *kalala*." Or the predicate is *kalalatun* and *yuwarathu* is a qualifier of *rajulun*, meaning: "if a man who is inherited is one who is *kala*lah, having neither child nor parent."

It is also read as *yuwarathu* (lightened) and *yuwarrathu* (intensified). Then *kalalatan* is an object or a circumstantial accusative, with the object omitted, meaning: "is inherited, and the intention is that he is in a state of *kalala*," or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "for the sake of *kalala*." *Kalala* is a verbal noun from *takallalahu al-nasab*, meaning the lineage encompassed him, and from it the crown (*iklil*) is named, because it encircles the head.

It refers to the deceased who has no child and no parent. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Umar, 'Ali, and the majority of scholars, and it is what the author of the *Kitab al-'Ayn*, Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, Ibn 'Arafa, al-Qutaybi, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ibn al-Anbari said. It has been said that this is a consensus.

Ibn Kathir said: This is the view of the people of Madina, Kufa, and Basra, and it is the view of the seven jurists and the four imams, and of the majority of later and earlier scholars, indeed of all of them. More than one person has reported the consensus on it, and a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) has been related about it. End of quotation.

Abu Hatim and al-Athram related from Abu 'Ubayda that he said: "*Kalala* is everyone who is not inherited by a father, a son, or a brother, and this is *kalala* according to the Arabs." Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Abu 'Ubayda's mention here of the brother alongside the father and son as conditions of *kalala* is an error with no basis, and no one else mentioned it as a condition of *kalala*. What is related from Abu Bakr and 'Umar, that *kalala* is only one who has no child, they both retracted.

Ibn Zayd said: *Kalala* refers to both the living and the dead together. They named relatives *kalala* because they surround the deceased on his sides while not being part of him, nor he of them, unlike the son and father, who are his two extremities; when they are gone, lineage encircles him. It has been said that *kalala* is derived from *kalal*, meaning fatigue, as if the inheritance reaches the heir from afar and with exertion. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *kalala* is the distant paternal cousins.

In sum: whoever reads *yuwarrithu* (with a kasra on the *ra'* and shadda) (this is some of the Kufans), or *yuwarithu* (lightened, read by al-Hasan and Ayyub), takes *kalala* to mean relatives. Whoever reads *yuwarathu* with a fatha on the *ra'* (this is the majority), it is possible that *kalala* means the deceased, and it is possible that it means the relatives. It has been related from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Sha'bi that *kalala* is whatever is other than a child and a parent among the heirs.

al-Tabari said: The correct view is that *kalala* are those who inherit the deceased apart from his child and parent, because of the soundness of the report of Jabir: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, only *kalala* inherit from me; shall I bequeath all my wealth?' He said, 'No.'" End of quotation. It is related from 'Ata' that he said: *kalala* is the wealth.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a weak view with no basis. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: *kalala* applies to three things: to one who leaves neither child nor parent; to one among those left behind who is neither child nor parent; and to relatives other than through child or parent. End of quotation.

**His words, "or a woman":** it is conjoined to "a man" and bound by the same restriction; that is: "or a woman who is inherited as *kalala*."

**His words, "and he has a brother or a sister":** Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read *min umm* ("from the mother"). The mention of who related that from him will come later.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars have agreed that the brothers here are the brothers on the mother's side. He said: There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that the full brothers or the paternal brothers do not receive this share. Their consensus indicates that the brothers mentioned in His words, "And if they are brothers and sisters, men and women, then the male has the equal share of two females" [4:176], are full brothers or paternal brothers. The pronoun in His words, "and he has a brother or a sister," is singular because each of them is intended, as is the custom of the Arabs when they mention two nouns equal in rule: they may use a singular pronoun referring to both, as in His words, "And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is burdensome" and His words, "those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah." They may also use a dual pronoun, as in His words, "If he is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them" [4:135].

We have previously given a discussion on this longer than what is mentioned here.

**His words, "But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third":** The reference of "that" in His words is to "and he has a brother or a sister," meaning: more than a single brother alone or a single sister alone. This applies when there are two or more, whether two males, two females, or a male and a female. It has been used as evidence that the male is like the female among the maternal siblings, since Allah made them partners in the third without mentioning the male's superiority over the female, as He mentioned for children and full or paternal siblings. Al-Qurtubi said: This is a consensus.

The verse indicates that when the maternal siblings complete the division, they take precedence over the full or paternal siblings. This applies in the case known as *al-himariyya* (the donkey problem), where the deceased leaves a husband, a mother, two maternal brothers, and full brothers. The husband receives one half, the mother one sixth, the two maternal brothers one third, and the full brothers receive nothing. The reasoning is that the condition under which the siblings on the mother's side inherit has been met, namely that the deceased is a *kalala*. This is supported by the hadith: "Give the fixed shares to their rightful owners, and what remains goes to the nearest male," which is in the two *Sahihs* and elsewhere. We have established the indication of the verse and the hadith on this in the treatise we named *al-Mabahith al-Durriyya fi al-Mas'ala al-Himariyya*. On this question there has been disagreement among the Companions and those after them, which is well known.

**His words, "after any bequest which is made or a debt":** the discussion of it is as previously stated.

**His words, "not causing harm":** that is, he makes the bequest while not harming his heirs in any form of harm, such as acknowledging something that is not owed, or making a bequest with no purpose except to harm the heirs, or bequeathing to an heir absolutely, or bequeathing to someone else more than a third when the heirs have not permitted it.
