His words: ﴿And how could you take it﴾ are a denial after a denial, containing the cause that requires prohibiting the taking: namely, al-ifḍāʾ (intimacy/going in together).

Al-Harawī said: It is when the two are under one blanket, whether he had intercourse or did not. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-ifḍāʾ is that a man and a woman are alone together, even if he has not had intercourse with her. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and al-Suddī said: al-ifḍāʾ in this verse is intercourse. The original meaning of al-ifḍāʾ in the language is mixing; it is said of a mixed thing that it is faḍāʾ, and it is said: the people are fawḍā and faḍāʾ, i.e., mixed together with no commander over them.

His words: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾ are coordinated with the sentence before it: i.e., the situation is that some of you have had intimacy with others, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant, which is the marriage contract. From it is His Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "You have taken them by the trust of Allah and have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." It was also said: it is His words: ﴿either keep them in good fashion or release them with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. And it was said: it is the children.

His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾: a prohibition against what the Jāhiliyyah used to do, marrying their fathers' wives after the fathers died. It begins an explanation of whom it is unlawful to marry among women and whom it is not unlawful.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the reason for the prohibition, saying: ﴿Indeed, it was immorality and hatred and an evil way.﴾ These three attributes indicate that it is among the most grievous and most abominable of the prohibited things. The Jāhiliyyah used to call it nikāḥ al-maqt (the marriage of hatred). Thaʿlab said: I asked Ibn al-Aʿrābī about nikāḥ al-maqt, and he said: it is that a man marries his father's wife after he divorces her or she is widowed from him. This is also called al-ḍayzam. The root of al-maqt is hatred, from maqatahu, yamqutuhu, maqtan, so he is mamqūt and maqīt.

His words: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ is an exception that is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), i.e., but what has already passed, leave it and forsake it. It was said: illā here means baʿda, i.e., after what has passed. It was said: the meaning is "nor what has passed." It was said: it is a connected exception from His words ﴿what your fathers married﴾, conveying emphasis in prohibition by framing the speech as contingent on the impossible: that is, if it is possible for you to marry what has already passed, then marry, but nothing else is lawful for you. His words: ﴿and an evil way﴾: it functions like bi's (evil) in dispraise and in action, and the one being dispraised is omitted; that is, an evil way is the way of that marriage. It was said: it functions like the rest of the verbs, and in it is a pronoun referring back to what precedes it.

Al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: When Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son wanted to marry his wife, and this had been theirs in the Jāhiliyyah, so Allah revealed ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: "This verse was revealed regarding Kubaysha bint Maʿmar ibn Maʿn ibn ʿĀṣim from the Aws. She was married to Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat. He died and left her, and his son became inclined toward her. So she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I did not inherit my husband, nor was I left to be married off.' So this verse was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Baylamānī regarding His words: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, and do not withhold them﴾, who said: These two verses were revealed, one of them concerning the affair of the Jāhiliyyah and the other concerning the affair of Islam. Ibn al-Mubārak said: ﴿to inherit women against their will﴾ is of the Jāhiliyyah, and ﴿do not withhold them﴾ is of Islam.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Abū Mālik regarding His words: ﴿and do not withhold them﴾, who said: Do not harm your wife so that she will ransom herself from you. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated from Mujāhid, ﴿and do not withhold them﴾, meaning: that they marry their husbands, like al-ʿaḍl in Sūrat al-Baqarah. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: ʿAḍl was among Quraysh in Makkah: a man would marry a noble woman, and perhaps she would not agree with him, so he would separate from her on condition that she not marry except with his permission. He would bring witnesses and have that written against her and have it witnessed. Then when a suitor proposed to her, if she gave him what he wanted and pleased him, he permitted her; otherwise he withheld her (ʿaḍalahā). We have already mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding the explanation of the occasion what you have known.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: ﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾, who said: It is hatred and rebelliousness. If she does that, then it becomes lawful for him to take a ransom from her. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated similarly from Qatādah. Ibn Jarīr also narrated similarly from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Ibn Jarīr narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: Here, immorality is fornication. Ibn Jarīr narrated similarly from Abū Qilābah and Ibn Sīrīn.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Suddī regarding His words: ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾, who said: Mix with them. Ibn Jarīr said: Some narrators distorted it; it is actually khāliqūhunna (be on good terms with them). Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: Her right over you is good companionship, clothing, and reasonable provision. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Muqātil regarding ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾, meaning: their companionship in what is reasonable. ﴿But if you dislike them, it may be that you dislike a thing, and he divorces her, and she marries a man after him, and Allah places for him a child from her, and Allah places in her marriage much good.* Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The much good is that he shows compassion toward her, so she is provided for with her child, and Allah places in her child much good.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted something similar from al-Suddi. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from al-Hasan something similar to what Muqatil said. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And if you desire to replace one spouse with another﴾ and the verse [continues], that he said: "If you dislike your wife and another woman pleases you, and you divorce this one and marry that one, then give this one her bridal gift (mahr), even if it is a qintar (a great treasure)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Abu Ya'la transmitted that Umar forbade people to increase women's bridal gifts beyond four hundred dirhams. A woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "Have you not heard what Allah revealed, saying: ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾?" He said: "O Allah, forgive me! Everyone has more understanding than Umar." Then he mounted the pulpit and said: "O people, I had forbidden you to increase women's bridal gifts beyond four hundred dirhams. Whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes may do so." Abu Ya'la said: "I think he also said: 'Whoever is content in his soul, let him do so.'" Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain (isnad) is good and strong, and this story has been narrated with different wordings; this is one of them." (Al-Suyuti graded it as having a good chain.)

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "al-ifda' (الإفْضاءُ) is intercourse (al-jima'), but Allah uses a euphemism (yakni)."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted something similar from Mujahid. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalizan)﴾, that he said: "al-ghalizh (الغَلِيظُ, the solemn) is either holding on with kindness (imsak bi-ma'ruf) or releasing with goodness (tasrih bi-ihsan)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah something similar and said: "That used to be taken from the groom in the marriage contract: 'By Allah upon you, you will either keep her with kindness or release her with goodness.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that Ibn Umar, whenever he married, would say: "I have married you according to what Allah has commanded: holding on with kindness or releasing with goodness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Anas ibn Malik something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ikrimah and Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾, that they said: "You took them with the trust of Allah, and you made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is the saying of the man: 'I have possessed (malaktu, مَلَكْتُ)'."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "It is the word of marriage (kalimat al-nikah) by which their private parts are made lawful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted regarding His words, exalted is He, ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ that it was revealed when Ibn Abi Qays ibn al-Aslat wished to marry his father's wife after his death.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿except what has already passed﴾: "except what was in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from al-Baraa, who said: "I met my maternal uncle, and he had the banner with him. I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to a man who married his father's wife after him, and he commanded me to strike off his neck and take his wealth.'"

This is connected to what preceded it concerning wives, and the purpose is to negate injustice against them. The address is to the guardians (awliyāʾ). The meaning of the verse becomes clear by knowing its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), which al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. He said: When a man died, his guardians had more right to his wife. If one of them wished, he would marry her; if they wished, they would marry her off; and if they wished, they would not marry her. So they had more right to her than her own family, and so it was revealed. In a wording of Abū Dāwūd from him regarding this verse: A man would inherit the wife of his relative and then withhold her (yaʿḍulu-hā) until she died or returned to him her dowry (ṣadāq). In a wording of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim from him: If she was beautiful, he married her; and if she was ugly, he confined her until she died, so that he would inherit her. This occasion has been related in various wordings. The meaning of ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ is: it is not lawful for you to take them by way of inheritance, claiming that you have more right to them than others, and keeping them for yourselves. And it is not lawful for you to withhold them (taʿḍulūhunna) from marrying others, in order to take their inheritance when they die, or so that they hand over their dowry to you when you permit them to marry.

Al-Zuhrī and Abū Mijlaz said: It was among their customs that when a man died leaving a wife, his son from another woman, or his closest agnate, would cast his garment over the woman, and he would become more entitled to her than she herself and than her guardians. If he wished, he would marry her without a dowry, except the dowry that the deceased had given her. If he wished, he would marry her to someone else and take her dowry, giving her nothing. And if he wished, he would withhold her so that she would ransom herself from him with what she had inherited from the deceased, or until she died and he inherited her. Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: The address is to the husbands of the women, when they confine them along with bad treatment, hoping to inherit them, or so that they will ransom themselves with part of their dowries. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah preferred this view, and said: The evidence for this is His words: ﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾. If a woman commits immorality, the guardian has no right to confine her until she departs with her wealth, by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the community; rather, that right belongs to the husband. Al-Ḥasan said: If a virgin commits fornication, she is to be flogged one hundred times and exiled, and she must return to her husband what she took from him.

Abū Qilābah said: If a man's wife commits adultery, there is no harm in his harming her and making things hard for her until she ransoms herself from him. Al-Suddī said: If they do that, then take their dowries.

Others said: The immorality (al-fāḥishah) is abusive speech with the tongue, and bad treatment is in word and deed. Mālik and a group of scholars said: The husband may take from a rebellious wife (nāshiz) all that she possesses.

All of this is based on the address in His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ being to the husbands. But you have understood from what we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation that the address in His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ is to those who were addressed by His words ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. The meaning then is: it is not lawful for you to prevent them from marriage ﴿in order that you may take away part of what you have given them﴾, i.e., what those whom you inherit from had given them, ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾, in which case it is permitted for you to keep them from husbands. And there is no concealing the strain (taʿassuf) in this, given that it is not permitted to confine a woman who has committed immorality from marrying and guarding her chastity from fornication. Just as making His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ an address to the guardians involves this strain, so making His words ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ an address to the husbands involves a manifest strain, together with its contradiction of the occasion of revelation of the verse that we have mentioned. The better view is that the address in His words ﴿it is not lawful for you﴾ is to the Muslims. That is: it is not lawful for you, O community of Muslims, to inherit women against their will as the Jāhiliyyah did; and it is not lawful for you, O community of Muslims, to withhold your wives (taʿḍulū azwājakum), i.e., to keep them with you while you have no desire for them, but rather in order that you may take away part of the dowry you gave them, which they ransom themselves with to be released from confinement and from remaining under you. And despite your dislike of them, ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾, it is permitted for you to separate from them (mukhāla‘ah) with part of what you have given them.

His words: مُبَيِّنَةٍ (mubayyinah, "clear"). Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with a kasrah under the yāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAbbās read مُبِينَةٍ (mubīnah) with a kasrah under the bāʾ and a sukūn on the yāʾ, from abāna al-shayʾ, so it is mubīn.

His words: ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾: i.e., in what is known (maʿrūf) in this sharīʿah and among its people of good companionship. It is an address to the husbands or to what is more general than them, and it varies with differences among husbands in wealth, poverty, nobility and lowliness. ﴿But if you dislike them﴾ for some reason, other than committing immorality or rebelliousness, ﴿it may be that you dislike a thing while Allah places in it much good﴾: it may be that the matter will turn to what you love, namely the disappearance of dislike and its replacement with affection, and therefore there will be in that much good, more than continuing the companionship and having children. So the consequent here is omitted, indicated by its cause; that is: if you dislike them, then be patient, ﴿for it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah places in it much good.﴾

His words: ﴿and you have given one of them a great amount (qintār)﴾: its explanation has already been given in Āl ʿImrān, and what is meant here is abundant wealth, so do not take anything from it. It was said: this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated), and it was said: it is mansūkh (abrogated) by His words, may He be exalted, in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is the saying of the man: 'I have possessed (malaktu, مَلَكْتُ)'."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "It is the word of marriage (kalimat al-nikah) by which their private parts are made lawful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted regarding His words, exalted is He, ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ that it was revealed when Ibn Abi Qays ibn al-Aslat wished to marry his father's wife after his death.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿except what has already passed﴾: "except what was in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from al-Baraa, who said: "I met my maternal uncle, and he had the banner with him. I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to a man who married his father's wife after him, and he commanded me to strike off his neck and take his wealth.'"

This is connected to what preceded it concerning wives, and the purpose is to negate injustice against them. The address is to the guardians (awliyāʾ). The meaning of the verse becomes clear by knowing its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), which al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. He said: When a man died, his guardians had more right to his wife. If one of them wished, he would marry her; if they wished, they would marry her off; and if they wished, they would not marry her. So they had more right to her than her own family, and so it was revealed. In a wording of Abū Dāwūd from him regarding this verse: A man would inherit the wife of his relative and then withhold her (yaʿḍulu-hā) until she died or returned to him her dowry (ṣadāq). In a wording of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim from him: If she was beautiful, he married her; and if she was ugly, he confined her until she died, so that he would inherit her. This occasion has been related in various wordings. The meaning of ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ is: it is not lawful for you to take them by way of inheritance, claiming that you have more right to them than others, and keeping them for yourselves. And it is not lawful for you to withhold them (taʿḍulūhunna) from marrying others, in order to take their inheritance when they die, or so that they hand over their dowry to you when you permit them to marry.

Al-Zuhrī and Abū Mijlaz said: It was among their customs that when a man died leaving a wife, his son from another woman, or his closest agnate, would cast his garment over the woman, and he would become more entitled to her than she herself and than her guardians. If he wished, he would marry her without a dowry, except the dowry that the deceased had given her. If he wished, he would marry her to someone else and take her dowry, giving her nothing. And if he wished, he would withhold her so that she would ransom herself from him with what she had inherited from the deceased, or until she died and he inherited her. Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: The address is to the husbands of the women, when they confine them along with bad treatment, hoping to inherit them, or so that they will ransom themselves with part of their dowries. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah preferred this view, and said: The evidence for this is His words: ﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾. If a woman commits immorality, the guardian has no right to confine her until she departs with her wealth, by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the community; rather, that right belongs to the husband. Al-Ḥasan said: If a virgin commits fornication, she is to be flogged one hundred times and exiled, and she must return to her husband what she took from him.

Abū Qilābah said: If a man's wife commits adultery, there is no harm in his harming her and making things hard for her until she ransoms herself from him. Al-Suddī said: If they do that, then take their dowries.

Others said: The immorality (al-fāḥishah) is abusive speech with the tongue, and bad treatment is in word and deed. Mālik and a group of scholars said: The husband may take from a rebellious wife (nāshiz) all that she possesses.

All of this is based on the address in His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ being to the husbands. But you have understood from what we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation that the address in His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ is to those who were addressed by His words ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. The meaning then is: it is not lawful for you to prevent them from marriage ﴿in order that you may take away part of what you have given them﴾, i.e., what those whom you inherit from had given them, ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾, in which case it is permitted for you to keep them from husbands. And there is no concealing the strain (taʿassuf) in this, given that it is not permitted to confine a woman who has committed immorality from marrying and guarding her chastity from fornication. Just as making His words ﴿and do not withhold them﴾ an address to the guardians involves this strain, so making His words ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ an address to the husbands involves a manifest strain, together with its contradiction of the occasion of revelation of the verse that we have mentioned. The better view is that the address in His words ﴿it is not lawful for you﴾ is to the Muslims. That is: it is not lawful for you, O community of Muslims, to inherit women against their will as the Jāhiliyyah did; and it is not lawful for you, O community of Muslims, to withhold your wives (taʿḍulū azwājakum), i.e., to keep them with you while you have no desire for them, but rather in order that you may take away part of the dowry you gave them, which they ransom themselves with to be released from confinement and from remaining under you. And despite your dislike of them, ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾, it is permitted for you to separate from them (mukhāla‘ah) with part of what you have given them.

His words: مُبَيِّنَةٍ (mubayyinah, "clear"). Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with a kasrah under the yāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAbbās read مُبِينَةٍ (mubīnah) with a kasrah under the bāʾ and a sukūn on the yāʾ, from abāna al-shayʾ, so it is mubīn.

His words: ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾: i.e., in what is known (maʿrūf) in this sharīʿah and among its people of good companionship. It is an address to the husbands or to what is more general than them, and it varies with differences among husbands in wealth, poverty, nobility and lowliness. ﴿But if you dislike them﴾ for some reason, other than committing immorality or rebelliousness, ﴿it may be that you dislike a thing while Allah places in it much good﴾: it may be that the matter will turn to what you love, namely the disappearance of dislike and its replacement with affection, and therefore there will be in that much good, more than continuing the companionship and having children. So the consequent here is omitted, indicated by its cause; that is: if you dislike them, then be patient, ﴿for it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah places in it much good.﴾

His words: ﴿and you have given one of them a great amount (qintār)﴾: its explanation has already been given in Āl ʿImrān, and what is meant here is abundant wealth, so do not take anything from it. It was said: this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated), and it was said: it is mansūkh (abrogated) by His words, may He be exalted, in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. The better view is that all of it is muḥkam, and what is meant here is other than the one who seeks khulʿ; it is not lawful for her husband to take anything of what he gave her.

His words: ﴿Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ The interrogative is for denial and rebuke. The sentence confirms the first sentence, which contains the prohibition. His words: ﴿And how could you take it﴾ are a denial after a denial, containing the cause that requires prohibiting the taking: namely, al-ifḍāʾ (intimacy/going in together).

Al-Harawī said: It is when the two are under one blanket, whether he had intercourse or did not. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-ifḍāʾ is that a man and a woman are alone together, even if he has not had intercourse with her. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and al-Suddī said: al-ifḍāʾ in this verse is intercourse. The original meaning of al-ifḍāʾ in the language is mixing; it is said of a mixed thing that it is faḍāʾ, and it is said: the people are fawḍā and faḍāʾ, i.e., mixed together with no commander over them.

His words: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾ are coordinated with the sentence before it: i.e., the situation is that some of you have had intimacy with others, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant, which is the marriage contract. From it is His Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "You have taken them by the trust of Allah and have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." It was also said: it is His words: ﴿either keep them in good fashion or release them with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. And it was said: it is the children.

His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾: a prohibition against what the Jāhiliyyah used to do, marrying their fathers' wives after the fathers died. It begins an explanation of whom it is unlawful to marry among women and whom it is not unlawful.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the reason for the prohibition, saying: ﴿Indeed, it was immorality and hatred and an evil way.﴾ These three attributes indicate that it is among the most grievous and most abominable of the prohibited things. The Jāhiliyyah used to call it nikāḥ al-maqt (the marriage of hatred). Thaʿlab said: I asked Ibn al-Aʿrābī about nikāḥ al-maqt, and he said: it is that a man marries his father's wife after he divorces her or she is widowed from him. This is also called al-ḍayzam. The root of al-maqt is hatred, from maqatahu, yamqutuhu, maqtan, so he is mamqūt and maqīt.

His words: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ is an exception that is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), i.e., but what has already passed, leave it and forsake it. It was said: illā here means baʿda, i.e., after what has passed. It was said: the meaning is "nor what has passed." It was said: it is a connected exception from His words ﴿what your fathers married﴾, conveying emphasis in prohibition by framing the speech as contingent on the impossible: that is, if it is possible for you to marry what has already passed, then marry, but nothing else is lawful for you. His words: ﴿and an evil way﴾: it functions like bi's (evil) in dispraise and in action, and the one being dispraised is omitted; that is, an evil way is the way of that marriage. It was said: it functions like the rest of the verbs, and in it is a pronoun referring back to what precedes it.

Al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: When Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son wanted to marry his wife, and this had been theirs in the Jāhiliyyah, so Allah revealed ﴿it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: "This verse was revealed regarding Kubaysha bint Maʿmar ibn Maʿn ibn ʿĀṣim from the Aws. She was married to Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat. He died and left her, and his son became inclined toward her. So she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I did not inherit my husband, nor was I left to be married off.' So this verse was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Baylamānī regarding His words: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, and do not withhold them﴾, who said: These two verses were revealed, one of them concerning the affair of the Jāhiliyyah and the other concerning the affair of Islam. Ibn al-Mubārak said: ﴿to inherit women against their will﴾ is of the Jāhiliyyah, and ﴿do not withhold them﴾ is of Islam.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Abū Mālik regarding His words: ﴿and do not withhold them﴾, who said: Do not harm your wife so that she will ransom herself from you. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated from Mujāhid, ﴿and do not withhold them﴾, meaning: that they marry their husbands, like al-ʿaḍl in Sūrat al-Baqarah. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: ʿAḍl was among Quraysh in Makkah: a man would marry a noble woman, and perhaps she would not agree with him, so he would separate from her on condition that she not marry except with his permission. He would bring witnesses and have that written against her and have it witnessed. Then when a suitor proposed to her, if she gave him what he wanted and pleased him, he permitted her; otherwise he withheld her (ʿaḍalahā). We have already mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding the explanation of the occasion what you have known.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: ﴿except that they commit a clear immorality﴾, who said: It is hatred and rebelliousness. If she does that, then it becomes lawful for him to take a ransom from her. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated similarly from Qatādah. Ibn Jarīr also narrated similarly from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Ibn Jarīr narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: Here, immorality is fornication. Ibn Jarīr narrated similarly from Abū Qilābah and Ibn Sīrīn.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Suddī regarding His words: ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾, who said: Mix with them. Ibn Jarīr said: Some narrators distorted it; it is actually khāliqūhunna (be on good terms with them). Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: Her right over you is good companionship, clothing, and reasonable provision. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Muqātil regarding ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾, meaning: their companionship in what is reasonable. ﴿But if you dislike them, it may be that you dislike a thing, and he divorces her, and she marries a man after him, and Allah places for him a child from her, and Allah places in her marriage much good.* Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The much good is that he shows compassion toward her, so she is provided for with her child, and Allah places in her child much good.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted something similar from al-Suddi. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from al-Hasan something similar to what Muqatil said. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And if you desire to replace one spouse with another﴾ and the verse [continues], that he said: "If you dislike your wife and another woman pleases you, and you divorce this one and marry that one, then give this one her bridal gift (mahr), even if it is a qintar (a great treasure)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Abu Ya'la transmitted that Umar forbade people to increase women's bridal gifts beyond four hundred dirhams. A woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "Have you not heard what Allah revealed, saying: ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾?" He said: "O Allah, forgive me! Everyone has more understanding than Umar." Then he mounted the pulpit and said: "O people, I had forbidden you to increase women's bridal gifts beyond four hundred dirhams. Whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes may do so." Abu Ya'la said: "I think he also said: 'Whoever is content in his soul, let him do so.'" Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain (isnad) is good and strong, and this story has been narrated with different wordings; this is one of them." (Al-Suyuti graded it as having a good chain.)

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "al-ifda' (الإفْضاءُ) is intercourse (al-jima'), but Allah uses a euphemism (yakni)."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted something similar from Mujahid. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalizan)﴾, that he said: "al-ghalizh (الغَلِيظُ, the solemn) is either holding on with kindness (imsak bi-ma'ruf) or releasing with goodness (tasrih bi-ihsan)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah something similar and said: "That used to be taken from the groom in the marriage contract: 'By Allah upon you, you will either keep her with kindness or release her with goodness.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that Ibn Umar, whenever he married, would say: "I have married you according to what Allah has commanded: holding on with kindness or releasing with goodness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Anas ibn Malik something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ikrimah and Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾, that they said: "You took them with the trust of Allah, and you made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is the saying of the man: 'I have possessed (malaktu, مَلَكْتُ)'."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "It is the word of marriage (kalimat al-nikah) by which their private parts are made lawful."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted regarding His words, exalted is He, ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ that it was revealed when Ibn Abi Qays ibn al-Aslat wished to marry his father's wife after his death.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿except what has already passed﴾: "except what was in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from al-Baraa, who said: "I met my maternal uncle, and he had the banner with him. I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to a man who married his father's wife after him, and he commanded me to strike off his neck and take his wealth.'"

(p. 284) His saying, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾: that is, marrying them. In this verse God, glory be to Him, has specified which women are lawful and which are unlawful. He forbade seven by blood relationship, and six by fosterage and affinity. The widely transmitted Sunnah (al-Sunnah al-mutawatirah) added the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt and with her maternal aunt, and there is consensus (al-ijma') on this. The seven forbidden by blood are: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers' daughters, and sisters' daughters.

The forbidden by affinity and fosterage are: foster mothers, foster sisters, mothers-in-law, stepdaughters, sons' wives, and combining two sisters. These are six. The seventh is wives of fathers, and the eighth is combining a woman with her aunt. Al-Tahawi said: all of this is among the clear (muhkam) rulings on which there is agreement, and it is not permissible to marry any of them by consensus, except the mothers-in-law whose daughters' husbands have not consummated the marriage. Most of the early scholars (al-salaf) held that the mother becomes forbidden upon the contract with the daughter, while the daughter is forbidden only upon consummation with the mother.

Some of the early scholars said: the mother-in-law and the stepdaughter are equal; neither becomes forbidden except by consummating the marriage with the other. They said: the meaning of His saying, ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾, is those with whom you have consummated [marriage]. They claimed that the condition of consummation applies to both the mothers and the stepdaughters. This was transmitted by Khilas from Ali ibn Abi Talib. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas, Jabir, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Mujahid.

Al-Qurtubi said: the report of Khilas from Ali cannot serve as proof, and its transmission is not sound according to the scholars of hadith; the authentic position from Ali is the same as the view of the majority. The majority's argument, that the condition of consummation refers to the mothers and the stepdaughters, has been answered on grounds of grammatical analysis (i'rab): if two predicates differ in their governing element, they cannot share one modifier. Thus, according to the grammarians, it is not permissible to say: مَرَرْتُ بِنِسائِكَ وهَوَيْتُ نِساءَ زَيْدٍ الظَّرِيفاتِ, making الظَّرِيفاتِ a modifier for all of them. Similarly, in the verse, the phrase "with whom you have consummated" cannot be a modifier for both, because the two clauses differ.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: the sound view is that of the majority, because all the mothers of wives are included in His saying, ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾. What supports the majority's position is what 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported by two routes from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If a man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether or not he has consummated [the marriage] with the daughter. And if he marries the mother and does not consummate with her, then divorces her, he may marry the daughter."

Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir, arguing for the majority: a report has been transmitted on this matter, but there is a question about its chain of transmission. He then mentioned this hadith and said: even though there is weakness in its chain, the consensus of the authoritative scholars on the validity of this view makes it unnecessary to cite other evidence for its soundness. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: they have agreed that the prohibition of the mothers of wives is absolute, while the prohibition of stepdaughters is conditional, as is apparent from the wording of God, exalted is He. End of quotation.

The claim of consensus is rejected because of the dissent of those who came before. Know that the word "mothers" includes their mothers and grandmothers, and the father's mother and grandmothers, however high they go, since all of them are "mothers" to whoever is born of them, however far down the line. The word "daughters" includes the daughters of children, however far down they go. The word "sisters" applies to a full sister (with the same two parents) or to a half-sister (sharing one parent). The word "paternal aunt" refers to any woman who shares with your father or grandfather either of their two parents, or one of them. An aunt can also be from the maternal side, who is the sister of the mother's father. The word "maternal aunt" refers to any woman who shares with your mother either of her two parents, or one of them. An aunt can also be from the paternal side, who is the sister of your father's mother. The "brother's daughter" is any female to whom your brother is a parent, directly or through an intermediary, however remote the descent; likewise the "sister's daughter."

His saying, ﴿and your mothers who have nursed you﴾: this is absolute, restricted by what is stated in the Sunnah about fosterage occurring within two years, except in cases like the nursing of Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah. The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that the rule of fosterage applies to whatever meets the definition of nursing both linguistically and legally. However, it has been restricted to five sucklings in sound hadiths. A full discussion of establishing and verifying this would be lengthy, and we have covered it thoroughly in our other works, where we have established what is correct in many of the issues concerning fosterage.

His saying, ﴿and your foster sisters﴾: a foster sister is one whom your mother nursed with your father's milk, whether she nursed alongside you or after or before you, among the brothers and sisters. A full sister by the mother is one whom your mother nursed with the milk of another man.

His saying, ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾: the discussion of whether consummation is required has already been covered.

The prohibitions by marriage (al-musahharah) are four: the wife's mother, her daughter, the father's wife, and the son's wife.

His saying, ﴿and your stepdaughters﴾: the rabibah (stepdaughter) is the daughter of a man's wife from another man. She is so named because he raises (yurabbi) her in his care, so she is marbubah, in the form fa'ilah with the meaning of maf'ulah. Al-Qurtubi said: the jurists agree that the stepdaughter becomes forbidden to the husband of her mother if he has consummated the marriage with the mother, even if the stepdaughter was not in his care. Some early scholars and the people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) deviated, saying: the stepdaughter is forbidden only if she is in the care of the one who married her mother; so if she lives in another country and he has separated from the mother, he may marry her. This was reported from Ali, but Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tahawi said: it has not been established from Ali, because its transmitter is Ibrahim ibn 'Ubayd, from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, from Ali, and this Ibrahim is not known.

Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir after citing this report from Ali: this is a strong chain, established from Ali ibn Abi Talib according to the standard of Muslim. The word "hujur" is the plural of hijr (care). The more likely view is that they are in the custody of their mothers, under the protection of their husbands, as is usually the case. It was also said that "hujur" means houses, i.e. in your houses; this was related by al-Athram from Abu 'Ubaydah.

His saying, ﴿but if you have not consummated [marriage] with them, there is no blame upon you﴾: that is, in marrying the stepdaughters. This explicitly states what is implied by the preceding statement.

The scholars differed on the meaning of consummation that makes the stepdaughters forbidden. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: consummation means sexual intercourse. This is the view of Tawus, 'Amr ibn Dinar, and others. Malik, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, and the Zaydis said: if a man touches the mother with desire, his stepdaughter becomes forbidden to him. This is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: there is consensus that the seclusion of a man with his wife does not make her daughter forbidden to him if he divorces her before touching her and before looking at her private part with desire, which indicates that the meaning of consummation is reaching her by intercourse. End of quotation. Al-Qurtubi also reported the consensus in this way, saying: the scholars agree that if a man marries a woman and then divorces her or she dies before he has consummated [the marriage], it is lawful for him to marry her daughter.

They differed concerning looking. Malik said: if he looks at her hair, her chest, or any of her attractions with desire, her mother and her daughter become forbidden to him. The Kufans said: if he looks at her private part with desire, it is the same as touching with desire, and al-Thawri said likewise, without mentioning desire. Ibn Abi Layla said: it is not forbidden by looking until he touches, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. What should be relied upon in such disagreement is to examine the meaning of consummation, either in law or in language. If it is specific to intercourse, there is no basis for extending it to anything else, whether touching, looking, or other things. If its meaning is broader than intercourse, such that it applies to any kind of sexual enjoyment, then that is the criterion for prohibition.

As for the stepdaughter in one's possession by right of ownership (milk al-yamin), it is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he disliked this. Ibn Abbas said: one verse permitted both, and another verse forbade both, and I would not do it. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: there is no disagreement among the scholars that it is not lawful for anyone to have intercourse with a woman and her daughter who are owned by right of possession, because God forbade this in marriage when He said: ﴿and the mothers of your wives and your stepdaughters, who are in your care, [born] of your wives﴾. According to them, ownership by right of possession follows marriage, except what was reported from 'Umar and Ibn Abbas, and none of the leading jurists or their followers agreed with it. End of quotation.

His saying, ﴿and the wives of your sons﴾: al-halail is the plural of halilah, meaning wife. She is so named because she is lawful (tahillu) with the husband wherever he is lawful; it is the form fa'ilah with the meaning of fa'ilah (active).

Al-Zajjaj and a group of scholars said that it comes from the word halal (lawful), so that she is halilah in the sense of muhallalah (made lawful). It was also said: because each of them makes lawful the other's garment. The scholars have agreed on the prohibition of what fathers have contracted for sons, and what sons have contracted for fathers, whether or not the contract was accompanied by intercourse, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾, and His saying: ﴿and the wives of your sons﴾. The jurists differed on whether a defective contract makes the prohibition apply, as is explained in the books of furu' (jurisprudence).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: all who are known to have knowledge among the scholars of the regions agreed that if a man has intercourse with a woman through a defective marriage contract, she becomes forbidden to his father and his son and to his grandfathers. The scholars agreed that a contract of purchase concerning a slave girl does not make her forbidden to his father or his son. So if he buys a slave girl and then touches or kisses her, she becomes forbidden to his father and his son. I know of no disagreement on this, so this prohibition is required as a matter of acceptance by them. Since they differed on whether she becomes forbidden by looking without touching, that view is not permitted due to their disagreement. He said: nothing has been authentically reported from any of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) contrary to what we have said.

His saying, ﴿who are from your loins﴾: this is a qualification of the sons; that is, excluding those whom you adopt from the children of others, as they used to do in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Zayd had no more need of her, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there would be no blame upon the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have no more need of them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Also His saying: ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4], and: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40].

As for the wife of a son by fosterage, the majority hold that she becomes forbidden to his father. It has been said that this is a consensus, even though a foster son is not one of the sons of the loins. The basis for this is what is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "What is forbidden by blood is forbidden by fosterage." There is no disagreement that the children of children, however far down, are in the same position as children of the loins regarding the prohibition of marrying their wives to their grandfathers.

The scholars have differed on whether intercourse through adultery (zina) makes marriage prohibited. Most scholars said: if a man has intercourse with a woman through adultery, marrying her is not forbidden to him because of it. Likewise, his wife is not forbidden to him if he commits adultery with her mother or her daughter. It is enough that the legal punishment (hadd) be carried out against him. Likewise, according to them, it is permissible for him to marry the mother of the woman he committed adultery with, and her daughter.

A group of scholars said: adultery does make marriage prohibited. This was reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y). It was also reported from Malik, but the authentic report from him is in agreement with the view of the majority.

The majority of scholars (al-Jumhur) cited His words, ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾, and His words, ﴿and the wives of your sons﴾. A woman who has been fornicated with (al-mawta'a bi'l-zina) is not truly described as one of their wives, nor as the wife of their son. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a man who committed fornication with a woman and then wished to marry her or her daughter. He said: 'What is unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful.'"

Those who hold that it is forbidden (al-muharrimun) cited the account of Jurayj, which is authentic in the Sahih, that he said: "O boy, who is your father?" He said: "So-and-so the shepherd." Thus the boy attributed himself to his father from fornication. This argument is invalid. They also cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah does not look at a man who looks at the private part of a woman and her daughter," and he did not distinguish between the lawful and the unlawful. It is answered that this is general (mutlaq) and restricted (muqayyad) by the evidences that indicate that what is unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful.

They differed concerning sodomy (al-liwat), whether it entails prohibition or not. Al-Thawri said: "If he sodomizes a boy, his mother becomes forbidden to him." This is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: "If he sodomizes the son of his wife, or her father, or her brother, his wife becomes forbidden to him." Al-Awza'i said: "If he sodomizes a boy and the one who was sodomized has a daughter, it is not permissible for the sodomizer to marry her, because she is the daughter of one with whom he has had intercourse."

The weakness and the collapse of the view of these scholars is not hidden. It falls far below the view of those who say that intercourse with what is unlawful entails prohibition by degrees, because the doubts that those scholars relied upon are not fit to support what they claim, namely that sodomy entails prohibition.

His words: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ mean: "And it is forbidden for you to combine two sisters." It is in the nominative position (mahall raf') by coordination (atf) upon the earlier prohibited persons. It includes combining them in marriage and in intercourse by right of ownership (bi-milk al-yamin).

It has been said that the verse is specific to combining them in marriage, not in ownership. As for intercourse by ownership, there is no right (haqq) to it through marriage. The community (al-ummah) has agreed on prohibiting their combination in a marriage contract. They differed concerning two sisters by right of ownership. The majority of scholars (kaffat al-'ulama') held that it is permissible to combine them in intercourse by ownership, and they agreed that it is permissible to combine them in ownership alone. Some of the early generations (al-salaf) hesitated concerning combining two sisters in intercourse by ownership, and that will be explained later. They differed concerning the permissibility of a marriage contract with the sister of a slave-girl who is being had sexually by ownership.

Al-Awza'i said: "If he has intercourse with a slave-girl of his by right of ownership, it is not permissible for him to marry her sister." Al-Shafi'i said: "Ownership of the right hand does not prevent marrying the sister." The Zahiris went to the permissibility of combining two sisters by right of ownership in intercourse, just as it is permissible to combine them in ownership. Ibn Abd al-Barr said, after mentioning what is narrated from Uthman ibn Affan concerning the permissibility of combining two sisters in intercourse by ownership: "The like of Uthman's view has been narrated from a group of the early generations, including Ibn Abbas, but they were disputed, and none of the jurists of the cities paid attention to that, neither in the Hijaz, nor in Iraq, nor what lies beyond it of the East, nor in Syria, nor in the West, except one who deviated from their community by following the apparent meaning (al-zahir) and rejecting analogy (al-qiyas)."

The one who deliberately does that is left alone. The body of jurists agree that it is not lawful to combine two sisters by right of ownership in intercourse, just as it is not lawful in marriage.

The Muslims have agreed that the meaning of His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, and your sisters﴾ to the end of the verse, is that marriage by right of ownership concerning all of these women is the same. Therefore, by analogy and reasoning, it must be that combining two sisters, the mothers of women, and the stepdaughters is likewise. So it is according to their majority, and this is the argument by which whoever opposes it and deviates from it is refuted. And Allah is the Praised. End of quotation.

I say: Here there is a difficulty. It is established that the word nikah is applied to the contract alone, and to intercourse alone, and the dispute is whether one of them is literal (haqiqa) and the other figurative (majaz), or whether both are literal, which is well known. If we take the prohibition mentioned in this verse, namely His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ to its end, to mean that the contract with them is forbidden, then in His words: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ there is no indication of the prohibition of combining two slave-women in intercourse by ownership. And what has occurred of the consensus of the Muslims, that His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, and your sisters﴾ to its end apply equally to free women and slave-women, does not require that the point of dispute, namely combining two sisters in intercourse by right of ownership, be like the point of consensus. Mere analogy in such a place does not establish proof, because of the counterexamples that may be raised against it. And if we take the prohibition mentioned in the verse to mean intercourse alone, that is not valid, because of the consensus on prohibiting the marriage contract with all of those mentioned from the beginning of the verse to its end. So nothing remains but to take the prohibition in the verse to mean the prohibition of the marriage contract. Then whoever holds the prohibition of combining two sisters in intercourse by ownership needs a proof, and it does not help him that this is the view of the majority, for truth is not known by men. If he brings it pure and free of any turbidity, then well and good; otherwise the original ruling is permissibility. It is also not valid to take the word nikah in the verse in both its meanings together, namely the contract and intercourse, because that is combining the literal and the figurative, which is prohibited, or combining the two meanings of a homonym (mushtarak), concerning which there is the well-known dispute in the principles of jurisprudence. So reflect on this.

The people of knowledge differed concerning a man who has intercourse with his slave-woman by ownership, and then wishes to have intercourse with her sister by ownership. Ali, Ibn Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: "It is not lawful for him to have intercourse with the second until the private part of the other becomes forbidden to him, by removing her from his ownership through sale, manumission, or by marrying her off." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "There is a second view from Qatada, namely that he intends to make the first forbidden to himself and does not approach her, then he refrains from her until the forbidden one has completed her waiting period (istibra'), and then he may approach the second." There is a third view, namely that he approaches neither of them. This is what al-Hakam and Hammad said, and the like of it is narrated from al-Nakha'i.

Malik said: "If he has two sisters by ownership, he may have intercourse with whichever of them he wishes, and refraining from the other is left to his trustworthiness. If he wishes to have intercourse with the other, he must make the first's private part forbidden to himself by an act he performs, such as removing her from ownership, marrying her off, selling her, manumitting her, granting her a writing of freedom (kitaba), or assigning her to long service. If he has intercourse with one of them and then pounces upon the other without making the first forbidden, he must stop with both of them, and it is not lawful for him to approach either until he makes the other forbidden, and that is not left to his trustworthiness, because he is suspected." Al-Qurtubi said: "The scholars have agreed that if a man divorces his wife with a divorce in which he may take her back, it is not permissible for him to marry her sister until the waiting period of the divorced woman has ended." 

They differed when he divorced her with a divorce in which he may not take her back. A group said: "It is not permissible for him to marry her sister, nor a fourth wife, until the waiting period of the one he divorced has ended." This was narrated from Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, Mujahid, Ata', al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Another group said: "He may marry her sister, and he may marry a fourth wife, for one who had four wives under him and divorced one of them with an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in)." This was narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, al-Qasim, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and Abu Ubayd. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I do not think it is other than the view of Malik." It is also one of the two narrations from Zayd ibn Thabit and Ata'.

His words: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ may mean the same as what preceded in His words: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾. It may also have another meaning, namely the permissibility of what has passed, that if the combining occurred in the Jahiliyyah the marriage was valid, and if it occurred in Islam one was given the choice between the two sisters. The correct interpretation is the first possibility.

His words: ﴿And the married women among the women﴾ are coordinated upon the prohibited persons mentioned. The root of tahassun is protection (al-tamannu'), and from it is His words: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80], meaning to protect you. From it also comes hisan (with a kasra on the ha') for a horse, because it protects its rider from destruction. And hasan (with a fatha on the ha') means a chaste woman, because she protects herself. From it is the verse of Hassan:

"A chaste and dignified woman, who is not suspected of any doubtful act, and who in the morning is hungry from the flesh of the heedless."

The verbal noun is hasana (with a fatha). Here "the married women" means women who have husbands.

Ihsan occurs in the Qur'an with several meanings. This is one of them. The second refers to a free woman, as in His words: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and His words: ﴿and the chaste women from among the believers, and the chaste women from among those given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. The third refers to a chaste woman, as in His words: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25; al-Ma'ida: 5]. The fourth refers to a Muslim woman, as in His words: ﴿And when they are chaste (uhsinna)﴾.

The people of knowledge differed in the interpretation of this verse, namely His words: ﴿And the married women among the women, except what your right hands possess.﴾ Ibn Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Qilaba, Makhul, and al-Zuhri said: "The meaning of the married women here is specifically the captured women who have husbands. That is: they are forbidden to you, except what your right hands possess by capture from the land of war, for those are lawful even if they have a husband." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, that is, captivity cuts the marital bond. It was also said by Ibn Wahb and Ibn Abd al-Hakam, who narrated it from Malik. Abu Hanifa and his companions, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr also said this. They differed concerning how the waiting period (istibra') for her is to be determined, as is recorded in the books of the branches of law (kutub al-furu').

Another group said: "The married women in this verse are the chaste women." This was said by Abu al-Aliya, Ubayda al-Salmani, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ata', and Ubayda narrated it from Umar. The meaning of the verse according to them is: every woman is forbidden except what your right hands possess; that is, you own their chastity by marriage, and you own their persons by purchase. Al-Tabari narrated that a man said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Did you not see Ibn Abbas, when he was asked about this verse, and he said nothing about it?" He said: "Ibn Abbas did not know it." Al-Tabari also narrated from Mujahid that he said: "If I knew someone who could explain this verse to me, I would ride camels' livers to him." End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse, and Allah knows best, is clear with no concealment. That is: "And there are forbidden to you the married women among the women," that is, those who have husbands, whether they are Muslims or disbelievers, "except what your right hands possess of them": either by captivity, in which case they are lawful even if they had a husband, or by purchase, in which case they are lawful even if they were married. The marriage that they had is annulled by their leaving the ownership of their master who had married them to someone. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, if Allah wills, and the reliance is on the generality of the wording, not on the specific cause.

It has been read as al-muhsanat with a fatha on the sad and with a kasra on it. The fatha reading means that husbands have made them chaste. The kasra reading means that they have made their private parts chaste from other than their husbands, or that they have made their husbands chaste. His words: ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ are in the accusative of the verbal noun, meaning: Allah decreed that upon you as a decree.

Al-Zajjaj and the Kufans said: it is in the accusative (manṣūb) as an *al-ighra'* (an exhortation to hold fast to something; a construction in which an imperative is implied), meaning: "Hold fast to the Book of God," or "The Book of God upon you." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi objected that in *al-ighra'* it is not permissible to place the object before the verb. This objection applies only to the view of those who say that it is in the accusative governed by *'alaykum* ("upon you") mentioned in the verse.

It is related from 'Ubayda al-Salmani that he said: the phrase ﴿The Book of God upon you﴾ refers to God's words ﴿two, three, or four﴾. This is far-fetched. Rather, it refers to the prohibition mentioned in His words ﴿You are forbidden﴾ to the end of the verse.

God's words ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾: Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read *wa-uḥilla* ("and it was made lawful") in the passive voice. The rest read it in the active voice (*wa-aḥalla*), coordinated with the verb implied in ﴿The Book of God upon you﴾. It was also said that it is coordinated with ﴿You are forbidden﴾. The difference between the two verbs does not undermine this. The verse indicates that it is lawful for them to marry those other than those mentioned. This general statement is specified by what is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt and with her maternal aunt.

Whoever said that the prohibition of combining the mentioned relatives is derived from this verse has gone too far, since it prohibits combining two sisters. Therefore what is similar to it in meaning has the same ruling, which is combining a woman with her paternal aunt and combining a woman with her maternal aunt. Likewise, the prohibition of marrying a slave woman for one who is able to marry a free woman, as will come, specifies this generality.

God's words ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ are in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a reason (*'illa*). That is: what was forbidden was forbidden to you, and what was made lawful was made lawful to you, for the sake of your seeking, with your wealth, women whom God has made lawful to you, and not seeking with it what is unlawful, so that you would become ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾, that is, guarding yourselves against adultery. ﴿Not fornicating﴾ means not committing adultery.

*Al-sifah* ("fornication") is adultery, and it derives from *safḥ al-ma'* ("pouring out water"), that is, pouring it out and letting it flow. It is as if He, glorified is He, commanded them to seek women with their wealth in the manner of marriage, not in the manner of fornication. It was also said that God's words ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ are an apposition (badal) of *mā* in His words ﴿beyond that﴾, meaning: and it is made lawful to you to seek with your wealth. The first view is preferable. By "the wealth mentioned," He, glorified is He, means what they pay as dowries for free women and as prices for slave women.

God's words ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages﴾: *mā* is a relative pronoun containing the meaning of a conditional, and the *fa'* in His words *fa-ātūhunna* is because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of the conditional. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: give them their wages for it.

The people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and others said: the meaning is, "So for what you have benefited from and enjoyed through intercourse with women by lawful marriage, *give them their wages*," that is, their dowries. The majority said that what is meant by this verse is the marriage of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), which existed in early Islam. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: *fa-mā istamta'tum bihi minhunna ilā ajalin musammā fa-ātūhunna ujūrahunna* ("So for those whom you have enjoyed of them for a specified term, give them their wages"). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade it, as is authentically established from the hadith of 'Ali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade temporary marriage and the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar." It is in the two Sahihs and others. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Sabra ibn Ma'bad al-Juhani, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said on the day of the Conquest of Mecca: "O people, I had permitted you to enjoy women, and God has forbidden that until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever has any of them, let him release her, and do not take anything of what you have given them." In another wording in Muslim, it was at the Farewell Pilgrimage. This is the abrogating (*nāsikh*) text.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was abrogated by the verses of inheritance, since temporary marriage carries no inheritance. 'A'isha and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: its prohibition and abrogation are in the Qur'an, namely His words ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 29–30]. A woman married temporarily is not one of their wives, nor one of what their right hands possess, for it is among the nature of a wife that she inherits and is inherited from, and a woman enjoyed temporarily is not like that.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said the permissibility of temporary marriage and that it remains, not abrogated. It is also related from him that he retracted this when the abrogating text reached him. A group of the Rafida also held that it is permissible, but their views are not to be considered. Some later scholars exhausted themselves by extensively discussing this question and strengthening what those who permit it have said, but this is not the place to demonstrate the falsehood of his words.

We have extended the discussion at length, and refuted the false doubts that those who permit it have relied upon, in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let it be referred to. God's word ﴿obligatory gift﴾ (*farīḍa*) is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkad*), or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: "as something obligated."

God's words ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾: that is, an increase or decrease in the dowry, for that is permissible by mutual consent. This is according to those who say that the verse concerns the lawful marriage. As for the majority, who say it concerns temporary marriage, the meaning is mutual agreement on increasing the term of the temporary marriage or decreasing it, or on increasing what he gives her in return for the enjoyment or decreasing it.

God's words ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾: *al-ṭawl* means wealth and capacity, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and the majority of the people of knowledge.

The meaning of the verse: "Whoever among you lacks wealth and means with which he can marry free believing women, then let him marry from your believing slave girls." It is said: *ṭala* (he was able) *yaṭūlu ṭawlan* in bestowing and being capable, and so-and-so is *dhū ṭawl*, that is, possessing capacity in his wealth. *Al-ṭawl* with a *ḍamma* is the opposite of shortness.

Qatada, al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', and al-Thawri said: *al-ṭawl* is patience. The meaning of the verse according to them is that whoever desires a slave girl to the point that he cannot marry anyone else, then he may marry her if he cannot control himself and fears he might commit wrong with her, even if he has the means to marry a free woman.

Abu Hanifa said, and it is related from Malik, that *al-ṭawl* is a free woman. So whoever has a free woman under him, it is not lawful for him to marry a slave girl, and whoever does not have a free woman under him may marry a slave girl even if he is wealthy. Abu Yusuf also held this, and Ibn Jarir chose it and argued for it. The first view is the one that matches the meaning of the verse, and whatever else differs from it involves strained interpretation. So it is not permissible for a man to marry a slave girl except when he is unable to marry a free woman, due to his lacking what is needed for her marriage, such as a dowry and other things.

The words ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾ have been used as evidence that it is not permissible to marry a slave girl who is of the People of the Book. The people of the Hijaz held this view, while the people of Iraq permitted it. The *fa'* in His words ﴿so from what your right hands possess﴾ enters because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional. And His words ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾ are in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). You have learned that it is not permissible for a free man to marry a slave woman except on the condition that he cannot afford a free woman. The second condition is what God, glorified is He, mentions at the end of the verse: ﴿That is for one who fears sin (*al-'anat*) among you﴾. So it is not lawful for a poor man to marry a slave woman except if he fears for himself *al-'anat* (sin/hardship). What is meant here is a slave woman owned by another. As for a man's own slave woman, there is consensus (*ijmā'*) that it is not permissible for him to marry her, since she is under his ownership, because rights conflict and differ.

*Fatayat* is the plural of *fatāh* (young woman), and the Arabs call a male slave *fatā* and a female slave *fatāh*. In the authentic hadith: "None of you should say: 'my slave (*'abdi*) and my slave-girl (*amati*)'; rather let him say: 'my young man (*fatāya*) and my young woman (*fatātī*)'."

God's words ﴿And God knows best your faith﴾: this contains consolation for the one who marries a slave woman when the two stated conditions are met together. That is: all of you are the children of Adam, and the most honored of you before God is the most pious. So do not disdain marrying slave women in times of necessity, for the faith of some slave women may be better than the faith of some free women. This clause is parenthetical (*i'tirāḍiyya*).

God's words ﴿Some of you are from some others﴾ are a subject and predicate, and their meaning is that they are connected in lineage, since they are all the children of Adam, or they are connected in religion, since they are all of one community, with one Book and one Prophet. The purpose of this is to prepare the souls of the Arabs, for they used to despise the children of slave women, belittle them, and look down on them. ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families﴾, that is, with the permission of their owners, because their services belong to them, and it is not permissible for anyone other than them to benefit from anything of them except with the permission of the one who owns them.

God's words ﴿And give them their wages in a fair manner﴾: that is, pay them their dowries in what is fair according to the Shari'a. Whoever said that the slave woman has more right to her dowry than her master has used this as evidence, and Malik held this view, while the majority held that the dowry belongs to the master. He attributed it to them because paying it to them is paying it to their master, since they are his property.

God's words ﴿chaste﴾ (*muḥṣanāt*): that is, modest.

Al-Kisa'i read *muḥṣināt* with a *kasra* on the *ṣād* throughout the Qur'an, except in His words ﴿And married women from among women﴾. The rest read it with a *fatḥa* throughout the Qur'an.

God's words ﴿not fornicating﴾ (*ghayra musāfiḥāt*): that is, not publicly committing adultery.

*Al-akhdān* are close companions. *Al-khidn* and *al-khadīn* refer to one who takes a companion (*mukhādin*), that is, one who keeps company. It was also said: *dhāt al-khidn* is the one who commits adultery in secret, as opposed to the *musāfiḥa*, who openly commits adultery. It was also said: the *musāfiḥa* is the one who gives herself freely, and *dhāt al-khidn* is one who commits adultery with a single man. The Arabs used to blame public adultery but did not blame taking secret companions. Then Islam abolished all of that. God says: ﴿And do not approach immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

God's words ﴿And when they are chaste (*uḥṣinna*)﴾: 'Asim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*. The rest read it with a *ḍamma*. Here, *iḥṣān* means Islam. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Anas, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and al-Suddi. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with an interrupted chain (*isnād munqaṭi'*), and it is what al-Shafi'i stipulated, and the majority held it. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Darda', Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, and others said: it means marriage. It was related from al-Shafi'i that according to the first view, there is no *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) for a non-Muslim slave woman, and according to the second view, there is no *ḥadd* for a slave woman who has not been married.

Al-Qasim and Salim said: her *iḥṣān* is her Islam and her chastity. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the two readings differs. Whoever reads *uḥṣinna* with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza*, its meaning is marriage, and whoever reads it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, its meaning is (p-289) Islam.

Some scholars said that the *ihsan* (the state of being chastened or protected, here meaning being married) mentioned in the verse refers to marriage, but the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) still applies to a Muslim slave woman who commits fornication before she marries, based on the Sunnah. This was the view of al-Zuhri. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The apparent meaning of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires that there is no *hadd* upon a slave woman, even if she is Muslim, unless after marriage. Then the Sunnah came with her being flogged even if she is not *muhsanah* (married or chaste), and this was an additional clarification. Al-Qurtubi said: The back of a Muslim is a protected sanctuary that may not be violated except with certainty, and there is no certainty in the presence of disagreement, except for what has come in the authentic Sunnah regarding flogging. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: The most evident view, and Allah knows best, is that the meaning of *ihsan* here is marriage, because the context of the verse indicates this, where He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾ up to His words: ﴿And when they are married, if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free married women﴾. So the whole context concerns believing young women, and it is therefore determined that the meaning of His words ﴿when they are married﴾ is "when they marry," as Ibn 'Abbas and those who followed him explained. He said: Both opinions present a problem for the position of the majority, because they say that if a slave woman commits fornication, she receives fifty lashes, whether she is Muslim or non-Muslim, married or a virgin, while the implication of the verse requires that there is no *hadd* upon slave women who are not married.

Their answers to this differed. Then it was mentioned that some of them answered, and they are the majority, by giving priority to the explicit wording of the hadiths over this implied meaning. Others acted upon the implied meaning of the verse and said: If she commits fornication and is not married, there is no *hadd* upon her, but she is disciplined by beating. He said: This is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Ubayd and Dawud al-Zahiri in one narration from him, held this view. These scholars gave priority to the implied meaning of the verse over the general wording.
