Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I do not think it is other than the view of Malik." It is also one of the two narrations from Zayd ibn Thabit and Ata'.

His words: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ may mean the same as what preceded in His words: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾. It may also have another meaning, namely the permissibility of what has passed, that if the combining occurred in the Jahiliyyah the marriage was valid, and if it occurred in Islam one was given the choice between the two sisters. The correct interpretation is the first possibility.

His words: ﴿And the married women among the women﴾ are coordinated upon the prohibited persons mentioned. The root of tahassun is protection (al-tamannu'), and from it is His words: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya': 80], meaning to protect you. From it also comes hisan (with a kasra on the ha') for a horse, because it protects its rider from destruction. And hasan (with a fatha on the ha') means a chaste woman, because she protects herself. From it is the verse of Hassan:

"A chaste and dignified woman, who is not suspected of any doubtful act, and who in the morning is hungry from the flesh of the heedless."

The verbal noun is hasana (with a fatha). Here "the married women" means women who have husbands.

Ihsan occurs in the Qur'an with several meanings. This is one of them. The second refers to a free woman, as in His words: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and His words: ﴿and the chaste women from among the believers, and the chaste women from among those given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. The third refers to a chaste woman, as in His words: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25; al-Ma'ida: 5]. The fourth refers to a Muslim woman, as in His words: ﴿And when they are chaste (uhsinna)﴾.

The people of knowledge differed in the interpretation of this verse, namely His words: ﴿And the married women among the women, except what your right hands possess.﴾ Ibn Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Qilaba, Makhul, and al-Zuhri said: "The meaning of the married women here is specifically the captured women who have husbands. That is: they are forbidden to you, except what your right hands possess by capture from the land of war, for those are lawful even if they have a husband." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, that is, captivity cuts the marital bond. It was also said by Ibn Wahb and Ibn Abd al-Hakam, who narrated it from Malik. Abu Hanifa and his companions, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr also said this. They differed concerning how the waiting period (istibra') for her is to be determined, as is recorded in the books of the branches of law (kutub al-furu').

Another group said: "The married women in this verse are the chaste women." This was said by Abu al-Aliya, Ubayda al-Salmani, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ata', and Ubayda narrated it from Umar. The meaning of the verse according to them is: every woman is forbidden except what your right hands possess; that is, you own their chastity by marriage, and you own their persons by purchase. Al-Tabari narrated that a man said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Did you not see Ibn Abbas, when he was asked about this verse, and he said nothing about it?" He said: "Ibn Abbas did not know it." Al-Tabari also narrated from Mujahid that he said: "If I knew someone who could explain this verse to me, I would ride camels' livers to him." End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse, and Allah knows best, is clear with no concealment. That is: "And there are forbidden to you the married women among the women," that is, those who have husbands, whether they are Muslims or disbelievers, "except what your right hands possess of them": either by captivity, in which case they are lawful even if they had a husband, or by purchase, in which case they are lawful even if they were married. The marriage that they had is annulled by their leaving the ownership of their master who had married them to someone. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, if Allah wills, and the reliance is on the generality of the wording, not on the specific cause.

It has been read as al-muhsanat with a fatha on the sad and with a kasra on it. The fatha reading means that husbands have made them chaste. The kasra reading means that they have made their private parts chaste from other than their husbands, or that they have made their husbands chaste. His words: ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ are in the accusative of the verbal noun, meaning: Allah decreed that upon you as a decree.

Al-Zajjaj and the Kufans said: it is in the accusative (manṣūb) as an *al-ighra'* (an exhortation to hold fast to something; a construction in which an imperative is implied), meaning: "Hold fast to the Book of God," or "The Book of God upon you." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi objected that in *al-ighra'* it is not permissible to place the object before the verb. This objection applies only to the view of those who say that it is in the accusative governed by *'alaykum* ("upon you") mentioned in the verse.

It is related from 'Ubayda al-Salmani that he said: the phrase ﴿The Book of God upon you﴾ refers to God's words ﴿two, three, or four﴾. This is far-fetched. Rather, it refers to the prohibition mentioned in His words ﴿You are forbidden﴾ to the end of the verse.

God's words ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾: Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read *wa-uḥilla* ("and it was made lawful") in the passive voice. The rest read it in the active voice (*wa-aḥalla*), coordinated with the verb implied in ﴿The Book of God upon you﴾. It was also said that it is coordinated with ﴿You are forbidden﴾. The difference between the two verbs does not undermine this. The verse indicates that it is lawful for them to marry those other than those mentioned. This general statement is specified by what is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt and with her maternal aunt.

Whoever said that the prohibition of combining the mentioned relatives is derived from this verse has gone too far, since it prohibits combining two sisters. Therefore what is similar to it in meaning has the same ruling, which is combining a woman with her paternal aunt and combining a woman with her maternal aunt. Likewise, the prohibition of marrying a slave woman for one who is able to marry a free woman, as will come, specifies this generality.

God's words ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ are in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a reason (*'illa*). That is: what was forbidden was forbidden to you, and what was made lawful was made lawful to you, for the sake of your seeking, with your wealth, women whom God has made lawful to you, and not seeking with it what is unlawful, so that you would become ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾, that is, guarding yourselves against adultery. ﴿Not fornicating﴾ means not committing adultery.

*Al-sifah* ("fornication") is adultery, and it derives from *safḥ al-ma'* ("pouring out water"), that is, pouring it out and letting it flow. It is as if He, glorified is He, commanded them to seek women with their wealth in the manner of marriage, not in the manner of fornication. It was also said that God's words ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ are an apposition (badal) of *mā* in His words ﴿beyond that﴾, meaning: and it is made lawful to you to seek with your wealth. The first view is preferable. By "the wealth mentioned," He, glorified is He, means what they pay as dowries for free women and as prices for slave women.

God's words ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages﴾: *mā* is a relative pronoun containing the meaning of a conditional, and the *fa'* in His words *fa-ātūhunna* is because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of the conditional. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: give them their wages for it.

The people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and others said: the meaning is, "So for what you have benefited from and enjoyed through intercourse with women by lawful marriage, *give them their wages*," that is, their dowries. The majority said that what is meant by this verse is the marriage of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), which existed in early Islam. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: *fa-mā istamta'tum bihi minhunna ilā ajalin musammā fa-ātūhunna ujūrahunna* ("So for those whom you have enjoyed of them for a specified term, give them their wages"). Then the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade it, as is authentically established from the hadith of 'Ali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade temporary marriage and the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar." It is in the two Sahihs and others. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Sabra ibn Ma'bad al-Juhani, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said on the day of the Conquest of Mecca: "O people, I had permitted you to enjoy women, and God has forbidden that until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever has any of them, let him release her, and do not take anything of what you have given them." In another wording in Muslim, it was at the Farewell Pilgrimage. This is the abrogating (*nāsikh*) text.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was abrogated by the verses of inheritance, since temporary marriage carries no inheritance. 'A'isha and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: its prohibition and abrogation are in the Qur'an, namely His words ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 29–30]. A woman married temporarily is not one of their wives, nor one of what their right hands possess, for it is among the nature of a wife that she inherits and is inherited from, and a woman enjoyed temporarily is not like that.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said the permissibility of temporary marriage and that it remains, not abrogated. It is also related from him that he retracted this when the abrogating text reached him. A group of the Rafida also held that it is permissible, but their views are not to be considered. Some later scholars exhausted themselves by extensively discussing this question and strengthening what those who permit it have said, but this is not the place to demonstrate the falsehood of his words.

We have extended the discussion at length, and refuted the false doubts that those who permit it have relied upon, in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let it be referred to. God's word ﴿obligatory gift﴾ (*farīḍa*) is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkad*), or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: "as something obligated."

God's words ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree upon after the obligation﴾: that is, an increase or decrease in the dowry, for that is permissible by mutual consent. This is according to those who say that the verse concerns the lawful marriage. As for the majority, who say it concerns temporary marriage, the meaning is mutual agreement on increasing the term of the temporary marriage or decreasing it, or on increasing what he gives her in return for the enjoyment or decreasing it.

God's words ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾: *al-ṭawl* means wealth and capacity, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and the majority of the people of knowledge.

The meaning of the verse: "Whoever among you lacks wealth and means with which he can marry free believing women, then let him marry from your believing slave girls." It is said: *ṭala* (he was able) *yaṭūlu ṭawlan* in bestowing and being capable, and so-and-so is *dhū ṭawl*, that is, possessing capacity in his wealth. *Al-ṭawl* with a *ḍamma* is the opposite of shortness.

Qatada, al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', and al-Thawri said: *al-ṭawl* is patience. The meaning of the verse according to them is that whoever desires a slave girl to the point that he cannot marry anyone else, then he may marry her if he cannot control himself and fears he might commit wrong with her, even if he has the means to marry a free woman.

Abu Hanifa said, and it is related from Malik, that *al-ṭawl* is a free woman. So whoever has a free woman under him, it is not lawful for him to marry a slave girl, and whoever does not have a free woman under him may marry a slave girl even if he is wealthy. Abu Yusuf also held this, and Ibn Jarir chose it and argued for it. The first view is the one that matches the meaning of the verse, and whatever else differs from it involves strained interpretation. So it is not permissible for a man to marry a slave girl except when he is unable to marry a free woman, due to his lacking what is needed for her marriage, such as a dowry and other things.

The words ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾ have been used as evidence that it is not permissible to marry a slave girl who is of the People of the Book. The people of the Hijaz held this view, while the people of Iraq permitted it. The *fa'* in His words ﴿so from what your right hands possess﴾ enters because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional. And His words ﴿from your believing slave girls﴾ are in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). You have learned that it is not permissible for a free man to marry a slave woman except on the condition that he cannot afford a free woman. The second condition is what God, glorified is He, mentions at the end of the verse: ﴿That is for one who fears sin (*al-'anat*) among you﴾. So it is not lawful for a poor man to marry a slave woman except if he fears for himself *al-'anat* (sin/hardship). What is meant here is a slave woman owned by another. As for a man's own slave woman, there is consensus (*ijmā'*) that it is not permissible for him to marry her, since she is under his ownership, because rights conflict and differ.

*Fatayat* is the plural of *fatāh* (young woman), and the Arabs call a male slave *fatā* and a female slave *fatāh*. In the authentic hadith: "None of you should say: 'my slave (*'abdi*) and my slave-girl (*amati*)'; rather let him say: 'my young man (*fatāya*) and my young woman (*fatātī*)'."

God's words ﴿And God knows best your faith﴾: this contains consolation for the one who marries a slave woman when the two stated conditions are met together. That is: all of you are the children of Adam, and the most honored of you before God is the most pious. So do not disdain marrying slave women in times of necessity, for the faith of some slave women may be better than the faith of some free women. This clause is parenthetical (*i'tirāḍiyya*).

God's words ﴿Some of you are from some others﴾ are a subject and predicate, and their meaning is that they are connected in lineage, since they are all the children of Adam, or they are connected in religion, since they are all of one community, with one Book and one Prophet. The purpose of this is to prepare the souls of the Arabs, for they used to despise the children of slave women, belittle them, and look down on them. ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families﴾, that is, with the permission of their owners, because their services belong to them, and it is not permissible for anyone other than them to benefit from anything of them except with the permission of the one who owns them.

God's words ﴿And give them their wages in a fair manner﴾: that is, pay them their dowries in what is fair according to the Shari'a. Whoever said that the slave woman has more right to her dowry than her master has used this as evidence, and Malik held this view, while the majority held that the dowry belongs to the master. He attributed it to them because paying it to them is paying it to their master, since they are his property.

God's words ﴿chaste﴾ (*muḥṣanāt*): that is, modest.

Al-Kisa'i read *muḥṣināt* with a *kasra* on the *ṣād* throughout the Qur'an, except in His words ﴿And married women from among women﴾. The rest read it with a *fatḥa* throughout the Qur'an.

God's words ﴿not fornicating﴾ (*ghayra musāfiḥāt*): that is, not publicly committing adultery.

*Al-akhdān* are close companions. *Al-khidn* and *al-khadīn* refer to one who takes a companion (*mukhādin*), that is, one who keeps company. It was also said: *dhāt al-khidn* is the one who commits adultery in secret, as opposed to the *musāfiḥa*, who openly commits adultery. It was also said: the *musāfiḥa* is the one who gives herself freely, and *dhāt al-khidn* is one who commits adultery with a single man. The Arabs used to blame public adultery but did not blame taking secret companions. Then Islam abolished all of that. God says: ﴿And do not approach immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

God's words ﴿And when they are chaste (*uḥṣinna*)﴾: 'Asim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*. The rest read it with a *ḍamma*. Here, *iḥṣān* means Islam. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Anas, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and al-Suddi. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with an interrupted chain (*isnād munqaṭi'*), and it is what al-Shafi'i stipulated, and the majority held it. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Darda', Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, and others said: it means marriage. It was related from al-Shafi'i that according to the first view, there is no *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) for a non-Muslim slave woman, and according to the second view, there is no *ḥadd* for a slave woman who has not been married.

Al-Qasim and Salim said: her *iḥṣān* is her Islam and her chastity. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the two readings differs. Whoever reads *uḥṣinna* with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza*, its meaning is marriage, and whoever reads it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, its meaning is (p-289) Islam.

Some scholars said that the *ihsan* (the state of being chastened or protected, here meaning being married) mentioned in the verse refers to marriage, but the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) still applies to a Muslim slave woman who commits fornication before she marries, based on the Sunnah. This was the view of al-Zuhri. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The apparent meaning of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires that there is no *hadd* upon a slave woman, even if she is Muslim, unless after marriage. Then the Sunnah came with her being flogged even if she is not *muhsanah* (married or chaste), and this was an additional clarification. Al-Qurtubi said: The back of a Muslim is a protected sanctuary that may not be violated except with certainty, and there is no certainty in the presence of disagreement, except for what has come in the authentic Sunnah regarding flogging. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: The most evident view, and Allah knows best, is that the meaning of *ihsan* here is marriage, because the context of the verse indicates this, where He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾ up to His words: ﴿And when they are married, if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free married women﴾. So the whole context concerns believing young women, and it is therefore determined that the meaning of His words ﴿when they are married﴾ is "when they marry," as Ibn 'Abbas and those who followed him explained. He said: Both opinions present a problem for the position of the majority, because they say that if a slave woman commits fornication, she receives fifty lashes, whether she is Muslim or non-Muslim, married or a virgin, while the implication of the verse requires that there is no *hadd* upon slave women who are not married.

Their answers to this differed. Then it was mentioned that some of them answered, and they are the majority, by giving priority to the explicit wording of the hadiths over this implied meaning. Others acted upon the implied meaning of the verse and said: If she commits fornication and is not married, there is no *hadd* upon her, but she is disciplined by beating. He said: This is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Tawus, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Ubayd and Dawud al-Zahiri in one narration from him, held this view. These scholars gave priority to the implied meaning of the verse over the general wording. They answered regarding hadiths such as that of Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Khalid in the two Sahihs and others, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, was asked about a slave woman who commits fornication and is not married, and he said: "If she commits fornication, flog her; then if she commits fornication, flog her; then if she commits fornication, flog her, then sell her even for a braided rope." They explained that the flogging here means discipline, and this is a forced interpretation. Also, it is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, say: "If the slave woman of one of you commits fornication, let him inflict the *hadd* upon her and not reproach her; then if she commits fornication again, let him inflict the *hadd* upon her." The hadith continues. In Muslim, from the hadith of 'Ali, he said: "O people, establish the *hadd* upon your slaves, whether they are married or not, for a slave woman of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, committed fornication, and he commanded me to flog her." The hadith continues. As for what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "There is no *hadd* upon a slave woman until she is married to a husband, and when she is married, then for her is half the punishment of free married women," Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Bayhaqi said: Its attribution to the Prophet is an error, and the correct version is that it is a statement of Ibn 'Abbas himself (*mawquf*).

His words: ﴿And if they commit immorality﴾. Here "immorality" (*fahishah*) means fornication. ﴿then for them is half of what is for free married women﴾, meaning free virgins, because the married woman's punishment is stoning, which cannot be divided. It was also said that "free married women" here means married women, because they are subject to flogging and stoning, and stoning cannot be divided, so for them is half of what they would receive of flogging.

By "punishment" (*'adhab*) is meant flogging here. The prescribed punishment for slave women was reduced compared to that of free women because they are weaker. It was also said: because they do not attain their desires as free women do. And it was said: because punishment is due according to the degree of blessing, as in His words: ﴿Her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. Allah, glorified be He, did not mention male slaves in this verse, but they are included with female slaves by analogy. Just as half the *hadd* applies to slave women and male slaves for fornication, so also half the *hadd* applies to them for slander and drinking.

His words: ﴿That is for one of you who fears hardship﴾, the reference is to marrying slave women. *Al-'Anat* means falling into sin, and its original linguistic sense is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, then it was used metaphorically for any hardship. ﴿But that you be patient﴾ [i.e., refrain] from marrying slave women is better for you than marrying them, meaning your patience is better for you, because marrying them leads to the enslavement of offspring and the diminishing of one's dignity.

His words: ﴿Allah wants to make clear to you﴾. The *lam* here is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*), which is interchangeable with *an*. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs interchange the *lam* of *kay* with *an*, so they use the *lam* that carries the meaning of *kay* in the place of *an* after *aradtu* (I wanted) and *amartu* (I ordered), so they say: "aradtu an taf'al" and "aradtu li-taf'al." From this is His words: ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾ [al-Saff: 8], ﴿And I have been commanded that I be just among you﴾ [al-Shura: 15], ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 71]. And from it is the verse of poetry:

*"I want to forget her memory, so it is as if*
*Layla appears to me on every path."*

Al-Zajjaj related this view and said: If the *lam* had the meaning of *an*, another *lam* would not enter upon it, as you say: "I came in order that you honor me," and then you say: "I came in order that (li-kay) you honor me." He recited:

*"I wanted, so that people may know that*
*It is the trousers of Qays, and the delegations are witnesses."*

It was also said: the *lam* is additional, to emphasize the meaning of the future, or to emphasize the will of clarification. The object of "to make clear" (*yubayyina*) is omitted, meaning: to make clear to you what has been hidden from you of good. It was also said: the object of "wants" is omitted, meaning: Allah wants this in order to make clear to you. This is the view of the Basran grammarians and is related from Sibawayh. It was also said: the *lam* itself governs the verb without the implied *an*, and it and what follows it is the object of the preceding verb, and this is similar to al-Farra's earlier view. Some Basran grammarians said: "wants" (*yuridu*) is interpreted as a verbal noun in the nominative case as the subject, like the proverb: "Hearing about al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him" (*tasma' bi-l-mu'aydi khayrun min an tarah*).

The meaning of the verse: Allah wants to make clear to you the interests of your religion, what is permitted and what is forbidden to you, and to guide you to the ways (*sunan*) of those before you, meaning their paths, who are the prophets and their followers, so that you may follow them. And that He may turn to you in mercy, meaning He wants to turn to you, so turn to Him in repentance and make up for what you have neglected through repentance; He will forgive your sins. ﴿And Allah wants to turn to you﴾ is an emphasis of what has already been understood from His earlier words: ﴿and turn to you in mercy﴾. It was also said: the first refers to guidance to acts of obedience, and the second to the performance of their causes. It was also said: the second is to explain the full benefit of His will, glorified be He, and the full harm of what those who follow desires want. The meaning of this is not merely the wanting of repentance, so that it would be a case of repetition for emphasis. It was said: this will of His, glorified be He, applies to all the rulings of the Sharia; and it was said: it applies only to marriage with slave women.

There is disagreement about identifying those who follow desires. It was said: they are fornicators. It was said: the Jews and Christians. It was said: only the Jews. It was said: the Magians, because they wanted the Muslims to follow them in marrying sisters through the father. The first view is the preferred one. Inclination (*mayl*) means deviating from the straight path. The desires here refer to what the Sharia has forbidden, but not what it has permitted. Describing the inclination as "great" is in relation to the inclination of one who commits a sin only occasionally.

His words: ﴿Allah wants to lighten your burden﴾, by what has passed of the concessions granted to you, or by everything in it that lightens for you. ﴿And man was created weak﴾, incapable, unable to master himself and restrain himself from his desires in fulfilling the duty of obligation. Therefore, from this aspect, he needs lightening. For this reason Allah, glorified be He, wills to lighten it for him.

Al-Bukhari and others related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Seven are forbidden by blood relation and seven by marriage. Then he recited: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ up to His words: ﴿and the daughters of a sister﴾. This is by blood relation. The rest of the verse is by marriage, and the seventh is: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾. Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related from 'Imran ibn Husayn regarding His words: ﴿and your wives' mothers﴾, he said: they are unspecified (*mubhamah*).

These same scholars related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: they are unspecified; when a man divorces his wife before he has consummated the marriage, or she dies, her mother is not permitted to him. These same scholars, except al-Bayhaqi, related from 'Ali concerning a man who marries a woman and then divorces her, or she dies before he consummates the marriage: is her mother permitted to him? He said: She is in the position of the stepdaughter (*rabibah*). These same scholars related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he used to say: if she dies while he is with her and he takes her inheritance, it is disliked for him to marry her mother; and if he divorces her before consummation, there is no harm in his marrying her mother. 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, who said regarding His words: ﴿and your wives' mothers and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾: both are meant with the condition of consummation together.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr who said: The stepdaughter and the mother are equal; there is no harm in either if he has not consummated the marriage with the woman. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related with an authentic chain from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan who said: I had a wife who died after she had borne me children, and I was grieved over her. Then 'Ali ibn Abi Talib met me and said: What is wrong with you? I said: The woman has died. 'Ali said: Does she have a daughter? I said: Yes, and she is in al-Ta'if. He said: Was she in your guardianship? I said: No. He said: Then marry her. I said: Then what about the words of Allah: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾? He said: She was not in your guardianship. We have already mentioned the view of those who said that this chain is established according to the condition of Muslim.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Entering" (*dukhul*) means intercourse. 'Abd al-Razzaq in the Musannaf, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ata' who said: We used to talk about how Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, when he married the wife of Zayd, the polytheists in Mecca spoke about it, so Allah revealed: ﴿and the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾, and ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4] was revealed, and ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40] was revealed.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ that he said: meaning in marriage. 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him regarding the verse that he said: That applies to free women; as for slaves, there is no harm. Ibn al-Mundhir related from him something similar through another route. Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan that a man asked him about two sisters in one's possession by right of ownership: may he have intercourse with both? He said: One verse permitted them and another verse forbade them, and I would not do that. So the man left him, then met a man from among the companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, whom I think was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and asked him about that. He said: If I had any authority over the matter, and I found anyone who did that, I would make him an example (*nakal*).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 23–30 (part 5 of 6):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ali that he was asked about a man who had two slave-girls who were sisters. He had had intercourse with one of them and wished to have intercourse with the other. He said: "No, not until he removes her from his ownership." It was said: "What if he marries her to his slave?" He said: "No, not until he removes her from his ownership."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about a man who combines two sister slave-girls, and he disliked it. It was said: "Allah says: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾." He said: "Your camel too is among what your right hand possesses."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi narrated through Abu Salih from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said concerning two sister slave-girls: "One verse has made them lawful and another verse has made them unlawful. I do not command or forbid, I do not make lawful or unlawful, and neither I nor the people of my household do it."

Ahmad narrated from Qays who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "Can a man have intercourse with a slave-woman and her daughter who are both his slaves?" He said: "One verse has made them lawful and another verse has made them unlawful, and I would not do it."

Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him concerning two sisters from among those in one's right hand: "One verse has made them lawful and another verse has made them unlawful."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Umar who said: "If a man has two slave-girls who are sisters, and he has had intercourse with one of them, then he should not approach the other until he removes the one he has had intercourse with from his ownership."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Muqatil ibn Sulayman who said: "Allah only said concerning the wives of fathers: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ because the Arabs used to marry the wives of their fathers. Then kinship and in-law relations were forbidden, so He did not say 'except what has already passed,' because the Arabs did not marry through kinship or in-law relations. And concerning the two sisters He said: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ because they used to combine the two of them, so He forbade combining them altogether, except what had already passed before the prohibition. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ for the intercourse with the two sisters that had occurred before the prohibition."

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent on the day of Hunayn an army to Awtas. They met an enemy and fought them, and they prevailed over them and took captives from them. Some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) seemed to be reluctant to have intercourse with them because of their husbands among the polytheists. So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And [prohibited to you are] the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾," meaning: "except what Allah has granted you as spoils."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: (p-291) ﴿And the married women among the women﴾ that he said: "Every woman who has a husband, having intercourse with her is adultery, except those who have been taken captive."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani narrated from Ali and Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words: "And the married women among the women, except those whom your right hands possess," that he said: "It is over polytheist women when they are taken captive; it becomes lawful for him." Ibn Mas'ud said: "[This applies to] polytheist women and Muslim women."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "If a slave-girl is sold while she has a husband, her master has more right to her womb."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And the married women among the women﴾ that he said: "Those who have husbands." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same from Anas ibn Malik. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And the married women﴾ that he said: "The chaste, sensible woman, from a Muslim or from the People of the Book."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning the verse that he said: "It is not lawful for him to marry more than four. Whatever is beyond four is unlawful to him, like his mother and his sister."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah concerning His words: ﴿And the married women among the women﴾ that he said: "He says: 'Marry what is good for you of women, two, three or four.' Then He forbade what He forbade of kinship and in-law relations. Then He said: ﴿And the married women among the women﴾, so He returned to the beginning of the surah and said: 'They are also unlawful, except for one who marries with a dowry, sunnah and witnesses.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubaydah who said: "Allah made four lawful to you at the beginning of the surah, and He forbade marrying every chaste woman beyond the four, except what your right hand possesses."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ihsan (chastity/protection) is of two kinds: ihsan of marriage and ihsan of chastity. Whoever reads it as 'al-muhsanat' with a kasrah on the sad, then they are the chaste ones, and whoever reads it as 'al-muhsanat' with a fathah, then they are the married ones." Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father said: "This is a munkar (rejected) hadith."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ that he said: "What is beyond this kinship." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi who said: "What is below four." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ata' who said: "What is beyond those of close kinship." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ that he said: "What your right hands possess." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the same from Ubaydah al-Salmani. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ that he said: "Not adulterers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the same from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿So give them their wages﴾ that he said: "If a man from among you marries a woman and then has intercourse with her once, her entire dowry becomes obligatory. The enjoyment (istimta') is the marriage contract itself, and that is His words: ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾ [al-Nisa': 4]."

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: "Temporary marriage (mut'ah) was at the beginning of Islam. They used to recite this verse: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages as an obligation﴾, the verse. A man would arrive in a town where he had no acquaintances, and he would marry for a period he thought sufficient to finish his need, to guard his belongings and to arrange his affairs. Until this verse was revealed: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾, and it abrogated the first. Thus temporary marriage was forbidden, and its confirmation from the Qur'an is: ﴿except from their spouses or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6]. Whatever is beyond this private part is unlawful."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, narrated that Ibn Abbas recited: "So for what you have enjoyed of them, until a specified term." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he recited it in that way.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that this verse concerns temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah). Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi. The reports about the permission of temporary marriage and then its prohibition, and whether its abrogation occurred once or twice, are mentioned in the books of hadith.

Ibn Jarir in his Tahdhib, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "What have you done? The riding camels have carried your fatwas away, and the poets have composed about them." He said: "And what did they say?" I said: They said:

"I say to the old man when his sitting has lengthened: O friend, do you have a desire for the fatwa of Ibn Abbas?
Do you have a desire for a soft-skinned girl, a comfort, who will be your abode until the people depart?"

He said: "We belong to Allah and to Him we return. No, by Allah, I did not issue a fatwa with this, nor did I intend this. I only made it lawful for the one compelled (by necessity)." In another wording: "I only made lawful from it what Allah made lawful from carrion, blood and the flesh of swine."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Hadrami that men used to set the dowry, then one of them might fall into hardship, so Allah said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you concerning what you mutually agree to after the obligation﴾. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And there is no blame upon you concerning what you mutually agree to﴾ that he said: "The consenting party is the one who pays her dowry in full, then gives her the choice."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Zayd concerning the verse that he said: "If she remits some of it for you, then it is permissible." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [the means] to marry free, believing women﴾, he said: "Whoever does not have means," ﴿to marry the chaste women﴾, he said: "The free women," ﴿then from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾, "then let him marry from the believing slave-women," ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾, meaning "chaste, not adulterers in secret or openly," ﴿nor those who take secret lovers﴾, meaning "boyfriends," ﴿And when they become chaste﴾, that is, when she marries a free man and then commits adultery, ﴿then upon them is half the punishment for free women﴾, he said: "of the lashes." ﴿That is for whoever among you fears hardship﴾, which is adultery. So none of the free men may marry a slave-woman, except if he cannot marry a free woman and fears hardship. ﴿But that you be patient﴾ concerning marrying slave-women ﴿is better for you.﴾

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [the means]﴾, meaning: "whoever does not find wealth to marry the chaste women, meaning the free women, then let him marry the believing slave-woman. Patience concerning marrying slave-women is better for you, and it is permissible." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "Among what Allah has granted this nation in ease is marrying a Christian or Jewish slave-woman, even if he is wealthy."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said: "It is not proper to marry slave-women of the People of the Book, because Allah says: ﴿from your believing young women﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Hasan that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that a slave-woman be married in addition to a free woman, or a free woman in addition to a slave-woman, and whoever finds the means to marry a free woman should not marry a slave-woman."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: "A free man should not marry more than one slave-woman." Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated the same from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil concerning His words: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your faith; you are of one another﴾ that he said: "You are brothers, some of you from others."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ that he said: "With the permission of their masters." ﴿And give them their wages﴾, he said: "Their dowries." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: "The fornicators (al-musafihat) are those who openly commit adultery, and those who take secret lovers are those who have one single lover."

He said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid what was apparent of adultery and make lawful what was hidden. So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not approach the immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ [al-An'am: 151]." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning ﴿And when they become chaste﴾: 'Their ihsan is their Islam.'"

Ali said: "Flog them." Ibn Abi Hatim said: "This is a munkar hadith." Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain contains weakness and an unnamed, unidentified narrator, and such a report cannot be a proof." Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: "The punishment of a slave who slanders a free person is forty."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him who said: "Al-anat is adultery." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And those who follow their desires wish﴾ that he said: "They are the Jews and the Christians." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And those who follow their desires wish﴾ that he said: "Adultery."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿Allah wishes to lighten for you﴾ that he said: "In the marrying of slave-women and in everything in which there is ease." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿Allah wishes to lighten for you﴾ that he said: "He granted you a concession in marrying slave-women." ﴿And man was created weak﴾ he said: "Had He not granted a concession to him in them."

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi (in al-Shu'ab) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Eight verses were revealed in Surat al-Nisa', they are better for this Ummah than everything upon which the sun rises and sets. The first of them is ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa': 26]. The second is ﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires want you to deviate with a great deviation﴾ [al-Nisa': 27]. The third is ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you, and man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa': 28]. The fourth is ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to a noble entrance﴾ [al-Nisa': 31]. The fifth is ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], the verse. The sixth is ﴿And whoever does a wrong or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], the verse. The seventh is ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48, 116], the verse. The eighth is ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them, those – He will give them their rewards﴾, and ﹙Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful to those who committed wrongs out of ignorance﹚ [al-Nisa': 152]."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verse 31:**

"Al-batil" (falsehood) is that which is not right (haqq), and its forms are many. Among falsehood are the sales transactions that the Sharia has forbidden. In the language, "tijarah" (trade) is an expression for exchange (mu'aradah). This exception is disjunctive (munqati'): that is, "but trade by mutual consent among you is permitted between you," or "but that trade by mutual consent among you be lawful for you." His saying ﴿by mutual consent﴾ is a qualifier of "trade" (tijarah): that is, existing by mutual consent. Allah, glory be to Him, specified trade over the rest of the types of exchange only because it is the most common and the most prevalent of them. "Tijarah" is also used, figuratively (majazan), for the reward of deeds from Allah, and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], and His saying: ﴿They hope for a trade that will never perish﴾ [Fatir: 29].

The scholars differed regarding "mutual consent" (taradi). One group said: its completion is that it becomes obligatory upon separation of the bodies after the contract of sale is concluded, or by one of the two saying to his companion, "Choose." As in the sound hadith: "The two parties to a sale have the option (khiyar) as long as they have not separated, or one of them says to the other, 'Choose.'"

This was the view of a group of the Companions and the Successors, and it was held by al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, Ibn 'Uyaynah, Ishaq, and others. Malik and Abu Hanifah said: the completion of the sale is that the contract is concluded verbally, whereby the option is thereby removed. They responded to the hadith with arguments that have no substance.

It has been recited as "tijarah" with a nominative (raf') vowel, taking "kana" as complete (tammah), and as "tijaratan" with an accusative (nasb) vowel, taking it as incomplete (naqisah).

His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ means: none of you, O Muslims, should kill another except for a cause established by the Sharia; or, do not kill yourselves by committing sins; or, the intended meaning is the prohibition against a person killing himself literally. There is no obstacle to applying the verse to all of these meanings. What indicates this is the argument of 'Amr ibn al-'As with it when he did not wash with cold water when he was in a state of major impurity (janabah) during the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil. The Prophet (ﷺ) endorsed his argument. It is in the Musnad of Ahmad, the Sunan of Abu Dawud, and others.

His saying: ﴿And whoever does that﴾ means: the killing specifically, or the consuming of people's wealth unjustly and the killing, transgressively and unjustly. It was said: it refers to everything that is prohibited in this surah. Ibn Jarir said: it refers to what was prohibited in the last warning, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾ [al-Nisa': 19], because every prohibition from the beginning of the surah was accompanied by a warning, except from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you﴾, for there is no warning after it except His saying: ﴿And whoever does that transgressively and unjustly﴾. "Al-'udwan" is exceeding the limit. "Al-zulm" is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It was said: the meaning of "al-'udwan" and "al-zulm" is one, and its repetition is for the purpose of emphasis, as in the words of the poet:

*"And I find her words to be lies and falsehood"* [p. 293]

Excluded by the qualifiers "transgressively" and "unjustly" is killing that is by right, such as retaliation (qisas), killing an apostate, all the legal prescribed punishments (hudud), and likewise accidental killing.

His saying: ﴿then We will drive him into the Fire﴾ is the answer to the condition: that is, We will admit him into a great fire. And that, that is, his being burned in the Fire, ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, because nothing can overpower Him. It has been recited as "nuslihi" with a fatha on the nun, which is reported from al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i, and on this recitation it is derived from "salla," and from it comes "shah musallayah" (a roasted sheep).

His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ means: if you avoid the major sins that Allah has forbidden you, ﴿We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾, that is, your sins which are minor. Interpreting "misdeeds" as minor sins here is required, because of the mention of the major sins before it, and because avoiding them is made a condition for the expiation of misdeeds.

The people of the principles of jurisprudence (usul, legal theory) have differed in establishing the meaning of "major sins" (kaba'ir), and then in their number. As for establishing its meaning, it was said: all sins are major, and only some of them are called minor in comparison to what is greater than them, just as it is said that fornication is minor in comparison to disbelief, and an unlawful kiss is minor in comparison to fornication. Something like this has been reported from al-Isfara'ini, al-Juwayni, al-Qushayri, and others. They said: the major sins whose avoidance is a cause for the expiation of misdeeds are polytheism (shirk). They based this on the recitation of one who recited "in tajtanibu kabira ma tunhawna 'anhu" (singular), and on the recitation in the plural, so the intended meaning is the categories of disbelief. They based what they said on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. They said: this verse specifies His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: a major sin is every sin that Allah concluded with a fire, or wrath, or a curse, or a punishment.

Ibn Mas'ud said: the major sins are what Allah forbade in this surah, up to thirty-three verses.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: every sin for which Allah attributed the Fire is a major sin.

A group of the people of the principles of jurisprudence said: major sins are every sin for which Allah prescribed a legal punishment (hadd) or explicitly stated a threat (wa'id) regarding it. Other things have been said which are not worth lengthening the discussion with.

As for the disagreement over their number: it was said they are seven; it was said seventy; it was said seven hundred; it was said they are not limited, but some of them are greater than others. What has been transmitted on this will come, Allah willing.

His saying: ﴿And We will admit you to an entrance﴾ means: a place of entering, which is Paradise, ﴿noble﴾, that is, good and pleasing. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and the Kufans recited "mud-khalan" with a damma on the mim. The people of Madinah recited it with a fatha on the mim. Both are nouns of place, and it is permissible for it to be a verbal noun (masdar).

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported, as al-Suyuti said with a sound chain, from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾, that he said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated); it has not been abrogated and will not be abrogated until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan regarding the verse, that he said: a man used to refrain from eating at the house of any of the people after this verse was revealed, so that verse was abrogated (nasakha) by the verse in al-Nur: ﴿Nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your houses﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and so on.

Ibn Majah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sale is only by mutual consent."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Salih and 'Ikrimah regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾, that they both said: He forbade them from killing one another.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported similar from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir reported similar from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Suddi: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾, he said: your co-religionists.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿And whoever does that transgressively and unjustly﴾, he meant: deliberately, transgressing without right. ﴿And that is easy for Allah﴾: he said: His punishment for him is easy for Allah.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj who said: I said to 'Ata': Do you see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does that transgressively and unjustly, We will drive him into the Fire﴾, is it about all of that, or about His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾? He said: rather, it is about His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Anas ibn Malik who said: What your Lord asked of you was minor: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Everything He forbade is a major sin, and the "glance" (tarfah) has been mentioned, meaning the look. Ibn Jarir reported from him who said: Everything in which Allah is disobeyed is a major sin. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him who said: Everything for which Allah promised the Fire is a major sin.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from him who said: The major sins are every sin that Allah concluded with a fire, or wrath, or a curse, or a punishment. Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr what we mentioned earlier from him.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about the major sins: "Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seventy."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that a man asked him: "Are the major sins seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven, except that there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence."

al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from him: Every sin that the servant persists in is a major sin, and whatever the servant repents of is not a major sin.

It is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins." They said: "And what are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah; killing a soul that Allah has forbidden except by right; sorcery; consuming usury; consuming the wealth of an orphan; fleeing on the day of battle; and slandering chaste, unaware, believing women."

It is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining, so he sat up and said: "Beware, and false speech and false testimony." He kept repeating it until we said, "Would that he had remained silent."

al-Bukhari and others reported from Ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The major sins are: associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, killing a soul" — Shu'bah was uncertain — "and the perjurous oath (yamin al-ghamus)."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the greatest of the major sins is that a man curses his parents." They said: "And how does a man curse his parents?" He said: "He insults the father of a man, so he insults his father, and insults his mother, so he insults his mother."

The hadiths concerning the enumeration and specification of the major sins are very numerous. Whoever wishes to become acquainted with what has been transmitted on this should refer to the book *al-Zawajir 'an Iqtiraf al-Kaba'ir*, for it has gathered and comprehensively covered it.

Know that it is necessary to qualify what is in this verse concerning the expiation of misdeeds by the mere avoidance of major sins, by what al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, that the Prophet (ﷺ) sat on the pulpit and then said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, there is no servant who prays the five prayers, fasts Ramadan, pays zakat, and avoids the seven major sins, except that the eight gates of Paradise will be opened for him on the Day of Resurrection, to the extent that they will be swinging." Then he recited: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾.

Abu 'Ubayd in his *Fada'il*, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn Mas'ud who said: Indeed, in Surah al-Nisa' there are five verses that would not please me to have the world and all that is in it in exchange for them. I know that the scholars, when they pass by them, recognize them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 31]; His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong an atom's weight﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 40]; His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 48, 116]; His saying: ﴿And if they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 64]; and His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 110].

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: "*And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others*." Tamanni (wishing, longing for something) is a kind of will (iradah) directed at the future, just as talahhuf (lamenting, grieving over what is lost) is a kind of it directed at the past. It contains a prohibition against a person wishing for what Allah has favoured another of mankind with over him. That is a kind of not being content with the portion which Allah has apportioned among His servants according to His will and His perfect wisdom. It also contains a kind of envy (hasad), which is forbidden, when it is accompanied by the desire for that blessing to be removed from the other person.

The scholars have differed over ghibtah (admiring emulation): is it permissible or not? It is that a person wishes to have a state like the state of his companion, without wishing for that state to be removed from his companion. The majority (al-jumhur) held that it is permissible, and they cited the authentic hadith: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given the Qur'an, and he stands with it through the hours of the night and the hours of the day; and a man whom Allah has given wealth, and he spends it through the hours of the night and the hours of the day." Al-Bukhari also gave it a chapter heading: "The chapter on ightibat (admiring emulation) in knowledge and judgment." The general wording of the verse requires the prohibition of wishing for that in which preference has been given, whether or not it is accompanied by what turns it into a kind of envy. What is related in the Sunnah of permissibility of that in specific matters serves as a specification (takhsis) of this generality. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, but what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

His saying: "*For men there is a share*" and so on. In it there is a specification after generalization, and a return to what the occasion of revelation of the verse contains, namely that Umm Salamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, men go out to fight, and we do not fight, nor do we engage in battle and so earn martyrdom, and we only have half of the inheritance." So the verse was revealed.

It was narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi. Something similar to this occasion has been related through various chains with differing wordings.

The meaning of the verse is that Allah has made for each of the two groups a share according to what His will and wisdom require. He expressed what is assigned to each of the two groups, men and women, by the word "share" (nasib) of what they have earned, by way of an indirect metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), likening the state of each group requiring its share to their earning it.

Qatadah said: "For men there is a share of what they have earned of reward and punishment, and likewise for women." Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is meant by that is inheritance and earning, according to this view, with the meaning we have mentioned."

His saying: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*." It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with his saying "and do not wish." The insertion of the causal clause "*For men there is a share*" and so on, between the coordinated element and that which it is coordinated with, serves to confirm what the prohibition contains. This command indicates the obligation of asking Allah, glorified is He, for His bounty, as a group of the people of knowledge have said.

His saying: "*And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and close relatives leave*." That is: We have appointed for every person heirs (mawali) who take up his inheritance. So "for each" is the second object, placed before the verb for emphasis of comprehensiveness. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it; that is, that each person should follow what Allah has allotted to him of inheritance, and not wish for what Allah has favoured another with over him. It has been said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying after it: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." It has also been said that it is the reverse, as Ibn Jarir narrated. The majority held that the abrogating text for "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*" is His, exalted is He, saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*" [al-Anfal: 75]. Mawali is the plural of mawla, which is used for the freed slave, the one who frees, the helper, the paternal cousin and the neighbour. It has been said that what is meant here is the 'asabah (male agnatic relatives), that is: and for each We have appointed 'asabah who inherit what the prescribed shares leave.

His saying: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." What is meant by them is the mawali of muwalah (contractual alliance): a man of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) would enter into a contract with a man, that is, make an alliance with him, and so he would deserve a share of his inheritance. Then this was established at the beginning of Islam by this verse, and then it was abrogated by His saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*."

The reading of the majority is "'aqadat" (عاقدت), and it is related from Hamzah that he read "'aqqadat" (عقّدت) with the qaf doubled, for intensification; that is: "and those to whom your oaths have tied the alliance," or "your oaths have tied their covenants." The estimate (taqdir) according to the reading of the majority is: "and those with whom your oaths have made a contract, give them their share," that is, what you have given them by means of the contract of alliance.

His saying: "*Men are the protectors (qawwamun) of women because Allah has favoured some of them over others*." This sentence is a new, independent sentence (mustanifah) containing an explanation of the reason by which men deserved the extra provision. It is as if it were said: how did men deserve what they deserved, of what women did not share with them? So He said: "*Men are the protectors*" and so on. What is meant is that they stand in charge by defending women, as rulers and commanders stand in charge by defending their subjects. They also provide what women need of maintenance, clothing and housing. The intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah) "qawwamun" is used to show their primacy in this matter. The ba' in "*because (bima) Allah has favoured*" is causal, and the pronoun in "*some of them over others*" refers to men and women; that is: they only deserved this excellence because Allah favoured men over women, with what He favoured them with, such as that among them are the caliphs, sultans, rulers, commanders, warriors and other matters.

His saying: "*and because (bima) they spend*." That is: and by reason of what they have spent of their wealth. "Ma" here is either verbal-masdariyyah or relative (mawsulah), and so it is in His saying "*bima fadala Allah*." "Min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah). What is meant is what they spend on the maintenance of women, and what they pay of their wealth as dowries for their wives, and likewise what they spend in jihad and what is obligatory for them in blood-money.

A group of scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of annulling a marriage when the husband is unable to maintain his wife in food and clothing. Malik, al-Shafi'i and others said this.

His saying: "*So the righteous women are devoutly obedient (qanitat), guarding in secret what Allah has guarded*." That is: the righteous women among them are devoutly obedient to Allah, performing what is obligatory upon them of the rights of Allah and the rights of their husbands. "*Guarding in secret*" means guarding what must be guarded in the absence of their husbands, of their own persons and of their husbands' property. "Ma" in "*bima hafiza Allah*" is verbal-masdariyyah; that is: by the guarding of Allah.

The meaning is: they guard the absence of their husbands by the guarding of Allah for them, His help and His making them firm. Or they guard [Allah's command] by what He has entrusted them with, namely fulfilling the trust to their husbands in the manner Allah has commanded. Or they guard [Allah] by Allah's guarding them, through what He enjoined husbands regarding them, of good companionship. "Ma" may also be relative, with a deleted returning pronoun.

Abu Ja'far read "*bima hafiza Allah*" (بما حفظ الله) with the noble name in the accusative (nasb). The meaning then is "by what they have guarded Allah," that is, they have guarded His command, or they have guarded His religion. The returning pronoun referring to them is deleted, since it is known. "Ma" in this reading is verbal-masdariyyah or relative, as in the first reading; that is, "by their guarding Allah," or "by that with which they guarded Allah."

His saying: "*And those (women) from whom you fear rebellion (nushuz)*." This is addressed to the husbands. It has been said: fear here is in its ordinary sense, a state that occurs in the heart at the occurrence of a disliked matter or at the supposition of its occurrence. It has also been said that what is meant by fear here is knowledge. Nushuz is disobedience. Its basic meaning in the language has already been explained. Ibn Faris said: "It is said: the woman rebelled (nasharat al-mar'ah): she became disobedient to her husband; and her husband rebelled against her (nashaza ba'luha 'alayha): when he struck her and was harsh to her."

"*Then admonish them*" that is: remind them of what Allah has made obligatory for them of obedience and good companionship, and encourage them and warn them. "*And abandon them in the beds*": it is said "hajarahu," meaning he distanced himself from him. The "madaji'" (beds) is the plural of madja', the place of lying down. That is: keep away from lying with them, and do not put them under what you place upon yourselves of garments during lying down. It has been said: it is that he turns his back to her when lying down. It has been said: it is a metaphor for abandoning intercourse with her. It has been said: he does not spend the night with her in the room where he lies down. "*And strike them*": a striking that is not severe (ghayr mubarrih).

The apparent wording of the Qur'anic text is that it is permissible for the husband to do all these things when he fears rebellion. It has been said that he should not abandon her except after the admonition has failed to have effect. If the admonition has an effect, he should not move on to abandonment; and if abandonment suffices, he should not move on to striking.

"*Then if they obey you*," as is obligatory, and abandon rebellion, "*then seek no means against them*," that is: do not approach them with anything they dislike, neither by word nor by deed. It has been said that the meaning is: do not burden them with loving you, for that does not fall within their choice.

"*Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great*." This is an indication to the husbands to lower the wing and be gentle to the side; that is: if you have power over them, remember Allah's power over you, for it is above every power, and Allah is watchful over you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "*And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others*": he said: a man should not wish and say, "I wish that I had the wealth and the family of so-and-so." So Allah, glorified is He, forbade that. Rather, he should ask Allah of His bounty. "*For men there is a share of what they have earned*": that is, of what the parents and close relatives leave; for the male is like the portion of two females.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that the women said: "If only our shares in the inheritance were made like the shares of the men!" And the men said: "We hope to be preferred over women with our good deeds in the Hereafter, as we were preferred over them in inheritance." The mention of the occasion of revelation has already been made.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*": he said: "It is not the goods of this world." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*": he said: "Worship; it is not of the affairs of this world."

al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ask Allah of His bounty, for Allah loves to be asked." al-Tirmidhi said: "Thus narrated Hammad ibn Waqid, and he is not a hafiz (memoriser of great learning); and Abu Nu'aym narrated it from Israil, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from a man, from the Prophet (ﷺ)." The hadith of Abu Nu'aym more closely resembles being the sounder. Thus also Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it, and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "*And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali)*": he said: "Inheritors." "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*": he said: When the Emigrants came to Madinah, the Emigrant would inherit from the Ansari to the exclusion of his blood relatives, because of the brotherhood which the Prophet (ﷺ) had established between them. Then when "*And for each We have appointed heirs*" was revealed, it was abrogated. Then He said: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract, give them their share*" — of help, of support and of counsel — though the inheritance has gone, a bequest is made for him.

Also narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas) by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, regarding ﴿And to each We have appointed heirs﴾, he said: "'Asabah (agnatic kinsmen)." ﴿And those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾: he said, "Two men would each inherit from the other, whichever of them died first. Then Allah revealed ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your allies﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 6]." He meant: except that they bequeath to their allies, with whom they had made a pact, a bequest, which is permissible for them from one-third of the estate of the deceased, and this is the kindness.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding the verse: "Before Islam, a man would make a pact with another man, saying, 'You inherit from me and I inherit from you.' The tribes would form alliances with one another. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Every alliance that existed in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), or any pact that Islam encountered, Islam only increases it in strength, and there is no pact or alliance in Islam.'" Then this was abrogated in Al-Anfal: ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another﴾."
