**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: "*And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others*." Tamanni (wishing, longing for something) is a kind of will (iradah) directed at the future, just as talahhuf (lamenting, grieving over what is lost) is a kind of it directed at the past. It contains a prohibition against a person wishing for what Allah has favoured another of mankind with over him. That is a kind of not being content with the portion which Allah has apportioned among His servants according to His will and His perfect wisdom. It also contains a kind of envy (hasad), which is forbidden, when it is accompanied by the desire for that blessing to be removed from the other person.

The scholars have differed over ghibtah (admiring emulation): is it permissible or not? It is that a person wishes to have a state like the state of his companion, without wishing for that state to be removed from his companion. The majority (al-jumhur) held that it is permissible, and they cited the authentic hadith: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given the Qur'an, and he stands with it through the hours of the night and the hours of the day; and a man whom Allah has given wealth, and he spends it through the hours of the night and the hours of the day." Al-Bukhari also gave it a chapter heading: "The chapter on ightibat (admiring emulation) in knowledge and judgment." The general wording of the verse requires the prohibition of wishing for that in which preference has been given, whether or not it is accompanied by what turns it into a kind of envy. What is related in the Sunnah of permissibility of that in specific matters serves as a specification (takhsis) of this generality. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, but what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

His saying: "*For men there is a share*" and so on. In it there is a specification after generalization, and a return to what the occasion of revelation of the verse contains, namely that Umm Salamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, men go out to fight, and we do not fight, nor do we engage in battle and so earn martyrdom, and we only have half of the inheritance." So the verse was revealed.

It was narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi. Something similar to this occasion has been related through various chains with differing wordings.

The meaning of the verse is that Allah has made for each of the two groups a share according to what His will and wisdom require. He expressed what is assigned to each of the two groups, men and women, by the word "share" (nasib) of what they have earned, by way of an indirect metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), likening the state of each group requiring its share to their earning it.

Qatadah said: "For men there is a share of what they have earned of reward and punishment, and likewise for women." Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is meant by that is inheritance and earning, according to this view, with the meaning we have mentioned."

His saying: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*." It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with his saying "and do not wish." The insertion of the causal clause "*For men there is a share*" and so on, between the coordinated element and that which it is coordinated with, serves to confirm what the prohibition contains. This command indicates the obligation of asking Allah, glorified is He, for His bounty, as a group of the people of knowledge have said.

His saying: "*And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and close relatives leave*." That is: We have appointed for every person heirs (mawali) who take up his inheritance. So "for each" is the second object, placed before the verb for emphasis of comprehensiveness. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it; that is, that each person should follow what Allah has allotted to him of inheritance, and not wish for what Allah has favoured another with over him. It has been said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying after it: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." It has also been said that it is the reverse, as Ibn Jarir narrated. The majority held that the abrogating text for "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*" is His, exalted is He, saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*" [al-Anfal: 75]. Mawali is the plural of mawla, which is used for the freed slave, the one who frees, the helper, the paternal cousin and the neighbour. It has been said that what is meant here is the 'asabah (male agnatic relatives), that is: and for each We have appointed 'asabah who inherit what the prescribed shares leave.

His saying: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." What is meant by them is the mawali of muwalah (contractual alliance): a man of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) would enter into a contract with a man, that is, make an alliance with him, and so he would deserve a share of his inheritance. Then this was established at the beginning of Islam by this verse, and then it was abrogated by His saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*."

The reading of the majority is "'aqadat" (عاقدت), and it is related from Hamzah that he read "'aqqadat" (عقّدت) with the qaf doubled, for intensification; that is: "and those to whom your oaths have tied the alliance," or "your oaths have tied their covenants." The estimate (taqdir) according to the reading of the majority is: "and those with whom your oaths have made a contract, give them their share," that is, what you have given them by means of the contract of alliance.

His saying: "*Men are the protectors (qawwamun) of women because Allah has favoured some of them over others*." This sentence is a new, independent sentence (mustanifah) containing an explanation of the reason by which men deserved the extra provision. It is as if it were said: how did men deserve what they deserved, of what women did not share with them? So He said: "*Men are the protectors*" and so on. What is meant is that they stand in charge by defending women, as rulers and commanders stand in charge by defending their subjects. They also provide what women need of maintenance, clothing and housing. The intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah) "qawwamun" is used to show their primacy in this matter. The ba' in "*because (bima) Allah has favoured*" is causal, and the pronoun in "*some of them over others*" refers to men and women; that is: they only deserved this excellence because Allah favoured men over women, with what He favoured them with, such as that among them are the caliphs, sultans, rulers, commanders, warriors and other matters.

His saying: "*and because (bima) they spend*." That is: and by reason of what they have spent of their wealth. "Ma" here is either verbal-masdariyyah or relative (mawsulah), and so it is in His saying "*bima fadala Allah*." "Min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah). What is meant is what they spend on the maintenance of women, and what they pay of their wealth as dowries for their wives, and likewise what they spend in jihad and what is obligatory for them in blood-money.

A group of scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of annulling a marriage when the husband is unable to maintain his wife in food and clothing. Malik, al-Shafi'i and others said this.

His saying: "*So the righteous women are devoutly obedient (qanitat), guarding in secret what Allah has guarded*." That is: the righteous women among them are devoutly obedient to Allah, performing what is obligatory upon them of the rights of Allah and the rights of their husbands. "*Guarding in secret*" means guarding what must be guarded in the absence of their husbands, of their own persons and of their husbands' property. "Ma" in "*bima hafiza Allah*" is verbal-masdariyyah; that is: by the guarding of Allah.

The meaning is: they guard the absence of their husbands by the guarding of Allah for them, His help and His making them firm. Or they guard [Allah's command] by what He has entrusted them with, namely fulfilling the trust to their husbands in the manner Allah has commanded. Or they guard [Allah] by Allah's guarding them, through what He enjoined husbands regarding them, of good companionship. "Ma" may also be relative, with a deleted returning pronoun.

Abu Ja'far read "*bima hafiza Allah*" (بما حفظ الله) with the noble name in the accusative (nasb). The meaning then is "by what they have guarded Allah," that is, they have guarded His command, or they have guarded His religion. The returning pronoun referring to them is deleted, since it is known. "Ma" in this reading is verbal-masdariyyah or relative, as in the first reading; that is, "by their guarding Allah," or "by that with which they guarded Allah."

His saying: "*And those (women) from whom you fear rebellion (nushuz)*." This is addressed to the husbands. It has been said: fear here is in its ordinary sense, a state that occurs in the heart at the occurrence of a disliked matter or at the supposition of its occurrence. It has also been said that what is meant by fear here is knowledge. Nushuz is disobedience. Its basic meaning in the language has already been explained. Ibn Faris said: "It is said: the woman rebelled (nasharat al-mar'ah): she became disobedient to her husband; and her husband rebelled against her (nashaza ba'luha 'alayha): when he struck her and was harsh to her."

"*Then admonish them*" that is: remind them of what Allah has made obligatory for them of obedience and good companionship, and encourage them and warn them. "*And abandon them in the beds*": it is said "hajarahu," meaning he distanced himself from him. The "madaji'" (beds) is the plural of madja', the place of lying down. That is: keep away from lying with them, and do not put them under what you place upon yourselves of garments during lying down. It has been said: it is that he turns his back to her when lying down. It has been said: it is a metaphor for abandoning intercourse with her. It has been said: he does not spend the night with her in the room where he lies down. "*And strike them*": a striking that is not severe (ghayr mubarrih).

The apparent wording of the Qur'anic text is that it is permissible for the husband to do all these things when he fears rebellion. It has been said that he should not abandon her except after the admonition has failed to have effect. If the admonition has an effect, he should not move on to abandonment; and if abandonment suffices, he should not move on to striking.

"*Then if they obey you*," as is obligatory, and abandon rebellion, "*then seek no means against them*," that is: do not approach them with anything they dislike, neither by word nor by deed. It has been said that the meaning is: do not burden them with loving you, for that does not fall within their choice.

"*Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great*." This is an indication to the husbands to lower the wing and be gentle to the side; that is: if you have power over them, remember Allah's power over you, for it is above every power, and Allah is watchful over you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "*And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others*": he said: a man should not wish and say, "I wish that I had the wealth and the family of so-and-so." So Allah, glorified is He, forbade that. Rather, he should ask Allah of His bounty. "*For men there is a share of what they have earned*": that is, of what the parents and close relatives leave; for the male is like the portion of two females.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that the women said: "If only our shares in the inheritance were made like the shares of the men!" This command indicates the obligation of asking Allah, glorified is He, for His bounty, as a group of the people of knowledge have said.

His saying: "*And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and close relatives leave*." That is: We have appointed for every person heirs (mawali) who take up his inheritance. So "for each" is the second object, placed before the verb for emphasis of comprehensiveness. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it; that is, that each person should follow what Allah has allotted to him of inheritance, and not wish for what Allah has favoured another with over him. It has been said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying after it: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." It has also been said that it is the reverse, as Ibn Jarir narrated. The majority held that the abrogating text for "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*" is His, exalted is He, saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*" [al-Anfal: 75]. Mawali is the plural of mawla, which is used for the freed slave, the one who frees, the helper, the paternal cousin and the neighbour. It has been said that what is meant here is the 'asabah (male agnatic relatives), that is: and for each We have appointed 'asabah who inherit what the prescribed shares leave.

His saying: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*." What is meant by them is the mawali of muwalah (contractual alliance): a man of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) would enter into a contract with a man, that is, make an alliance with him, and so he would deserve a share of his inheritance. Then this was established at the beginning of Islam by this verse, and then it was abrogated by His saying: "*But those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another*."

The reading of the majority is "'aqadat" (عاقدت), and it is related from Hamzah that he read "'aqqadat" (عقّدت) with the qaf doubled, for intensification; that is: "and those to whom your oaths have tied the alliance," or "your oaths have tied their covenants." The estimate (taqdir) according to the reading of the majority is: "and those with whom your oaths have made a contract, give them their share," that is, what you have given them by means of the contract of alliance.

His saying: "*Men are the protectors (qawwamun) of women because Allah has favoured some of them over others*." This sentence is a new, independent sentence (mustanifah) containing an explanation of the reason by which men deserved the extra provision. It is as if it were said: how did men deserve what they deserved, of what women did not share with them? So He said: "*Men are the protectors*" and so on. What is meant is that they stand in charge by defending women, as rulers and commanders stand in charge by defending their subjects. They also provide what women need of maintenance, clothing and housing. The intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah) "qawwamun" is used to show their primacy in this matter. The ba' in "*because (bima) Allah has favoured*" is causal, and the pronoun in "*some of them over others*" refers to men and women; that is: they only deserved this excellence because Allah favoured men over women, with what He favoured them with, such as that among them are the caliphs, sultans, rulers, commanders, warriors and other matters.

His saying: "*and because (bima) they spend*." That is: and by reason of what they have spent of their wealth. "Ma" here is either verbal-masdariyyah or relative (mawsulah), and so it is in His saying "*bima fadala Allah*." "Min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah). What is meant is what they spend on the maintenance of women, and what they pay of their wealth as dowries for their wives, and likewise what they spend in jihad and what is obligatory for them in blood-money.

A group of scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of annulling a marriage when the husband is unable to maintain his wife in food and clothing. Malik, al-Shafi'i and others said this.

His saying: "*So the righteous women are devoutly obedient (qanitat), guarding in secret what Allah has guarded*." That is: the righteous women among them are devoutly obedient to Allah, performing what is obligatory upon them of the rights of Allah and the rights of their husbands. "*Guarding in secret*" means guarding what must be guarded in the absence of their husbands, of their own persons and of their husbands' property. "Ma" in "*bima hafiza Allah*" is verbal-masdariyyah; that is: by the guarding of Allah.

The meaning is: they guard the absence of their husbands by the guarding of Allah for them, His help and His making them firm. Or they guard [Allah's command] by what He has entrusted them with, namely fulfilling the trust to their husbands in the manner Allah has commanded. Or they guard [Allah] by Allah's guarding them, through what He enjoined husbands regarding them, of good companionship. "Ma" may also be relative, with a deleted returning pronoun.

Abu Ja'far read "*bima hafiza Allah*" (بما حفظ الله) with the noble name in the accusative (nasb). The meaning then is "by what they have guarded Allah," that is, they have guarded His command, or they have guarded His religion. The returning pronoun referring to them is deleted, since it is known. "Ma" in this reading is verbal-masdariyyah or relative, as in the first reading; that is, "by their guarding Allah," or "by that with which they guarded Allah."

His saying: "*And those (women) from whom you fear rebellion (nushuz)*." This is addressed to the husbands. It has been said: fear here is in its ordinary sense, a state that occurs in the heart at the occurrence of a disliked matter or at the supposition of its occurrence. It has also been said that what is meant by fear here is knowledge. Nushuz is disobedience. Its basic meaning in the language has already been explained. Ibn Faris said: "It is said: the woman rebelled (nasharat al-mar'ah): she became disobedient to her husband; and her husband rebelled against her (nashaza ba'luha 'alayha): when he struck her and was harsh to her."

"*Then admonish them*" that is: remind them of what Allah has made obligatory for them of obedience and good companionship, and encourage them and warn them. "*And abandon them in the beds*": it is said "hajarahu," meaning he distanced himself from him. The "madaji'" (beds) is the plural of madja', the place of lying down. That is: keep away from lying with them, and do not put them under what you place upon yourselves of garments during lying down. It has been said: it is that he turns his back to her when lying down. It has been said: it is a metaphor for abandoning intercourse with her. It has been said: he does not spend the night with her in the room where he lies down. "*And strike them*": a striking that is not severe (ghayr mubarrih).

The apparent wording of the Qur'anic text is that it is permissible for the husband to do all these things when he fears rebellion. It has been said that he should not abandon her except after the admonition has failed to have effect. If the admonition has an effect, he should not move on to abandonment; and if abandonment suffices, he should not move on to striking.

"*Then if they obey you*," as is obligatory, and abandon rebellion, "*then seek no means against them*," that is: do not approach them with anything they dislike, neither by word nor by deed. It has been said that the meaning is: do not burden them with loving you, for that does not fall within their choice.

"*Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great*." This is an indication to the husbands to lower the wing and be gentle to the side; that is: if you have power over them, remember Allah's power over you, for it is above every power, and Allah is watchful over you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "*And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others*": he said: a man should not wish and say, "I wish that I had the wealth and the family of so-and-so." So Allah, glorified is He, forbade that. Rather, he should ask Allah of His bounty. "*For men there is a share of what they have earned*": that is, of what the parents and close relatives leave; for the male is like the portion of two females.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that the women said: "If only our shares in the inheritance were made like the shares of the men!" And the men said: "We hope to be preferred over women with our good deeds in the Hereafter, as we were preferred over them in inheritance." The mention of the occasion of revelation has already been made.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*": he said: "It is not the goods of this world." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "*And ask Allah of His bounty*": he said: "Worship; it is not of the affairs of this world."

al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ask Allah of His bounty, for Allah loves to be asked." al-Tirmidhi said: "Thus narrated Hammad ibn Waqid, and he is not a hafiz (memoriser of great learning); and Abu Nu'aym narrated it from Israil, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from a man, from the Prophet (ﷺ)." The hadith of Abu Nu'aym more closely resembles being the sounder. Thus also Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it, and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "*And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali)*": he said: "Inheritors." "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract*": he said: When the Emigrants came to Madinah, the Emigrant would inherit from the Ansari to the exclusion of his blood relatives, because of the brotherhood which the Prophet (ﷺ) had established between them. Then when "*And for each We have appointed heirs*" was revealed, it was abrogated. Then He said: "*And those with whom your oaths have made a contract, give them their share*" — of help, of support and of counsel — though the inheritance has gone, a bequest is made for him.

Also narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas) by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, regarding ﴿And to each We have appointed heirs﴾, he said: "'Asabah (agnatic kinsmen)." ﴿And those with whom your oaths have bound you﴾: he said, "Two men would each inherit from the other, whichever of them died first. Then Allah revealed ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your allies﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 6]." He meant: except that they bequeath to their allies, with whom they had made a pact, a bequest, which is permissible for them from one-third of the estate of the deceased, and this is the kindness.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding the verse: "Before Islam, a man would make a pact with another man, saying, 'You inherit from me and I inherit from you.' The tribes would form alliances with one another. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Every alliance that existed in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), or any pact that Islam encountered, Islam only increases it in strength, and there is no pact or alliance in Islam.'" Thus this verse abrogated it: ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another﴾ [Al-Anfal: 75].

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi also narrated from him regarding the verse: "A man would form an alliance with a man with whom he had no kinship, so that one of them would inherit from the other. Then this was abrogated in Al-Anfal: ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another﴾."

Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan: "A man from the Ansar slapped his wife, and she came seeking retribution (qisas, legal retaliation). The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered qisas between them. Then there was revealed ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell silent, and the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ and so on. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'We wanted one thing, and Allah wanted something else.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated similarly from 'Ali.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾: meaning "rulers (umara')." They must obey him in what Allah has commanded her to obey Him in, and her obedience to him is to be good to his family and to guard his property. ﴿Because Allah has made some of them to excel others﴾: He preferred him over them through his provision and his effort. ﴿So righteous women are devoutly obedient﴾: he said, "obedient." ﴿Guarding in secret what Allah has guarded﴾: meaning, when they are like this, then be good to them.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿guarding in secret﴾: "They guard in secret what Allah has entrusted to them of His right, and they guard the secrets of their husbands."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid: "﴿Guarding in secret﴾ for the husbands."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi: "She guards her husband's property and her chastity until he returns, as Allah has commanded her."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And those from whom you fear disobedience (nushuz)﴾: "That woman rebels and makes light of her husband's right and does not obey his command. So Allah commanded him to admonish her and remind her of Allah and to magnify his right over her. If she accepts, well and good; otherwise he should forsake her in the bed and not speak to her, without divorcing her; and this is a severe measure for her. If she returns, well and good; otherwise he may strike her with a light blow that is not severe, and not break any bone for her or wound her."

﴿And if they obey you, then do not seek a way against them﴾: he means, if she obeys you, do not seek pretexts against her.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And forsake them in the beds﴾: "He does not have intercourse with her." 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "He forsakes her with his tongue, speaks to her harshly, but does not abandon intercourse." 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated similarly from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ata': he asked Ibn 'Abbas about a non-severe striking, and he said: "With a siwak (tooth-stick) or the like."

At-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas that he attended the Farewell Sermon with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in it the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware! Treat women well, for they are but prisoners (awan) with you; you have no control over them except that, unless they commit a clear indecency. If they do, then forsake them in their beds and strike them with a blow that is not severe. ﴿And if they obey you, then do not seek a way against them﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Zam'ah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Does one of you strike his wife as he strikes a slave, and then lie with her at the end of the day?"

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah 4, verse 35:

The meaning of shiqaq (discord, enmity) has already been explained in al-Baqarah. Its root sense is that each of them takes a side (shiqq) other than the side of his companion; that is, a direction other than his direction. The noun shiqaq is here construed with the adverbial expression (zarf) bayna-hima, treating it as if it were a direct object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it is the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33], and in the line of verse: "O thief of the night, (you who have struck) the people of the house."

The address is to the rulers and judges. The pronoun in His saying "bayna-hima" refers to the spouses, since what indicates them has already been mentioned, namely the mention of "men" and "women." So "send an arbiter (hakam) to the two spouses who will judge between them," chosen from those who are fit for this task in intellect, religion and fairness.

Allah, glorified is He, specified that the two arbiters should be from the families of the spouses, because they are the most knowledgeable of their circumstances. If no one from the families of the spouses is fit to judge between them, then the two arbiters may be from others. This applies when their matter is unclear and it has not become evident which of them is the wrongdoer. But if the wrongdoer is known, then the right is taken from him for his companion. The two arbiters must strive to reconcile the couple to the best of their ability. If they are able to do so, they act accordingly. If they are unable to reconcile their situation and they see separation between them as the course, it is permissible for them to do so without an order from the ruler of the land and without the spouses delegating separation to them. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i and Ishaq, and it is related from Uthman, Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Kathir reports it from the majority (al-jumhur). They say: because Allah said, ﴿send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family﴾, and this is an explicit statement from Allah, glorified is He, that the two are judges, not agents, nor witnesses.

The Kufans, 'Ata', Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i said: separation belongs to the imam or the ruler of the land, not to the two arbiters, unless the spouses delegate them or the imam and ruler order them, because they are two emissaries and witnesses, so separation is not theirs to decide. What points to this is His saying: if the two arbiters (yuridu, i.e. they) intend reconciliation between the spouses, ﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾, since it mentions only reconciliation and not separation. The meaning of ﴿if they intend reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾ is: Allah will cause agreement between the spouses so that they return to affection and good companionship.

The meaning of "intention" (iradah) is the sincerity of their intention for the improvement of the spouses' situation. It is also said that the pronoun in ﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾ refers to the two arbiters, as in ﴿if they intend reconciliation﴾, meaning: Allah will bring harmony between the two arbiters in the unity of their word and the attainment of their aim. It is also said that both pronouns refer to the spouses, meaning: if they intend to remedy the discord between them, Allah will cause affection and accord to arise between them. And if the two arbiters disagree, their ruling is not binding, and their word is not obligatory to accept without dispute.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿and if you fear a breach between the two﴾, he said: "This concerns the man and the woman when the relationship between them has deteriorated. Allah commanded you to send a righteous man from the man's family and a man like him from the woman's family, and they look at which of them is the wrongdoer. If the man is the wrongdoer, they keep his wife away from him and compel him to provide maintenance; if the woman is the wrongdoer, they compel her to return to her husband and withhold maintenance from her. If their opinion agrees on separating or reuniting them, their decision is permitted. If they decide to reunite them, and one spouse is pleased while the other dislikes it, and then one of them dies, the one who was pleased inherits from the one who disliked it, but the one who disliked does not inherit from the one who was pleased." ﴿If they intend reconciliation﴾, he said: "They are the two arbiters." ﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾, and likewise every reconciler, Allah guides him to the truth and the right.

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, 'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani concerning this verse, that he said: "A man and a woman came to Ali with a large group of people. Ali ordered them, and they sent an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family. Then Ali said to the two arbiters: 'Do you know what is incumbent upon you? If you see that you should reunite them, then reunite them; and if you see that you should separate them, then separate them.' The woman said: 'I am content with the Book of Allah, with what is upon me and what is mine in it.' The man said: 'As for separation, no.' Ali said: 'You have lied, by Allah, until you acknowledge what she has acknowledged.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I and Mu'awiyah were sent as two arbiters. We were told: 'If you see that you should reunite them, reunite them; and if you see that you should separate them, separate them.' And it was Uthman who sent them."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Hasan, who said: "The two arbiters are only sent to reconcile and to bear witness against the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing. As for separation, it is not in their hands." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of this from Qatadah. Al-Bayhaqi related from Ali, who said: "If one of the two arbiters rules and the other does not rule, his ruling is nothing until the two of them agree."

The meaning of worship (ʿibadah) has already been explained. "Shay'an" (anything) may be the object: that is, "do not associate with Him anything among things," without distinguishing between the living and the dead, inanimate objects and animals. Or it may be a verbal noun (maṣdar): that is, "do not commit any association (shirk) with Him," without distinguishing between major and minor shirk, or between open and hidden shirk. His saying "iḥsānan" (good treatment) is a verbal noun for a deleted verb: that is, "Be good to your parents, with goodness."

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it in the nominative (iḥsānun). The mention of good treatment toward the two parents after the command to worship Allah and the prohibition of associating partners with Him indicates the greatness of their right. Similar to this is His saying, ﴿Be grateful to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqmān: 14]. So He commanded that they be thanked along with Him. His saying, ﴿and to the near of kin﴾, means the person with kinship, that is, one to whom the name "near of kin" can rightly apply, even if the relationship is distant.

﴿and the orphans and the needy﴾: their interpretation has already been given. The meaning is: "Be good to the near of kin," through to the end of what is mentioned in this verse. ﴿and the neighbor who is near of kin﴾: that is, the neighbor who is close by. It was said that he is one who, along with being a neighbor in the same dwelling, has kinship by lineage. ﴿and the neighbor who is a stranger﴾, the one at a distance, who is the opposite of the near neighbor. What is meant is one to whom the name of neighbor truly applies, even though his house is far away. In this there is evidence for extending good treatment to all neighbors, whether their dwellings are near or distant, and that neighborly relations are a respected right that is commanded. It also refutes those who think that the neighbor is only the adjacent one and not the one with a barrier between, or only the near one and not the distant one. It was said that what is meant by "the neighbor who is a stranger" here is the foreigner, and it was said that it is the unrelated person who has no kinship between himself and the one living beside him.

Al-Aʿmash and al-Mufaḍḍal read "al-jāri al-janb" (the neighbor who is a stranger) with a fatḥah on the jīm and a sukūn on the nūn, that is, "dhī al-janb" (the one at the side), which means the side. Al-Akhfash recited:

"The people are a side, and the commander is a side."

It was said that what is meant by "the neighbor who is near of kin" is the Muslim, and by "the neighbor who is a stranger" is the Jew and the Christian. The scholars differed over the amount of space within which the name of neighbor applies and the neighbor acquires the right. It is reported from al-Awzāʿī and al-Ḥasan that it extends to forty houses from each side. Something similar is reported from al-Zuhrī. It was said: whoever hears the call to prayer (iqāmat al-ṣalāh). It was said: when both are in the same quarter (maḥallah). It was said: whoever hears the call (al-nidāʾ).

The better view is that the meaning of "neighbor" should be referred to the Sharīʿah (sacred law). If the law contains something that clarifies it and states that a neighbor is one within a certain number of dwellings or a certain distance of land, then acting on it is required. If nothing is found, the meaning is referred to its linguistic or customary sense. The Sharīʿah does not contain anything stating that the neighbor is the one who is a certain distance from his neighbor, nor has anything in the language of the Arabs been reported indicating this. Rather, the meaning of "neighbor" in the language is "one who lives adjacent," and the term is used for several meanings.

(p-298) In al-Qāmūs, it says: "al-jār" (the neighbor) is the one who lives adjacent; the one whom you have given protection (ajartahu) from being wronged; the one who grants protection (al-mujīr); the one who seeks protection (al-mustajīr); the partner in trade; the husband of a woman, and she is his jārah (female neighbor); the private part of a woman; what is near the dwellings; the buttocks, like al-jārah; the divider (al-qāsim); the ally (al-ḥalīf); and the helper (al-nāṣir). End of quote.

Al-Qurṭubī said in his tafsīr: It is reported that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "I have settled in the quarter of a people, and the nearest of them to me as a neighbor is the one who harms me most." So the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿAlī to call out at the doors of the mosques: "Beware! Forty houses are a neighborhood, and whoever does not feel safe from his neighbor's mischief will not enter Paradise." End of quote.

If this were established, it would suffice without anything else. But he has narrated it, as you see, without attributing it to any of the well-known books of hadith. Although he is an imam in the science of narration, the proof is not established by what he narrates without a mentioned chain (sanad) and without transmission from a well-known book, especially since he frequently mentions weak reports, as he does in his Tadhkirah. The Qur'an has indicated that living together in a city means being neighbors. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist...﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Then they will not be your neighbors therein except briefly﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 60]. So He made their gathering in Medina a neighborhood. As for customary practices regarding the notion of neighborhood, they differ according to the people's customs, and it is not valid to interpret the Qur'an according to customs in common use and conventional terms agreed upon among people.

His saying, ﴿and the companion at your side﴾: it was said that this is the fellow traveler. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn Abī Laylā said: it is the wife. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the one who accompanies you and stays with you, hoping for your benefit. It is not far-fetched that the verse includes all that is in these sayings, along with more beyond them. It is anyone to whom the description "companion at the side" truly applies, that is, one at your side, such as one who stands beside you in acquiring knowledge, learning a craft, engaging in trade, or the like.

His saying, ﴿and the wayfarer﴾: Mujāhid said: he is the one who passes by you in transit. The sabīl is the road, so the traveler is named after it because he passes along it and keeps to it. It is therefore better to interpret it as one who is on a journey, since the resident is obliged to treat him well. It was said: he is the one cut off from his means. It was said: he is the guest.

His saying, ﴿and those your right hands possess﴾: that is, be good to those your right hands possess, with goodness. They are the male and female slaves. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that they be fed from what their master eats and clothed from what he wears. Al-mukhtāl is one who has self-admiration (khuyalāʾ), which is arrogance and conceit; that is, Allah does not love one who is proud, conceited toward people, and boastful over them. Fakhr is praising oneself, showing superiority, and enumerating virtues. He singled out these two attributes because they lead their possessor to disdain what Allah has enjoined in this verse.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān transmitted through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, ﴿and the neighbor who is near of kin﴾, that he meant: the one with whom you have kinship; ﴿and the neighbor who is a stranger﴾, that he meant: the one with whom you have no kinship.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Nawf al-Bikālī, who said: "the neighbor who is near of kin" is the Muslim, and "the neighbor who is a stranger" is the Jew and the Christian. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, ﴿and the companion at your side﴾, that he said: it is the fellow traveler. Ibn Jarīr transmitted the same from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid. Al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding ﴿and the companion at your side﴾, that he said: it is your companion at home, your fellow traveler on a journey, and your wife who lies beside you. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from ʿAlī, who said: it is the woman. These and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd the same.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās the same. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid regarding His saying, ﴿and those your right hands possess﴾, that he said: "from what Allah has entrusted to you, so treat its companionship well"; all of this is what Allah has enjoined. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Muqātil something similar.

Traditions have also come from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in raised (marfūʿ) form concerning kindness to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, goodness to orphans, goodness to neighbors, and providing for what slaves need. Numerous hadiths are contained in the books of Sunnah, and there is no need for us to expand on them here. Likewise, what is well known has come concerning the condemnation of arrogance, self-admiration, and boasting.

The Ayah begins with ﴿Those who are stingy﴾. It is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿one who is arrogant and boastful﴾, or it is in an accusative position by way of blame (dhamm). It may also be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate (khabar) placed before it, meaning: for them is such-and-such punishment. It is permissible for it to be nominative as a substitute for the hidden pronoun in ﴿arrogant and boastful﴾. It is also permissible for it to be accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni), or nominative as a predicate, with an implied subject, meaning: they are those who are stingy, and the clause is then in the accusative position as a substitute.

Blameworthy stinginess (bukhl) in the Shari'ah is refraining from paying what Allah has made obligatory. The people mentioned in this Ayah combined with the stinginess, which is among the worst of evil traits, something even more repugnant and more indicative of the baseness of the doer and of how far his vileness has reached. That is, although they are stingy with their wealth and conceal what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty, ﴿and they command people to be stingy﴾, as if they feel distress and resentment in their hearts at the generosity of others with their wealth. So may Allah not increase the likes of you among His servants. "These are your possessions, of which you are stingy because you think that they will diminish if you spend some of them in their proper places. So why are you stingy with the wealth of others, when no harm will reach you from that? Is this anything but the utmost blame, the extreme of foolishness, meanness, ugly dispositions, and bad choice?" The variant readings concerning bukhl have already been discussed.

It has been said that this Ayah refers to the Jews, for they combined arrogance and boasting, stinginess with wealth, and concealing what Allah revealed in the Torah. It has also been said that it refers to the hypocrites. It is not hidden that the wording is broader than that, more comprehensive, and of more general benefit.

﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) on ﴿those who are stingy﴾. The reasoning is that the first group were negligent through stinginess, through commanding people to be stingy, and through concealing what Allah had given them of His bounty. The second group went to excess by spending their wealth in places other than their proper ones, merely for show and reputation, as one does who wants people to hear that he is generous, to elevate himself over others by this, and to be proud over them. Added to this spending, which returns to him as harm, is the lack of faith in Allah and in the Last Day.

﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion﴾: there is an implied ellipsis (idmar) in the speech, and the sense is: "They do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, so Satan is their companion." ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, evil is he as a companion.﴾ The qarin is the one who accompanies, and it means the companion and close friend. The meaning is: whoever accepted Satan in this world has accompanied him in it, or he is his companion in the Fire, and Satan is an evil companion.

﴿And what would be upon them﴾, that is, upon these groups, ﴿if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them﴾, seeking His Face and complying with His command? That is: what harm would come upon them if they did that?

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (even) an atom's weight.﴾ Mithqal is a pattern (mif'al) from weight (thiql), like miqdar from qadr. It is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) for an omitted object: He does not wrong anything (by) an atom's weight. Dharrah is a single unit of dharr, which are small ants; it is said to be the head of an ant, it is said to be a mustard seed, and it is said to be every part of the dust particles that appear in sunlight entering through a window or otherwise. The first is the linguistic meaning, which the Qur'an must be taken to mean. The intended sense of the speech is that Allah does not wrong, neither a little nor a lot; that is, He does not diminish from the reward of their deeds, nor does He increase the punishment for their sins by the weight of an atom, let alone more than that.

﴿And if it is a good deed, He doubles it﴾: the people of the Hijaz read ḥasanatun with a nominative ending (raf'), and others read it with an accusative ending (nasb). The meaning according to the first reading is: if a good deed exists, with kana being the complete (tammah) verb, not the incomplete (naqisah). According to the second reading: if his act is a good deed, He doubles it. It has been said that the implied sense is: if the weight of the atom is a good deed; the pronoun of mithqal is feminine because it is in construct with a feminine noun. The first is preferable.

Al-Hasan read nudaa'if-ha with the letter nun, and the rest read it with the letter ya', and the latter is more preferred because of His saying: ﴿and gives from Himself a great reward﴾. The discussion of doubling has already been mentioned, and what is meant is the doubling of the reward of a good deed.

﴿So how (will it be) when We bring from every nation a witness﴾: kayfa is in the accusative by an implied verb, as is the view of Sibawayh, or its position is nominative as a subject, as is the view of others. The reference in His saying "these" is to the disbelievers. It has been said that it refers specifically to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The meaning: how will the state of these disbelievers be on the Day of Resurrection when We bring a witness from every nation, and bring you as a witness against these? This interrogation carries the meaning of rebuke and reproach.

﴿On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth would be leveled over them.﴾ Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read tussawwa with a fatha on the ta' and a shaddah on the sin. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the ta' and no shaddah on the sin. The rest read it with a damma on the ta' and no shaddah on the sin. The meaning according to the first and second readings is that the earth is what is leveled over them; that is, they wish that the earth had opened up for them so that they would sink into it. It has been said that the ba' in His saying "with them" means "upon", i.e., the earth is leveled upon them.

According to the third reading the verb is passive, meaning: if Allah levels the earth with them, making them and the earth equal, so that they are not resurrected.

﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ is coordinated on "will wish", meaning: on that Day, those who disbelieved will wish, and on that Day they will not conceal from Allah any statement, nor will they be able to do so.

Al-Zajjaj said: Some said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ is a new sentence (musta'nif), because what they did is manifest to Allah, and they cannot conceal it. Others said: it is coordinated, and the meaning is: they will wish that the earth were leveled over them and that they had not concealed from Allah any statement, because their lie became apparent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Kardam ibn Yazid, the ally of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Usamah ibn Habib, Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi', Bahri ibn 'Amr, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut used to come to men of the Ansar, giving them sincere advice. They would say: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you if it is lost, and do not hasten to spend, for you do not know what will happen." So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Those who are stingy and command people to be stingy﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever Knowing of them.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that it was revealed concerning the Jews. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from Qatadah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (even) an atom's weight﴾ that he said: "the head of a red ant." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾ that it is the weight of an atom; if it exceeds his evil deeds, He doubles it. As for the polytheist, the punishment is lightened for him by it, and he will never leave the Fire.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Recite to me." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, I love to hear it from others." So I recited Surah al-Nisa' until I came to this Ayah: ﴿So how (will it be) when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ He said: "That is enough for now." Then his eyes were shedding tears.

Al-Hakim also narrated it and authenticated it from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Hurayth.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Were the earth leveled over them﴾ that it means: that the earth be leveled with the mountains, and the earth over them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning the Ayah that he said: they wished that the earth would split open over them, so they would sink into it. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ that he said: "with their limbs."

Others said: it is coordinated, and the meaning is: they will wish that the earth were leveled over them and that they had not concealed from Allah any statement, because their lie became apparent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Kardam ibn Yazid, the ally of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Usamah ibn Habib, Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi', Bahri ibn 'Amr, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut used to come to men of the Ansar, giving them sincere advice. They would say: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you if it is lost, and do not hasten to spend, for you do not know what will happen." So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Those who are stingy and command people to be stingy﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever Knowing of them.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that it was revealed concerning the Jews. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from Qatadah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (even) an atom's weight﴾ that he said: "the head of a red ant." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾ that it is the weight of an atom; if it exceeds his evil deeds, He doubles it. As for the polytheist, the punishment is lightened for him by it, and he will never leave the Fire.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Recite to me." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, I love to hear it from others." So I recited Surah al-Nisa' until I came to this Ayah: ﴿So how (will it be) when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ He said: "That is enough for now." Then his eyes were shedding tears.

Al-Hakim also narrated it and authenticated it from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Hurayth.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Were the earth leveled over them﴾ that it means: that the earth be leveled with the mountains, and the earth over them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning the Ayah that he said: they wished that the earth would split open over them, so they would sink into it. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ that he said: "with their limbs."
