**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 1 of 3):**

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ He made the address specific to the believers, because they used to approach the prayer while intoxicated. As for the disbelievers, they do not approach it, neither intoxicated nor sober.

His saying: ﴿do not approach﴾. The lexicographers said: When it is said *lā taqrab* with a fatḥah on the *rāʾ*, its meaning is "do not engage in the act." When it is *lā taqrub* with a ḍammah on the *rāʾ*, its meaning is "do not come near it." What is intended here is the prohibition of engaging in the prayer and entering upon it. This is the view of a group of exegetes, and Abū Ḥanīfah adopted it. Others said that what is intended is the places of prayer, and al-Shāfiʿī held this view. On this reading, a *muḍāf* (an elided noun, "the places of") must be supplied. This is strengthened by His saying: ﴿nor in a state of major impurity, except for those passing through [a way]﴾. Another group said that what is intended is both the prayer and its places together, because at that time they did not come to the mosque except for the prayer, and did not pray except in congregation, so the two were mutually connected.

His saying: ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾. The clause is in a position of *naṣb* as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Sukārā* is the plural of *sakrān*, like *kusālā* is the plural of *kaslān*. Al-Nakhaʿī read *sakrā* with a fatḥah on the *sīn*, which is a broken plural of *sakrān*. Al-Aʿmash read *sukrā* like *ḥublā*, as a singular adjective. All the scholars agree that what is meant by intoxication here is intoxication by wine, except al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said that what is meant is the intoxication of sleep. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later, and by it the views that contradict what is correct are refuted.

His saying: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾. This is the limit (*ghāyah*) of the prohibition of approaching the prayer while intoxicated; that is, until the effect of intoxication leaves you and you know what you are saying. The intoxicated person does not know what he says. Those who held that the divorce of an intoxicated person does not take effect have relied on this, since if he does not know what he is saying, intention is absent. This was the view of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāʾūs, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Qāsim and Rabīʿah, and it is the view of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr and al-Muzanī. Al-Ṭaḥāwī chose it and said: The scholars agreed that the divorce of one who is *maʿtūh* (mentally incapacitated) is not valid, and the intoxicated person is *maʿtūh* like one who is afflicted with waswās (obsessive delusion). A group permitted the taking effect of his divorce, and this is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Muʿāwiyah and a group of the Successors. It is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Thawrī and al-Awzāʿī. The opinion of al-Shāfiʿī on this differed. Mālik said: Divorce binds him, and retaliation (*qawad*) applies to wounds and killing, but marriage and sale do not bind him.

His saying: ﴿nor in a state of major impurity﴾ is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on the position of the circumstantial clause, which is His saying: ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾. *Junub* (in a state of major impurity) does not take a feminine form, nor a dual, nor a plural, because it is treated as a verbal noun, like *al-buʿd* and *al-qurb*. Al-Farrāʾ said: It is said *januba al-rajul* and *ajnaba* from *al-janābah*. It was also said that *junub* is pluralized in one dialect as *ajnāb*, like *ʿunuq* and *aʿnāq*, and *ṭunub* and *aṭnāb*.

His saying: ﴿except for those passing through [a way]﴾ is an exceptive construction with a missing antecedent (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*); that is, do not approach it in any state except in the state of passing through a way. What is meant here is travel. The place of this exceptive construction is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lā taqrabū*, after restricting it by the second circumstance, which is His saying: *nor in a state of major impurity*, and not by the first circumstance, which is His saying: *while you are intoxicated*. The meaning thus becomes: Do not approach the prayer while you are in a state of major impurity, except in the state of travel, for it is permitted for you to pray with *tayammum* (dry ablution). This is the view of ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥakam and others. They said: It is not valid for anyone to approach the prayer while in major impurity until after washing, except the traveller, who performs *tayammum*, because water may be unavailable during travel but not generally at home, as it is usually not unavailable.

Ibn Masʿūd, ʿIkrimah, al-Nakhaʿī, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: *ʿĀbir al-sabīl* is the one who crosses through the mosque. This is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. On this reading, the meaning of the verse is: Do not approach the places of prayer, which are the mosques, in a state of major impurity, except if you are passing through them from one side to the other. The first view has strength in that the prayer remains in its literal meaning, and weakness in that taking *ʿābir al-sabīl* to mean the traveller implies that he approaches the prayer when water is unavailable by means of *tayammum*, whereas this ruling applies to the resident as well when water is unavailable, just as it applies to the traveller. The second view has strength in that it avoids strained interpretation in the meaning of His saying: *except for those passing through*, and weakness in that it requires taking the prayer to mean its places. In sum, the first circumstance, namely His saying: *while you are intoxicated*, strengthens the retention of the prayer in its literal meaning without supplying an elided noun, and likewise the occasion of revelation to be mentioned later strengthens this. His saying: *except for those passing through* strengthens the supplying of the elided noun, that is: Do not approach the places of prayer.

It may be said: Some of the restrictions of the prohibition, namely *do not approach* together with His saying *while you are intoxicated*, indicate that the prayer is meant in its literal sense, and some restrictions of the prohibition, namely His saying *except for those passing through*, indicate that the places of prayer are meant. There is no obstacle to considering each of the two with its indicating restriction, and this is like two prohibitions each restricted by a condition: Do not approach the prayer, which is the one with its remembrances and pillars, while you are intoxicated; and do not approach the places of prayer while in major impurity, except while passing through the mosque from one side to the other. The most that can be said about this is that it is a combination of the literal and the figurative (*majāz*), which is permitted according to a well-known interpretation. Ibn Jarīr, after reporting the two views, said: The most preferable is the view of the one who said: *Nor in a state of major impurity, except for those passing through [a way]* means only those crossing through a path in it, because the ruling on the traveller who finds no water while in major impurity has already been stated in His saying: ﴿And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself, or you have contacted women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it﴾. So it was already known from that. That is, if His saying *nor in a state of major impurity, except for those passing through, until you wash* were meant of the traveller, there would be no understood meaning in repeating it in His saying: (p-301) ﴿And if you are ill, or on a journey﴾. The ruling was already mentioned before that. If this is so, then the interpretation of the verse is: O you who have believed, do not approach the mosques for prayer, praying in them, while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying; and do not approach them either while in major impurity until you wash, except for those passing through. He said: *ʿĀbir al-sabīl* is one who crosses by passing and traversing. It is said of this: *ʿabartu hādhā al-ṭarīq*, "I crossed this road," *fa-anā aʿburuhu ʿabran wa-ʿubūran*. From this it is said: *ʿabara fulān al-nahr*, "so-and-so crossed the river," when he traversed and passed over it. From this also it is said of a strong she-camel: *hiya ʿabr asfār*, "she is one that crosses journeys," because of her strength in covering journeys.

Ibn Kathīr said: This which he (i.e., Ibn Jarīr) supported is the view of the majority, and it is the apparent meaning of the verse. End.

His saying: ﴿until you wash﴾ is a limit (*ghāyah*) of the prohibition of approaching the prayer or its places while in major impurity. The meaning: Do not approach them while in major impurity until you wash, except while passing through the way.

His saying: ﴿And if you are ill﴾. *Maraḍ* (illness) is an expression for the body's departure from the limit of balance and normal condition into deviation and abnormality, and it is of two kinds: severe and slight. What is meant here is that one fears for his life from destruction or harm by using water, or one is weak in his body and cannot reach the place of water. It is reported from al-Ḥasan that he should perform purification even if he dies. This is false, and it is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any difficulty in religion﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 78], and His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 29], and His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

His saying: ﴿or on a journey﴾. In it is the permissibility of *tayammum* for one to whom the name "traveller" applies. The disagreement is elaborated in the books of jurisprudence. The majority held that it is not required that it be a journey that allows shortening the prayer (*safar qaṣr*), and a group said that this is necessary. The scholars have agreed on the permissibility of *tayammum* for the traveller. They differed concerning the resident. Mālik and his companions, Abū Ḥanīfah and Muḥammad said that it is permitted both at home and on a journey. Al-Shāfiʿī said: It is not permitted for the healthy resident to perform *tayammum* unless he fears destruction.

His saying: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself﴾. *Ghāʾiṭ* is a low-lying place, and *al-majīʾ minhu* (coming from it) is a metaphor (*kināyah*) for a minor impurity (*ḥadath*). The plural is *ghiyṭān* and *aghwāṭ*. The Arabs used to go to this kind of place to relieve themselves, concealing themselves from people's eyes. Then the minor impurity that comes out of a person was called *ghāʾiṭ* by extension. Included in *al-ghāʾiṭ* are all the events that nullify ablution.

His saying: ﴿or you have contacted women﴾. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read *lāmastum* (with an alif), and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read *lamastum* (without an alif). It was said: What is meant by both readings is intercourse. It was said: What is meant is simple physical contact. It was said: It includes both things together. Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad said: The preferable meaning in the language is that *lāmastum* means "you kissed" and the like, and *lamastum* means "you covered" (i.e., had intercourse).

The scholars differed about the meaning of this in several views. One group said: Here *mulāmasah* (contact) is restricted to the hand, excluding intercourse. They said: The one in major impurity has no way to perform *tayammum*; rather, he washes or leaves the prayer until he finds water. This was reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Ibn Masʿūd. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: None of the jurists of the cities, from among the people of opinion and the transmitters of reports, held the view of these two on this question. End. Also, the authentic hadiths refute and invalidate it, such as the hadith of ʿAmmār, ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn and Abū Dharr concerning the *tayammum* of the one in major impurity.

Another group said: It is intercourse, as in His saying: ﴿Then if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 49], and His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. This is reported from ʿAlī, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ṭāʾūs, al-Ḥasan, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Shaʿbī, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and Abū Ḥanīfah. Mālik said: The one who touches by intercourse performs *tayammum*, and the one who touches with the hand performs *tayammum* if he experienced pleasure (*iltadha*); if he touched her without desire, there is no ablution. Aḥmad and Isḥāq said the same.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: If a man's body makes contact with any part of a woman's body, whether by hand or by another limb, his purity is nullified; otherwise it is not. Al-Qurṭubī reported this from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Zuhrī and Rabīʿah. Al-Awzāʿī said: If the touching is by the hand, it nullifies purity; if it is by other than the hand, it does not nullify it, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾. They argued with proofs, each group claiming that its proof indicates that the contact mentioned in the verse is what it holds. This is not the case. The Companions and those after them differed about the meaning of the contact mentioned in the verse. Even on the assumption that it is clearly about intercourse, the reading reported from Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī with the wording *aw lamastum* is established, and it is undoubtedly possible. With possibility there is no argument from what is possible. This ruling affects everyone and establishes a general obligation, so it is not permissible to establish it by a possibility, and the dispute has occurred concerning its understanding. Once you know this, the authentic Sunnah has established the obligation of *tayammum* on one who avoids water and does not find it. So the one in major impurity is included in the verse by this evidence, and even if he were not included, the Sunnah suffices for that.

As for the obligation of ablution or *tayammum* on one who touches a woman with his hand or some part of his body, it is not valid to hold it by this verse, because of the possibility you have come to know. As for what they cited as evidence, that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about a man who met a woman whom he did not know? A man does nothing with his wife except that he does everything with her except that he does not have intercourse with her." So Allah revealed: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember﴾ [Hūd: 114].

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Mu'adh. They said: he (ﷺ) ordered him to perform wudu' (ablution) because he had touched a woman without having intercourse with her. But it should not escape you that this hadith is no evidence on the point in dispute, for the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to perform wudu' only so that he could pray the prayer that Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in this verse, since there is no prayer without wudu'. Moreover, the hadith is munqati' (disconnected in its chain), because it is narrated by Ibn Abi Layla from Mu'adh, and he did not meet him. Once you know this, the default position is the absence of this ruling, so it is not established except by clear evidence free of the defects that would invalidate it, since this hadith falls short of being a proof.

Also, it has been established from 'A'ishah through several chains that she said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would perform wudu', then kiss, then pray without performing wudu' again." This hadith has been narrated with different wordings. It was related by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. As for what has been said, that it is from the narration of Habib ibn Abi Thabit from Urwah from 'A'ishah, and that he did not hear from Urwah, it was narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad from the hadith of Hisham ibn Urwah from his father from 'A'ishah. Ibn Jarir narrated it from the hadith of Layth from 'Ata' from 'A'ishah. Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i also narrated it from the hadith of Abu Rawq al-Hamdani from Ibrahim al-Taymi from 'A'ishah. Ibn Jarir also narrated it from the hadith of Umm Salamah, and he narrated it from the hadith of Zaynab al-Sahmiyyah.

The wording of the hadith of Umm Salamah is: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would kiss her while he was fasting, and he would not break his fast, nor would he renew his wudu'." The wording of the hadith of Zaynab al-Sahmiyyah is: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) would kiss, then pray, without performing wudu'."

Ahmad narrated it from Zaynab al-Sahmiyyah from 'A'ishah.

His saying: ﴿and you find no water﴾. This condition, if it refers to everything mentioned before it after the conditional clause, namely illness, travel, coming from the toilet, and touching women, then there is evidence that illness and travel by themselves do not permit tayammum (dry ablution with earth). Rather, the absence of water must accompany one of the two causes. Thus it is not permissible for the sick person to perform tayammum unless he finds no water, and it is not permissible for the traveller to perform tayammum unless he finds no water. However, this raises a difficulty: the healthy person who finds no water performs tayammum, and likewise the traveller, for the absence of water is usual in his case. And if the condition refers only to the last two cases, namely His saying: ﴿or one of you comes from the toilet, or you have touched women﴾, as some exegetes have said, then there is a difficulty, namely that whoever is truly called sick or a traveller is permitted to perform tayammum even if he has water and is able to use it. It has been said that this condition refers to the last two cases, although it is also required in the first two, because it is rare for those two to occur without it.

You know well that this is a worthless statement and a cold interpretation. Malik and those who followed him said: Allah mentioned illness and travel as conditions for tayammum, taking into account what is usual for one who does not find water, unlike the resident, for water is usually available to him. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, did not specify it for him. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that illness by itself permits tayammum, even if water is present, if using it would harm him at present or in the future. The fear of destruction is not considered. Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185], and He says: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj 22:78]. The Prophet (ﷺ) says: "The religion is ease." And he says: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." He said: "They killed him, may Allah kill them." And he says: "I have been sent with the tolerant (samhah) sharia." So if we say that the condition of not finding water refers to all cases, the reason for mentioning illness is that it is permissible for him to perform tayammum while water is present and available, if using it would harm him. Thus the consideration of that condition applies to him when using water would not harm him, for in illness alone, when using water does not cause harm, there is a likelihood of his being unable to search for water, because a kind of weakness accompanies illness. As for the reason for mentioning the traveller, there is no doubt that travelling on the earth is a likely cause of the scarcity of water in some places and not others.

His saying: ﴿then perform tayammum﴾. Tayammum linguistically means intention, aim. It is said: "I tayammamtu the thing," meaning I aimed at it; "I tayammamtu the earth," meaning I deliberately went to it; "I tayammamtu it with my arrow and my spear," meaning I aimed at it rather than anything else. Al-Khalil recited:

*I aimed the spear at him sideways, then I said to him: "This is valour, not the play of the ones who play with swords."*

Imru' al-Qays said:

*I aimed for her from Adhri'at, and her people were at Yathrib, the nearest of her dwellings a high gaze.*

And he said:

*The eye aimed at the spring near Darij, whose shade falls upon its mossy bank, thirsty.*

Ibn al-Sikkit said: His saying "fa-tayammamu" means: aim. Then the usage of this word became common until tayammum came to mean wiping the face and hands with dust. Ibn al-Anbari said regarding their saying "the man has performed tayammum": it means he wiped dust over his face.

This is a confusion by them of the linguistic meaning with the sharia meaning. The Arabs did not know tayammum in the sense of wiping the face and hands. It is only a sharia meaning. The apparent command is obligation, and there is consensus on this. The hadiths on this subject are numerous.

His saying: ﴿ṣa'īdan (clean earth)﴾. The ṣa'īd is the surface of the earth, whether or not it has dust on it, as said by al-Khalil, Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: I know of no disagreement among the lexicographers about this. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed We will make what is on it a barren, dry ground﴾ [al-Kahf 18:8], meaning a hard earth that produces nothing. He said: ﴿So it will become a bare, slippery ground﴾ [al-Kahf 18:40]. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*As if in the forenoon he throws the ṣa'īd with it, and his tooth in the bones of the head is a snout.*

It was called ṣa'īd because it is the furthest point of the earth that one ascends to. The plural of ṣa'īd is ṣu'adāt. The people of knowledge differed regarding what tayammum may be performed with. Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri and al-Tabari said: it is valid with the whole surface of the earth, whether dust, sand or stones, and they interpreted His saying ﴿ṭayyiban (clean)﴾ as meaning pure, not impure.

Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and their companions said: tayammum is valid only with dust. They used as evidence His saying ﴿ṣa'īdan zalaqan﴾ [al-Kahf 18:40], meaning smooth clean dust. They also used His saying ﴿ṭayyiban﴾, and said: the ṭayyib is the dust that produces vegetation. The meaning of ṭayyib has been disputed: it has been said it means pure, as previously mentioned; it has been said it means productive, as here; and it has been said it means lawful.

What is only possible cannot serve as a proof. Even if the only thing with which one could perform tayammum were what is in the Noble Book, the truth would be what the earlier scholars said. But it is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have been favoured over the people in three ways: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the whole earth has been made a mosque for us; and its dust has been made a purifier for us when we do not find water." In another wording: "and its dust has been made a purifier for us." So this clarifies the meaning of ṣa'īd mentioned in the verse, or specifies its generality, or restricts its absoluteness. This is supported by what Ibn Faris related from the Kitab of al-Khalil: "He performed tayammum upon the ṣa'īd," meaning he took from its dust. End of quote. A bare stone has no dust.

His saying: ﴿then wipe your faces and your hands﴾. This wiping is absolute. It covers wiping with one strike or two strikes, and it covers wiping up to the elbows or up to the wrists. The Sunnah has explained it clearly. We have combined what came regarding wiping with one strike and with two strikes, and what came regarding wiping up to the wrist and up to the elbows, in our commentary on al-Muntaqa and our other works, in a way that needs nothing else.

His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, meaning: He has pardoned you, forgiven your shortcoming, and shown you mercy by granting you a concession and making things easy for you.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf prepared food for us, invited us, and gave us wine to drink. The wine took effect on us, and the prayer time came. They made me lead, and I recited: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun 109:1–2], while we were worshipping what you worship. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that the one who led them in prayer was Abd al-Rahman.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ikrimah regarding the verse that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Sa'd. Ali prepared food and drink for them, and they ate and drank. Then he led them in the Maghrib prayer and recited: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ until he finished it, then said: "I have my religion and you have yours." So it was revealed.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse that he said: it was abrogated by ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling...﴾ the verse [al-Ma'idah 5:90].

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: it did not mean intoxicants; it meant only the drowsiness of sleep.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾ that he said: it means drowsiness. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ali.

His saying: ﴿nor [approach prayer while] in a state of janabah, except while passing through [the mosque]﴾. He said: it was revealed concerning the traveller who becomes junub, so he performs tayammum and prays. In another wording he said: "He should not approach prayer except if he is a traveller who has become junub, and does not find water, so he performs tayammum and prays until he finds water."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "Do not approach prayer while you are junub if you find water. But if you do not find water, I have permitted you to wipe yourselves with the earth." Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid that he said: the junub and the menstruating woman should not pass through the mosque. The verse ﴿nor [approach prayer while] in a state of janabah, except while passing through﴾ was revealed only for the traveller, who performs tayammum and then prays.

Al-Daraqutni, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan and Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Asla' ibn Sharik, who said: "I was saddling the camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I became junub on a cold night, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wanted to set off. I disliked saddling his camel while I was junub, and I feared that if I washed with cold water I would die or fall ill. So I ordered a man from the Ansar, and he saddled it. Then I heated stones and heated water with them, and I washed. Then I caught up with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. He said: 'O Asla', what is the matter? I see your mount has changed.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I did not saddle it; a man from the Ansar saddled it.' He said: 'And why?' I said: 'I became junub, and I feared the cold for myself, so I ordered him to saddle it, and I heated stones and heated water and washed with it.' Then Allah revealed: 'O you who believe…' up to His saying: ﴿nor [approach prayer while] in a state of janabah, except while passing through﴾."

Ibn Sa'd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi narrated through another route from Asla', who said: "I used to serve the Prophet (ﷺ) and saddle his camel for him. One night he said to me: 'O Asla', get up and saddle for me.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have become junub.' He remained silent with me for a while, until Jibril came with the verse of ṣa'īd. He said: 'Get up, O Asla', and perform tayammum.'" The hadith [continues].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Abi Hatim related through the route of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Do not approach prayer﴾ that he said: "The mosques." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related through the route of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani from him regarding ﴿nor [approach] while impure, except as travellers on the way﴾ that he said: "Do not enter the mosque while you are in a state of janabah, except as travellers passing through." He said: "You pass through it without stopping and do not sit."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Masʿud something similar. ʿAbd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from him that he used to permit the one in a state of janabah to pass through the mosque without sitting in it, then he recited his saying: ﴿nor [approach] while impure, except as travellers on the way﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi related from Anas something similar. Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Jabir that he said: "One of us would pass through the mosque while in a state of janabah, passing through."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding his saying ﴿And if you are ill﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar who was ill and was unable to stand up and perform wudu', and he had no servant to assist him. So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and Allah revealed this verse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding his saying ﴿And if you are ill﴾ that he said: "It refers to the man who has a skin disease, or has wounds or sores, who becomes junub and fears that if he washes he will die, so he performs tayammum."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were struck by wounds which spread among them, then they were afflicted with janabah, so they complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and ﴿And if you are ill﴾ [the verse] was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related through various routes from Ibn Masʿud regarding his saying ﴿or you have touched women﴾ that he said: "Touching is less than intercourse, and kissing is from it, and wudu' is required for it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿUmar that he used to perform wudu' due to a woman's kiss, and would say: "It is al-lamas (touching)."

al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim related from ʿUmar that he said: "Indeed, kissing is from touching, so perform wudu' because of it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAli that he said: "Al-lams is intercourse, but Allah has referred to it indirectly."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd (p-304) Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr who said: "We were in the room of Ibn ʿAbbas, with us were ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and a group of the mawali (non-Arab clients), and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and a group of the Arabs. We discussed al-lamis (the one who touches). I, ʿAṭāʾ and the mawali said: 'Lams is by the hand.' ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and the Arabs said: 'It is intercourse.' So I entered upon Ibn ʿAbbas and informed him, and he said: 'The mawali were overcome, and the Arabs were correct.' Then he said: 'Indeed, lams, mass and mubashara do not refer to intercourse by themselves, but Allah alludes with whatever He wills to whatever He wills.'"

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The best of the ṣaʿīd (earth) is the land of tillage."

The Prophet's name appears in the text as "النَّبِيّ" or "رَسُولَ اللَّهِ" and is rendered as "the Prophet (ﷺ)" or "the Messenger of God (ﷺ)".

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 44–48:

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Book?﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), and the address is to everyone among the Muslims who is able to see. The "nasib" (share) means "portion" (ḥaẓẓ), and what is meant is the Jews, who were given a share of the Torah. His saying: "yashtarūn" (they purchase) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and what is meant by "al-ishtirā'" (purchasing) is "al-istibdāl" (exchanging), and its precise meaning has already been established. The meaning is: the Jews exchanged error (ḍalālah), which is remaining upon Judaism after the proof of the truth of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ) had become clear. His saying: ﴿and they wish that you would go astray from the way﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with his saying "yashtarūn," sharing with it in explaining the evil of their conduct and the weakness of their choice. That is: they were not content with what they had brought upon themselves of exchanging guidance for error, but rather, along with their own error, they wanted to reach, through their concealment and denial, that you, O believers, would go astray from the straight path, which is the path of truth.

﴿And God knows best your enemies﴾, O believers, and what they intend for you of misguidance. The sentence is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah). ﴿And God suffices as a Protector﴾ for you, ﴿and God suffices as a Helper﴾ who will help you in the places of war. So be content with His guardianship and His help, and do not take as protector anyone other than Him, nor seek help from anyone else. The "bāʾ" in his saying "bi-Llāh" in both places is superfluous (zāʾidah).

His saying: ﴿of those who are Jews﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: if it is connected to what precedes, then one does not stop at His saying "nasīran" (helper); but if it is taken as disconnected (munqaṭiʿah), then it is permissible to stop at "nasīran," and the estimated meaning is: "of those who are Jews, there are people who distort," then it was omitted. This is the view of Sibawayh, and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"Had you said: there is no one among her people who was not sinful, surpassing her in lineage and in appearance."

They said: the meaning is: had you said: there is no one among her people who surpasses her, then it was omitted. Al-Farrāʾ said: the omitted element is the word "man" (whoever); that is: "of those who are Jews, whoever distorts the words," like His saying: ﴿and there is none of us but has a known station﴾, meaning "whoever has." From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"So they remained, and among them is one whose tears are running ahead of him,"

meaning: "whose tears." Al-Mubarrid and al-Zajjaj denied this, because omitting the relative pronoun is like omitting part of a word. It was also said: His saying "of those who are Jews" is an explanation of His saying "those who were given a share of the Book."

And "al-taḥrīf" (distortion) is inclination and removal; that is: they incline it and remove it from its places and put something else in its place. Or what is meant is that they interpret it in other than its proper interpretation. God, mighty and majestic, censured them for this, because they do it out of obstinacy and rebellion and to serve worldly aims.

His saying: ﴿and they say: "We hear and we disobey"﴾, that is: "We hear your words and we disobey your command." ﴿And hear, without being heard﴾, that is: hear while you are unheard. It may be a supplication against the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: "Hear, may you not hear!" It may also mean: hear without being heard anything unpleasant, or: hear without being answered.

The discussion of "rāʿinā" has already been given. The meaning of ﴿twisting with their tongues﴾ is that they twist them away from the truth, that is, they incline them toward what is in their hearts. The root of "al-layy" is twisting (al-fatl), and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it may also be an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). His saying: ﴿and defaming the religion﴾ is coordinated with "layyan" (twisting); that is: they slander the religion by saying: "If he were a prophet, he would know that we are cursing him," so God, glorified be He, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of that.

﴿And if they had said: "We hear" your words "and we obey" your command, "and hear what we say," and "look at us"﴾, that is: if they had said this in place of their saying "rāʿinā"—﴿it would have been better for them﴾ than what they said, ﴿and more upright﴾, that is: more just and more fitting than their first saying, which is their saying: ﴿"We hear and we disobey, and hear without being heard, and rāʿinā"﴾, because of the opposition and bad manners in it, and the possibility of blame in "rāʿinā." But they did not take the good course nor bring what is better for them and more upright. For this reason, ﴿God cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: except a little belief, which is belief in some of the Books and not others, and in some of the messengers and not others.

His saying: ﴿O you who were given the Book﴾. He, glorified be He, first mentioned that they were given a share of the Book, and here He mentions that they were given the Book. What is meant is that they were given a share of it, because they did not act upon all that is in it, but rather distorted and altered. His saying "muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

"Al-ṭamas" (obliteration) is the eradication of the trace of a thing, and from it is His saying: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾ [al-Mursalat: 8]. It is said "naṭmis" with kasra or ḍamma on the mīm in the future tense, both being dialects. It is said: "ṭamasa al-athar," meaning he erased the trace entirely. From it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾ [Yunus: 88], meaning: destroy it. It is also said: "huwa maṭmūs al-baṣar" (his sight is obliterated), and from it is His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ [Ya-Sin: 66], meaning: We would have blinded them.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of this verse: is it literal, so that the face becomes like the nape, and the nose, mouth, eyebrows and eyes are removed? Or is it a metaphor for misguidance in their hearts and the removal of success? One group went to the first view, and others went to the second. On the first view, what is meant by His saying ﴿then We will turn them back upon their backs﴾ is that We make them into a nape, that is, We remove the traces of the face and its features until it becomes in the shape of a nape. It was also said that after obliteration He returns them to the place of the nape, and the nape to their places. This is closest to the meaning indicated by His saying ﴿then We will turn them back upon their backs﴾.

It was said: how could He threaten them with obliterating faces if they do not believe, when He did not do that to them? It was answered: when these people and those who followed them believed, the threat was lifted from the rest. Al-Mubarrid said: the threat remains pending, and he said: there must be obliteration among the Jews, and abrogation (naskh) before the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿Or We will curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of the faces. It was said: what is meant by the curse here is transformation (maskh), for the purpose of comparing it with the curse of the people of the Sabbath, and the curse of the people of the Sabbath was their transformation into apes and swine. It was also said: what is meant is the curse itself, and they are cursed in every tongue. What is meant is the occurrence of one of the two matters: either obliteration or cursing. The cursing has occurred, but the comparison of this cursing with the cursing of the people of the Sabbath strengthens the first view. His saying: ﴿And the command of God is ever accomplished﴾, that is: existing and present without doubt; or "amr" may mean "the thing commanded" (al-maʾmūr).

The meaning is that whenever He wills it, it is, as in His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. This ruling encompasses all groups of disbelievers, from the People of the Book and others, and is not specific to the disbelievers of the warring enemies, because the Jews said: "Uzayr is the son of God," the Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of God," and they said: "The third of three."

There is no disagreement among the Muslims that a polytheist who dies in his polytheism is not among the people of forgiveness that God bestows upon those other than the people of polytheism, according to what His will requires. As for the sinful Muslims other than the people of polytheism, they are included under the will: He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. Ibn Jarir said: this verse has made clear that every person who commits a major sin is under the will of God, mighty and majestic: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He pardons him, so long as his major sin is not polytheism with God, mighty and majestic. Its apparent meaning is that forgiveness from Him, glorified be He, occurs for whomever His will requires, as a bounty and mercy from Him, even if that sinner does not repent. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that required repentance for forgiveness) restricted this to repentance. His saying, exalted be He, has already been given: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], and it indicates that God, glorified be He, forgives the misdeeds of whoever avoids the major sins, so the one who avoids major sins is among those for whom God has willed the forgiveness of his misdeeds.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut was one of the leaders of the Jews, and when he spoke to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he twisted his tongue and said: "Make your hearing attentive to us, O Muhammad, until we understand you." Then he slandered Islam and disparaged it, so God revealed about him: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a share of the Book?﴾ to the end of the verse. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾, that he meant: they distort the limits of God in the Torah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾, he said: it is the Jews' alteration of the Torah. ﴿And they say: "We hear and we disobey"﴾: they said: "We hear what you say and we will not obey you." ﴿And hear, without being heard﴾: he said: unacceptable to what you say. ﴿Twisting with their tongues﴾: he said: opposition, they twist their tongues with it. ﴿And hear and look at us﴾: he said: make us understand, do not hasten against us. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿And hear, without being heard﴾, he said: they say, "Hear, may you not hear!"

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Leaders of the rabbis of the Jews spoke with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among them ʿAbd Allah ibn Suriya and Kaʿb ibn Asad. He said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, fear God and submit, for by God, you know that what I have brought you is the truth.' They said: 'We do not know that, O Muhammad.' And God revealed about them: ﴿O you who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾, he said: their obliteration is that they become blind. ﴿Then We will turn them back upon their backs﴾: he said: We will make their faces from the direction of their napes, so they walk backward, and We will make one of them have two eyes in his nape. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾, he said: from the path of truth. ﴿Then We will turn them back upon their backs﴾, he said: into misguidance.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan something similar. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have a nephew who does not refrain from the forbidden.' He said: 'And what is his religion?' He said: 'He prays and affirms the oneness of God.' He said: 'Ask him to give you his religion as a gift, and if he refuses, buy it from him.' The man asked him for that, but he refused. So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: 'I found him stingy about his religion.' Then God revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn al-Duraysi, Abu Yaʿla, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn ʿAdi transmitted with a sound chain from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "We used to refrain from asking forgiveness for the people of major sins, until we heard from our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, and he said: 'I have stored up my supplication and my intercession for the people of major sins from my community.' So we refrained from much of what had been in our hearts." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "When God revealed: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], to the end of the verse, a man stood up and said: 'And polytheism, O Prophet of God?' The Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that, and he said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ to the end of the verse." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abu Mijlaz that this man's question was the occasion of revelation of ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾.

Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (al-Nasikh) and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said concerning this verse: God forbade forgiveness to whoever dies while a disbeliever, and He left the people of monotheism to His will, and did not make them despair of forgiveness. al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded as good (hasan) from ʿAli, who said: "The verse most beloved to me in the Qur'an is: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ to the end of the verse."

The Prophet's name appears in the text as "النَّبِيّ" or "رَسُولَ اللَّهِ" and is rendered as "the Prophet (ﷺ)" or "the Messenger of God (ﷺ)".

For this reason, ﴿God cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: except a little belief, which is belief in some of the Books and not others, and in some of the messengers and not others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿And hear, without being heard﴾, he said: they say, "Hear, may you not hear!"

He said: 'And what is his religion?' He said: 'He prays and affirms the oneness of God.' He said: 'Ask him to give you his religion as a gift, and if he refuses, buy it from him.' The man asked him for that, but he refused. So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: 'I found him stingy about his religion.' The Prophet's name appears in the text as "النَّبِيّ" or "رَسُولَ اللَّهِ" and is rendered as "the Prophet (ﷺ)" or "the Messenger of God (ﷺ)".

The meaning: "Rather, they envy the people," that is, the Jews envy the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, or they envy him and his companions for what God has given them of His bounty, namely prophethood, victory, and subjugating the enemies. His saying: ﴿For We have already given the family of Abraham﴾ is a proof against the Jews through what they acknowledge and do not deny. The meaning: what We have given Muhammad and his companions of Our bounty is no novelty, so that the Jews should envy them for it. They know of what We gave the family of Abraham, and they are the forefathers of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The tafsir of the Book, the wisdom, and the great kingdom has already been mentioned. It was said: the great kingdom is the kingdom of Solomon. Ibn Jarir chose this. ﴿So among them﴾, that is, among the Jews, ﴿is one who believes in him﴾, that is, in the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿and among them is one who turns away from him﴾, that is, turns away from him. It was also said: the pronoun in "in him" refers to what was mentioned of the story of the family of Abraham. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Abraham.

[p. 307] The meaning: among the family of Abraham, some believed in Abraham and some turned away from him. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Book. The first is preferable. ﴿And sufficient is Jahannam as a blazing fire﴾, that is, a kindled fire.

Ibn Jarir narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Jews said: 'Our forefathers have died, and they are a means of nearness to God for us, and they will intercede for us and purify us.' So God said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: The Jews used to bring forward their children to lead them in prayer and offer their sacrifices, claiming they had no sins or wrongdoings. They lied. God said: "I do not make one who has a sin bear another who has no sin." Then God sent down: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that tazkiyah was their saying: ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved ones﴾, and they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged a fatil﴾ that he said: "The fatil is what comes out between the two fingers." In another wording from him: "It is that you rub between your two fingers, and whatever comes out of them is that." Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: "The naqir is the notch that is in the pit from which the palm tree sprouts. The fatil is what is on the split of the pit. The qitmir is the skin that is on the pit." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: "The fatil is what is in the split in the belly of the pit."

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from him, who said: "Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf came to Mecca to Quraysh and allied with them to fight the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said to them: 'You are the people of ancient knowledge and the People of the Book, so inform us about us and about Muhammad.' They said: 'What are you? And what is Muhammad?' They said: 'We slaughter the she-camel of the rich, we give milk on water, we release captives, we give drink to the pilgrims, and we maintain the ties of kinship.' They said: 'And what is Muhammad?' They said: 'He is a sunbur (a lone, weak one), who has severed our ties of kinship, and the Banu Ghifar, plunderers of pilgrims, have followed him.' They said: 'No, rather you are better than him and better guided in the way.' So God sent down: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in al-jibt and al-taghut?﴾ to the end of the verse." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from 'Ikrimah as a mursal report. It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and from 'Ikrimah with another wording. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from al-Suddi from Abu Malik. al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn 'Asakir in his History also narrated something similar from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "al-jibt and al-taghut are two idols."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Umar concerning the tafsir of al-jibt and al-taghut what we have already cited from him. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and al-taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-jibt is the idols, and al-taghut is the one who stands before the idols and expresses lies about them to mislead the people." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-jibt is the name of Satan in Abyssinian, and al-taghut is the soothsayers of the Arabs." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom?﴾ that he said: "They have no share; and if they had a share, they would not give the people a naqir." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through multiple chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The naqir is the dot on the back of the pit."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The People of the Book said: 'Muhammad claims that he has been given what he has been given in humility, yet he has nine wives and his only aspiration is marriage. What kingdom is greater than this?' So God sent down this verse: ﴿Or do they envy the people﴾ to His saying: ﴿a great kingdom﴾, meaning the kingdom of Solomon." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "The 'people' in this place refers specifically to the Prophet." Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "They are this tribe of the Arabs."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 56–57:

His saying: "bi-ayatina" (with Our signs). The apparent meaning is that there is no specification of some signs over others. "Sawfa" (soon, shortly) is a word used for threat; so said Sibawayh. The sin (s) takes its place. The meaning of "nusli" has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. The intended meaning is: "We will make them enter a great fire." Humayd ibn Qays read "nasliihim" with a fatha on the nun.

His saying: ﴿Whenever their skins are roasted through﴾. It is said: "nada al-shay'u nudjan wa-nidajan" (the thing became ripe), "nada al-lahmu" (the meat became cooked), and "fulanun nadiju al-ra'y" (so-and-so is mature of opinion), i.e., its firm one. The meaning is: whenever their skins are burned, Allah replaces them with other skins, i.e., He gives them, in place of every burned skin, another skin that is not burned. This is more intense in punishment for the person, because his perception of the fire's effect on the skin that has not burned is more intense than his perception of its effect on the burned skin. It was said: the intended meaning of "skins" is the garments (sarabil) which He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their garments of tar﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. There is no reason to abandon the literal meaning here, although it is permissible to apply "skins" to garments figuratively, as in the saying of the poet:

"Meanness clothed Taym in green in their skins, so woe to Taym from their green garments."

It was said: the meaning is that We restored the first skin as new. But the meaning of replacement rejects that. His saying: ﴿that they may taste the punishment﴾: i.e., that the complete tasting may be realized for them through that replacement. It was also said its meaning is: that the punishment may remain for them and not cease.

Then He followed the description of the state of the disbelievers with the description of the state of the believers. The explanation of "the gardens beneath which rivers flow" has already been mentioned.

His saying: ﴿For them therein are purified spouses﴾: i.e., purified from the impurities found in the women of this world. "Zillun zalil" (dense shade): the thick one into which there does not enter what enters the shade of this world of heat, scorching wind, and the like. It was said: it is the collective shade of trees and palaces. It was said: "zillun zalil" is the lasting one which does not pass away; and the derivation of the adjective from the word of the described thing is for emphasis, as one says "laylun alil" (a very dark night).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Umar, regarding His saying: (p-308) ﴿Whenever their skins are roasted through﴾, that he said: "If their skins are burned, We replace them with white skins like parchments." Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted from him, with a weak chain, that he said: "It was recited in the presence of Umar: ﴿Whenever their skins are roasted through﴾, the verse. Mu'adh said: 'I have its explanation: it is replaced a hundred times in an hour.' Umar said: 'Thus did I hear it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted that the speaker was Ka'b, and that he said: it is replaced twenty and a hundred times in a single hour. Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that the thickness of the skin of the disbeliever is forty-two cubits. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His saying: ﴿a dense shade﴾ that he said: it is the shade of the Throne, which does not pass away.

This verse is one of the mother verses (ummahat al-ayat) that contain many rulings of the Sharia. The apparent meaning is that the address includes all people, in all trusts (amanat). It has been narrated from Ali, Zayd ibn Aslam and Shahr ibn Hawshab that the address is directed to the rulers of the Muslims. The first view is more apparent. That the verse was revealed on a particular occasion, as will come, does not negate the generality of its wording. The consideration is therefore given to the generality of the wording, not to the specificity of the occasion, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). The rulers enter this address first and foremost, so it is obligatory upon them to render the trusts they hold, to return wrongful seizures, and to seek justice in their judgments. Other people also enter the address, so it is obligatory upon them to return the trusts they hold, and to seek truthfulness in testimonies and reports. Among those who said that the address is general were al-Bara' ibn Azib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The majority of exegetes adopted this view, among them Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). They agreed that the trusts are to be returned to their owners, both the righteous among them and the wicked, as Ibn al-Mundhir said. The word amanat is the plural of amanah, and it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), i.e., "that which is entrusted."

His words: ﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾. That is: and Allah commands you, when you judge between people, that you judge with justice. Justice ('adl) is the just determination of a judgment according to what is in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). It is not judgment by mere opinion (ra'y mujarrad). Such judgment is not from the truth at all, except when no evidence for that judgment is found in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. In that case there is no harm in the judge exercising independent reasoning (ijtihad al-ra'y), provided he knows the ruling of Allah, the Exalted, and what is closest to the truth when there is no explicit text. As for the judge who does not know the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, nor what is closest to them, he does not know what justice is, because he does not comprehend the proof when it comes to him, let alone judge by it among the servants of Allah.

His words: "ni'imma ma" (how excellent is that which). It is either descriptive (mawsufah) or relative (mawsulah), and we have already discussed such matters.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah and took the keys of the Ka'bah from Uthman ibn Talhah, Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with the command to return the key. So the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned Uthman ibn Talhah, returned it to him, and recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that this verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Talhah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) took from him the key of the Ka'bah, then summoned him and handed it to him.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ali, who said: It is incumbent upon the ruler to judge by what Allah has revealed and to render the trust. When he does that, it is incumbent upon the people to listen to him, to obey him, and to respond when they are called.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." It is also established in the Sahih that: "Whoever betrays when he is entrusted, there is in him a characteristic of hypocrisy."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 59:

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded the judges and rulers, when they judge between people, to judge with truth, He then commanded the people to obey them here. Obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is complying with His commands and prohibitions, and obedience to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is in what he commanded and what he forbade.

"Those in authority" (ulu al-amr) are the imams, the sultans, the judges, and everyone who holds a legitimate authority (wilaya shar'iyya), not a tyrannical authority (wilaya taghutiyya). What is meant is obedience to them in what they command and forbid, so long as it is not sinful. There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to Allah, as has been established from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. Jabir ibn Abd Allah and Mujahid said: "Those in authority are the people of the Qur'an and knowledge," and this is also the view of Malik and al-Dahhak. It is narrated from Mujahid that they are the Companions of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. Ibn Kaysan said: "They are the people of intellect and opinion." The preferred view is the first.

His saying: ﴿Then if you dispute concerning anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Al-munazaʿa (dispute) is mutual pulling (al-mujadhaba), and al-nazʿ is pulling (al-jadhb), as though each party snatches at the other's argument and draws it toward himself. What is meant is disagreement and contention. The apparent sense of His saying "concerning anything" covers the affairs of religion and of the world, but since He said "refer it back to Allah and the Messenger," it becomes clear that the matter in dispute is restricted to the affairs of religion, not the affairs of worldly life. Referring back to Allah is referring back to His Mighty Book, and referring back to the Messenger is referring back to his purified Sunnah after his death; during his lifetime, referring to him means asking him. This is the meaning of referring back to both. It has been said that the meaning of referring back is to say "Allah knows best," but this is a fallen view and a cold interpretation. The referring back in this verse is none other than the referring mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who draw conclusions from it among them would have known it﴾ [al-Nisa: 83].

His saying: ﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ contains evidence that this referring back is obligatory upon those in dispute, and that it is the characteristic of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day. The indication in His saying "that" refers to the referring back commanded: ﴿That is better for you and more excellent in outcome﴾. Ta'wil here means outcome or return, from awala, yaulu, meaning "to come to such-and-such," i.e., to arrive at it. The meaning is that this referring back is better for you and a more excellent destination to which you return. It is also possible that the meaning is that referring back is a more excellent interpretation (ta'wil) than your own interpretation to which you resort when disputing.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ (p-309), that he said: it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa ibn Qays ibn Adi, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, sent him in a military expedition (sariyya), and his story is well known. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ata regarding the verse, he said: obedience to Allah and the Messenger is following the Book and the Sunnah, and "those in authority" are "those of understanding and knowledge."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayra that he said: ﴿Those in authority among you﴾ are the commanders, and in another wording: they are the commanders of the expeditions. Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah regarding His saying: ﴿And those in authority among you﴾, that he said: they are the people of knowledge. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn Jarir also narrated from Abu al-Aliya something similar. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿Then if you dispute concerning anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾, that he said: "To the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger." Then he recited: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who draw conclusions from it among them would have known it﴾ [al-Nisa: 83]. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran regarding the verse, he said: "Referring back to Allah is referring back to His Book, and referring back to His Messenger is while he is alive; when he has passed away, it is to his Sunnah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada and al-Suddi something similar. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿That is better and more excellent in interpretation﴾, that he said: "That is more excellent in reward and better in consequence."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And more excellent in interpretation﴾, that he said: "And more excellent in recompense."

Many hadiths have come concerning obedience to rulers, established in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, restricted to the condition that it be in what is right (al-ma'ruf), and that there is no obedience in disobedience to Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 4, verses 60–65:

His saying, ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾: this is an expression of wonder directed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning the state of those who claimed for themselves that they had combined faith in what was sent down to the Messenger of God, namely the Qur'an, and in what was sent down to the prophets before him. Yet they did something that refutes this claim against them, invalidates it at its root, and makes clear that they had no part of it at all: they wished to have their disputes judged by the *taghut* (false authority, idol, or transgressor). They had been commanded, in what was sent down to the Messenger of God and to those before him, to reject it. The explanation of the reason for the revelation of the verse will come, and through it its meaning becomes clear. The exegesis of *taghut* and the disagreement over its meaning have already been mentioned.

His saying, ﴿And Satan wishes﴾: this is conjoined with his saying "they wish," and both sentences are brought to explain the object of the wonder, as if it were said: "What do they do?" Then it was said: "They wish such-and-such, and Satan wishes such-and-such." His saying, *ḍalālan* (going far astray), is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the mentioned verb with its extra letters removed, like His saying: ﴿And God caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾. Or it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb indicated by the mentioned verb, and the sense is: "Satan wishes to lead them astray, so that they go astray with a going astray."

﴿When it is said to them, "Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾ *Ṣudūd* (aversion) is a noun functioning as a verbal noun; according to al-Khalil it is *al-ṣadd* (turning away), while according to the Kufans they are two verbal nouns. That is, they turn away from you with turning away.

His saying, ﴿How then, when a calamity befalls them because of what their hands have sent ahead﴾: this explains the outcome of their affair and what their state comes to. That is, how will their condition be ﴿when a calamity befalls them﴾, that is, at the time it befalls them? For they will be unable at that time and will not be able to repel it.

What is meant by ﴿what their hands have sent ahead﴾ is the acts of disobedience they committed, among which is their seeking judgment from the *taghut*. Then they came to you swearing oaths, making excuses for their conduct. This is conjoined to "befalls them," and his saying "swearing" (*yaḥlifūn*) is a circumstantial clause: they came to you while swearing. ﴿We desired nothing but good and conciliation﴾: that is, by our seeking judgment from other than you we desired only good, not harm, and conciliation between the two parties, not opposition to you. Ibn Kaysan said: its meaning is "We desired nothing but justice and truth," like His saying: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We desired only the best"﴾ [al-Tawba: 107].

Then God gave the lie to them by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows﴾, namely the hypocrisy and enmity toward the truth in them. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that God has indeed known that they are hypocrites. ﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, from punishing them; it was also said: from accepting their excuse. ﴿And admonish them﴾: that is, frighten them away from hypocrisy. ﴿And speak to them in their own selves﴾: that is, concerning their own persons. It was also said that its meaning is: speak to them privately, with no one else present, ﴿a far-reaching word﴾, that is, one that reaches its aim in their admonition and has an effect upon them. This is by threatening them with the shedding of their blood, the taking of their women captive, and the seizing of their property.

﴿And We sent no messenger﴾: here *min* is a superfluous particle for emphasis, ﴿except to be obeyed by God's leave﴾ in what he commanded and forbade, ﴿by His knowledge﴾. It was also said: by His enabling. ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ by abandoning obedience to you and seeking judgment from others, ﴿they had come to you, seeking your intercession, and asked forgiveness of God for their sins, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Oft-Returning and Merciful﴾. That is, they would have found Him abundantly accepting their repentance and showing mercy to them. His saying, ﴿they had come to you﴾, is in the manner of *iltifāt* (a shift of grammatical person), with the aim of magnifying the status of the Messenger (ﷺ). And His saying, ﴿and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾, is in the same manner, with the same aim.

His saying: ﴿So no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾.

Ibn Jarir said: His saying "so no" is a response to what was mentioned before. Its sense is: "The matter is not as they claim, that they have believed in what was sent down to you and what was sent down before you." Then He began the oath with His saying: ﴿By your Lord, they do not believe﴾. It was also said that He placed *lā* (no) before the oath to give emphasis to the negation and to show its strength, then repeated it after the oath for confirmation. It was also said that *lā* is superfluous, to emphasize the meaning of the oath and not the meaning of negation, and the sense is: "By your Lord, they do not believe," as in His saying: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75].

Or it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb indicated by the mentioned verb, and the sense is: "Satan wishes to lead them astray, so that they go astray with a going astray."

That is, how will their condition be ﴿when a calamity befalls them﴾, that is, at the time it befalls them? For they will be unable at that time and will not be able to repel it.

What is meant by ﴿what their hands have sent ahead﴾ is the acts of disobedience they committed, among which is their seeking judgment from the *taghut*. Then God gave the lie to them by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows﴾, namely the hypocrisy and enmity toward the truth in them. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that God has indeed known that they are hypocrites. ﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, from punishing them; it was also said: from accepting their excuse. ﴿And admonish them﴾: that is, frighten them away from hypocrisy. ﴿And speak to them in their own selves﴾: that is, concerning their own persons. It was also said that its meaning is: speak to them privately, with no one else present, ﴿a far-reaching word﴾, that is, one that reaches its aim in their admonition and has an effect upon them. This is by threatening them with the shedding of their blood, the taking of their women captive, and the seizing of their property.

﴿And We sent no messenger﴾: here *min* is a superfluous particle for emphasis, ﴿except to be obeyed by God's leave﴾ in what he commanded and forbade, ﴿by His knowledge﴾. It was also said: by His enabling. ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ by abandoning obedience to you and seeking judgment from others, ﴿they had come to you, seeking your intercession, and asked forgiveness of God for their sins, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Oft-Returning and Merciful﴾. That is, they would have found Him abundantly accepting their repentance and showing mercy to them. His saying, ﴿they had come to you﴾, is in the manner of *iltifāt* (a shift of grammatical person), with the aim of magnifying the status of the Messenger (ﷺ). And His saying, ﴿and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾, is in the same manner, with the same aim.

His saying: ﴿So no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾.

Its sense is: "The matter is not as they claim, that they have believed in what was sent down to you and what was sent down before you." Then He began the oath with His saying: ﴿By your Lord, they do not believe﴾. It was also said that He placed *lā* (no) before the oath to give emphasis to the negation and to show its strength, then repeated it after the oath for confirmation. It was also said that its meaning is "they bring their disputes to you," and there is no compulsion for that. ﴿In what is in dispute among them﴾: that is, what has become disputed and confused among them.
