That is, how will their condition be ﴿when a calamity befalls them﴾, that is, at the time it befalls them? For they will be unable at that time and will not be able to repel it.

What is meant by ﴿what their hands have sent ahead﴾ is the acts of disobedience they committed, among which is their seeking judgment from the *taghut*. Then they came to you swearing oaths, making excuses for their conduct. This is conjoined to "befalls them," and his saying "swearing" (*yaḥlifūn*) is a circumstantial clause: they came to you while swearing. ﴿We desired nothing but good and conciliation﴾: that is, by our seeking judgment from other than you we desired only good, not harm, and conciliation between the two parties, not opposition to you. Ibn Kaysan said: its meaning is "We desired nothing but justice and truth," like His saying: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We desired only the best"﴾ [al-Tawba: 107].

Then God gave the lie to them by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows﴾, namely the hypocrisy and enmity toward the truth in them. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that God has indeed known that they are hypocrites. ﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, from punishing them; it was also said: from accepting their excuse. ﴿And admonish them﴾: that is, frighten them away from hypocrisy. ﴿And speak to them in their own selves﴾: that is, concerning their own persons. It was also said that its meaning is: speak to them privately, with no one else present, ﴿a far-reaching word﴾, that is, one that reaches its aim in their admonition and has an effect upon them. This is by threatening them with the shedding of their blood, the taking of their women captive, and the seizing of their property.

﴿And We sent no messenger﴾: here *min* is a superfluous particle for emphasis, ﴿except to be obeyed by God's leave﴾ in what he commanded and forbade, ﴿by His knowledge﴾. It was also said: by His enabling. ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ by abandoning obedience to you and seeking judgment from others, ﴿they had come to you, seeking your intercession, and asked forgiveness of God for their sins, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Oft-Returning and Merciful﴾. That is, they would have found Him abundantly accepting their repentance and showing mercy to them. His saying, ﴿they had come to you﴾, is in the manner of *iltifāt* (a shift of grammatical person), with the aim of magnifying the status of the Messenger (ﷺ). And His saying, ﴿and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾, is in the same manner, with the same aim.

His saying: ﴿So no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾.

Ibn Jarir said: His saying "so no" is a response to what was mentioned before. Its sense is: "The matter is not as they claim, that they have believed in what was sent down to you and what was sent down before you." Then He began the oath with His saying: ﴿By your Lord, they do not believe﴾. It was also said that He placed *lā* (no) before the oath to give emphasis to the negation and to show its strength, then repeated it after the oath for confirmation. It was also said that *lā* is superfluous, to emphasize the meaning of the oath and not the meaning of negation, and the sense is: "By your Lord, they do not believe," as in His saying: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75].

﴿Until they make you judge﴾: that is, they make you an arbiter between them in all their affairs, not making anyone other than you judge. It was also said that its meaning is "they bring their disputes to you," and there is no compulsion for that. ﴿In what is in dispute among them﴾: that is, what has become disputed and confused among them. From this comes *al-shajar* (tree), because of the interlacing of its branches. From this is the verse of Tarafa:

*And they are the judges, the lords of guidance, and the mediators of people in matters of dispute (al-shajar).*

That is, the disputed matter. From this also comes *tashājur al-rimāḥ* (the interlocking of spears), that is, their clashing. ﴿Then they find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾: it was said this is conjoined to an implied element to which the speech leads: that is, "You judge between them, then they find no discomfort." *Ḥaraj* means constriction; it was also said to mean doubt. From it comes the phrase for a thick-clustered tree: *ḥaraj* and *ḥarijah*, whose plural is *ḥirāj*. It was also said that *ḥaraj* means sin, that is, they find within themselves no sin in rejecting what you have decided. ﴿And submit in full submission﴾: that is, they yield to your command and judgment with a yielding in which they do not oppose it in anything. Al-Zajjaj said: *taslīman* (full submission) is an emphatic verbal noun, that is, they submit to your ruling with a submission in which they introduce into themselves no doubt or ambiguity regarding it.

The apparent meaning is that this encompasses every individual in every ruling, as His saying supports: ﴿And We sent no messenger except to be obeyed by God's leave﴾. As for after his death, it is the judgment by the Book and the Sunna, and the judgment of a judge by what is in them, from among the imams and qadis, provided he does not judge by mere opinion when there is evidence in the Book and the Sunna or in one of them, and provided he understands what is presented to him of the proofs of the Book and the Sunna. That means he must know the Arabic language and what relates to it of grammar, morphology, meanings, and rhetoric, be acquainted with what is needed of the science of the fundamentals (*uṣūl*), be discerning in the purified Sunna, distinguish between the authentic and what resembles it and the weak and what resembles it, be fair and not partisan to any school of thought or any sect, and be pious, not deviating or inclining in his judgment. Whoever is like this stands in the station of prophethood, conveying it and judging by its rulings.

In this severe warning there is that which makes the skins shudder and the hearts tremble. For first He swore by Himself, confirming this oath with the particle of negation, that they do not believe. He negated from them faith, which is the capital of the righteous servants of God, until the goal is attained which is their making the Messenger of God (ﷺ) judge. Then God did not suffice with that, but said: ﴿Then they find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾, adding to judgment another matter, which is the absence of constriction, that is, constriction in their breasts. Mere judgment and submission are not sufficient unless it comes from the core of the heart, with contentment, tranquility, the calm of the heart, and the goodness of the soul. Then He did not suffice with all this, but added to it His saying "and submit," that is, yield and comply outwardly and inwardly. Then He did not suffice with that, but added to it the emphatic verbal noun, saying "in full submission." Thus faith is not established for a servant until this judgment occurs from him, he finds no constriction in his breast regarding what is decided against him, and he submits to the judgment and law of God, with a submission that is not mixed with rejection and is not tainted by opposition.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted, with a chain which al-Suyuti said is sound, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Barzah al-Aslami was a soothsayer who judged between the Jews in matters over which they disputed. Some Muslims went to him to dispute, so God revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: Al-Jullas ibn al-Samit, before his repentance, and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and Rafi' ibn Zayd, were claiming to be Muslims. Men from their own people who were Muslims invited them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning a dispute that was between them. But they invited them to the soothsayers, the judges of the Jahiliyya, so the aforementioned verse was revealed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿They wish to seek judgment from the *taghut*﴾, he said: The *taghut* was a man of the Jews called Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. When they were called to what God had sent down and to the Messenger to judge between them, they would say: "Rather, we will bring our dispute to Ka'b." So the verse was revealed. Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Dahhak a similar report.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others transmitted from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that: al-Zubayr disputed with a man of the Ansar who had witnessed Badr with the Prophet (ﷺ), before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), concerning water channels from the *harra* (lava field), with which both of them irrigated palm trees. The Ansari said: "Let the water flow through." But he refused. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then send the water to your neighbour." The Ansari became angry and said: "O Messenger of God, is he the son of your aunt?" The face of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) changed color, then he said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold the water until it reaches the *jidr* (the bank or wall), then send the water to your neighbour." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had previously given the Zubayr a ruling in which he intended a broad allowance for him and for the Ansari. But when the Ansari provoked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he gave Zubayr his full right in an explicit judgment. Al-Zubayr said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿So no, by your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge in what is in dispute among them.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through Ibn Lahi'a from al-Aswad that the reason for the revelation of the verse was: two men brought a dispute before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he judged between them. The one against whom judgment was given said: "Send us back to Umar." So he sent them back. Umar killed the one who had said "send us back," and the verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) nullified the blood of the slain man.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted it in *Nawadir al-Usul* from Makhul, mentioning something similar, and clarified that the one whom Umar killed was a hypocrite. Both are *mursal* reports (with a missing companion in the chain), the narrative is strange, and Ibn Lahi'a has weakness in it.

(p-311) "Law" (لَوْ) is a particle of negation of consequence (ḥarf imtināʿ), and "an" (أنْ) is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah) or an explanatory particle (tafsiriyyah), since kataba ("He prescribed") here carries the sense of amara ("He commanded"). The meaning is: if Allah, glorified is He, had prescribed killing and expulsion from homes upon these existing Jews, only a few of them would have done it; or, if He had prescribed that upon the Muslims, only a few of them would have done it. The pronoun in His saying "fa'alūhu" ("they did it") refers either to the thing prescribed that is indicated by "kataba" (we prescribed), or to the killing and expulsion indicated by the two verbs. The singular pronoun in such a context has been explained earlier. As for His saying "illā qalīlun" ("except a few"), the majority of readers recite it in the nominative (rafʿ) as a substitute (badal). ʿAbdullah ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recite "illā qalīlan" in the accusative (naṣb) as an exception (istithnāʾ), and it is so in the codices of the people of Syria; but the nominative is better according to the grammarians (nuḥāh).

His saying: "Wa law annahum fa'alū mā yūʿaẓūna bihi" ("And if they had done what they were admonished with") — namely, following the Law and submitting to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — "la-kāna dhālika khayran lahum fi l-dunyā wa l-ākhirah" ("that would have been better for them in this world and the Hereafter"), "wa ashadda tathbītan" ("and firmer in establishing them"), meaning that their feet would be steadfast upon the truth, so they would not waver regarding the matter of their religion.

"Wa idhan" means: at the time of their doing what they are admonished with. "La-ātaynāhum min ladunnā ajran ʿaẓīman wa la-hadaynāhum ṣirāṭan mustaqīman" ("We would have given them from Us a great reward and guided them to a straight path") with no crookedness in it, so that they would reach the good that is attained by one who complies with what he was commanded and submits to whoever calls him to the truth.

His saying: "Wa man yuṭiʿi llāha wa l-rasūla" ("And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger") is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf) explaining the excellence of obedience to Allah and the Messenger. The reference in His saying "fa-ulā'ika" ("then those") is to the obedient, as is conveyed by "maʿa lladhīna anʿama llāhu ʿalayhim" ("with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor") — by entering Paradise and attaining what Allah has prepared for them. "Al-ṣiddīq" is one who is intensive in truthfulness, as the form indicates; it is said that they are the excellent followers of the prophets.

"Al-shuhadāʾ" are those for whom martyrdom is established, and "al-ṣāliḥūn" are the people of righteous deeds. "Al-rafīq" is derived from "al-rifq," which is gentleness of the side, and what is meant by it is the companion whose company you find advantage in; from it comes "al-rufqah" (company of travelers), for some of them benefit from others. It is in the accusative either as a specification (tamyīz) or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), as al-Akhfash said.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid regarding His saying: "Wa law annā katabnā ʿalayhim an uqtulū anfusakum" ("Had We prescribed for them: kill yourselves"): they are the Jews, just as He commanded the companions of Moses to kill one another. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sufyān that it was revealed concerning Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from al-Suddī something similar. It has been narrated through several chains that a group of the Companions said when this verse was revealed: "If our Lord had done it, we would have done it." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted it from al-Ḥasan. Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted it from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and also from Shurayḥ ibn ʿUbayd. Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilyah, and al-Ḍiyāʾ al-Maqdisī in Ṣifat al-Jannah (and he graded it ḥasan), transmitted from ʿĀ'ishah, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than myself, you are dearer to me than my children, and when I am at home I remember you and I cannot be patient until I come and look at you. But when I remember my death and your death, and I know that when you enter Paradise you will be raised with the prophets, and that if I enter Paradise I fear I will not see you" — and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not answer him until Jibrīl descended with this verse: "And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor..." — the verse." Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from Ibn ʿAbbās.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 71–76:**

His words, "O you who have believed": this is an address to the sincere believers, and a command to them to fight the disbelievers and to set out in the way of Allah. *Al-ḥadhar* (caution) and *al-ḥidhr* are two forms, like *al-mathal* and *al-mithl*. Al-Farra' said: "Most usage is *al-ḥidhr*. *Al-ḥadhar* is also attested, as in the saying *khudh ḥadharaka*, meaning 'take your precaution', i.e. 'be cautious'." It was also said that the meaning of the verse is a command to them to take up weapons as a precaution, because weapons are the means of caution.

His words, "*fa-nfirū*" (then go forth): *nafara* (to set out), *yanfiru*, with the vowel of the *fā'* in the past tense being *kasra*, *nafīran*. *Nafarat al-dābba* (the animal bolted), *tanfuru*, with a *ḍamma* on the *fā'*, *nufūran*.

The meaning: rise up to fight the enemy. Alternatively, *al-nafīr* is a term for the people who go forth. Its root is from *al-nifār* and *al-nufūr*, which means alarm or fright. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turned their backs in flight, repelling﴾ [al-Isrā' 46], meaning: fleeing.

His words, "*thubāt*" (in groups): it is the plural of *thubah*, meaning a company. The meaning is: go forth in scattered companies. His words, "*aw infirū jamī'an*" (or go forth all together): meaning, gathered together as one army. The meaning of the verse is a command to them to go forth in one of the two ways, so that this is more severe upon their enemy and so that they are safe from the enemy snatching them away, when each one of them goes forth alone or something similar. It was said that this verse is abrogated (*mansūkha*, subject to naskh, i.e. abrogation) by His words: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah 41], and by His words: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ [al-Tawbah 39]. The correct view is that both verses are muḥkam (definitive, not abrogated): the one applies at the time when the whole body is needed to go forth, and the other applies when going forth by a part is sufficient without the rest.

His words, "*wa-inna minkum la-man la-yubaṭṭi'anna*" (and indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind): *al-tabṭi'a* and *al-ibṭā'* mean delay. The intended ones are the hypocrites, who used to hold back from going out and would make others hold back. The meaning: among your intimates, your kind, and those who showed their faith to you while being hypocrites, is one who delays the believers and discourages them. The *lām* in His words *la-man* is the *lām* of emphasis. In His words *la-yubaṭṭi'anna*, the *lām* is the *lām* of the answer to the oath, and *man* is in the accusative position, with the clause as its complement. Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and al-Kalbi read *la-yubṭi'anna* with the lightened form.

﴿So if a calamity strikes you﴾ from killing, defeat, or the loss of wealth, this hypocrite says: "Allah has favoured me in that I was not with them, so that what has struck them has not struck me." ﴿And if a bounty from Allah comes to you﴾ in the form of spoils or conquest, (p. 312) this hypocrite will certainly say, as a regretful envier would say: ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement."﴾

His words, "*ka-an lam takun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah*" (as if there had never been any affection between you and him): this is a parenthetical clause between the verb, which is *la-yaqūlanna* (will certainly say), and its object, which is *yā laytanī* (oh, I wish). It was also said that there is a transposition (*taqdīm wa-ta'khīr*) in the speech. It was said that the meaning is: "will certainly say, as if there had not been an agreement between you and him concerning jihad." It was also said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Ḥasan read *la-yaqūlu* with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, according to the sense of *man*. Ibn Kathir and Ḥafs from ‘Āṣim read *ka-an lam takun* with the *tā'*, according to the wording of *mawaddah*.

His words, "*fa-afūza*" (so that I would achieve): in the accusative, as the answer to the wish (*jawāb al-tamannī*). Al-Ḥasan read *fa-afūzu* with a *ḍamma*.

His words: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾. This is a command to the believers. He placed the adverbial phrase before the subject for emphasis. ﴿Those who sell﴾ means "those who exchange", and they are the believers. The *fā'* in His words *fa-l-yuqātil* (so let him fight) is the answer to an assumed condition: that is, if those previously mentioned, who were described as among them being one who will certainly lag behind, do not fight, then let the sincere ones fight, those who give up their souls and sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. Then He promised those who fight in the way of Allah that He will give them a great reward that cannot be measured. That is, if he is killed, he achieves martyrdom, which is the highest rank of reward. If he prevails and triumphs, he has the reward of one who fought in the way of Allah, along with what he has attained of elevation in this world and spoils. The apparent sense of this requires equality between the one who is killed as a martyr and the one who returns victorious. It may be said that the equality between them is only in the granting of the great reward, and it does not follow that their reward is equal, for being great is one of the relative matters, where something may be great in comparison to what is below it and small in comparison to what is above it.

His words: ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of Allah﴾: an address to the believers who were commanded to fight, by way of *iltifāt* (a shift of address). His words, "*wa-l-mustaḍ‘afīn*" (and the oppressed): it is in the genitive, being joined to the noble name, i.e. "why should you not fight in the way of Allah and in the way of the oppressed, until you free them from captivity and relieve them from the hardship they are in?"

It is permissible for it to be in the accusative by specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), i.e. "and I single out the oppressed, for they are among the greatest of what the way of Allah truly applies to." Al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari preferred the first. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "I prefer that the meaning be: 'and in (the cause of) the oppressed', so that it is joined to *al-sabīl* (the way)." The intended meaning of "the oppressed" here is those believers in Makkah who were under the humiliation of the disbelievers, and they are the ones for whom the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray, saying: "O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, and the oppressed among the believers," as is in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

It is not far-fetched to say that the wording of the verse is broader, and the consideration is the generality of the wording, were it not for its restriction by His words: ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers"﴾. This indicates that it is specific to the oppressed who were in Makkah, because the exegetes have agreed that the intended "town whose people are wrongdoers" is Makkah. His words: ﴿of the men and the women and the children﴾ are an explanation of "the oppressed".

His words: ﴿Those who believed fight in the way of Allah﴾: this is an encouragement for the believers and an incitement to them that their fighting is for this purpose and not for any other. ﴿And those who disbelieved fight in the way of the *ṭāghūt*﴾, i.e. the way of Satan, or the soothsayers, or the idols. Interpreting *al-ṭāghūt* here as Satan is preferable, because of His words: ﴿So fight the allies of Satan; indeed, the plan of Satan is ever weak﴾, i.e. his scheming and the scheming of those disbelievers who followed him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning His words, ﴿go forth in groups﴾, that he said: "*ʿuṣub* (bands), meaning separate detachments," ﴿or go forth all together﴾, meaning: all of you.

Abu Dawud in his *Nāsikh* (book on abrogation), and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from him that he said, concerning Surah al-Nisa': ﴿Take your precaution, then go forth in groups or go forth all together﴾ was abrogated by ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah 122].

‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His words, "*thubāt*": "that is, small groups." Qatada related concerning His words, ﴿or go forth all together﴾: "that is, when the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) goes forth, no one may remain behind him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from al-Suddi. ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾ up to His words: ﴿then We will give him a great reward﴾, that everything in between is about the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan concerning the verse, that he said: "It is, as we have been informed, ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the leader of the hypocrites."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His words, "*fa-l-yuqātil*": "that is, let him fight the polytheists in the way of Allah, in obedience to Allah." ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed﴾: that is, the enemy kills him, ﴿or triumphs﴾: that is, he prevails over the enemy among the polytheists, ﴿then We will give him a great reward﴾: that is, an abundant recompense in Paradise. Thus he made the one who is killed and the one who survives among the Muslims in fighting the polytheists equal partners in the reward.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning His words, ﴿in the way of Allah and of the oppressed﴾, that he said: "And in (the cause of) the oppressed." Ibn Jarir related from al-Zuhri that he said: "And the way of the oppressed." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, by way of al-‘Awfi, that he said: "The oppressed are Muslim people who were in Makkah and could not leave it." al-Bukhari related from him that he said: "I and my mother are among the oppressed." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "The town whose people are wrongdoers is Makkah." Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from ‘Ā’ishah.

‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas that he said: "If you see Satan, do not fear him, but charge at him." ﴿Indeed, the plan of Satan is ever weak﴾. Mujahid said: "Satan used to appear to me during prayer, so I would remember the saying of Ibn ‘Abbas and charge at him, and he would leave me."

It was also said that the meaning of the verse is a command to them to take up weapons as a precaution, because weapons are the means of caution.

His words, "*fa-nfirū*" (then go forth): *nafara* (to set out), *yanfiru*, with the vowel of the *fā'* in the past tense being *kasra*, *nafīran*. *Nafarat al-dābba* (the animal bolted), *tanfuru*, with a *ḍamma* on the *fā'*, *nufūran*.

The meaning: rise up to fight the enemy. Alternatively, *al-nafīr* is a term for the people who go forth. Its root is from *al-nifār* and *al-nufūr*, which means alarm or fright. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turned their backs in flight, repelling﴾ [al-Isrā' 46], meaning: fleeing.

His words, "*thubāt*" (in groups): it is the plural of *thubah*, meaning a company. The meaning is: go forth in scattered companies. His words, "*aw infirū jamī'an*" (or go forth all together): meaning, gathered together as one army. The meaning of the verse is a command to them to go forth in one of the two ways, so that this is more severe upon their enemy and so that they are safe from the enemy snatching them away, when each one of them goes forth alone or something similar. It was said that this verse is abrogated (*mansūkha*, subject to naskh, i.e. abrogation) by His words: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah 41], and by His words: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ [al-Tawbah 39]. The correct view is that both verses are muḥkam (definitive, not abrogated): the one applies at the time when the whole body is needed to go forth, and the other applies when going forth by a part is sufficient without the rest.

His words, "*wa-inna minkum la-man la-yubaṭṭi'anna*" (and indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind): *al-tabṭi'a* and *al-ibṭā'* mean delay. The intended ones are the hypocrites, who used to hold back from going out and would make others hold back. The meaning: among your intimates, your kind, and those who showed their faith to you while being hypocrites, is one who delays the believers and discourages them. The *lām* in His words *la-man* is the *lām* of emphasis. In His words *la-yubaṭṭi'anna*, the *lām* is the *lām* of the answer to the oath, and *man* is in the accusative position, with the clause as its complement. Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and al-Kalbi read *la-yubṭi'anna* with the lightened form.

﴿So if a calamity strikes you﴾ from killing, defeat, or the loss of wealth, this hypocrite says: "Allah has favoured me in that I was not with them, so that what has struck them has not struck me." ﴿And if a bounty from Allah comes to you﴾ in the form of spoils or conquest, (p. 312) this hypocrite will certainly say, as a regretful envier would say: ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement."﴾

His words, "*ka-an lam takun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah*" (as if there had never been any affection between you and him): this is a parenthetical clause between the verb, which is *la-yaqūlanna* (will certainly say), and its object, which is *yā laytanī* (oh, I wish). It was also said that there is a transposition (*taqdīm wa-ta'khīr*) in the speech. It was said that the meaning is: "will certainly say, as if there had not been an agreement between you and him concerning jihad." It was also said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Ḥasan read *la-yaqūlu* with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, according to the sense of *man*. Ibn Kathir and Ḥafs from ‘Āṣim read *ka-an lam takun* with the *tā'*, according to the wording of *mawaddah*.

His words, "*fa-afūza*" (so that I would achieve): in the accusative, as the answer to the wish (*jawāb al-tamannī*). Al-Ḥasan read *fa-afūzu* with a *ḍamma*.

His words: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾. This is a command to the believers. He placed the adverbial phrase before the subject for emphasis. ﴿Those who sell﴾ means "those who exchange", and they are the believers. The apparent sense of this requires equality between the one who is killed as a martyr and the one who returns victorious. It may be said that the equality between them is only in the granting of the great reward, and it does not follow that their reward is equal, for being great is one of the relative matters, where something may be great in comparison to what is below it and small in comparison to what is above it.

The meaning: among your intimates, your kind, and those who showed their faith to you while being hypocrites, is one who delays the believers and discourages them. The *lām* in His words *la-man* is the *lām* of emphasis. In His words *la-yubaṭṭi'anna*, the *lām* is the *lām* of the answer to the oath, and *man* is in the accusative position, with the clause as its complement. Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and al-Kalbi read *la-yubṭi'anna* with the lightened form.

﴿So if a calamity strikes you﴾ from killing, defeat, or the loss of wealth, this hypocrite says: "Allah has favoured me in that I was not with them, so that what has struck them has not struck me." ﴿And if a bounty from Allah comes to you﴾ in the form of spoils or conquest, (p. 312) this hypocrite will certainly say, as a regretful envier would say: ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement."﴾

His words, "*ka-an lam takun baynakum wa-baynahu mawaddah*" (as if there had never been any affection between you and him): this is a parenthetical clause between the verb, which is *la-yaqūlanna* (will certainly say), and its object, which is *yā laytanī* (oh, I wish). It was also said that there is a transposition (*taqdīm wa-ta'khīr*) in the speech. It was said that the meaning is: "will certainly say, as if there had not been an agreement between you and him concerning jihad." It was also said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Ḥasan read *la-yaqūlu* with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, according to the sense of *man*. Ibn Kathir and Ḥafs from ‘Āṣim read *ka-an lam takun* with the *tā'*, according to the wording of *mawaddah*.

His words, "*fa-afūza*" (so that I would achieve): in the accusative, as the answer to the wish (*jawāb al-tamannī*). Al-Ḥasan read *fa-afūzu* with a *ḍamma*.

His words: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾. This is a command to the believers. He placed the adverbial phrase before the subject for emphasis. ﴿Those who sell﴾ means "those who exchange", and they are the believers. The *fā'* in His words *fa-l-yuqātil* (so let him fight) is the answer to an assumed condition: that is, if those previously mentioned, who were described as among them being one who will certainly lag behind, do not fight, then let the sincere ones fight, those who give up their souls and sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. Then He promised those who fight in the way of Allah that He will give them a great reward that cannot be measured. That is, if he is killed, he achieves martyrdom, which is the highest rank of reward. If he prevails and triumphs, he has the reward of one who fought in the way of Allah, along with what he has attained of elevation in this world and spoils. The apparent sense of this requires equality between the one who is killed as a martyr and the one who returns victorious. It may be said that the equality between them is only in the granting of the great reward, and it does not follow that their reward is equal, for being great is one of the relative matters, where something may be great in comparison to what is below it and small in comparison to what is above it.

His words: ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of Allah﴾: an address to the believers who were commanded to fight, by way of *iltifāt* (a shift of address). His words, "*wa-l-mustaḍ‘afīn*" (and the oppressed): it is in the genitive, being joined to the noble name, i.e. "why should you not fight in the way of Allah and in the way of the oppressed, until you free them from captivity and relieve them from the hardship they are in?"

It is permissible for it to be in the accusative by specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), i.e. "and I single out the oppressed, for they are among the greatest of what the way of Allah truly applies to." Al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari preferred the first. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "I prefer that the meaning be: 'and in (the cause of) the oppressed', so that it is joined to *al-sabīl* (the way)." The intended meaning of "the oppressed" here is those believers in Makkah who were under the humiliation of the disbelievers, and they are the ones for whom the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray, saying: "O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, and the oppressed among the believers," as is in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

It is not far-fetched to say that the wording of the verse is broader, and the consideration is the generality of the wording, were it not for its restriction by His words: ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers"﴾. This indicates that it is specific to the oppressed who were in Makkah, because the exegetes have agreed that the intended "town whose people are wrongdoers" is Makkah. His words: ﴿of the men and the women and the children﴾ are an explanation of "the oppressed".

His words: ﴿Those who believed fight in the way of Allah﴾: this is an encouragement for the believers and an incitement to them that their fighting is for this purpose and not for any other. ﴿And those who disbelieved fight in the way of the *ṭāghūt*﴾, i.e. the way of Satan, or the soothsayers, or the idols. Interpreting *al-ṭāghūt* here as Satan is preferable, because of His words: ﴿So fight the allies of Satan; indeed, the plan of Satan is ever weak﴾, i.e. his scheming and the scheming of those disbelievers who followed him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning His words, ﴿go forth in groups﴾, that he said: "*ʿuṣub* (bands), meaning separate detachments," ﴿or go forth all together﴾, meaning: all of you.

Abu Dawud in his *Nāsikh* (book on abrogation), and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from him that he said, concerning Surah al-Nisa': ﴿Take your precaution, then go forth in groups or go forth all together﴾ was abrogated by ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah 122].

‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His words, "*thubāt*": "that is, small groups." Qatada related concerning His words, ﴿or go forth all together﴾: "that is, when the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) goes forth, no one may remain behind him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from al-Suddi. ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾ up to His words: ﴿then We will give him a great reward﴾, that everything in between is about the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan concerning the verse, that he said: "It is, as we have been informed, ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the leader of the hypocrites."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His words, "*fa-l-yuqātil*": "that is, let him fight the polytheists in the way of Allah, in obedience to Allah." ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed﴾: that is, the enemy kills him, ﴿or triumphs﴾: that is, he prevails over the enemy among the polytheists, ﴿then We will give him a great reward﴾: that is, an abundant recompense in Paradise. Thus he made the one who is killed and the one who survives among the Muslims in fighting the polytheists equal partners in the reward.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning His words, ﴿in the way of Allah and of the oppressed﴾, that he said: "And in (the cause of) the oppressed." Ibn Jarir related from al-Zuhri that he said: "And the way of the oppressed." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, by way of al-‘Awfi, that he said: "The oppressed are Muslim people who were in Makkah and could not leave it." al-Bukhari related from him that he said: "I and my mother are among the oppressed." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "The town whose people are wrongdoers is Makkah." Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from ‘Ā’ishah.

‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas that he said: "If you see Satan, do not fear him, but charge at him." ﴿Indeed, the plan of Satan is ever weak﴾. Mujahid said: "Satan used to appear to me during prayer, so I would remember the saying of Ibn ‘Abbas and charge at him, and he would leave me."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 71–76:**

His words, "O you who have believed": this is an address to the sincere believers, and a command to them to fight the disbelievers and to set out in the way of Allah. *Al-ḥadhar* (caution) and *al-ḥidhr* are two forms, like *al-mathal* and *al-mithl*. Al-Farra' said: "Most usage is *al-ḥidhr*. *Al-ḥadhar* is also attested, as in the saying *khudh ḥadharaka*, meaning 'take your precaution', i.e. 'be cautious'." It was also said that the meaning of the verse is a command to them to take up weapons as a precaution, because weapons are the means of caution.

His words, "*fa-nfirū*" (then go forth): *nafara* (to set out), *yanfiru*, with the vowel of the *fā'* in the past tense being *kasra*, *nafīran*. *Nafarat al-dābba* (the animal bolted), *tanfuru*, with a *ḍamma* on the *fā'*, *nufūran*.

The meaning: rise up to fight the enemy. Alternatively, *al-nafīr* is a term for the people who go forth. Its root is from *al-nifār* and *al-nufūr*, which means alarm or fright. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turned their backs in flight, repelling﴾ [al-Isrā' 46], meaning: fleeing.

His words, "*thubāt*" (in groups): it is the plural of *thubah*, meaning a company. The meaning is: go forth in scattered companies. His words, "*aw infirū jamī'an*" (or go forth all together): meaning, gathered together as one army. The meaning of the verse is a command to them to go forth in one of the two ways, so that this is more severe upon their enemy and so that they are safe from the enemy snatching them away, when each one of them goes forth alone or something similar. It was said that this verse is abrogated (*mansūkha*, subject to naskh, i.e. abrogation) by His words: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah 41], and by His words: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ [al-Tawbah 39]. (p-313) His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands"?﴾ and the rest of the verse. It is said that they were a group of the Companions who were ordered to refrain from fighting in Makkah, after they had been hasty in seeking it. When fighting was prescribed for them in Madinah, they hung back from it, not out of doubt in the religion, but out of fear of death and dread of the terror of killing. It is also said that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, and it is said concerning the hypocrites who had embraced Islam before fighting was prescribed, and when it was prescribed they disliked it. This is closer to the context, given His saying: ﴿And they say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us to a near term."﴾ and His saying: ﴿And if a good thing befalls them...﴾ and the rest of the verse. But such conduct is unlikely to have come from the Companions.

His saying: ﴿as the fear of Allah﴾ is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., a fear like the fear of Allah. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., "you fear them resembling those who fear Allah," and the verbal noun is attached to its object, i.e., "like their fear of Allah."

His saying: ﴿or even more intense in fear﴾ is coordinated with "as the fear of Allah" in the position of a genitive. Or it is coordinated with the prepositional phrase as a whole, so that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause like the thing it is coordinated with. Or it is for classification (lil-tanwīʿ), in the sense that the fear of some of them is like the fear of Allah, and the fear of others is more intense than that.

His saying: ﴿And they say﴾ is coordinated with what is indicated by His saying "when a group of them..." i.e., "when fighting was prescribed for them, a group of them suddenly feared people as they fear Allah. And they said, 'Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us'," i.e., "Why did You not delay us?" They desired a respite to another time near the time at which fighting was prescribed for them. So He, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, and He said: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little"﴾, swift in its passing, not lasting for its companion. And the reward of the Hereafter is better for you than the little enjoyment, for those among you who are mindful (of Allah) and who desire the lasting reward. ﴿And you will not be wronged the least bit (fatīl)﴾, i.e., anything trivial and insignificant. The explanation of "fatīl" has already been given shortly before. And since your rewards are paid in full and not diminished in the least, how can you turn away from that and occupy yourselves with the enjoyment of this world, despite its scarcity and its cessation?

His saying: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ is an independent statement. In it is an exhortation for those who sat back from fighting out of fear of death, and a demonstration of the corruption of what has mixed with them of fear and penetrated them. For death, when it is certainly inevitable, then:

> Whoever does not die by the sword dies by other means.

"Al-burūj" is the plural of "burj," which is a high building. "Al-mushayyadah" means the lofty ones, from "shāda al-qaṣr" when he raised it and plastered it with "al-shīd," which is gypsum (jiṣṣ). The answer to "law lā" (even if) is omitted, because of what precedes it indicating it.

It has been disputed what these "burūj" are. It is said they are fortresses on the earth. It is said they are palaces. Al-Zajjāj and al-Qutaybī said: the meaning of "mushayyadah" is "elongated" (muṭawwalah). It is said its meaning is "plastered with al-shīd, which is gypsum." It is said the intended "burūj" are constructed towers in the lowest heaven, related by Makkī from Mālik, who said: "Do you not see His saying: ﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾ [al-Burūj: 1], ﴿He has placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqān: 61], ﴿And We have placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 16]?" It is also said that the intended "burūj al-mushayyadah" here are palaces of iron.

Ṭalḥah ibn Sulaymān read ﴿yudrikukumu al-mawt﴾ with a nominative (raf') according to the estimation of a "fā'" (so that it reads "fa-yudrikukum"), as in the saying of the poet:

> And their scout said, "Halt, let us try them (nuzāwiluhā)."

His saying: ﴿And if a good thing befalls them﴾. This and what follows is specific to the hypocrites; i.e., if a blessing befalls them, they attribute it to Allah, the Exalted, and if a trial and calamity befalls them, they attribute it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah refuted that claim against them with His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, it is not as you claim. Then He attributed them to ignorance and lack of understanding, saying: ﴿So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾, i.e., what has happened to them that they are like this?

His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾. This address is either to everyone among the people to whom it applies, or to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as an indirect address to his community. I.e., whatever abundance, ease, health, and safety befalls you is from Allah by His grace and mercy, and whatever hardship, affliction, or distress befalls you is from yourself, due to a sin you committed, for which you were punished. It is also said that this is from the statement of those who do not understand any statement; i.e., they say, "Whatever good befalls you is from Allah." It is also said that the interrogative alif is implied; i.e., "Is it from yourself?" A similar instance is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And is this a favour (of which) you remind me?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 22], meaning "Is that a favour?" A similar instance is His saying: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾ [al-Anʿām: 77], i.e., "Is this my Lord?" And from it is the saying of Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī:

> They shot at me and said, "O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,"
> but I replied, denying the faces, "They are they (hum hum)."

i.e., "Are they they?" This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The Noble Book has already included what conveys the same sense as this verse, such as His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shūrā: 30], and His saying: ﴿Why, when a disaster struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much, do you say, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 165].

It may be thought that His saying: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ contradicts His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, and His saying: ﴿And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 166], and His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 35], and His saying: ﴿And when Allah intends for a people harm, there is no averting it, and they have no protector besides Him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. But the matter is not so. Reconciliation is possible, as is established in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. In it is a clarification of the generality of his message (ﷺ) to all, as indicated by the emphasis by the verbal noun and the generality in "mankind." A similar instance is His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾ [Sabaʾ: 28], and His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 158], and ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 28] upon that.

His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. In it is that obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah. In this is an honouring of the nobility of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the exaltation of his station, and the elevation of his rank, beyond what can be measured or reached. I.e., whatever abundance, ease, health, and safety befalls you is from Allah by His grace and mercy, and whatever hardship, affliction, or distress befalls you is from yourself, due to a sin you committed, for which you were punished. It is also said that this is from the statement of those who do not understand any statement; i.e., they say, "Whatever good befalls you is from Allah." It is also said that the interrogative alif is implied; i.e., "Is it from yourself?" A similar instance is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And is this a favour (of which) you remind me?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 22], meaning "Is that a favour?" A similar instance is His saying: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾ [al-Anʿām: 77], i.e., "Is this my Lord?" And from it is the saying of Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī:

> They shot at me and said, "O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,"
> but I replied, denying the faces, "They are they (hum hum)."

i.e., "Are they they?" This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The Noble Book has already included what conveys the same sense as this verse, such as His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shūrā: 30], and His saying: ﴿Why, when a disaster struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much, do you say, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 165].

It may be thought that His saying: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ contradicts His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, and His saying: ﴿And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 166], and His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 35], and His saying: ﴿And when Allah intends for a people harm, there is no averting it, and they have no protector besides Him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. But the matter is not so. Reconciliation is possible, as is established in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. In it is a clarification of the generality of his message (ﷺ) to all, as indicated by the emphasis by the verbal noun and the generality in "mankind." A similar instance is His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾ [Sabaʾ: 28], and His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 158], and ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 28] upon that.

His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. In it is that obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah. In this is an honouring of the nobility of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the exaltation of his station, and the elevation of his rank, beyond what can be measured or reached. Its basis is that the Messenger commands only what Allah has commanded, and forbids only what Allah has forbidden. ﴿And whoever turns away﴾, i.e., turns away, ﴿then We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, i.e., a guardian of their deeds. Your duty is only to convey.

(p-314) It is said that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword (naskh, abrogation, i.e., the replacement of a ruling by a later one).

﴿And they say, "Obedience"﴾ is in the nominative (marfūʿ), as the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., "our affair is obedience," or "our concern is obedience." Al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī, and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim read it in the accusative as a verbal noun; i.e., "we obey with obedience." This is about the hypocrites according to the statement of most exegetes; i.e., they say when they are in your presence, ﴿"Obedience," but when they go out from your presence﴾, i.e., leave you, ﴿a group of them plots at night﴾, i.e., a group of these sayers devises other than what you tell them and command them, or other than what they tell you of obedience to you. It is also said its meaning is: they altered, changed, and distorted your word regarding what you had entrusted to them. "Al-tabyīt" is alteration, and from it is the poet's saying:

> They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they had plotted,
> and they had come to me with an abhorrent matter.

It is said: "The man plotted the matter" when he considered it at night. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they plot at night what He does not approve of in speech﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 108]. ﴿And Allah records what they plot﴾, i.e., He preserves it in the records of their deeds to recompense them for it. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that He sends it down to you in the Book.

His saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, i.e., leave them and their affair, until it becomes possible to take vengeance upon them. It is also said its meaning is: do not inform about their names. It is also said its meaning is: do not punish them. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him and trust in Him for victory over His enemy. It is said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbās that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and some of his companions came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Prophet of Allah, we were in honour while we were polytheists, and when we believed we became humiliated?" He said: "I have been commanded to pardon, so do not fight the people." When Allah transferred him to Madinah, He commanded him to fight, and they held back. So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands"?﴾ and the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatādah in the explanation of the verse something similar to this.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Mujāhid that it was revealed concerning the Jews.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related through al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿So when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a group of them﴾ and the verse, he said: Allah forbade this community from doing what they did.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Suddī concerning His saying "until a near term," he said: it is death. They both related something similar from Ibn Jurayj.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatādah concerning ﴿in towers well-built﴾, he said: in fortified palaces. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, who said: they are palaces in the sky. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related something similar from Sufyān. ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatādah concerning His saying: ﴿And if a good thing befalls them﴾, he says: a blessing; ﴿and if an evil befalls them﴾, he said: a calamity; ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, he said: the blessings and the calamities. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Abū al-ʿĀliyah concerning His saying: ﴿And if a good thing befalls them﴾, he said: this is in ease and hardship; and concerning His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾, he said: this is in good deeds and bad deeds.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, he says: good and evil are both from Allah. As for good, He bestowed it upon you; and as for evil, He tested you with it. And concerning His saying: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you﴾, he said: what befell him on the day of Uḥud, that his face was wounded and his front tooth broken. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related through al-ʿAwfī from him concerning His saying: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, he said: this is the day of Uḥud; he says: whatever calamity came was because of your sin, and I decreed that. Ibn al-Mundhir related through Mujāhid that Ibn ʿAbbās used to recite: "And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself, and I have written it against you." Mujāhid said: and so is the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd. Ibn al-Anbārī related something like Mujāhid's statement in the Maṣāḥif (codices). Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related through al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿And they say, "Obedience"﴾, he said: they are people who used to say in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "We believe in Allah and His Messenger," so that they would be safe for their blood and property. But when they went out from the presence of the Messenger of Allah, ﴿a group of them plotted﴾, he said: they opposed what they had said in his presence, so Allah reproached them. Ibn Jarīr related from him: those people altered what the Prophet (ﷺ) had said.

The hamza in His words "Do they not then reflect (أفَلا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ)" is for rebuke, and the fa' (الفاءُ) is coordinating with an implied clause, meaning: "Do they then turn away from the Qur'an and not reflect upon it?" It is said: "I contemplated (تَدَبَّرْتُ) the matter," meaning I considered its outcome and examined it. Then the word was used for every kind of careful consideration. Tadbir (التَّدْبِيرُ) means that a person arranges his affair as though he is looking at where its outcome will lead. This verse, and His words, "Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?" [Muhammad: 24], indicate the obligation to reflect upon the Qur'an so that its meaning may be known.

The meaning is: if they had reflected upon it as it deserves, they would have found it harmonious and free of discord, sound in its meanings, strong in its structure, and reaching the highest degree of eloquence. "Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy": that is, variation and contradiction. This does not include the differences in the lengths of verses and surahs, because what is meant is contradictory discrepancy and lack of conformity with reality. This is the nature of human speech, especially when it is long and its speaker ventures into reporting the unseen, for then little of it, rare as it is, will be correct and conform to reality.

His words: "When there comes to them some matter of security or fear, they spread it abroad." It is said: adhā'a al-shay' and adhā'a bihi (أذاعَ الشَّيْءَ وأذاعَ بِهِ) when one disseminates and reveals it. These people were a group of the weaker Muslims who, when they heard something of the affairs of the Muslims that carried security, such as the victory of the Muslims and the killing of their enemy, or that carried fear, such as the defeat of the Muslims and their being killed, would spread it, thinking that there was no harm for them in doing so.

His words: "But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them" (p-315): these are the people of knowledge and sound intellect whom they consult in their affairs, or they are the rulers over them, "those among them who would have known it who can investigate it": that is, who would extract it through their reflection and the soundness of their minds.

The meaning is: if they had left off spreading news until the Prophet (ﷺ) himself was the one to disseminate it, or until those in authority among them were the ones who handled it, because they know what should be spread and what should be concealed. Istinbat (الِاسْتِنْباطُ) is derived from istanbaṭtu al-mā' (اسْتَنْبَطْتُ الماءَ), meaning when you extract water.

Al-nabaṭ (النَّبَطُ) is the water that is first extracted when a well is dug. It is also said that these weak people used to hear the rumours of the hypocrites against the Muslims and spread them, so that harm resulted.

His words: "Had it not been for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few." That is: had it not been for what Allah graciously bestowed upon you by sending His Messenger and sending down His Book, you would have followed Satan and remained in your disbelief, except for a few of you. Or: except for a few followers among you. It is also said that the meaning is: they spread it, except for a few of them who did not spread it and did not disclose it. This was said by al-Kisā'ī, al-Akhfash, al-Farrā', Abū 'Ubayda, Abū Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr. It is also said that the meaning is: "those who would have known it who can investigate it, except for a few of them," as said by al-Zajjāj.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported from Qatāda regarding "Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy," that he said: the word of Allah does not differ; it is true and contains no falsehood, whereas the words of people do differ.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Muslim and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported through the chain of Ibn ʿAbbās from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) withdrew from his wives, I entered the mosque and found people striking pebbles with stones and saying: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives." So I stood at the door of the mosque and called out at the top of my voice: "He has not divorced his wives." Then this verse was revealed: "When there comes to them some matter of security or fear, they spread it abroad. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who would have known it who can investigate it would have known it." So I was the one who had investigated that matter.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim has reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding "When there comes to them," that he said: they are the people of hypocrisy. Ibn Jarīr has reported the same from Abū Muʿādh.

His words: "But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them" (p-315): these are the people of knowledge and sound intellect whom they consult in their affairs, or they are the rulers over them, "those among them who would have known it who can investigate it": that is, who would extract it through their reflection and the soundness of their minds.

The meaning is: if they had left off spreading news until the Prophet (ﷺ) himself was the one to disseminate it, or until those in authority among them were the ones who handled it, because they know what should be spread and what should be concealed. Istinbat (الِاسْتِنْباطُ) is derived from istanbaṭtu al-mā' (اسْتَنْبَطْتُ الماءَ), meaning when you extract water.

Al-nabaṭ (النَّبَطُ) is the water that is first extracted when a well is dug. It is also said that these weak people used to hear the rumours of the hypocrites against the Muslims and spread them, so that harm resulted.

His words: "Had it not been for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few." That is: had it not been for what Allah graciously bestowed upon you by sending His Messenger and sending down His Book, you would have followed Satan and remained in your disbelief, except for a few of you. Or: except for a few followers among you. It is also said that the meaning is: they spread it, except for a few of them who did not spread it and did not disclose it. This was said by al-Kisā'ī, al-Akhfash, al-Farrā', Abū 'Ubayda, Abū Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr. It is also said that the meaning is: "those who would have known it who can investigate it, except for a few of them," as said by al-Zajjāj.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported from Qatāda regarding "Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy," that he said: the word of Allah does not differ; it is true and contains no falsehood, whereas the words of people do differ.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Muslim and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported through the chain of Ibn ʿAbbās from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) withdrew from his wives, I entered the mosque and found people striking pebbles with stones and saying: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has divorced his wives." So I stood at the door of the mosque and called out at the top of my voice: "He has not divorced his wives." Then this verse was revealed: "When there comes to them some matter of security or fear, they spread it abroad. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who would have known it who can investigate it would have known it." So I was the one who had investigated that matter.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir have reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding the verse that he said: this concerns news; when a detachment of the Muslims went on a raid, people reported about it, saying: "The Muslims suffered such and such from their enemy, and the enemy suffered such and such from the Muslims," and they spread it among themselves without the Prophet (ﷺ) being the one who informed them of it.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim has reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding "When there comes to them," that he said: they are the people of hypocrisy. Ibn Jarīr has reported the same from Abū Muʿādh.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: "Had it not been for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan," that he said: here the speech ends.

As for His words "except for a few": it occurs at the beginning of the verse, where it informs about the hypocrites. He said: "When there comes to them some matter of security or fear, they spread it abroad," meaning: by the few believers.

The **fa'** in His saying ﴿So fight﴾ is said to be connected to His saying ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 74], etc.; meaning: for the sake of this, fight. It is also said to be connected to His saying ﴿And why do you not fight in the way of Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 75], so fight. It is also said to be the response to an omitted condition indicated by the context, its estimate being: if the matter is as mentioned, namely the non-obedience of the hypocrites, then fight; or, if they leave you alone and abandon you, then fight.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to wage jihad even if he fights alone, because He had guaranteed him victory. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the apparent meaning of the wording. However, nothing has ever come in a report that fighting was obligated upon him alone without the Ummah. So the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the address is to him in wording, but in meaning it is to him and to his Ummah; that is, you, O Muhammad, and every one of your Ummah, it is said to him: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾, meaning: you are not burdened with anything other than yourself, and you are not obligated to the act of others. This is a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it, because the restriction of his obligation to his own act is among the requirements of his directly fighting alone. It was also read as **lā tukallaf** with a **jazm** (jussive) as a prohibition, and it was read with a **nūn**.

His saying ﴿And urge the believers﴾: that is, urge them to fighting and jihad. It is said: *ḥarraḍtu fulānan ʿalā kadhā* (I urged so-and-so to such-and-such) when you command him to it. *Ḥāraḍa fulān ʿalā al-amr*, *akabba ʿalayhi* and *wāẓaba ʿalayhi* have the same meaning. His saying ﴿It may be that Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾: in it is an expectation given to the believers that Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve from them. And the giving of such hope from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is, is obligatory; so it is a promise from Him, glorified is He, and His promise is certainly to occur. ﴿And Allah is greater in might﴾: that is, greater in assault and more mighty in authority, ﴿and greater in punishment﴾: that is, in penalty. It is said: *nakkaltu bi-l-rajul tankīlan*, from *al-nakāl*, which is torment. And *al-munakkil* is the thing that punishes a person.

﴿Whoever intercedes with an intercession that is good will have a share of it﴾. The origin of *al-shafāʿa* (intercession), *al-shufʿa* (pre-emption) and the like is from *al-shafʿ*, which is a pair. From it comes *al-shafīʿ* (the intercessor), because he becomes a pair with the person in need. From it also comes *nāqa shafūʿ*, when she gathers two milkings in one milking; and *nāqa shafīʿ*, when a pregnancy and an offspring following her are gathered for her.

*Al-shafʿ* is joining one to one. *Al-shufʿa* is joining the ownership of a partner to one's own ownership. So *al-shafāʿa* is joining another to your standing and your means. It is, in verification, a manifestation of the rank of the intercessor with the one interceded with, and the arrival of a benefit to the one for whom intercession is made.

A good intercession is in righteousness and obedience. A bad intercession is in sins. Whoever intercedes in good, so that he benefits, has a share of it, that is, of its reward. And whoever intercedes in evil, like one who carries tale-bearing and backbiting, has a portion of it, that is, a share of its burden.

*Al-kifl* is burden and sin. Its derivation is from the cloth which the rider places on the hump of a camel so that it does not fall. It is said: *iktafaltu al-baʿīr*, when you place a cloth on its hump and ride upon it, because he has not used the whole back but has used a portion of it. It is used for a portion of good and evil. From its use in good is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28]. ﴿And Allah is ever Muqīt over all things﴾: that is, Capable (muqtadir), as al-Kisa'i said.

Al-Farra' said: *al-Muqīt* is the One who gives each person his sustenance. It is said: *qutthu aqūtuhu qūtan*, and *aqattuhu uqītuhu iqātatan*, so I am *qā'it* and *muqīt*. Al-Kisa'i reported *aqāta yuqītu*. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-Muqīt* is the Guardian. Al-Nahhas said: Abu 'Ubayda's saying is preferable, because it is derived from *al-qūt*, and *al-qūt* means the amount that preserves a person. Ibn Faris said in *al-Mujmal*: *al-Muqīt* is the one who is capable (*al-muqtadir*), and *al-Maqīt* is the Guardian and the Witness. As for the saying of the poet:

*Is the excess mine, or is it against me, if I am reckoned? Indeed I am a sustainer over the reckoning.*

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: it is from a different meaning than this.

His saying ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it﴾. *Al-taḥiyya* is a *taf'ila* form from *ḥayiytu*, and the original is *taḥiyya*, like *tarḍiya* and *tasmiya*, so they assimilated the *yā'* into the *yā'*. Its origin is the supplication for life. *Al-taḥiyya* is greeting (*al-salām*), and this is the meaning intended here. Similar is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they come to you they greet you with what Allah has not greeted you with﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8]. To this went the majority of the exegetes. And it was narrated from Malik that what is meant by *al-taḥiyya* here is the blessing of one who sneezes (*tashmīt al-ʿāṭis*).

The companions of Abu Hanifa said: *al-taḥiyya* here is a gift (*hadiyya*), because of His saying "or return it", and it is not possible to return the greeting of peace itself. This is corrupt and one should not turn to it.

What is meant by His saying ﴿then greet with better than it﴾ is that one adds to the reply upon what the initiator said. So if the initiator says: "Peace be upon you," the responder says: "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah." And if the initiator adds a word, the responder adds to the whole of what the initiator brought, with a word or words, such as: "and His blessings, and His good pleasure, and His greetings."

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars have agreed that initiating with peace is a Sunnah that is encouraged, and returning it is obligatory, because of His saying: ﴿then greet with better than it, or return it﴾. They differed about whether, if one person among a group returns it, it suffices or not. Malik and al-Shafi'i went to its sufficiency, and the Kufans went to its not sufficing for others. Against them is the hadith of 'Ali from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It suffices for a group when they pass by that one of them greets, and it suffices for those who are sitting that one of them returns it." It was reported by Abu Dawud. In its chain is Sa'id ibn Khalid al-Khuza'i al-Madani, and there is nothing wrong with him, though some have declared him weak. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr declared the hadith good (hasan).

The meaning of His saying "or return it" is limiting oneself to the like of the wording with which the initiator came. So if he says: "Peace be upon you," the responder says: "And upon you be peace." The pure Sunnah has come with what suffices here, without expansion, in specifying who initiates with peace, who deserves the greeting, and who does not deserve it.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever over all things a Reckoner﴾: He will call you to account for everything. It is said: its meaning is Guardian (*ḥafīẓ*). It is said: sufficient (*kāfiyan*), from their saying *aḥsabanī kadhā*, meaning: it sufficed me. Similar is ﴿Allah is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64].

His saying: "Allah, there is no god but Him": a subject and predicate. The *lām* in His saying "He will surely gather you" is the response to an omitted oath; meaning: by Allah, Allah will surely gather you by the resurrection until the Day of Resurrection, that is, until the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection. It is said: *ilā* is in the sense of *fī* (in). It is said: it is superfluous. The meaning: He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, and the Day of Resurrection is the Day of standing up from the graves. ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: that is, in the Day of Resurrection, or in the gathering, meaning a gathering in which there is no doubt. ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾: a denial that anyone could be more truthful than Him, glorified is He.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-man azdaqu* with a *zāy*. The rest read with a *ṣād*, and the *ṣād* is the original. It may be changed to a *zāy* because their points of articulation are close.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿Whoever intercedes with an intercession that is good﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: it is people's intercession for one another. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿will have a share of it﴾, that he said: a portion of it. And regarding His saying ﴿a share of it﴾, he said: *al-kifl* is sin. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, who said: *al-kifl* is a portion. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Muqīt over all things﴾, that he said: Guardian.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha that a man asked him about the saying of Allah ﴿And Allah is ever Muqīt over all things﴾, and he said: He gives each person sustenance according to the measure of his deeds. Its chain contains an unknown man. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿Muqīt﴾, that he said: a witness. Ibn Jarir reported from him, ﴿Muqīt﴾: a witness, a reckoner, a guardian.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Muqīt﴾, that he said: capable. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: *al-Muqīt* is *al-Qadīr* (the Capable). He also reported the same from Ibn Zayd. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak, who said: *al-Muqīt* is *al-Razzāq* (the Provider). Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Whoever greets you from among Allah's creation, return it to him, even if he is a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. That is because Allah says: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported; al-Suyuti said with a good chain (sanad hasan), from Salman al-Farisi, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "And upon you be the mercy of Allah." Then another came and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, and the mercy of Allah." He said: "And upon you be the mercy of Allah and His blessings." Then another came and said: "Peace be upon you, the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said to him: "And upon you." The man said to him: "O Prophet of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, so-and-so and so-and-so came to you and greeted you, and you returned more to them than you returned to me?" He said: "You did not leave anything for us. Allah says: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it﴾, so we have returned it to you."

al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* reported from Abu Hurayra that a man passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in a gathering, and he said: "Peace be upon you." He said: "Ten good deeds." Then another man passed and said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah." He said: "Twenty good deeds." Then another man passed and said: "Peace be upon you, the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said: "Thirty good deeds."

al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. al-Bayhaqi also reported from Sahl ibn Hunayf, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well. Ahmad, al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it good, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well, and added that after each time, the Prophet (ﷺ) returned it to him, then said: "Ten," to its end. Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas al-Juhani, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and added after his saying "and His blessings": "and His forgiveness." He said: "Forty," meaning good deeds.
