Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha that a man asked him about the saying of Allah ﴿And Allah is ever Muqīt over all things﴾, and he said: He gives each person sustenance according to the measure of his deeds. Its chain contains an unknown man. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿Muqīt﴾, that he said: a witness. Ibn Jarir reported from him, ﴿Muqīt﴾: a witness, a reckoner, a guardian.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Muqīt﴾, that he said: capable. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: *al-Muqīt* is *al-Qadīr* (the Capable). He also reported the same from Ibn Zayd. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak, who said: *al-Muqīt* is *al-Razzāq* (the Provider). Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Whoever greets you from among Allah's creation, return it to him, even if he is a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. That is because Allah says: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported; al-Suyuti said with a good chain (sanad hasan), from Salman al-Farisi, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "And upon you be the mercy of Allah." Then another came and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, and the mercy of Allah." He said: "And upon you be the mercy of Allah and His blessings." Then another came and said: "Peace be upon you, the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said to him: "And upon you." The man said to him: "O Prophet of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, so-and-so and so-and-so came to you and greeted you, and you returned more to them than you returned to me?" He said: "You did not leave anything for us. Allah says: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it﴾, so we have returned it to you."

al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* reported from Abu Hurayra that a man passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in a gathering, and he said: "Peace be upon you." He said: "Ten good deeds." Then another man passed and said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah." He said: "Twenty good deeds." Then another man passed and said: "Peace be upon you, the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said: "Thirty good deeds."

al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. al-Bayhaqi also reported from Sahl ibn Hunayf, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well. Ahmad, al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who declared it good, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well, and added that after each time, the Prophet (ﷺ) returned it to him, then said: "Ten," to its end. Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas al-Juhani, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and added after his saying "and His blessings": "and His forgiveness." He said: "Forty," meaning good deeds.

The interrogative in His saying (ﷺ)... no, correct: The interrogative in His saying ﴿What is [the matter] with you regarding the hypocrites?﴾ is for rebuke (*li-l-inkar*), and the interrogative noun is the subject (*mubtada'*), with what follows it as its predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is: "What is it that exists for you concerning the hypocrites, that is, regarding their affair and their state, while you are two groups concerning that?" The essential point is a denial directed at the addressees that there should be anything for them that necessitates their disagreement about the state of the hypocrites.

The grammarians differed over the case-ending (*intisab*, the accusative) of *fi'atayn* ("two groups"). Al-Akhfash and the Basrans (*al-Basriyyun*, the grammarians of Basra) said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), as in your saying: *ma laka qa'iman?* ("What is the matter with you, standing?"). The Kufans (*al-Kufiyyun*, the grammarians of Kufa) said that its accusative is because it is the predicate of *kana* (“to be”), which is elided, and the estimated construction is: *fa-ma lakum fi l-munafiqin kuntum fi'atayn* ("then what is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, you being two groups").

The occasion of revelation of the verse is what will come, and the meaning becomes clear through it. His saying ﴿And Allah has reverted them﴾ means: He returned them to disbelief because of what they earned. Al-Farra', al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and al-Kisa'i related *arkasahum* and *rakasahum*, meaning: He returned them to disbelief and overturned them. *Al-rak's* and *al-nak's* mean turning a thing upon its head, or returning its beginning to its end. *Al-mankus* and *al-markus* are one who has been overturned. In the reading of Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy it is *wa-llahu rakasahum* ("and Allah overturned them"). From this is the saying of Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

*Urkisu fi fi'atin mudhlimatin / ka-sawadi al-layli yatluha fitan*
("They were overturned into a dark faction, like the blackness of night, followed by trials.")

The *ba'* in His saying ﴿because of what they earned﴾ is causal (*sababiyya*), meaning: He overturned them because of their earning, which is their joining the abode of disbelief. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke, and in it is evidence that guidance by a human being has no effect upon whom Allah has led astray. ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

His saying ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way﴾ means: a path to guidance.

His saying ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, and that you would be alike﴾ is a resumed statement (*kalam mustanaf*) that includes a clarification of the state of these hypocrites, and an explanation that they wish the believers would disbelieve as they disbelieved, and that they would desire this out of obstinacy, extremism in disbelief, and persistence in error. The *kaf* in His saying *kama* ("as") is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (*na't masdar mahdhuf*), meaning: a disbelief like their disbelief; or it is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), as is related from Sibawayh.

His saying ﴿so that you would be alike﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) upon His saying "that you would disbelieve" and falls under its ruling, meaning: they wish your disbelief to be like their disbelief, and they wish for your equality with them.

His saying ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾ is the response (*jawab*) of an elided condition, meaning: if their state is as mentioned, then do not take from among them allies until they believe and actualize their faith through emigration (*hijra*). If they turn away from that, then seize them wherever you find them and kill them, when you have power over them, ﴿wherever you find them﴾ within the sacred territory and outside it, ﴿and do not take from among them a protector﴾ whom you befriend, ﴿nor a helper﴾ whom you seek help from.

His saying ﴿except those who are connected to a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ is an exception (*istithna'*) from His saying "seize them and kill them", meaning: except those who join and enter into a people between whom and you there is a covenant through protection (*jiwar*) and alliance (*hilf*). Do not kill them, because between them and those between whom and you there is a covenant is a pact and a covenant, for the pact includes them. This is the most sound of what has been said regarding the meaning of the verse. It has also been said that "connection" here is the connection of lineage, meaning: except those who trace their descent to a people between whom and you there is a covenant. This was said by Abu Ubayda, but the scholars rejected this of him, because lineage does not prevent fighting by consensus (*ijma'*), for there were kinship ties between the Muslims and the polytheists, and that did not prevent fighting.

It has been disputed who these people were, with whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a covenant. It is said they were Quraysh, with whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had a covenant, and those who joined Quraysh were the Banu Mudlij. It is said it was revealed concerning Hilal ibn Uwaymir, Suraqa ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn Amir ibn Abd Manaf, who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It is said it was Khuza'a, and it is said it was Banu Bakr ibn Zayd.

His saying ﴿or they come to you with their hearts constricted﴾ is coordinated upon His saying "connect" and falls under the ruling of the exception, meaning: except those who connect, and those who come to you. It may also be coordinated upon the description of "a people": except those who connect to a people between whom and you there is a covenant, and those who connect to a people who come to you with their hearts constricted, meaning: their hearts are straitened from fighting, so they refrain from it. *Al-hasr* means constriction and contraction.

Al-Farra' said: "It (*hasirat sudooruhum*, 'their hearts constricted') is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) from the pronoun of the subject in *ja'uukum*, as you say: 'So-and-so came, his mind gone,' meaning: his mind has indeed gone."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a predicate after a predicate, meaning: they came to you, then He informed: their hearts are constricted. In this case *hasirat* is a substitute (*badal*) for *ja'uukum*." It was also said that *hasirat* is in the genitive position as a qualifier (*na't*) of "a people," and it was said that the estimate is: "or men or a people came to you whose hearts were constricted." Al-Hasan read *aw ja'uukum hasiratan sudooruhum* with the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier.

It has been recited *hasirat* and *hasirat* (in other forms), and al-Mubarrad (Muhammad ibn Yazid) said: "*hasirat sudooruhum*" is an invocation against them, just as you say: "May Allah curse the disbeliever." Some commentators weakened this. It was also said that *aw* here has the meaning of *waw* ("and").

His saying ﴿that they would fight you or fight their own people﴾ is connected to His saying "*hasirat sudooruhum*", meaning: their hearts are constricted from fighting you and from fighting alongside you (*ma'akum*) against their people, so their hearts are straitened from fighting either of the two groups, and they dislike that. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾, as a trial from Him for you and a test, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and are steadfast, and We test your reports﴾ [Muhammad: 31]; or as a purification for you, or as punishment for your sins. But He, glorified is He, did not will that. The *lam* in His saying ﴿so they would have fought you﴾ is the response of *law* ("if"), repeating the response, meaning: if Allah had willed, He would have given them power and they would have fought you. The *fa'* is for sequence.

﴿And if they withdraw from you﴾ and do not confront you in fighting, ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, they submit to you and comply, ﴿then Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾, meaning: a path. So it is not lawful for you to kill them, nor to take them captive, nor to plunder their wealth. This submission prevents that and forbids it.

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people﴾; they show Islam to you and show disbelief to their people, so that they may be safe from both groups. They are a people from the inhabitants of Tihama who sought safety from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that they might be safe with him and with their people. It was also said that it concerns some people from Makka, and it was said it concerns Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, for he used to make both the Muslims and the polytheists feel secure. It was also said it concerns a group of hypocrites, and it was said it concerns Asad and Ghatafan.

﴿Every time they are returned to dissension﴾, that is, their people call them to it and ask them to fight the Muslims, ﴿they are plunged back into it﴾, meaning: they are turned over in it, so they return to their people and fight the Muslims. The meaning of *al-irtikas* is *al-intikas* (a reversal).

﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾, meaning: these who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their people, ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, submit to you, enter into your covenant and treaty, withdraw from their people, and restrain their hands from fighting you, ﴿then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾, that is: wherever you find them and gain power over them. ﴿And those⁠—⁠We have given you against them a clear authority﴾, meaning: a manifest proof by which you have dominion over them and subdue them, because of what is in their hearts of sickness, and what is in their breasts of corruption, and their reversal into dissension with the easiest action and the least effort.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have related from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to Uhud, and some people who had gone out with him returned. The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became two groups concerning them: one group said, 'We should kill them,' and another group said, 'No.' So Allah revealed: ﴿What is [the matter] with you regarding the hypocrites, two groups?﴾ the whole verse. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, it is good (*tayyiba*), and it expels impurity as fire expels the impurity of silver.'"

This is the most sound of what has been narrated regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, though other occasions have been narrated. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And Allah has reverted them﴾ that he said: "He caused them to fall." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "He turned them back." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except those who are connected to a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning Hilal ibn Uwaymir and Suraqa ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, and concerning the Banu Khuzayma ibn Amir ibn Abd Manaf."

Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh* (abrogating work), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from him regarding His saying ﴿except those who are connected⁠—⁠﴾ the verse, that he said: "It was abrogated by *Bara'a* (Surah al-Tawba): ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding ﴿their hearts are constricted﴾ that he said: "Their hearts were straitened." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' regarding ﴿and offer you peace﴾ that he said: "Reconciliation." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿And if they withdraw from you﴾, the verse, that he said: "It was abrogated by ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan and Ikrima regarding this verse that he said: "It was abrogated by *Bara'a*." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿You will find others﴾, the verse, that he said: "Some people from Makka used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and greet him out of showing off, then return to their people and revert to the idols, seeking by that to be safe here and there. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud.

The meaning is: "What is it that exists for you concerning the hypocrites, that is, regarding their affair and their state, while you are two groups concerning that?" The essential point is a denial directed at the addressees that there should be anything for them that necessitates their disagreement about the state of the hypocrites.

The grammarians differed over the case-ending (*intisab*, the accusative) of *fi'atayn* ("two groups"). Al-Akhfash and the Basrans (*al-Basriyyun*, the grammarians of Basra) said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), as in your saying: *ma laka qa'iman?* ("What is the matter with you, standing?"). The Kufans (*al-Kufiyyun*, the grammarians of Kufa) said that its accusative is because it is the predicate of *kana* (“to be”), which is elided, and the estimated construction is: *fa-ma lakum fi l-munafiqin kuntum fi'atayn* ("then what is the matter with you regarding the hypocrites, you being two groups").

The occasion of revelation of the verse is what will come, and the meaning becomes clear through it. His saying ﴿And Allah has reverted them﴾ means: He returned them to disbelief because of what they earned. Al-Farra', al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and al-Kisa'i related *arkasahum* and *rakasahum*, meaning: He returned them to disbelief and overturned them. *Al-rak's* and *al-nak's* mean turning a thing upon its head, or returning its beginning to its end. *Al-mankus* and *al-markus* are one who has been overturned. In the reading of Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy it is *wa-llahu rakasahum* ("and Allah overturned them"). From this is the saying of Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

*Urkisu fi fi'atin mudhlimatin / ka-sawadi al-layli yatluha fitan*
("They were overturned into a dark faction, like the blackness of night, followed by trials.")

The *ba'* in His saying ﴿because of what they earned﴾ is causal (*sababiyya*), meaning: He overturned them because of their earning, which is their joining the abode of disbelief. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke, and in it is evidence that guidance by a human being has no effect upon whom Allah has led astray. ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

His saying ﴿And whomever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way﴾ means: a path to guidance.

His saying ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, and that you would be alike﴾ is a resumed statement (*kalam mustanaf*) that includes a clarification of the state of these hypocrites, and an explanation that they wish the believers would disbelieve as they disbelieved, and that they would desire this out of obstinacy, extremism in disbelief, and persistence in error. The *kaf* in His saying *kama* ("as") is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (*na't masdar mahdhuf*), meaning: a disbelief like their disbelief; or it is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), as is related from Sibawayh.

His saying ﴿so that you would be alike﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) upon His saying "that you would disbelieve" and falls under its ruling, meaning: they wish your disbelief to be like their disbelief, and they wish for your equality with them.

His saying ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾ is the response (*jawab*) of an elided condition, meaning: if their state is as mentioned, then do not take from among them allies until they believe and actualize their faith through emigration (*hijra*). If they turn away from that, then seize them wherever you find them and kill them, when you have power over them, ﴿wherever you find them﴾ within the sacred territory and outside it, ﴿and do not take from among them a protector﴾ whom you befriend, ﴿nor a helper﴾ whom you seek help from.

His saying ﴿except those who are connected to a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ is an exception (*istithna'*) from His saying "seize them and kill them", meaning: except those who join and enter into a people between whom and you there is a covenant through protection (*jiwar*) and alliance (*hilf*). Do not kill them, because between them and those between whom and you there is a covenant is a pact and a covenant, for the pact includes them. This is the most sound of what has been said regarding the meaning of the verse. It has also been said that "connection" here is the connection of lineage, meaning: except those who trace their descent to a people between whom and you there is a covenant. This was said by Abu Ubayda, but the scholars rejected this of him, because lineage does not prevent fighting by consensus (*ijma'*), for there were kinship ties between the Muslims and the polytheists, and that did not prevent fighting.

It has been disputed who these people were, with whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a covenant. It is said they were Quraysh, with whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had a covenant, and those who joined Quraysh were the Banu Mudlij. It is said it was revealed concerning Hilal ibn Uwaymir, Suraqa ibn Ju'shum, and Khuzayma ibn Amir ibn Abd Manaf, who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ). It is said it was Khuza'a, and it is said it was Banu Bakr ibn Zayd.

His saying ﴿or they come to you with their hearts constricted﴾ is coordinated upon His saying "connect" and falls under the ruling of the exception, meaning: except those who connect, and those who come to you. It may also be coordinated upon the description of "a people": except those who connect to a people between whom and you there is a covenant, and those who connect to a people who come to you with their hearts constricted, meaning: their hearts are straitened from fighting, so they refrain from it. *Al-hasr* means constriction and contraction.

Al-Farra' said: "It (*hasirat sudooruhum*, 'their hearts constricted') is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) from the pronoun of the subject in *ja'uukum*, as you say: 'So-and-so came, his mind gone,' meaning: his mind has indeed gone."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a predicate after a predicate, meaning: they came to you, then He informed: their hearts are constricted. In this case *hasirat* is a substitute (*badal*) for *ja'uukum*." It was also said that *hasirat* is in the genitive position as a qualifier (*na't*) of "a people," and it was said that the estimate is: "or men or a people came to you whose hearts were constricted." Al-Hasan read *aw ja'uukum hasiratan sudooruhum* with the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier.

It has been recited *hasirat* and *hasirat* (in other forms), and al-Mubarrad (Muhammad ibn Yazid) said: "*hasirat sudooruhum*" is an invocation against them, just as you say: "May Allah curse the disbeliever." Some commentators weakened this. It was also said that *aw* here has the meaning of *waw* ("and").

His saying ﴿that they would fight you or fight their own people﴾ is connected to His saying "*hasirat sudooruhum*", meaning: their hearts are constricted from fighting you and from fighting alongside you (*ma'akum*) against their people, so their hearts are straitened from fighting either of the two groups, and they dislike that. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾, as a trial from Him for you and a test, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and are steadfast, and We test your reports﴾ [Muhammad: 31]; or as a purification for you, or as punishment for your sins. But He, glorified is He, did not will that. The *lam* in His saying ﴿so they would have fought you﴾ is the response of *law* ("if"), repeating the response, meaning: if Allah had willed, He would have given them power and they would have fought you. The *fa'* is for sequence.

﴿And if they withdraw from you﴾ and do not confront you in fighting, ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, they submit to you and comply, ﴿then Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾, meaning: a path. It was also said that it concerns some people from Makka, and it was said it concerns Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, for he used to make both the Muslims and the polytheists feel secure. It was also said it concerns a group of hypocrites, and it was said it concerns Asad and Ghatafan.

The meaning of *al-irtikas* is *al-intikas* (a reversal).

His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾. This negation has the meaning of a prohibition that implies unlawfulness, like His saying: ﴿It is not for you to hurt the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. If this negation were on its literal meaning, it would be a report, and that would require its truth, so that no believer would ever have killed a believer. It was said: the meaning is, it was not permissible for him in the covenant of Allah. It was said: the meaning is, it was not permissible for him in the past, just as it is not permissible for him now in any way. Then He made an exception from it, an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category as what precedes it), saying: ﴿except by mistake﴾, meaning: it was never permissible for him to kill him at all, but if he killed him by mistake, then upon him is such-and-such. This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj. It was also said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning is: it was not established, nor found, nor permissible for a believer to kill a believer, except by mistake, since he is then overpowered. It was also said that the meaning is: "nor by mistake." Al-Nahhas said: this is not known in the speech of the Arabs, and it is not correct in meaning, because mistake is not forbidden. It was also said that the meaning is: it is not proper for him to kill him for any reason of the reasons, except for mistake alone. In that case, His saying ﴿khata'an﴾ (by mistake) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: except a killing by mistake. The forms of mistake are many, and they are governed by the absence of intent. Khata' is the noun from akhta'a when one does not do something deliberately.

His saying: [p. 319] ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, meaning: upon him is the freeing of a believing slave, whom he sets free as an expiation (kaffarah) for killing by mistake. He expressed "slave" by "neck," meaning the whole person. The scholars differed over the definition of "believing slave." It was said: he is the one who has prayed and understood faith, so a young child does not suffice. This was the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and others.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: it suffices to free a young child born among Muslims. A group, including Malik and al-Shafi'i, said: whoever is judged to be obligated to pray over him if he dies suffices. According to the majority of scholars, a blind person, a paralyzed person, or one with a withered limb does not suffice. According to most, a lame person and a one-eyed person suffice. Malik said: except if the lameness is severe. According to most of them, an insane person does not suffice. On this matter there are lengthy details mentioned in the science of furu' (positive law).

His saying: ﴿and a diyah (blood-money) delivered to his family﴾. The diyah is what is given as compensation for the blood of the slain to his heirs. The musallamah (delivered) is what is paid and handed over. "The family" intended here are the heirs. The kinds of diyah and its details have been explained by the pure Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition). His saying: ﴿unless they remit it﴾, meaning: unless the family of the slain give the diyah to the killer as charity. Pardoning it is called charity to encourage it.

Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) read: ﴿unless they give charity﴾ (yatasaddaqu). This excepted clause is connected to His saying "diyah delivered," meaning: upon him is a diyah delivered, unless the heirs pardon it.

His saying: ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you﴾, meaning: if the slain was from a people hostile to you, namely the non-Muslim combatants. This is the case of a believer whom the Muslims kill in the lands of the unbelievers, among whom he was, who then embraced Islam but did not emigrate, and they think he has not become Muslim and remains upon the religion of his people. Then there is no diyah upon his killer; rather, upon him is the freeing of a believing slave. They differed over the reason for the diyah being dropped. It was said: the reason is that the victim's guardians are unbelievers and have no right to the diyah. It was said: the reason is that this one who believed but did not emigrate has little sanctity, based on Allah's saying: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate—you owe them no guardianship at all until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Some scholars said: his diyah is obligatory to the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

His saying: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, meaning: a covenant that is either time-limited or unlimited. Al-Hasan read: "and he is a believer, a diyah delivered to his family," meaning: upon his killer is a diyah paid to his family from among the people of Islam, who are his heirs, ﴿and the freeing of a believing slave﴾ as previously mentioned. ﴿So whoever does not find﴾, meaning: the slave, and his wealth does not extend to buying one, ﴿then fasting two consecutive months﴾, meaning: upon him is fasting two consecutive months, in which no breaking of the fast during the daytime separates any two days of the fasting. If he breaks it, he begins again. This is the view of the majority. As for breaking the fast for a legitimate excuse, such as menstruation and the like, it does not require beginning again. There is disagreement about breaking the fast due to the onset of illness.

His saying: ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: He prescribed that for you as repentance, that is, acceptance of your repentance; or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: He turned to you in repentance; or it was said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: while He is one who has a repentance proceeding from Allah.

His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾. When He explained the ruling for the one who kills by mistake, He explained the ruling for the one who kills intentionally. The scholars differed over the meaning of intention ('amd). 'Ata', al-Nakha'i and others said: it is killing with an iron implement, such as a sword, a dagger, the tip of a spear, or the like of sharp things, or with what is known to cause death, such as heavy stones or the like. The majority said: it is every killing by a killer intending the act, with iron, with a stone, with a stick, or with other than these. Some scholars restricted it to killing with what would normally kill such a person. Some scholars held that killing is divided into three categories: intentional, quasi-intentional (shibh 'amd), and by mistake. They argued for this with evidences that this place is not suited to elaborate. Others held that it is divided into two categories: intentional and by mistake, with no third. They argued that the Qur'an mentions only these two. This is answered by saying that the Qur'an's limiting itself to two categories does not negate the establishment of a third category by the Sunnah, and this has been established in the Sunnah.

This verse came with severe punishment for the intentional killer, combining in it: that Hell is his recompense, meaning he deserves it because of this sin; that he remains in it forever; that Allah is angry with him and curses him; and that He has prepared for him a great punishment. There is no severity beyond this severity, and no threat like this threat.

The accusative of khalidan (abiding) is a circumstantial state. His saying: ﴿and Allah is angry with him﴾ is conjoined to something omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: He made his recompense Hell, or He judged against him, or He requited him and was angry with him; ﴿and prepared for him﴾.

The scholars differed over whether the intentional killer has repentance or has no repentance. Al-Bukhari narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: the scholars of Kufa differed about it, so I traveled to Ibn Abbas and asked him about it. He said: this verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ was revealed, and it is the last to be revealed, and nothing has abrogated it. al-Nasa'i narrated something similar from him. al-Nasa'i narrated something similar from Zayd ibn Thabit. Among the early scholars who held that he has no repentance were Abu Hurayrah, Abdullah ibn Amr, Abu Salamah, Ubayd ibn Umayr, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, as transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from them.

The majority held that his repentance is accepted. They argued with verses such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114], and His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. They also said: reconciliation is possible between this verse of al-Nisa' and the verse of al-Furqan, so that their meaning is: his recompense is Hell except for the one who repents, especially since the cause is one, namely killing, and the consequence, namely the threat of punishment, is one. They also argued with the hadith mentioned in the two Sahihs from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pledge allegiance to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor commit fornication, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except with right." Then he said: "Whoever commits any of that and Allah conceals it, it is up to Allah: if He wills, He pardons him, and if He wills, He punishes him." And with the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which Muslim narrated in his Sahih and others, about the man who killed a hundred souls. A group, including Abu Hanifah and his companions and al-Shafi'i, held that the intentional killer falls under the will of Allah, whether he repented or not. I have clarified in my commentary on al-Muntaqa the argument of each party. The truth is that the door of repentance has not been closed to every sinner; rather, [p. 320] it is open to everyone who intends it and seeks to enter through it. If shirk, which is the greatest and gravest of sins, is erased by repentance to Allah, and the one who commits it is accepted if he leaves it and enters the door of repentance, then how about what is less than it of sins, among which is intentional killing? But the repentance of the intentional killer must include acknowledging the killing and surrendering himself to retaliation (qisas) if it is obligatory, or surrendering the diyah if retaliation is not obligatory and the killer is wealthy and able to pay it or part of it. As for mere repentance by the intentional killer and his resolve not to return to killing anyone, without acknowledgment or surrender of himself, we do not assert its acceptance. And Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful, He who judges between His servants concerning that over which they used to differ.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, that he said: it was not for him to do that, regarding what came to him from his Lord of the covenant of Allah which was made with him.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah killed a believing man who had been tormenting him, along with Abu Jahl, who was his maternal brother, in pursuit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ayyash thought that man was an unbeliever. A clearer context than this is what Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, who said: al-Harith ibn Yazid of the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy used to torment Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah along with Abu Jahl. "Then he went out emigrating to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning al-Harith, and Ayyash met him at al-Harrah and struck him with the sword, thinking that he was an unbeliever. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ to the end of the verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited it over him, then said to him: 'Stand up and free [a slave].'" Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Suddi something longer than this. It has also been narrated through chains other than these.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd who said: it was revealed concerning a man whom Abu al-Darda' killed. He was in a military expedition, and Abu al-Darda' turned aside to a mountain pass for a need of his, and found a man from the people among his sheep. He charged at him with the sword, and the man said: "There is no god but Allah," and he struck him. Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym narrated something similar, but in it: the one who killed the one seeking refuge with the word of testimony was Bakr ibn Harithah al-Juhani.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, that he said: by "believing" is meant one who has understood faith and prayed. Every slave in the Qur'an which is not described as believing, then it is permissible for one who is a child or older and who has no disability. Concerning His saying: ﴿and a diyah delivered to his family unless they give it as charity﴾, he said: upon him is the diyah delivered, unless it is given to him as charity.

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah that he said: in the reading of Ubayy: "then the freeing of a believing slave, in which a child does not suffice." Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a black slave-girl and said: "O Messenger of Allah, upon me is the freeing of a believing slave." He said to her: "Where is Allah?" She pointed to the sky with her finger. He said to her: "Who am I?" She pointed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the sky, meaning: you are the Messenger of Allah. He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."

It has been narrated through several chains, and it is in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami. There are also many hadiths on fixing the diyah (blood-money, compensation paid for a killing), on the difference between the diyah for accidental killing (khata') and the diyah for quasi-deliberate killing (shibh al-'amd), and on the diyah of a Muslim versus that of a disbeliever. These are well known, so there is no need for us to mention them at this point.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i concerning His saying ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾: "This refers to a Muslim whose heirs are Muslims." Concerning ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer﴾: "This refers to a Muslim man whose people are polytheists, and there is no treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah." Concerning ﴿But if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾: "This refers to a Muslim man whose people are polytheists, but there is a treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He is killed, so his inheritance goes to the Muslims, and his diyah goes to his people, because they bear the diyah on his behalf (ya'qilun 'anhu)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer﴾: he said, "If he is among the people of war, and he is a believer, and one kills him by mistake, then the killer must atone by freeing a believing slave, or by fasting two consecutive months, and there is no diyah upon him." And concerning His saying ﴿But if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾: he said, "If he is a disbeliever under your protection (dhimma) and he is killed, then the killer must pay the diyah, delivered to his family, and free a slave."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib from Abu 'Ayyash, who said: "A man would come, embrace Islam, then go back to his people, who were polytheists, and remain among them. Then the armies of the Prophet ﷺ would raid them, and the man would be killed among those who were killed. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, and he has no diyah."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported through 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib from Abu Yahya from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾: he meant "a pardon from Allah for this community, in that He made expiation (kaffara) mandatory for accidental killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrima that a man from the Ansar killed the brother of Miqyas ibn Subaba. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the diyah and he accepted it, then he attacked the killer of his brother. And concerning this the verse was revealed. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar, and in it: Miqyas ibn Subaba later joined Makkah and apostatized from Islam.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ was revealed eight years after the one in Surat al-Furqan, which is His saying ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ up to His saying ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ was revealed six months after His saying ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, who said: "This verse in Surat al-Nisa' was revealed four months after His saying ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]." The reports from the Companions on this are very numerous, (p-321) and the truth is what we have made known to you.

His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾. This negation has the meaning of a prohibition that implies unlawfulness, like His saying: ﴿It is not for you to hurt the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. If this negation were on its literal meaning, it would be a report, and that would require its truth, so that no believer would ever have killed a believer. It was said: the meaning is, it was not permissible for him in the covenant of Allah. It was said: the meaning is, it was not permissible for him in the past, just as it is not permissible for him now in any way. Then He made an exception from it, an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category as what precedes it), saying: ﴿except by mistake﴾, meaning: it was never permissible for him to kill him at all, but if he killed him by mistake, then upon him is such-and-such. This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj. It was also said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning is: it was not established, nor found, nor permissible for a believer to kill a believer, except by mistake, since he is then overpowered. It was also said that the meaning is: "nor by mistake." Al-Nahhas said: this is not known in the speech of the Arabs, and it is not correct in meaning, because mistake is not forbidden. It was also said that the meaning is: it is not proper for him to kill him for any reason of the reasons, except for mistake alone. In that case, His saying ﴿khata'an﴾ (by mistake) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: except a killing by mistake. The forms of mistake are many, and they are governed by the absence of intent. Khata' is the noun from akhta'a when one does not do something deliberately.

His saying: [p. 319] ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, meaning: upon him is the freeing of a believing slave, whom he sets free as an expiation (kaffarah) for killing by mistake. He expressed "slave" by "neck," meaning the whole person. The scholars differed over the definition of "believing slave." It was said: he is the one who has prayed and understood faith, so a young child does not suffice. This was the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and others.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: it suffices to free a young child born among Muslims. A group, including Malik and al-Shafi'i, said: whoever is judged to be obligated to pray over him if he dies suffices. According to the majority of scholars, a blind person, a paralyzed person, or one with a withered limb does not suffice. According to most, a lame person and a one-eyed person suffice. Malik said: except if the lameness is severe. According to most of them, an insane person does not suffice. On this matter there are lengthy details mentioned in the science of furu' (positive law).

His saying: ﴿and a diyah (blood-money) delivered to his family﴾. The diyah is what is given as compensation for the blood of the slain to his heirs. The musallamah (delivered) is what is paid and handed over. "The family" intended here are the heirs. The kinds of diyah and its details have been explained by the pure Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition). His saying: ﴿unless they remit it﴾, meaning: unless the family of the slain give the diyah to the killer as charity. Pardoning it is called charity to encourage it.

Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) read: ﴿unless they give charity﴾ (yatasaddaqu). This excepted clause is connected to His saying "diyah delivered," meaning: upon him is a diyah delivered, unless the heirs pardon it.

His saying: ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you﴾, meaning: if the slain was from a people hostile to you, namely the non-Muslim combatants. This is the case of a believer whom the Muslims kill in the lands of the unbelievers, among whom he was, who then embraced Islam but did not emigrate, and they think he has not become Muslim and remains upon the religion of his people. Then there is no diyah upon his killer; rather, upon him is the freeing of a believing slave. They differed over the reason for the diyah being dropped. It was said: the reason is that the victim's guardians are unbelievers and have no right to the diyah. It was said: the reason is that this one who believed but did not emigrate has little sanctity, based on Allah's saying: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate—you owe them no guardianship at all until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. Some scholars said: his diyah is obligatory to the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

His saying: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, meaning: a covenant that is either time-limited or unlimited. Al-Hasan read: "and he is a believer, a diyah delivered to his family," meaning: upon his killer is a diyah paid to his family from among the people of Islam, who are his heirs, ﴿and the freeing of a believing slave﴾ as previously mentioned. ﴿So whoever does not find﴾, meaning: the slave, and his wealth does not extend to buying one, ﴿then fasting two consecutive months﴾, meaning: upon him is fasting two consecutive months, in which no breaking of the fast during the daytime separates any two days of the fasting. If he breaks it, he begins again. This is the view of the majority. As for breaking the fast for a legitimate excuse, such as menstruation and the like, it does not require beginning again. There is disagreement about breaking the fast due to the onset of illness.

His saying: ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: He prescribed that for you as repentance, that is, acceptance of your repentance; or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: He turned to you in repentance; or it was said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: while He is one who has a repentance proceeding from Allah.

His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾. When He explained the ruling for the one who kills by mistake, He explained the ruling for the one who kills intentionally. The scholars differed over the meaning of intention ('amd). 'Ata', al-Nakha'i and others said: it is killing with an iron implement, such as a sword, a dagger, the tip of a spear, or the like of sharp things, or with what is known to cause death, such as heavy stones or the like. The majority said: it is every killing by a killer intending the act, with iron, with a stone, with a stick, or with other than these. Some scholars restricted it to killing with what would normally kill such a person. Some scholars held that killing is divided into three categories: intentional, quasi-intentional (shibh 'amd), and by mistake. They argued for this with evidences that this place is not suited to elaborate. Others held that it is divided into two categories: intentional and by mistake, with no third. They argued that the Qur'an mentions only these two. This is answered by saying that the Qur'an's limiting itself to two categories does not negate the establishment of a third category by the Sunnah, and this has been established in the Sunnah.

This verse came with severe punishment for the intentional killer, combining in it: that Hell is his recompense, meaning he deserves it because of this sin; that he remains in it forever; that Allah is angry with him and curses him; and that He has prepared for him a great punishment. There is no severity beyond this severity, and no threat like this threat.

The accusative of khalidan (abiding) is a circumstantial state. His saying: ﴿and Allah is angry with him﴾ is conjoined to something omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: He made his recompense Hell, or He judged against him, or He requited him and was angry with him; ﴿and prepared for him﴾.

The scholars differed over whether the intentional killer has repentance or has no repentance. Al-Bukhari narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: the scholars of Kufa differed about it, so I traveled to Ibn Abbas and asked him about it. He said: this verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ was revealed, and it is the last to be revealed, and nothing has abrogated it. al-Nasa'i narrated something similar from him. al-Nasa'i narrated something similar from Zayd ibn Thabit. Among the early scholars who held that he has no repentance were Abu Hurayrah, Abdullah ibn Amr, Abu Salamah, Ubayd ibn Umayr, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, as transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from them.

The majority held that his repentance is accepted. They argued with verses such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114], and His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. They also said: reconciliation is possible between this verse of al-Nisa' and the verse of al-Furqan, so that their meaning is: his recompense is Hell except for the one who repents, especially since the cause is one, namely killing, and the consequence, namely the threat of punishment, is one. They also argued with the hadith mentioned in the two Sahihs from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pledge allegiance to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor commit fornication, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except with right." Then he said: "Whoever commits any of that and Allah conceals it, it is up to Allah: if He wills, He pardons him, and if He wills, He punishes him." And with the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which Muslim narrated in his Sahih and others, about the man who killed a hundred souls. A group, including Abu Hanifah and his companions and al-Shafi'i, held that the intentional killer falls under the will of Allah, whether he repented or not. I have clarified in my commentary on al-Muntaqa the argument of each party. The truth is that the door of repentance has not been closed to every sinner; rather, [p. 320] it is open to everyone who intends it and seeks to enter through it. If shirk, which is the greatest and gravest of sins, is erased by repentance to Allah, and the one who commits it is accepted if he leaves it and enters the door of repentance, then how about what is less than it of sins, among which is intentional killing? But the repentance of the intentional killer must include acknowledging the killing and surrendering himself to retaliation (qisas) if it is obligatory, or surrendering the diyah if retaliation is not obligatory and the killer is wealthy and able to pay it or part of it. As for mere repentance by the intentional killer and his resolve not to return to killing anyone, without acknowledgment or surrender of himself, we do not assert its acceptance. And Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful, He who judges between His servants concerning that over which they used to differ.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, that he said: it was not for him to do that, regarding what came to him from his Lord of the covenant of Allah which was made with him.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah killed a believing man who had been tormenting him, along with Abu Jahl, who was his maternal brother, in pursuit of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ayyash thought that man was an unbeliever. A clearer context than this is what Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, who said: al-Harith ibn Yazid of the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy used to torment Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah along with Abu Jahl. "Then he went out emigrating to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning al-Harith, and Ayyash met him at al-Harrah and struck him with the sword, thinking that he was an unbeliever. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ to the end of the verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited it over him, then said to him: 'Stand up and free [a slave].'" Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Suddi something longer than this. It has also been narrated through chains other than these.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd who said: it was revealed concerning a man whom Abu al-Darda' killed. He was in a military expedition, and Abu al-Darda' turned aside to a mountain pass for a need of his, and found a man from the people among his sheep. He charged at him with the sword, and the man said: "There is no god but Allah," and he struck him. Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym narrated something similar, but in it: the one who killed the one seeking refuge with the word of testimony was Bakr ibn Harithah al-Juhani.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, that he said: by "believing" is meant one who has understood faith and prayed. Every slave in the Qur'an which is not described as believing, then it is permissible for one who is a child or older and who has no disability. Concerning His saying: ﴿and a diyah delivered to his family unless they give it as charity﴾, he said: upon him is the diyah delivered, unless it is given to him as charity.

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah that he said: in the reading of Ubayy: "then the freeing of a believing slave, in which a child does not suffice." Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a black slave-girl and said: "O Messenger of Allah, upon me is the freeing of a believing slave." He said to her: "Where is Allah?" She pointed to the sky with her finger. He said to her: "Who am I?" She pointed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the sky, meaning: you are the Messenger of Allah. He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."

It has been narrated through several chains, and it is in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami. There are also many hadiths on fixing the diyah (blood-money, compensation paid for a killing), on the difference between the diyah for accidental killing (khata') and the diyah for quasi-deliberate killing (shibh al-'amd), and on the diyah of a Muslim versus that of a disbeliever. These are well known, so there is no need for us to mention them at this point.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i concerning His saying ﴿and a compensation paid to his family﴾: "This refers to a Muslim whose heirs are Muslims." Concerning ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer﴾: "This refers to a Muslim man whose people are polytheists, and there is no treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah." Concerning ﴿But if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾: "This refers to a Muslim man whose people are polytheists, but there is a treaty between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He is killed, so his inheritance goes to the Muslims, and his diyah goes to his people, because they bear the diyah on his behalf (ya'qilun 'anhu)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer﴾: he said, "If he is among the people of war, and he is a believer, and one kills him by mistake, then the killer must atone by freeing a believing slave, or by fasting two consecutive months, and there is no diyah upon him." And concerning His saying ﴿But if he is from a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾: he said, "If he is a disbeliever under your protection (dhimma) and he is killed, then the killer must pay the diyah, delivered to his family, and free a slave."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib from Abu 'Ayyash, who said: "A man would come, embrace Islam, then go back to his people, who were polytheists, and remain among them. Then the armies of the Prophet ﷺ would raid them, and the man would be killed among those who were killed. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿But if he is from a people hostile to you, and he is a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave﴾, and he has no diyah."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported through 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib from Abu Yahya from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾: he meant "a pardon from Allah for this community, in that He made expiation (kaffara) mandatory for accidental killing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrima that a man from the Ansar killed the brother of Miqyas ibn Subaba. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the diyah and he accepted it, then he attacked the killer of his brother. And concerning this the verse was revealed. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar, and in it: Miqyas ibn Subaba later joined Makkah and apostatized from Islam.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ was revealed eight years after the one in Surat al-Furqan, which is His saying ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ up to His saying ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ was revealed six months after His saying ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, who said: "This verse in Surat al-Nisa' was revealed four months after His saying ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]." The reports from the Companions on this are very numerous, (p-321) and the truth is what we have made known to you.

This is connected to the mention of jihad and fighting. *Ḍarb* means travelling on the earth. The Arabs say *ḍarabtu fi al-ardh* ("I travelled in the land") when one travels for trade, for raiding, or for other purposes. They say *ḍarabtu al-ardh* without *fi* when one intends to relieve oneself. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let no two men go out relieving themselves together" (*yaḍribāni al-ghā'iṭ*).

His words, *fa-tabayyanū* ("then verify"), come from *al-tabayyun*, which means careful consideration. This is the reading of the majority, except Ḥamzah, who read *fa-tathabbatū* ("then be firm and careful") from *al-tathabbut*.

Abu 'Ubayda and Abu Ḥātim preferred the first reading. They said: whoever is commanded to verify has also been commanded to be careful. The reason that the command to verify is specifically tied to travel, although verifying and being careful in matters of killing are obligatory both at home and while travelling without dispute, is that the incident which was the occasion of revelation of the verse took place during a journey, as will come.

His words, *wa-lā taqūlū li-man alqā ilaykumu al-salāma* ("Do not say to one who offers you peace"), have also been read as *al-salama*, and the meaning of both is one. Abu 'Ubayda preferred *al-salām*. The people of reasoning (*ahl al-naẓar*) disagreed with him and said that *al-salam* is more suitable here, because it means submission and surrender. The intended meaning is: do not say to one who has laid down his arms before you and submitted, "You are not a believer." So *al-salam* and *al-salām* both mean submission. It was also said that both mean Islam, i.e., "Do not say to one who offers you Islam, that is, its word, which is the testimony of faith, 'You are not a believer.'" It was also said that both mean the greeting that is the salutation of the people of Islam, i.e., "Do not say to one who offers you the greeting and says, 'Peace be upon you,' 'You are not a believer.'"

The intended meaning is the prohibition on the Muslims against neglecting what the unbeliever brings of evidence for his Islam, and saying that he only did that as a means of seeking protection or out of *taqiyya* (dissimulation to avoid harm). Abu Ja'far read *lasta mu'ammanan* ("you are not one who has been given safety"), from *amman*: if you grant someone protection, he is *mu'ammam* (protected).

This verse has been used as evidence that whoever kills an unbeliever after he has said "There is no god but Allah" is to be killed in retaliation (*qutila bihi*), because by this word he has secured his blood, property and family. The killing was dropped from those who did this in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) only because they interpreted (the situation) and thought that whoever said it out of fear of the weapon would not be a Muslim, and his blood would not be protected by it, and that he must say this word while being calm and not afraid. Within the ruling on speaking the word of Islam is the showing of submission, by saying, "I am a Muslim" or "I am upon your religion," because, as you know, the meaning of the verse is submission and surrender, and this is achieved by everything that indicates Islam, whether by word or deed. Among these is the word of testimony and the word of greeting. Thus the other two sayings regarding the meaning of the verse are included under the first saying.

His words, *tabtaghūna 'araḍa al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* ("seeking the transient goods of worldly life"): this clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: do not say that statement while seeking spoils (*al-ghanīma*), so that the prohibition applies to both the condition and the conditioned, not to the condition alone. The goods of this world are called *'araḍ* because they are passing and perishing, not permanent. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said that all the goods of this world are *'arad* with a fatha on the ra'. As for *'ard* with a sukun on the ra', it means everything other than gold and silver coins. So every *'ard* with sukun is an *'arad* with fatha, but not every *'arad* with fatha is an *'ard* with sukun.

In *Kitāb al-'Ayn*: *al-'arad* is what is obtained of this world. From this is the saying of the Most High: ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾ [al-Anfal: 67], and its plural is *'urūḍ*. In *al-Mujmal* of Ibn Fāris: *al-'arad* is what befalls a person of sickness or the like, and *'arad al-dunyā* is whatever wealth there is in it, whether little or much. *Al-'arḍ* among household goods is whatever is not cash.

His words, *fa-'inda Allāhi maghānimu kathīra* ("With Allah are abundant spoils"): this is a reason given for the prohibition. That is: with Allah, from what is lawful for you without committing any forbidden act, are many spoils which you may gain and by which you may be free from killing one who has submitted and surrendered and from seizing his property. ﴿Thus you were before﴾, that is, you were unbelievers, so your blood was protected when you spoke the word of testimony. Or: thus you were before, concealing your faith from your people out of fear for yourselves, until Allah bestowed His favour upon you by strengthening His religion, so you displayed the faith and proclaimed it. The command to verify is repeated for emphasis, since it is obligatory with no latitude or concession.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Some Muslims met a man who had with him his spoils (*ghanīma*). He said, "Peace be upon you." They killed him and took his spoils, so the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah, verify﴾ and so on.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Aḥmad, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man from Banu Sulaym passed by a group of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was driving his sheep. He greeted them with peace. They said, "He greeted us only so that he might seek refuge from us." So they rushed at him, killed him, and brought his sheep to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah﴾.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Aḥmad, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ḥadrad al-Aslami, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us to Idam. I went out with a group of Muslims, among whom were Abu Qatada al-Ḥārith ibn Rib'i and Muḥallam ibn Jaththama ibn Qays al-Laythi. We set out until, when we were in the valley of Idam, 'Amir ibn al-Aḍbaṭ al-Ashja'i passed by us on a she-camel of his, with a small bag (*mutay'*) and a skin of milk. When he passed by us, he greeted us with the greeting of Islam. We held back from him, but Muḥallam ibn Jaththama attacked him because of something that had been between them, killed him, and took his camel and his bag. When we came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him the news, the Qur'an was revealed concerning us: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah, verify﴾ and so on.

In a version in Ibn Isḥāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim, from the narration of this Abu Ḥadrad: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Muḥallam, 'Did you kill him after he said, "I believe in Allah"?'" And the Qur'an was revealed.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from the narration of Ibn 'Umar: "Muḥallam sat before the Prophet (ﷺ) to ask him for forgiveness, and he said, 'May Allah not forgive you.' So he got up while wiping his tears with his two cloaks. Not an hour had passed before he died, and they buried him, but the earth cast him out. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said, '(p-322) The earth accepts one who is worse than your companion, but Allah wanted to admonish you.' Then they threw him onto a mountain and cast stones upon him, and the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth﴾."

Al-Bazzar, al-Dāraquṭnī in *al-Afrād*, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Ḍiyā' in *al-Mukhtāra* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad killed a man after he had said, "There is no god but Allah." There are many narrations concerning the occasion of revelation, and this that we have mentioned is the best of them.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His words, ﴿Thus you were before﴾, that he said: You conceal your faith as this shepherd concealed his faith; he meant those who killed him after he had offered them the greeting. In another wording: "You hide your faith from the polytheists." ﴿Then Allah bestowed His favour upon you﴾, so he displayed Islam, and you proclaimed your faith, so verify. He said: This is a second warning from Allah.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Qatada concerning His words, ﴿Thus you were before﴾, that he said: You were unbelievers until Allah bestowed His favour upon you with Islam and guided you to it.

The difference between the ranks of those who stayed behind from jihad without an excuse and the ranks of those who strove in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves, although this is already known. But by this announcement Allah, glory be to Him, intended to stir up the mujahidin so that they would be eager, and to rebuke those who stayed behind so that they would feel shame. His saying: ﴿Other than those who have a harm﴾. The people of Kufa and Abu 'Amr read it in the nominative (raf'), as an attribute (wasf) of "those who sit (al-qa'idin)," as al-Akhfash said, because they are not meant as particular people, so they became like an indefinite noun, and so it was permissible to describe them with "other than."

Abu Haywa read it in the genitive (kasr) of the ra', as an attribute of "the believers (al-mu'minin)." The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina) read it with a fatha on the ra', as an exception (istithna') from "those who sit" or from "the believers," meaning: except those who have a harm, for they are equal to the mujahidin.

It is permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "those who sit," meaning: those who sit, healthy, in their state of health are not equal. The circumstantial state is permissible from them because their wording is definite. The scholars said: "those with a harm" are the people of excuses, because these excuses harmed them to the point that they prevented them from jihad. The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording is that the person with an excuse is given a reward like the reward of the mujahid. It was also said: he is given his reward without multiplication, so the mujahid surpasses him by the multiplication because of the direct participation. Al-Qurtubi said: "The first is more correct, God willing, because of the authentic hadith on this: 'There are men in Madina who, whenever you crossed a valley or traveled a journey, were with you; they are people whom the excuse held back.'" He said: "In this meaning is what has come in a report: 'When the servant falls ill, Allah, the Exalted, says: Write for My servant what he used to do in health until he recovers or I take him to Me.'"

His saying: ﴿Allah has preferred the mujahidin with their wealth and their selves over those who sit by a degree﴾. This is an explanation of the difference between the two groups, which is understood from the mention of non-equality in general terms. The meaning here is "other than those with a harm," taking the unrestricted (mutlaq) to be interpreted by the restricted (muqayyad). He said here "a degree (darajatan)" and said afterwards "degrees (darajat)." Some said: the preference by "a degree" and then by "degrees" is only emphasis, clarification and confirmation. Others said: Allah preferred the mujahidin over those who sit among the people with a harm by one degree, and Allah preferred the mujahidin over those who sit, other than the people with a harm, by degrees. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others. It was also said: the meaning of "a degree" is elevation, i.e., He raised their mention and elevated them with praise and commendation. "A degree" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) or as a verbal noun (masdar), since it stands in the place of a single instance of preference, meaning: Allah preferred them with His preference, or by removing the preposition, or as a circumstantial state (hal) of the mujahidin, meaning: possessors of a degree.

His saying: "Each (kullan)" is the first object of His saying "Allah promised (wa'ada Allahu)." It is placed before it to convey restriction (qasr), meaning: each one of the mujahidin and of those who sit, Allah has promised him "the best (al-husna)," that is, the reward, which is Paradise. His saying: "a reward (ajran)" is in the accusative as a specification. It was also said: as a verbal noun, because "preferred (fadalla)" here means "rewarded (ajara)," so the estimate is: He rewarded them with a reward. It was also said: it is a second object of "preferred," because it includes the meaning of giving. It was also said: it is in the accusative by removing the preposition. It was also said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) from "degrees," placed before it.

﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy; and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. As for the accusative of "degrees, forgiveness and mercy," they are in apposition (badal) to "a reward." It was also said: the verbs governing "forgiveness and mercy" are implied, meaning: He forgave them a forgiveness and showed them mercy with mercy.

Al-Bukhari, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others have related from Zayd ibn Thabit that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dictated to him: "Not equal are those who sit among the believers and those who strive in the way of Allah." Then Ibn Umm Maktum came while he was dictating it to me and said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I were able to fight, I would fight." He was blind. So Allah revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ), while his thigh was on my thigh: ﴿other than those who have a harm﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related this meaning from the hadith of al-Bara'. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, have also related it from the hadith of Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit from his father.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: ﴿Not equal are those who sit among the believers, other than those with a harm﴾ concerning Badr, and those who went out to Badr. 'Abd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have also related it from him. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi have related from him that he said: It was revealed concerning people whom sicknesses and pains occupied, so Allah sent down their excuse from the heavens. Sa'id ibn Mansur and ʿAbd ibn Humayd have related from Anas ibn Malik who said: This verse was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, and I saw him in some of the battlefields of the Muslims, with the banner with him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying: ﴿Allah has preferred the mujahidin with their wealth and their selves over those who sit by a degree﴾ that he said: over the people of harm. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ that he said: Paradise.

Ibn Jarir has related from Ibn Jurayj who said: It used to be said: Islam is a degree, and emigration is a degree within Islam, and jihad within emigration is a degree, and being killed in jihad is a degree. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn Muhayriz concerning His saying: "degrees (darajat)" that he said: The degrees are seventy degrees, and the distance between two degrees is the gallop of a well-bred, trained horse for seventy years.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq in his Musannaf has related something similar from Abu Mijlaz. Al-Bukhari and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat have related from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed in Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for the mujahidin in the way of Allah; the distance between two degrees is like the distance between the heaven and the earth. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Paradise and the highest of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth."
