**Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 4, verses 97–100**

His saying: (*tawaffahum*) may be a past-tense verb, with the feminine marker dropped because the feminine gender of "the angels" is not real (*ghayr haqiqi*). It may also be a future (*mustaqbal*) verb, the original being *tatawaffahum*, with one of the two *ta'*s dropped. Ibn Furak reported from al-Hasan that the meaning is "He will gather them (*tahshuruhum*) to the Fire." It was also said that it means "He will seize their souls (*taqbid arwahahum*)," and this is the most apparent meaning.

By "the angels" is meant the angels of death, based on God's saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you in death﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. His saying: (﴿zalimi anfusihim﴾) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while they were wronging themselves. The angels' saying: ﴿What was your condition?﴾ is a question of rebuke, meaning: "In what matter of your religion were you?" It was also said that the meaning is: "Were you among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), or were you polytheists?" And it was said that the purpose of the question is to reproach them for having held no part of the religion at all.

Their saying: ﴿We were oppressed in the land﴾ means Mecca, because the occasion of revelation concerns those who embraced Islam there but did not emigrate, as will come. Then the angels confronted them with their religion, established the proof against them, and cut off their excuse, so they said: ﴿Was not the earth of God spacious, so that you could have emigrated therein?﴾ It was said that by "this earth" is meant Medina. But the better view is generality, taking into account the generality of the wording rather than the specificity of the occasion, as is the truth. Thus "the earth" means every region of the earth suitable for emigration to, and the first "earth" means every land from which emigration is appropriate.

His saying: (﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾) This clause is the predicate of ﴿those﴾ (*ula'ika*), and the whole sentence is the predicate of *inna* in his saying: (﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾). The *fa'* is inserted because the subject of *inna* contains the meaning of a conditional (*sharṭ*). And ﴿evil is it as a destination﴾, that is, Hell, (*masiran*), meaning: a place to which they arrive.

His saying: (﴿except the oppressed﴾) is an exception from the pronoun in ﴿their refuge﴾. It was also said that it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), because the oppressed are not included in the relative clause and its pronoun. His saying: ﴿from among the men and the women and the children﴾ is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "being among them." By "the oppressed men" are meant the disabled and the like. The "children" are like Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah and Salamah ibn Hisham. He mentioned the children despite their not being obligated, in order to emphasize the matter of emigration, and to imply that it is obligatory even for one who is not accountable if he is able to do it, so how much more so for one who is accountable. It was also said that by "the children" he meant those approaching puberty and the slaves.

His saying: (﴿they cannot devise a plan﴾) is a descriptive (*sifah*) for "the oppressed," or for "the men and the women and the children," or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "the oppressed." It was said: *al-hilah* is a general term for the kinds of means of escape, meaning: they do not find a plan or a way to that. It was also said: *al-sabil* means the way to Medina. ﴿Those﴾ refers to the oppressed described with what has been mentioned. ﴿Perhaps God will pardon them﴾: the word of hope (*kalimat al-itmi'*) is used to affirm the matter of emigration, so that one thinks that abandoning it by one for whom it is not obligatory would be a sin requiring the seeking of pardon for it.

His saying: ﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of God will find in the earth many a refuge and abundance﴾. This sentence contains encouragement toward emigration and stirring up of desire for it. His saying: *in the way of God* indicates that emigration must be with a sound intention and a sincere purpose, not mixed with any worldly matter. From this is the sound hadith: "Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for a worldly thing he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for."

The meaning of God's saying (﴿will find in the earth a refuge (*muraghaman*)﴾) has been disputed. Ibn Abbas and a group of the Successors and those after them said: *al-muraghan* means the place of moving away and the path. Mujahid said: *al-muraghan* means the one who withdraws (*al-mutazahzih*).

Ibn Zayd said: *al-muraghan* means the place of emigration, and Abu Ubaydah said likewise. Al-Nahhas said: These sayings are agreed in meaning. So *al-muraghan* is the path and the place of moving, which is the place where one is opposed (*yuraghamu*) in it. It is derived from *al-raghām*, which is dust; and "the nose of so-and-so was humbled (*raghima anfu fulan*)," meaning he was pressed into the dust. And "I opposed so-and-so (*raghamtu fulanan*)" means I abandoned him and was hostile to him, and did not care that his nose was humbled. It was also said: he was named an emigrant and an opponent because a man, when he embraced Islam, became hostile to his people and abandoned them, so his leaving was named *muraghaman*, and his journey to the Prophet (ﷺ) was named *hijrah*.

The summary of the meaning of the verse is that the emigrant finds on the earth a place to dwell in despite the noses of his people whom he emigrated from, that is, despite their humiliation and their degradation. His saying: (*wa sa'ah*) means: in the lands. It was also said: in provision. There is no obstacle to understanding *al-sa'ah* in a sense more general than that.

His saying: ﴿Whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to God and His Messenger, then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed fallen upon God﴾. It has been read *yudrikhu* (with a jussive *-h*, *yudrikhu* as *yudrikh*) by way of conjunction with the conditional verb; and with a *ḍamma* as the predicate of an omitted subject; and with a *fatḥa* by way of an implied *an*. The meaning: whoever death overtakes before he reaches his goal, which is the place he intended to emigrate to, or the matter for which he intended to emigrate, ﴿his reward has indeed fallen upon God﴾, that is: it is established with Him as an establishment that does not fail. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾, that is, abundant in forgiveness, ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, abundant in mercy.

This verse has been cited as evidence that emigration is obligatory upon everyone who is in the abode of polytheism, or in an abode where the disobedience of God is openly practiced, if he is able to emigrate and is not among the oppressed, because of the generality in this noble verse, even though the occasion of revelation is specific, as has preceded. Its apparent meaning is that there is no difference between one place and another, or one time and another. Hadiths have been transmitted concerning emigration, and some have come indicating that there is no emigration after the Conquest. We have clarified the truth in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let one refer to it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* have transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: A group of people from Mecca had embraced Islam and were concealing their Islam. The polytheists brought them out with them on the day of Badr, and some of them were struck and some were killed. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were coerced; so ask forgiveness for them." Then this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. He said: So it was written to those Muslims who remained in Mecca about this verse, and that they had no excuse. So they went out, and the polytheists caught up with them and inflicted trial upon them. Then this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10], to the end of the verse. So the Muslims wrote to them with that, and they grieved and despaired of every good. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then fought and were patient—indeed, your Lord thereafter is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. So they wrote to them with that, that God has made for you a way out, so come out. They came out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Al-Bukhari and others have transmitted it from him, abbreviating it to its beginning.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and evil is it as a destination﴾. He said: It was revealed concerning Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Aswad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. He said: When the polytheists of Quraysh and their followers went out to prevent Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and the caravan of Quraysh from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions, and to seek what had been taken from them on the day of Nakhlah, they went out with them with young men who were unwilling, who had embraced Islam, and they gathered at Badr without a prior appointment. So they were killed at Badr as unbelievers, and they had turned back from Islam; and they are the ones we have named. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from Ibn Ishaq, and something like this has been related through several chains.

Al-Bukhari and others have transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he recited this verse: ﴿except the oppressed among the men and the women and the children﴾, and said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed: I was among the children and my mother was among the women."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying: (﴿they cannot devise a plan﴾), he said: "strength." Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿they cannot devise a plan﴾, he said: "rising up toward Medina," and ﴿nor are they guided to a way﴾, he said: "a path to Medina." Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: (﴿muraghaman kathiran wa sa'ah﴾), he said: "*al-muraghan* is the moving from land to land, and *al-sa'ah* is provision." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, "*muraghaman*," he said: "withdrawing from what he dislikes." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ata' concerning His saying: (﴿wa sa'ah﴾), he said: "and ease." He also transmitted from Malik, who said: "*sa'at al-bilad*" (the vastness of the lands).

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani—al-Suyuti said, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy—transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Dhamrah ibn Jundub left his house as an emigrant and said to his people: "Carry me and take me out of the land of polytheism to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." But he died on the road before reaching the Prophet (ﷺ), so the revelation came down: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to God﴾, the verse. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from him by another route.

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Abd Allah ibn Atik, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Whoever leaves his house striving in the way of God—and where are the strivers in the way of God?—then he falls from his mount and dies, his reward has fallen upon God; or a beast stings him and he dies, his reward has fallen upon God; or he dies by his nose-death (*bi-hatf anfihi*), that is, upon his bed, his reward has fallen upon God." By God, it is indeed a word I had not heard from any Arab before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). "And whoever is killed in a sudden death (*qa'sa'*) has earned Paradise."

Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever goes out on pilgrimage and dies, there is written for him the reward of a pilgrim until the Day of Resurrection; whoever goes out as a performer of the minor pilgrimage (*'umrah*) and dies, there is written for him the reward of one performing 'umrah until the Day of Resurrection; and whoever goes out as a warrior in the way of God and dies, there is written for him the reward of a warrior until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a strange hadith through this route.

It was said: *al-hilah* is a general term for the kinds of means of escape, meaning: they do not find a plan or a way to that. And "I opposed so-and-so (*raghamtu fulanan*)" means I abandoned him and was hostile to him, and did not care that his nose was humbled. It was also said: he was named an emigrant and an opponent because a man, when he embraced Islam, became hostile to his people and abandoned them, so his leaving was named *muraghaman*, and his journey to the Prophet (ﷺ) was named *hijrah*.

The summary of the meaning of the verse is that the emigrant finds on the earth a place to dwell in despite the noses of his people whom he emigrated from, that is, despite their humiliation and their degradation. The meaning: whoever death overtakes before he reaches his goal, which is the place he intended to emigrate to, or the matter for which he intended to emigrate, ﴿his reward has indeed fallen upon God﴾, that is: it is established with Him as an establishment that does not fail. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾, that is, abundant in forgiveness, ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, abundant in mercy.

Its apparent meaning is that there is no difference between one place and another, or one time and another. Hadiths have been transmitted concerning emigration, and some have come indicating that there is no emigration after the Conquest. We have clarified the truth in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let one refer to it.

The polytheists brought them out with them on the day of Badr, and some of them were struck and some were killed. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims, but they were coerced; so ask forgiveness for them." Then this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. So they went out, and the polytheists caught up with them and inflicted trial upon them. Then this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10], to the end of the verse. So the Muslims wrote to them with that, and they grieved and despaired of every good. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then fought and were patient—indeed, your Lord thereafter is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. They came out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Al-Bukhari and others have transmitted it from him, abbreviating it to its beginning.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and evil is it as a destination﴾. He said: When the polytheists of Quraysh and their followers went out to prevent Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and the caravan of Quraysh from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions, and to seek what had been taken from them on the day of Nakhlah, they went out with them with young men who were unwilling, who had embraced Islam, and they gathered at Badr without a prior appointment. So they were killed at Badr as unbelievers, and they had turned back from Islam; and they are the ones we have named. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from Ibn Ishaq, and something like this has been related through several chains.

Al-Bukhari and others have transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he recited this verse: ﴿except the oppressed among the men and the women and the children﴾, and said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed: I was among the children and my mother was among the women."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: (﴿muraghaman kathiran wa sa'ah﴾), he said: "*al-muraghan* is the moving from land to land, and *al-sa'ah* is provision." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, "*muraghaman*," he said: "withdrawing from what he dislikes." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ata' concerning His saying: (﴿wa sa'ah﴾), he said: "and ease." He also transmitted from Malik, who said: "*sa'at al-bilad*" (the vastness of the lands).

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani—al-Suyuti said, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy—transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Dhamrah ibn Jundub left his house as an emigrant and said to his people: "Carry me and take me out of the land of polytheism to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." But he died on the road before reaching the Prophet (ﷺ), so the revelation came down: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to God﴾, the verse. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from him by another route.

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Abd Allah ibn Atik, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Whoever leaves his house striving in the way of God—and where are the strivers in the way of God?—then he falls from his mount and dies, his reward has fallen upon God; or a beast stings him and he dies, his reward has fallen upon God; or he dies by his nose-death (*bi-hatf anfihi*), that is, upon his bed, his reward has fallen upon God." By God, it is indeed a word I had not heard from any Arab before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). "And whoever is killed in a sudden death (*qa'sa'*) has earned Paradise."

Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever goes out on pilgrimage and dies, there is written for him the reward of a pilgrim until the Day of Resurrection; whoever goes out as a performer of the minor pilgrimage (*'umrah*) and dies, there is written for him the reward of one performing 'umrah until the Day of Resurrection; and whoever goes out as a warrior in the way of God and dies, there is written for him the reward of a warrior until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a strange hadith through this route.

His statement, "﴿And when you travel through the land﴾": the explanation of *darb fi al-ard* (travelling through the land) has already been given shortly before.

His statement, "﴿there is no blame upon you﴾": this is evidence that *qasr* (shortening the prayer) is not obligatory. This is the view of the majority. A minority held that it is obligatory, including ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, the Kufans, the judge Ismaʿil, and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, and this view is also attributed to Malik. They argued with the hadith of ʿAʾishah, which is authentic in the Sahih: "The prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs. It was increased for the resident and left as it was for the traveller." The fact that she contradicted what she narrated does not weaken this, since action is based on the second report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Similar is the hadith of Yaʿla ibn Umayya, who said: "I asked ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, 'Upon you there is no blame if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you,' while the people are now secure." ʿUmar said to me, "I was amazed at what you were amazed at (p-325) so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity.'" Narrated by Ahmad, Muslim, and the authors of the Sunan. The apparent meaning of his words, "so accept His charity," is that shortening is obligatory.

His statement, "﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾": the apparent meaning of this condition is that shortening the prayer during travel is permitted only with fear of tempting by the disbelievers, not in security. However, it has been established by the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) shortened the prayer in security," as you know. Thus shortening in fear is established by the Book, and shortening in security is established by the Sunnah. The implication of a condition cannot stand against what has been transmitted with certainty (mutawatir) from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding shortening in security.

It has been said that this condition came in the form of what is usual, because what was usual for the Muslims at that time was shortening due to fear during journeys. For this reason Yaʿla ibn Umayya said to ʿUmar what he said, as has passed. In the reading of Ubayy: "﴿that you shorten the prayer, if you fear that they may tempt you﴾" without "﴿if you fear﴾" (the second occurrence), and the meaning according to this reading is "lest those who disbelieve tempt you."

A group of scholars held that this verse only permits shortening during travel for one who fears the enemy. Whoever is secure has no shortening. Others held that his statement "if you fear" is not connected to what precedes it, and that the speech ended at "the prayer," then began anew: "﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾," so establish for them, O Muhammad, the prayer of fear.

His statement, "﴿Indeed, the disbelievers have ever been to you an open enemy﴾," is parenthetical. Al-Jurjani, al-Mahdawi, and others mentioned this meaning, and al-Qushayri and the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi rejected it. Al-Qurtubi related from Ibn ʿAbbas the meaning mentioned by al-Jurjani and those with him. What refutes and repels this is the conjunction "wa" in his statement, "﴿And when you are among them﴾." Some commentators made an effort and said that the "wa" is superfluous and that the response (jawab) of the condition mentioned, namely "﴿if you fear﴾," is his statement "then let a party of them stand," but some people held that the mention of fear was abrogated (naskh) by the Sunnah, namely the hadith of ʿUmar that we mentioned earlier and what has come with a similar meaning.

His statement, "that those who disbelieve may tempt you." Al-Farraʾ said: The people of the Hijaz say *fatantu al-rajul* (فَتَنْتُ الرَّجُلَ), while Rabiʿah, Qays, Asad, and all the people of Najd say *aftantu al-rajul* (أفْتَنْتُ الرَّجُلَ). Al-Khalil and Sibawayh distinguished between them, saying: *fatantuhu* means I put *fitnah* in him, like *kahaltuhu* (I applied kohl to him), while *aftantuhu* means I made him subject to *fitnah* (I made him tempted). Al-Asmaʿi claimed that he did not know *aftantahu*.

The intended meaning of *fitnah* here is fighting and attacking with what is disliked.

His statement, "﴿an enemy﴾" (ʿaduwwan): meaning enemies (aʿdaʾ).

His statement, "﴿And when you are among them and establish for them the prayer﴾": this is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to those after him among the leaders (ahl al-amr), and the ruling applies to them as is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Similar is His statement, "﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾" [al-Tawbah: 103] and similar. This is the view of the majority of scholars. Abu Yusuf and Ismaʿil ibn ʿUlayyah deviated, saying: the prayer of fear is not performed after the Prophet (ﷺ), because this address is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They said: no one else is attached to him, because of the great distinction the Prophet (ﷺ) possessed. This is rejected, for Allah has commanded us to follow His Messenger and take him as a model. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pray as you have seen me pray." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are more knowledgeable about the meanings of the Qur'an, and they performed it after his death on more than one occasion, as is well known. The meaning of "﴿establish for them the prayer﴾" is "you intend to establish it," like His statement, "﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾," and His statement, "﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾" [al-Nahl: 98].

His statement, "﴿let a party of them stand with you﴾": meaning, after you make them into two groups: one group stands facing the enemy, and another group stands with you in prayer. "﴿And let them take their weapons﴾": meaning the group that prays with him. It was said that the pronoun refers to the group facing the enemy, but the first is more apparent, because the group standing facing the enemy must necessarily be standing with its weapons. The command to do that is needed only for those who are in prayer, because they might think that carrying weapons is forbidden during prayer. So Allah commanded them to be holding their weapons, meaning not putting them down. The intended meaning is not taking them in hand, but that they should be carrying their weapons so they can grab them from nearby if they need them, and so that this is more effective in cutting off the hope of their enemy of finding an opportunity against them.

Ibn ʿAbbas held that the pronoun in "﴿and let them take their weapons﴾" refers to the group facing the enemy, saying: because the group praying does not fight. Others said the pronoun refers to the praying group. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas allowed that this is a command to both groups together, because it is more frightening to the enemy. The Ahl al-Zahir (literalists) made taking up weapons in this prayer obligatory, interpreting the command as obligatory.

Abu Hanifah held that those praying do not carry weapons, and that doing so invalidates the prayer. This is rejected by what is in this verse and by the authentic hadiths.

His statement, "﴿So when they have prostrated﴾": meaning, those standing in prayer. "Then let them be behind you," meaning the group facing the enemy should be behind you, i.e., behind those praying.

It is possible that the meaning is: "So when those praying with him have prostrated," meaning they completed the rak'ah, using prostration to refer to the whole rak'ah or to the whole prayer. "Then let them be behind you," meaning, after finishing, they should turn to face the enemy as guards. "And let another group come, which is the group facing the enemy that did not pray, and let them pray with you in the manner in which the first group prayed." "﴿And let them take﴾" (wa-l-yaʾkhudhu), meaning this other group, "﴿their precaution and their weapons﴾," an added instruction to the other group to take precaution together with taking up weapons. It was said that the reason is that this time there is a likelihood that the disbelievers will notice that the group standing with the Prophet (ﷺ) is occupied with something distracting. As for the first time, they might think they are standing for battle. It was also said: because the enemy does not delay its intent until this time, since it is the end of the prayer. The weapon is that by which a person defends himself in war. The noble verse does not specify how long each of the two groups prays. The prayer of fear has come in the purified Sunnah in various forms and different descriptions, and all of them are authentic and sufficient. Whoever performs any one of them has done what he was commanded. Whoever among the scholars chose one form over the others has strayed from what is correct. We have clarified this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa and in all our other works.

His statement, "﴿The disbelievers wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, so they could come upon you in one attack﴾": this sentence contains the reason for which Allah commanded them to take precaution and carry weapons. (p-326) Meaning: they wished for your neglect of taking up weapons and of precaution, so that they could reach their aim and gain their opportunity, and then attack you in one assault. The *amtiʿah* (belongings) are what one uses for enjoyment during war, including provisions and mounts.

His statement, "﴿And there is no blame upon you if you are troubled by rain or if you are ill, to put down your weapons﴾": He, glorified is He, permitted them to put down weapons when they are troubled by rain or when they are ill, because carrying weapons becomes difficult in these two situations. Then He commanded them to take precaution, lest the enemy come upon them unexpectedly while they are heedless. Ibn Abi Shaybah and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Handhalah who said: I asked Ibn ʿUmar about the prayer during travel. He said: "Two rak'ahs." I said: "Then what about His statement, 'if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you,' while we are secure?" He said: "It is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Umayyah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Khalid ibn Usayd that he asked Ibn ʿUmar: "Tell me about shortening the prayer during travel. We do not find it in the Book of Allah; we only find mention of the prayer of fear." Ibn ʿUmar said: "O son of my brother, Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) and we know nothing. We only do what we have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) doing. Shortening the prayer during travel is a Sunnah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) established."

In the two Sahihs and others, from Harithah ibn Wahb al-Khuzaʿi who said: "I prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) the Dhuhr and the ʿAsr at Mina, when the people were at their most numerous and most secure, two rak'ahs."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, and al-Nasaʾi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) between Makkah and Madinah while we were secure, fearing nothing, two rak'ahs."

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿAli who said: "A group of merchants asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, we travel through the land, so how should we pray?' Then Allah revealed, '﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾.' Then the revelation ceased. After a year, the Prophet (ﷺ) went on a military expedition and prayed the Dhuhr. The polytheists said: 'Muhammad and his Companions have been placed before you from behind; why did you not attack them?' One of them said: 'Indeed, they have another prayer after it, equal to it.' So Allah revealed between the two prayers, '﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you, indeed the disbelievers have ever been to you an open enemy﴾' and '﴿And when you are among them﴾' until His statement, '﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾.' Then the prayer of fear was revealed."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 103–104:

(قَضَيْتُمْ) means "you finished" (faraghtum) from the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), and it is one of the meanings of qada' (completion, fulfilment). Similar to it is ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] and ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. As for His saying: ﴿Remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾, it means: in all circumstances, even in the state of fighting. The majority of scholars (jumhur al-'ulama') held that this remembrance commanded here is what follows the prayer of fear; that is, when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah in these states. It was also said that the meaning of His saying: (﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾) is: when you pray, then pray standing, sitting, or on your sides, as the situation requires at the moment of close combat. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 239].

As for His saying: (﴿So when you are secure﴾), it means: when you are safe and your hearts are at rest. Tuma'nina (tranquillity) is the calm of the soul from fear. ﴿Then establish the prayer﴾ means: perform the prayer whose time has entered in its prescribed form with its prescribed remembrances and pillars, and do not do less than what is possible, for that concession applies only in the state of fear. It was also said that the meaning in the verse is that they make up what they prayed during the state of close fighting, because that is a state of agitation, distress, and shortcoming in the remembrances and pillars; this is related from al-Shafi'i. The first view is more preponderant. ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been prescribed upon the believers at fixed times﴾; that is, specified and determined. It is said: waqatahu, so it is mawqut (fixed), and waqqatahu, so it is muwaqqat (appointed).

The meaning is: Allah has obligated His servants to the prayers and prescribed them upon them at their specified times; it is not permissible for anyone to perform them outside that time except for a legitimate excuse such as sleep, forgetfulness, or the like.

His saying: ﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy﴾ means: do not be weak in seeking them, and show strength and endurance. His saying: ﴿If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾ is a reason for the prohibition mentioned before it; that is, the pain of wounds and the toil of fighting that you find is not specific to you, but is a matter shared between you and them. They are no more deserving than you of patience in the heat of battle and the bitterness of war. Yet you have an advantage over them that they do not have: you hope from Allah for reward and great recompense that they do not hope for, because of their disbelief and denial. Therefore you are more worthy of patience than they are and more entitled to not weakening than they are, for your souls are strong, since they see death as gain, while they see it as loss. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]. It was also said that "hope" here means "fear," because whoever hopes for something is not certain of obtaining it, so he is never free of fear of what he hopes for.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "hope" is not used in the sense of "fear" except with negation, as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for Allah to be dignified?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning: you do not fear His greatness.

Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj read (أنْ تَكُونُوا) with a fatha on the hamza, meaning li-an takunu (because you are). Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir read (تِيلَمُونَ) with a kasra on the taa'; but according to the Basrians, it is not permissible to use a kasra on the taa' because of its heaviness.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾ that he said: "By night and by day, on land and at sea, while traveling and at home, in wealth and in poverty, in sickness and in health, in secret and in public, and in every state."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ibn Mas'ud that it reached him that some people remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and he said: "This is only when a man is unable to pray standing; he prays sitting."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning (﴿So when you are secure﴾) that he said: "When you leave the abode of travel for the abode of residence, then establish the prayer," he said: "Complete it." Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related similarly from Qatadah, and Ibn al-Mundhir related similarly from Ibn Jurayj.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been prescribed upon the believers at fixed times﴾ that he meant: obligatory (mafrudan). Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "Mawqut means obligatory (wajib)." Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning (ولا تَهِنُوا) that he said: "do not weaken." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning (﴿تَأْلَمُونَ﴾) that he said: "you are hurt," and concerning (﴿وتَرْجُونَ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا يَرْجُونَ﴾) that he said: "you hope for good."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 103–104:

(قَضَيْتُمْ) means "you finished" (faraghtum) from the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), and it is one of the meanings of qada' (completion, fulfilment). Similar to it is ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] and ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. As for His saying: ﴿Remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾, it means: in all circumstances, even in the state of fighting. The majority of scholars (jumhur al-'ulama') held that this remembrance commanded here is what follows the prayer of fear; that is, when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah in these states. It was also said that the meaning of His saying: (﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾) is: when you pray, then pray standing, sitting, or on your sides, as the situation requires at the moment of close combat. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 239].

As for His saying: (﴿So when you are secure﴾), it means: when you are safe and your hearts are at rest. Tuma'nina (tranquillity) is the calm of the soul from fear. ﴿Then establish the prayer﴾ means: perform the prayer whose time has entered in its prescribed form with its prescribed remembrances and pillars, and do not do less than what is possible, for that concession applies only in the state of fear. It was also said that the meaning in the verse is that they make up what they prayed during the state of close fighting, because that is a state of agitation, distress, and shortcoming in the remembrances and pillars; this is related from al-Shafi'i. The first view is more preponderant. ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been prescribed upon the believers at fixed times﴾; that is, specified and determined. It is said: waqatahu, so it is mawqut (fixed), and waqqatahu, so it is muwaqqat (appointed).

The meaning is: Allah has obligated His servants to the prayers and prescribed them upon them at their specified times; it is not permissible for anyone to perform them outside that time except for a legitimate excuse such as sleep, forgetfulness, or the like.

His saying: ﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy﴾ means: do not be weak in seeking them, and show strength and endurance. His saying: ﴿If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾ is a reason for the prohibition mentioned before it; that is, the pain of wounds and the toil of fighting that you find is not specific to you, but is a matter shared between you and them. They are no more deserving than you of patience in the heat of battle and the bitterness of war. Yet you have an advantage over them that they do not have: you hope from Allah for reward and great recompense that they do not hope for, because of their disbelief and denial. Therefore you are more worthy of patience than they are and more entitled to not weakening than they are, for your souls are strong, since they see death as gain, while they see it as loss. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]. It was also said that "hope" here means "fear," because whoever hopes for something is not certain of obtaining it, so he is never free of fear of what he hopes for.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "hope" is not used in the sense of "fear" except with negation, as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for Allah to be dignified?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning: you do not fear His greatness.

His saying: "by what Allah has shown you," either by revelation or by what proceeds according to the patterns of what Allah has revealed. The intended meaning here is not seeing with the eye, since a ruling cannot be seen. Rather, it means by what Allah has made known to him and guided him to.

His saying: (﴿And do not be a disputant for the treacherous﴾), meaning: do not be an advocate on behalf of the treacherous, that is, do not argue on their behalf, disputing with the upright because of them. This indicates that it is not permitted for anyone to argue on behalf of another unless he knows that the other is in the right.

His saying: (﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾) is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to seek forgiveness. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, "Seek forgiveness from Allah for your sin in your disputing on behalf of the treacherous." The reason the verse was revealed will be explained later, and through it the intended meaning becomes clear. It was also said that the meaning is: "Seek forgiveness from Allah on behalf of the sinners among your community and those who dispute falsely."

His saying: ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾, meaning: do not argue on behalf of those who betray their own souls. Al-mujadalah (disputation) is derived from al-jadal, which means twisting. It was also said it is derived from al-jaddalah, which is the surface of the earth, because each of the two adversaries wants to throw his opponent down upon it. Their sin is called betrayal of themselves because the harm of their disobedience returns to them. Al-khawwan means one who commits much betrayal, and al-atheem means one who commits much sin. Not loving them is a metaphor for hatred.

His saying: (﴿They conceal themselves from people﴾), meaning: they hide from them, like His saying: (﴿and one who hides himself by night﴾) [al-Ra'd: 10], meaning: one who hides. It was also said that the meaning is: ﴿They conceal themselves from people, yet they do not conceal themselves from Allah﴾, meaning: they do not hide from Him or are not ashamed before Him, while He is with them in all their circumstances, knowing what they are engaged in. So how can they hide from Him when they plot at night? Tabyit (plotting) means they devise a plan among themselves. It is called tabyit because devising a plan usually takes place at night, of speech that does not please Him, that is, of the plan they devised among themselves. It is called speech because it only comes about after discussion among them.

His saying: (﴿Here you are﴾), meaning the people who argued on behalf of their companion the thief, as will come. The phrase is a subject and predicate.

Al-Zajjaj said: (ulaa') means "those who," and (jadaltum) means "you argued" in the life of this world. ﴿So who will dispute with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ The interrogative is for denial and rebuke, meaning: who will argue and dispute with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection when they are punished for their sins? ﴿Or who will be a guardian over them?﴾, meaning a disputant and an advocate. Al-wakil (guardian) originally means one who manages affairs.

The meaning is: who will take charge of their affair when Allah seizes them with His punishment?

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, who said: There was a household among us called the Banu Ubayriq: Bishr, Bushayr, and Mubashshir. Bishr was a hypocrite who composed poetry satirizing the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he would attribute it to some of the Arabs, saying: "So-and-so said such and such, so-and-so said such and such." When the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard that poetry, they would say: "By Allah, no one composes this poetry except this wicked man." Then he said:

*"Whenever men compose a poem, they are silenced, and they say: 'It was composed by Ibn al-Ubayriq.'"*

He said: They were a household of need and poverty in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. The people of Madinah ate only dates and barley. When a man had means and a caravan of provisions arrived from al-Sham, containing fine wheat flour, a man would buy from it and keep it for himself, while his dependents ate only dates and barley. "A caravan arrived from al-Sham, and my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Rafi' bought a load of fine flour and placed it in a storehouse, and in the storehouse were his weapons: two coats of mail, two swords, and what was needed to maintain them. A thief came upon him in the night, the storehouse was broken into, and the food and weapons were taken. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said: 'O nephew, you know that we were attacked during this night; our storehouse was broken into, and our food and weapons were taken.' He said: 'We searched the house and asked around, and we were told: We have seen the Banu Ubayriq kindle a fire this night, and we do not think, from what we see, that it was anything but some of your food.' He said: The Banu Ubayriq said, while we were asking around the house, 'By Allah, we do not think your companion is anyone but Labid ibn Sahl, a man among us who has righteousness and Islam.' When Labid heard this, he drew his sword, then came to the Banu Ubayriq and said: 'Am I a thief? By Allah, this sword will either reach you, or you will reveal this theft!' They said: 'Away from us, O man! By Allah, you are not its perpetrator.' We searched the house until we had no doubt that they were its perpetrators. My uncle said to me: 'O nephew, if you went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him.'" Qatadah said: "So I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a household among us, people of harshness, attacked my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Zayd, broke into his storehouse, and took his weapons and food. Let them return our weapons to us; as for the food, we have no need of it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will look into this matter.' When the Banu Ubayriq heard this, they went to a man among them called Usayr ibn Urwah and spoke to him about it, and a group of people from the household gathered around him. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man and his uncle have targeted a household among us, people of Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof.'" Qatadah said: "So I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke to him, and he said: 'You have targeted a household mentioned for Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof?'" Qatadah said: "So I returned, and I wished that I had lost some of my property rather than having spoken to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it. Then my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said: 'O nephew, what have you done?' So I told him what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to me, and he said: 'Allah is the One sought for help.'" Then it was not long before the Qur'an was revealed: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be a disputant for the treacherous﴾), meaning the Banu Ubayriq. (﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾), meaning for what you said to Qatadah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then whoever seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], meaning: if they had sought forgiveness from Allah, He would have forgiven them. (﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾) [al-Nisa': 111] up to His saying: (﴿has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾) [al-Nisa': 112], referring to their words about Labid. And His saying: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you﴾ [al-Nisa': 113], meaning Usayr ibn Urwah. When the Qur'an was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought the weapons and returned them to Rifa'ah. Qatadah said: "When I brought the weapons to my uncle, he was an elderly man who had been overcome in the Jahiliyyah, meaning he had grown old. I used to think his Islam was tainted. But when I brought him the weapons, he said: 'O nephew, it is in the way of Allah.' So I knew that his Islam was sound." When the Qur'an was revealed, Bushayr joined the polytheists and stayed with Sulafah bint Sa'd. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa': 115] up to His saying: (﴿far astray﴾) [al-Nisa': 115–116]. When he stayed with Sulafah, Hassan ibn Thabit satirized him with verses of poetry, so she took his saddle, placed it on her head, went out, threw it into al-Abtah, and said: "You brought me the poetry of Hassan; you never brought me any good." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a gharib (singular) hadith; we know of no one who transmitted it with a full chain except Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Harrani.

It was also related by Yunus ibn Bukayr and others, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah, as a mursal (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain), without mentioning "from his father, from his grandfather." Ibn Abi Hatim related it from Hashim ibn al-Qasim al-Harrani, from Muhammad ibn al-Sani', who said: Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, and he mentioned it in full. Abu al-Shaykh al-Isbahani related it in his tafsir from Muhammad ibn al-Abbas ibn Ayyub and al-Hasan ibn Ya'qub, both from al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani, from Muhammad ibn Salamah with the same wording. Then at its end he said: Muhammad ibn Salamah said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il heard this hadith from me." Al-Hakim also related it in al-Mustadrak from Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm, from Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Utaridi, from Yunus ibn Bukayr, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, with a similar meaning but more complete, and then said: This is sahih according to the conditions of Muslim.

Ibn Sa'd related it from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: Bushayr went out and mentioned it in brief. This story has been related in both brief and extended forms from a group of the Successors.

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, who said: There was a household among us called the Banu Ubayriq: Bishr, Bushayr, and Mubashshir. Bishr was a hypocrite who composed poetry satirizing the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he would attribute it to some of the Arabs, saying: "So-and-so said such and such, so-and-so said such and such." When the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard that poetry, they would say: "By Allah, no one composes this poetry except this wicked man." Then he said:

*"Whenever men compose a poem, they are silenced, and they say: 'It was composed by Ibn al-Ubayriq.'"*

He said: They were a household of need and poverty in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. The people of Madinah ate only dates and barley. When a man had means and a caravan of provisions arrived from al-Sham, containing fine wheat flour, a man would buy from it and keep it for himself, while his dependents ate only dates and barley. A thief came upon him in the night, the storehouse was broken into, and the food and weapons were taken. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said: 'O nephew, you know that we were attacked during this night; our storehouse was broken into, and our food and weapons were taken.' He said: 'We searched the house and asked around, and we were told: We have seen the Banu Ubayriq kindle a fire this night, and we do not think, from what we see, that it was anything but some of your food.' He said: The Banu Ubayriq said, while we were asking around the house, 'By Allah, we do not think your companion is anyone but Labid ibn Sahl, a man among us who has righteousness and Islam.' When Labid heard this, he drew his sword, then came to the Banu Ubayriq and said: 'Am I a thief? By Allah, this sword will either reach you, or you will reveal this theft!' They said: 'Away from us, O man! By Allah, you are not its perpetrator.' We searched the house until we had no doubt that they were its perpetrators. My uncle said to me: 'O nephew, if you went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him.'" Qatadah said: "So I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a household among us, people of harshness, attacked my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Zayd, broke into his storehouse, and took his weapons and food. Let them return our weapons to us; as for the food, we have no need of it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will look into this matter.' When the Banu Ubayriq heard this, they went to a man among them called Usayr ibn Urwah and spoke to him about it, and a group of people from the household gathered around him. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man and his uncle have targeted a household among us, people of Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof.'" Qatadah said: "So I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke to him, and he said: 'You have targeted a household mentioned for Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof?'" Qatadah said: "So I returned, and I wished that I had lost some of my property rather than having spoken to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it. Then my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said: 'O nephew, what have you done?' So I told him what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to me, and he said: 'Allah is the One sought for help.'" Then it was not long before the Qur'an was revealed: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be a disputant for the treacherous﴾), meaning the Banu Ubayriq. (﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾), meaning for what you said to Qatadah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then whoever seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], meaning: if they had sought forgiveness from Allah, He would have forgiven them. (﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾) [al-Nisa': 111] up to His saying: (﴿has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾) [al-Nisa': 112], referring to their words about Labid. And His saying: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to mislead you﴾ [al-Nisa': 113], meaning Usayr ibn Urwah. When the Qur'an was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought the weapons and returned them to Rifa'ah. Qatadah said: "When I brought the weapons to my uncle, he was an elderly man who had been overcome in the Jahiliyyah, meaning he had grown old. I used to think his Islam was tainted. But when I brought him the weapons, he said: 'O nephew, it is in the way of Allah.' So I knew that his Islam was sound." When the Qur'an was revealed, Bushayr joined the polytheists and stayed with Sulafah bint Sa'd. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa': 115] up to His saying: (﴿far astray﴾) [al-Nisa': 115–116]. Qatadah said: "When I brought the weapons to my uncle, he was an elderly man who had been overcome in the Jahiliyyah, meaning he had grown old. I used to think his Islam was tainted. But when I brought him the weapons, he said: 'O nephew, it is in the way of Allah.' So I knew that his Islam was sound." When the Qur'an was revealed, Bushayr joined the polytheists and stayed with Sulafah bint Sa'd. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa': 115] up to His saying: (﴿far astray﴾) [al-Nisa': 115–116]. When he stayed with Sulafah, Hassan ibn Thabit satirized him with verses of poetry, so she took his saddle, placed it on her head, went out, threw it into al-Abtah, and said: "You brought me the poetry of Hassan; you never brought me any good." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a gharib (singular) hadith; we know of no one who transmitted it with a full chain except Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Harrani.

It was also related by Yunus ibn Bukayr and others, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah, as a mursal (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain), without mentioning "from his father, from his grandfather." Ibn Abi Hatim related it from Hashim ibn al-Qasim al-Harrani, from Muhammad ibn al-Sani', who said: Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, and he mentioned it in full. Abu al-Shaykh al-Isbahani related it in his tafsir from Muhammad ibn al-Abbas ibn Ayyub and al-Hasan ibn Ya'qub, both from al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani, from Muhammad ibn Salamah with the same wording. Then at its end he said: Muhammad ibn Salamah said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il heard this hadith from me." Al-Hakim also related it in al-Mustadrak from Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm, from Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Utaridi, from Yunus ibn Bukayr, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, with a similar meaning but more complete, and then said: This is sahih according to the conditions of Muslim.

Ibn Sa'd related it from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: Bushayr went out and mentioned it in brief. This story has been related in both brief and extended forms from a group of the Successors.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 110–113:

This is part of the completion of the preceding story. What is meant by "evil" (su') is the ugly deed by which one harms others, or by which one wrongs oneself through committing a sin of disobedience or a transgression that does not extend to others. ﴿Then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾ asks Him to forgive him for the sin he has committed. ﴿Will find Allah Forgiving﴾ of his sin, ("Merciful") toward him. In this there is encouragement for the one who committed the theft from the Banu Ubayriq to repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness, and that He is Forgiving to whoever seeks His forgiveness and Merciful to him.

Al-Dahhak said: this verse was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah. He had associated partners with Allah and killed Hamzah, then came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Is there repentance for me?" So it was revealed. In any case, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specific cause, so it applies to every servant of Allah's servants who commits a sin and then seeks forgiveness from Allah, glorified is He.

His saying: ﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾ of the sins by a wrong he commits, ﴿then he earns it only against himself﴾, meaning: its consequence returns upon him. Kasb (earning) is what a person draws to himself as benefit or wards off as harm by it; for this reason the act of the Lord is not called kasb, as al-Qurtubi said. ﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin﴾. It was said: these two have the same meaning and are repeated for emphasis. Al-Tabari said: khati'ah (fault) may occur intentionally or unintentionally, while ithm (sin) occurs only intentionally. It was also said: khati'ah is the minor sin and ithm is the major sin. His saying: ﴿then throws it upon an innocent⦆ — the singular pronoun is used because the conjunction is "or" (aw), or to give precedence to ithm over khati'ah. It was also said that it refers back to kasb.

His saying: ﴿then he has certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾. Since sins cling to their doers, they are like a burden that is carried, and similar is His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. Buhtan (slander) is derived from buht, which is lying against the innocent with that which bewilders and confounds him. It is said: "bahatahu bahtan wa buhtanan" when he said about him what he did not say. It is also said: "bahita al-rajul" (with kasra) when a man is astonished and bewildered, and "buhita" (with damma). From this is His saying: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. Ithm mubin (manifest sin) is the clear one.

His saying: ﴿And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). What is meant by this favor and mercy toward the Messenger of Allah is that he was alerted to the truth in the story of the Banu Ubayriq. It was also said that what is meant by them is prophethood and protection (ismah). ﴿A party of them would have certainly intended﴾, meaning: of the group who supported the Banu Ubayriq, as previously mentioned, ﴿to mislead you from the truth, but they do not mislead except themselves﴾, because the harm of that returns upon them, ﴿and they do not harm you at all﴾, because Allah, glorified is He, is the One who protects you from the people, and because you acted on the apparent evidence, and there is no harm to you in judging by it before the revelation descended. The prepositional phrase is in a position of nasb as a verbal noun (masdar); meaning: they do not harm you with any harm whatsoever.

His saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book﴾. It was said: this is the beginning of a new statement. It was also said the waw is for the state (hal); meaning: they do not harm you with anything while Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, or together with Allah's sending that down to you. His saying: ﴿And taught you that which you did not know﴾ is coordinated with "sent down", meaning: He taught you through revelation what you did not know before. ﴿And ever has the favor of Allah upon you been enormous﴾, since there is no greater favor than prophethood and the descent of revelation.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever does a wrong or wrongs himself﴾ — the verse — he said: Allah informed His servants of His forbearance, pardon, generosity, vastness of mercy and forgiveness. Whoever commits a sin, small or great, then seeks forgiveness from Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful, even if his sins were greater than the heavens, the earth and the mountains.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: whoever recites these two verses from Surat al-Nisa' and then seeks forgiveness from Allah, He will forgive him: ﴿And whoever does a wrong or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness from Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and ﴿And if they had, when they wronged themselves, come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 64] — the verse. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And taught you that which you did not know﴾ that he said: Allah taught him the explanation of this world and the Hereafter, clarifying His lawful and unlawful, so that He might establish proof with it against His creation. He also narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: He taught him good and evil. Numerous hadiths about the acceptance of seeking forgiveness, and that it erases sin, have been recorded in the books of the Sunnah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 114–118:

An-najwa (secret conversation): a secret between two persons or a group. One says: "najaytu fulanan munajatan wa-najaan" (I conferred privately with so-and-so), and "hum yantijuna wa-yatanajawna" (they confer privately). Also, "najawtu fulanan anjuhu najwan," meaning "najaytuhu" (I conferred with him privately). So najwa is derived from "najawtu al-shay'a anjuhu," meaning "khallastuhu wa-afradtuhu" (I separated it out and set it apart). A najwa of the land (naj'wa) is the elevated ground, because it stands apart by its height from what surrounds it. Thus najwa, as a verbal noun, means private whispering. It may also be used for the group itself, as one says "qawmun 'adl" (a just people). God the Exalted said: ﴿And when they are a secret council﴾ [al-Isra' 47]. According to the first usage, the exception (illa) is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "for everyone who commands charity"; or it is connected (muttasil) on the assumption of "except the secret conversation of one who commands charity." According to the second usage, the exception is connected and in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for "kathir" (much): "there is no good in much of it except in one who commands charity."

A group of exegetes have said that najwa is the speech of a group that has withdrawn apart, or of two persons, whether it is secret or spoken aloud, and al-Zajjaj said this as well.

His saying "bi-sadaqatin" (with charity): the apparent meaning is voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'). It has been said it is obligatory charity (sadaqat al-fard), but the well-known meaning is voluntary charity, and the first is more appropriate. Al-ma'ruf (what is good and known) is a general term that includes all kinds of righteousness.

Muqatil said: al-ma'ruf here is loaning (al-qard), but the first is more appropriate. From it is the saying of al-Hutay'a:

"Whoever does good shall not lack its reward; the good deed does not perish between God and people."

From it is also the hadith: "Every ma'ruf is charity, and among ma'ruf is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face." It has also been said: al-ma'ruf is relieving the distressed (ighathat al-malhuf).

Reconciliation between people (al-islah bayn al-nas) is general, concerning lives, honour and wealth, and in every matter where discord occurs. His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾ refers to the matters mentioned. He made the mere commanding of them good, then he encouraged doing them with his words ﴿And whoever does that﴾, because doing them is closer to God than merely commanding them, since the excellence of commanding them is only because it is a means to doing them.

His saying ﴿seeking the pleasure of God﴾ is the cause (illa) of the action, because whoever does it for other than that does not deserve this praise and reward; rather he may not be free from sin, and actions are by intentions.

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him﴾: al-mushaqqa means enmity and opposition, and the clarity of guidance is its manifestation, by his knowing the truth of the message through the proofs indicating it, and then he commits opposition. ﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾: that is, other than their path, which is the religion of Islam and adherence to its rulings. ﴿We shall turn him to what he has turned to﴾: that is, We shall make him master of the error he has chosen. ﴿And burn him in Hell﴾. Asim, Hamzah and Abu 'Amr read nuwallihi and nuslihi with sukun on the ha' in both places, while the rest read them with kasra, and both are dialects. It was also read naslihi with fath on the nun, from salahu, and its explanation has already preceded.

A group of the people of knowledge have used this verse as evidence for the authority of consensus (ijma'), by His saying ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾. But there is no proof in that according to me, because what is meant by "other than the way of the believers" here is leaving the religion of Islam for another, as the wording indicates and the occasion of revelation confirms. It has been said: it was repeated here because of the story of the Banu Ubayriq. It has also been said: it was revealed here for a reason other than the story of the Banu Ubayriq, namely what al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi related in their tafsirs, on the authority of al-Dahhak: that an old man from the Bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am an old man who is immersed in sins and transgressions. That is, cut. The disbelievers did this in compliance with Satan's command and following his traces, so they slit the ears of the baha'ir and the sawa'ib, as is well known.

His saying: ﴿and I will surely command them, so they will change the creation of Allah﴾: that is, "I will surely command them to change the creation of Allah, so they will change it by the compulsion of my command to them." The scholars differed about what this change is. One group said: it is castration, gouging out eyes and cutting off ears. Others said: what is meant by this change is that Allah, glorified is He, created the sun, the moon, stones, fire and similar created things for what He created them for, and the disbelievers changed them by making them worshipped deities. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. It has been said: what is meant by this change is the change of the natural disposition (fitra) upon which Allah created mankind. (p-331) There is no objection to understanding the verse in all these senses, either comprehensively or alternatively.

A group of scholars have permitted the castration of animals when the purpose is to increase their benefit, such as for fattening or other reasons, while others disliked it. As for the castration of human beings, it is forbidden. Some people disliked buying a eunuch. al-Qurtubi said: The scholars do not differ that the castration of human beings is not lawful nor permissible, that it is mutilation and a change of Allah's creation; and likewise the cutting off of any of their limbs without a prescribed punishment or retaliation. Said by Abu 'Umar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr.

﴿And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah﴾: by following him and complying with what he commands, without following what Allah has commanded and without complying with Him, ﴿has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾: that is, evident and manifest. He promises them false promises and gives them vain hopes. ﴿And Satan does not promise them except delusion﴾: that is, Satan does not promise them, through the empty whisperings he places in their minds, anything except delusion, by which he deceives them and shows them benefit in it, while it is pure harm. The accusative of (ghurura) is either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "a promise of delusion," or as a second object, or as a verbal noun not from its own verb.

Ibn 'Arafa said: delusion (ghurur) is that you see in something an apparent aspect you love while it has a hidden aspect that is hateful. This sentence is parenthetical.

His saying: (﴿Those﴾) refers to the protectors of Satan. This is the subject, and its predicate is the sentence: (﴿their refuge is Hell﴾). His saying: (maHisan) means a place of escape, from haasa yahiisu. It has been said: a refuge and a means of salvation; al-mahis is a noun of place, and it has been said it is a verbal noun.

His saying: (﴿And those who believe﴾), etc. He made this promise to those who believe coupled with the preceding threat against the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿The promise of Allah is true﴾. In al-Kashshaf it is said: these are two verbal nouns; the first emphasizes itself, and the second emphasizes something else. Its explanation is that the first emphasizes the content of the nominal sentence, and its content is "promise" (wa'd), and the second emphasizes something else; that is, "that is truly true."

His saying: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ This sentence emphasizes what precedes it. The qil is a verbal noun of qala, like qawl; that is, I do not find anyone more truthful in speech than Allah, mighty and majestic. It has been said that qila is a noun, not a verbal noun, and that it is in the accusative as a specification.

al-Tirmidhi transmitted from the hadith of 'Ali that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with None, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾." al-Tirmidhi said: hasan gharib.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abu Malik regarding His saying ﴿They invoke besides Him none but female [deities]﴾ that he said: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, all of them feminine. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse that he said: "With every idol there is a female jinn."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿They invoke besides Him none but female [deities]﴾ that he said: "Dead objects." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from al-Hasan. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir also transmitted the like of it from Qatada. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: "Every tribe of the Arabs had an idol they worshipped, which they called 'the female of the Banu so-and-so.' So Allah revealed ﴿They invoke besides Him none but female [deities]﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "The polytheists said: the angels are the daughters of Allah, and we only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in position." He said: "They took them as lords and fashioned them in the forms of maidens, adorned them and hung ornaments on them, and said: 'These resemble the daughters of Allah whom we worship,' meaning the angels." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil ibn Hayyan regarding His saying ﴿And he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants"﴾, etc., that he said: "This is Iblis saying: from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine go to the Fire and one to Paradise."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted the like of it from al-Rabi'. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿so they will slit the ears of the cattle﴾ that he said: "Slitting was in the baHira and the sa'iba: they slit their ears for their idols (taghut)." 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas that he disliked castration and said: "It is concerning this that the verse ﴿and I will surely command them, so they will change the creation of Allah﴾ was revealed." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted the like of it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the castration of animals and horses." Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade sabr al-ruh (tying up a living creature to be shot at) and the castration of animals." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through various chains from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and I will surely command them, so they will change the creation of Allah﴾ that he said: "The religion of Allah." Ibn Jarir transmitted the like of it from al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted the like of it also from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: "It is tattooing."

His saying: (﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with None,﴾) The tafsir of this verse has already preceded, and its repetition with the same wording is for emphasis. It has been said: it was repeated here because of the story of the Banu Ubayriq. It has also been said: it was revealed here for a reason other than the story of the Banu Ubayriq, namely what al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi related in their tafsirs, on the authority of al-Dahhak: that an old man from the Bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am an old man who is immersed in sins and transgressions. However, I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him and believed in Him, nor have I taken any patron besides Him, nor have I committed acts of disobedience out of audacity toward Allah or defiance of Him. And indeed I am regretful, repentant and seeking forgiveness. So what is my state with Allah?" Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with None﴾, the verse, and ﴿Whoever associates others with Allah has certainly strayed far astray﴾, because shirk is the greatest kind of misguidance and the furthest from what is correct.

It has been said: what is meant by "females" is lifeless objects having no spirit, such as a piece of wood or a stone. It has also been said: what is meant by "females" is the angels, because of their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It has been read as (wuthunan) with a damma on the waw and the tha', the plural of wathan (idol); this reading was transmitted by Ibn al-Anbari from A'isha.

Ibn 'Abbas read (illa uthunan), also the plural of wathan, and its origin is wathan, the waw being replaced by a hamza. al-Hasan read (illa unuthan) with a damma on the hamza and the nun, followed by a thaa' with three dots, the plural of anith, like ghadir and ghadr. al-Tabari related that it is the plural of inath, like thimar and thamar.

Abu 'Amr al-Dani transmitted this reading from the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu Haywa also recited it." On all these readings, this statement comes in the form of a rebuke to the polytheists, a belittling of them and a disparagement of their intellects, because they worshipped besides Allah a weak kind of thing.

﴿And they invoke none but a rebellious Satan﴾: that is, they invoke besides Allah none but a rebellious Satan, namely Iblis, may Allah curse him, because when they obey him in what he embellishes for them, they have in fact worshipped him. The derivation of the word shaytan has already been mentioned. The murid is the defiant, obstinate one, from marada, meaning "he became insolent."

Ibn arafa said: it is the one whose evil has become manifest. It is said of a tree that is "marda'" when its leaves have fallen and its branches have appeared; and from this it is said of a man that he is "amrad," meaning the place of hair on his cheeks is bare.

His saying: (may Allah curse him): the origin of la'n (cursing) is expulsion and distancing, which has already been mentioned; and in common usage it is distancing accompanied by wrath.

His saying: ﴿and he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion"﴾ is coordinated with his saying "may Allah curse him," and the two clauses are descriptions of Satan; that is, a rebellious Satan combining Allah's curse upon him with this vile statement. The appointed portion (nasib mafrud) is that which is cut off and determined; that is: "I will surely make a determined piece of the servants of Allah subject to my misguidance and to my leading astray, until I bring them out from the worship of Allah to disbelief in Him."

His saying: (﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾): the lam is the answer to an omitted oath, and misguidance (idlal) is diverting from the path of guidance to the path of error. Likewise the lam in His saying (﴿and I will surely arouse in them desires﴾ and ﴿and I will surely command them﴾). What is meant by the false desires with which Satan beguiles them are the vain hopes arising from his embellishment and his whisperings.
