Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 4, verses 123–126:

Abu Ja'far read ﴿أَمَانِي﴾ (*amani*) with the *ya'* lightened (*takhfif*) in both places, and the subject of *laysa* (ليس, "is not") is omitted. The meaning is: entering Paradise, bounty, or nearness to God is not by your wishful desires (*amani*) nor by the wishful desires of the People of the Book. This is what the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) that follows indicates. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the promise of God, but this is a weak view. Among the wishful desires of the People of the Book is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 111), and their saying: ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 18), and their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 80).

His saying: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾. It has been said that the intended "evil" is polytheism (*shirk*), but the apparent meaning of the verse is more general than that. Whoever does any evil, of whatever kind, will be recompensed for it, without distinction between the Muslim and the disbeliever. In this sentence there is a severe threat that makes hearts tremble, and when it was revealed it had a great effect on the hearts of the Muslims, as is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Be close to the right course and strive to be steadfast. For everything by which a Muslim is afflicted there is an expiation, even the prick he is pricked with and the thorn that pricks him.'"

His saying: ( ﴿ولا يجد﴾ ) (*wa la yajid*, "and he will not find"). The majority read it in the jussive (*bi-l-jazm*), coordinating it with the conditional (*al-jaza'*). Ibn Bakkar related from Ibn 'Amir the reading ﴿ولا يَجِدُ﴾ with *raf'* (*wa la yajidu*), as a new independent clause (*isti'naf*). The meaning is: for the one who does evil there is no protector (*waliyy*) besides God who will befriend him, nor any helper (*nasir*) who will support him.

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾, i.e., some of them, while being male or female, and while being a believer. The first circumstantial phrase (*hal*) specifies who does the deed, and the second circumstantial phrase serves to state that faith is a condition for every righteous deed. The phrase ﴿those﴾ (*fa-ula'ika*) refers to the deed characterized by faith.

﴿They will enter Paradise﴾. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yudkhalun﴾ with a *damma* on the first letter of the imperfect, in the passive voice (*bina' li-l-majhul*). The rest read it with a *fatha*, in the active voice (*bina' li-l-ma'lum*). ﴿And they will not be wronged the slightest bit (*naqir*)﴾, i.e., they will not be deprived of anything, however small. The meaning of *naqir* has already been explained.

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to God﴾, i.e., dedicates himself sincerely to Him while doing good, that is, performing good deeds. ﴿And follows the religion of Abraham﴾, i.e., his religion, while being a *hanif*, that is, inclining away from false religions toward the religion of truth, which is Islam. ﴿And God took Abraham as an intimate friend (*khalil*)﴾, i.e., He made him His chosen one and singled him out with His honors. Tha'lab said: the *khalil* was only called *khalil* because his love penetrates (*yatakhallal*) the heart and leaves no room in it except that it fills it. He recited the verse of Bashshar:

*You have penetrated the path of the spirit within me, and by this the khalil was named khalil.*

*Khalil* is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of the active participle (*fa'il*), like *'alim* meaning *'alim* (knower). It has also been said that it is in the sense of the passive participle (*maf'ul*), like *habib* meaning *mahbub* (beloved). Abraham, peace be upon him, was both loved by God and a lover of Him. It has also been said that *khalil* derives from *ikhtisas* (specialization), so God specialized Abraham with His message at that time and chose him for it. An-Nahhas chose this view, and az-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *khalil* is one in whose love there is no defect (*khalal*).

﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. This contains an indication that He took Abraham as a friend for His obedience, not because He needed him, nor to increase His numbers through him, nor to strengthen Himself through his companionship. ﴿And God is ever, of all things, Encompassing﴾. This sentence confirms the meaning of the sentence before it, i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything: ﴿He leaves nothing small or great but that He has enumerated it﴾ (Al-Kahf: 49).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: The Arabs said, "We will not be resurrected and we will not be called to account." The Jews and Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians" (Al-Baqarah: 111), and they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few days" (Al-Baqarah: 80). So God revealed: ﴿Not by your wishful desires, nor by the wishful desires of the People of the Book. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Masruq, who said: The Muslims and the People of the Book argued. The Muslims said, "We are better guided than you," and the People of the Book said, "We are better guided than you." So it was revealed, and the Muslims prevailed over them by this verse: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Masruq, who said: The Christians and the people of Islam boasted, and these said, "We are better than you," and those said, "We are better than you," so it was revealed. The meaning of these reports has come through many chains, both brief and lengthy.

'Abd ibn Humayd, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Bakr as-Siddiq that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him when this verse was revealed: "As for you and your companions, O Abu Bakr, you will be recompensed for it in this world until you meet God with no sins upon you. As for the others, it will be gathered for them until they are recompensed for it on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id that they both heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "No fatigue, nor illness, nor sickness, nor sorrow afflicts the believer, not even the worry that troubles him, except that God expiates by it some of his misdeeds." Many hadiths have come with this meaning.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn 'Umar met him and asked him about this verse (﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾). He said: "The obligatory duties (*al-fara'id*)."

Al-Hakim related and declared authentic, from Jundab, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say before he died: "God has taken me as a friend (*khalil*) just as He took Abraham as a friend." Al-Hakim also related and declared authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do you wonder that intimate friendship (*khullah*) belongs to Abraham, speech belongs to Moses, and the vision belongs to Muhammad (ﷺ)?"

The Occasion of Revelation of this verse: some of the Companions asked about the matter of women and their rulings concerning inheritance and other things. So Allah commanded His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them (﴿Allah gives you a ruling﴾), meaning: He will explain to you the ruling on what you asked about. This verse is a return to what the surah began with regarding the matter of women, and some rulings had remained which they did not know, so they asked, and it was said to them: (﴿Allah gives you a ruling﴾).

His saying: (﴿and what is recited to you﴾) is coordinated with His saying (﴿Allah gives you a ruling﴾), and the meaning is: "and the Qur'an that is recited to you gives you a ruling concerning them."

What is recited in the Book with regard to orphans is His Exalted saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. It is also permissible that His saying (﴿and what is recited﴾) be coordinated with the pronoun in His saying (yuftikum, "gives you a ruling"), which refers back to the subject, because of the separation between the coordinated and the element it is coordinated with by the object and the prepositional phrase. It is also permissible that it be the subject, with (fi al-Kitab, "in the Book") as its predicate, on the basis that what is meant by it is the Preserved Tablet. Other grammatical analyses of it have been mentioned besides what we have stated, but we have not mentioned them because of their weakness. His saying: (﴿concerning the orphan women﴾) is, according to the first and second possibilities, a relative clause (silah) for His saying (yutla, "is recited"), and according to the third possibility, an apposition (badal) for His saying (fihinna, "concerning them").

﴿to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾: that is, what has been obligated for them of inheritance and other things. (﴿and you desire﴾) is coordinated with His saying (﴿you do not give﴾), a coordination of an affirmative clause upon a negative clause. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (tu'tunahunna, "you give them"). As for His saying (an tankihuhunna, "to marry them"), it may be that the implied meaning is "in that you marry them", i.e., you desire to marry them for their beauty; and it may be that the implied meaning is "and you desire to refrain from marrying them because of their lack of beauty."

His saying: ﴿and the oppressed among the children﴾ is coordinated with "orphan women"; that is: what is recited to you concerning the orphan women and concerning the oppressed among the children, which is His Exalted saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. The people of the Jahiliyyah did not give inheritance to women nor to any child who was weak, as has passed; they gave inheritance only to the men who fought and performed all the other duties.

His saying: ﴿and that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾, like "the oppressed"; that is: what is recited to you concerning the orphan women, and concerning the oppressed, and concerning your standing up for orphans with justice, i.e., with equity. It is also permissible that it be in a position of accusative case (nasb); that is: "and He commands you to stand up..." ﴿And whatever good you do﴾ concerning the rights of those mentioned, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it: He will reward you according to your deeds, whether good or evil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning women﴾ the verse, that he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah did not give inheritance to a newborn until he grew up, nor did they give inheritance to a woman. When Islam came, He said: ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book﴾ at the beginning of the surah, concerning the obligatory shares.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah did not give women nor children any inheritance at all. They used to say: "They do not go out to fight and they do not acquire any booty." So Allah prescribed for them inheritance as a binding right. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to it, more extensive than it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Ibrahim concerning the verse that he said: When a girl was an orphan and unattractive, they would not give her her inheritance, and they would withhold her from marriage until she died, so that they would inherit her. So Allah revealed this. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from 'A'ishah concerning His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning women﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ she said: It is the man who has an orphan girl in his care, he is her guardian and her heir, she has shared with him in his property, even in the palm-tree; so he desires to marry her and dislikes to give her in marriage to another man, lest she share with him in his property, so he prevents her; so this verse was revealed. Ibn al-Mundhir related through the chain of Ibn 'Awn, from al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin concerning this verse, one of them said: "targhabuna fihinna" (you desire them), and the other said: "targhabuna 'anhunna" (you turn away from them).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 128–130:

(ٱمْرَأَةٌ) is in the nominative, governed by a verb that is understood and is explained by what follows it. That is, "and if a woman fears..." The verb *khafat* (feared) here means she anticipates what she fears from her husband. It was also said that it means she is certain, but this is an error. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband﴾ is the continuation of *nushuz* (marital discord, the wife's or husband's disobedience and estrangement). Al-Nahhas said: the difference between *nushuz* and *i'rad* (turning away) is that *nushuz* is distance, while *i'rad* is that he does not speak to her and does not feel at ease with her. The apparent meaning of the verse is that reconciliation is permitted when there is fear of any *nushuz* or any *i'rad*. The ruling depends on the general wording, not on the specific occasion of revelation that will be mentioned later. Its apparent meaning is also that reconciliation is permitted in any form: by waiving the turn (of nights), or part of it, or part of the maintenance, or part of the dower (*mahr*).

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, and Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Sawda feared that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she said: O Messenger of God, do not divorce me, and give my day to ʿĀʾisha. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 131–134:

His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. This sentence is resumptive (mustanfa'ah), establishing the completeness of His, glorified is He, vastness and the comprehensiveness of His power. ﴿And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you﴾: We commanded them, concerning what We revealed to them of the books. The lam in al-Kitab (the Scripture) is for the generic (li-l-jins, referring to the category as a whole). "Wa-iyyakum" (and you) is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the relative pronoun (al-mawsul). ﴿That fear Allah﴾: that is, We commanded them and commanded you with taqwa (God-consciousness). It is in a position of nasb (accusative) by its being the object of "waṣṣaynā" (We instructed), or it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid). Al-Akhfash said: that is, "bi-an ittaqu Allah" (that fear Allah). It is also permissible that "an" be explanatory (mufassirah), since the act of instruction (tawsiyah) carries the meaning of saying (qawl).

His saying: ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. It is coordinated upon His saying "an ittaqu" (that you fear). That is: We instructed them and you with taqwa, and We said to them and to you: if you disbelieve. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 135–136:

His saying: "qawwamina" (ever-standing firm) is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah), meaning that standing firm in justice should be repeated among you. Justice (al-qist) is equity in your testimony against yourselves, which is acknowledging the rights that are owed by you. As for his testifying against his parents, it is by testifying against them for a right belonging to another; and likewise testimony against the nearest of kin. He mentioned the two parents because of the obligation of showing them kindness and because they are the most beloved of creation to him. Then he mentioned the nearest of kin, because they are the most likely object of affection and partisanship. So when they bear witness against these people for what is due from them, a stranger among people is even more deserving that they testify against him.

It has been said: the meaning of testimony against oneself is that one bears witness with the truth against someone from whom harm to oneself is feared; but this is far-fetched.

His saying: "shuhada'a lillah" (witnesses for Allah) is a predicate following another predicate of kana (was), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is not declined because it contains the feminine alif (alif al-ta'nith). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the circumstantial reading here is weak in meaning, because it restricts standing firm in justice to the sense of testimony alone. His saying: "lillah" means for His good pleasure and His reward. His saying: "wa law 'ala anfusikum" (even if against yourselves) is connected to "shuhada'" (witnesses). This is the apparent meaning of the verse. It has also been said: the meaning of "shuhada'a lillah" is witnessing to His oneness (al-wahdaniyyah), so that "wa law 'ala anfusikum" is connected to "qawwamin." The first is preferable.

His saying: "in yakun ghaniyyan aw faqiran" (whether he be rich or poor): the subject of kana is implied; that is, if the one testified against is rich, he is not to be considered on account of his wealth, seeking to gain his benefit or out of compassion for him, so that one abandons testimony against him; or if he is poor, he is not to be considered on account of his poverty, out of mercy toward him and compassion for him, so that one abandons testimony against him. He said: "fa-Allahu awla bihima" (Allah is more worthy of both of them) and did not say "bihi" (of him), even though the option (of choice) indicates attainment by one; because the meaning is that Allah is more worthy of each one of them. Al-Akhfash said: "aw" here carries the meaning of "wa" (and). It has been said that this is permissible when both have been mentioned before, as in His saying: "wa lahu akhun aw ukhtun fa-li-kulli wahidin minhuma al-sudus" (and if he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth) [al-Nisa': 12]. What is more detailed than this has already been discussed earlier in similar contexts.

Ubayy read "fa-Allahu awla bihim" (plural). Ibn Mas'ud read "in yakun ghaniyyun aw faqirun," taking kana as complete (taammah).

"fa-la tattabi'u al-hawa" (so do not follow desire): He forbade them from following desire. His saying: "an ta'dilu" (that you deviate) is in the accusative position, and it may be either from "al-'adl" (justice), as if He said: "so do not follow desire, out of aversion to being just among people"; or from "al-'udul" (deviation), as if He said: "so do not follow desire, for fear that you deviate from the truth," or "out of aversion to deviating from the truth."

His saying: "wa in talwu" (and if you distort) is from al-layy (twisting). It is said: "lawaytu fulanan haqqahu" (I withheld his right from him) when you repel it from him. What is meant is twisting the testimony out of inclination toward the one testified against. Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read "wa in talu" from al-wilayah (authority); that is, if you take on the testimony and abandon what is obligatory upon you of discharging it in the proper manner of truth. It has been said that this reading conveys two meanings: wilayah (authority) and i'rad (turning away). The first reading conveys only one meaning, which is i'rad. Some grammarians claimed that the second reading is an error and a solecism (lahn), because there is no sense of wilayah here.

Al-Nahhas and others said: this does not necessarily follow; rather, talu is in the sense of talwu. The original form was talawu, the damma was felt heavy on the waw followed by another waw, so the vowel was transferred onto the lam and one of the two waws was deleted due to the meeting of two consonants (sakinan). Al-Zajjaj mentioned something similar.

His saying: "aw tu'ridu" (or you turn away): that is, from giving testimony at all, "fa-inna Allaha kana bima ta'malruna khabiran" (indeed Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do): that is, with what you do of twisting and turning away, or with every deed. In this is a severe warning for whoever does not bring testimony as it is obligatory upon him. It has been narrated that this verse includes both the judge and the witnesses. As for the witnesses, it is clear; as for the judge, it applies when he turns away from one of the two litigants or twists his speech with one of them. It has been said that it is specific to the witnesses.

His saying: "ya ayyuha alladhina amanu, amminu billahi wa rasulihi" (O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger): that is, remain steadfast in your faith and persist in it. The address here is to all believers. "wa al-kitabi alladhi nazzala 'ala rasulihi" (and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger) is the Qur'an, and the definite article is for specific reference. "wa al-kitabi alladhi anzala min qablu" (and the Book which He sent down before) is every Book, and the definite article is generic. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "nuzzila" and "unzila" with a damma; the rest read both with a fatha. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the meaning is: O you who believe outwardly, be sincere to Allah. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning the polytheists, and the meaning is: O you who believe in al-Lat and al-'Uzza, believe in Allah; and both of those are weak.

His saying: "wa man yakfur billahi wa malaikatihi wa kutubihi wa rusulihi wa al-yawmi al-akhiri" (and whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day): that is, in any of these, "faqad dalla" (has certainly strayed) from the right course, "dalalan ba'idan" (a far-off straying). He mentioned the Messenger earlier in reference to the Book that was sent down upon him, and mentioned the messengers here in reference to the Books in general, so the mention of messengers in general is appropriate. The angels are placed before the messengers because they are the intermediaries between Allah and His messengers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: "ya ayyuha alladhina amanu kunu qawwamina" (O you who believe, be steadfast upholders of justice) through the end of the verse, that he said: Allah commanded the believers to speak the truth, even if against themselves, or their fathers, or their sons; they should not favour the rich for his wealth, nor show mercy to the poor for his poverty. And concerning His saying: "fa-la tattabi'u al-hawa" (do not follow desire), lest you abandon the truth and so transgress; "wa in talwu" (and if you distort), meaning with your tongues in testimony; "aw tu'ridu" (or you turn away) from it.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from him regarding the meaning of the verse, that he said: "Two men sit before the judge, and the judge's twisting and turning away is toward one of the two men against the other."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, al-Baqarah was the first surah revealed, then he followed it with Surat al-Nisa'. He said: A man would have testimony before his cousin or his relatives, so he would twist his tongue with it, or conceal it, because of the hardship he saw in them, until he became wealthy, and then he would settle it when he became wealthy. Then "kunu qawwamina bil-qist" (be steadfast upholders of justice) was revealed through the end of the verse. Ibn Jarir also narrated from him: "wa in talwu aw tu'ridu" means: you twist your tongue away from the truth, and this is evasiveness (al-lajlajah), so you do not establish the testimony in its proper form.

Al-I'rad means: abandonment.

al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Abdullah ibn Salam, Asad and Usayd, the two sons of Ka'b, Tha'labah ibn Qays, Salam the son of 'Abdullah ibn Salam's sister, Salamah his brother's son, and Yamin ibn Yamin came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and your Book, and in Musa and the Torah, and in 'Uzayr, and we disbelieve in what is other than that of the Books and messengers." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rather, believe in Allah and His Messenger Muhammad, and His Book, the Qur'an, and in every Book that came before it." They said: "We will not do so." So "ya ayyuha alladhina amanu amminu billah" (O you who believe, believe in Allah) through the end of the verse was revealed.

The authenticity of this must be examined, for al-Tha'labi, may Allah have mercy on him, is not among the transmitters of narration, and he does not distinguish between the sound and the fabricated.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning this verse, that he said: It refers to the People of the Book. Allah had taken their covenant in the Torah and the Gospel, and they acknowledged against themselves that they would believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). When Allah sent His Messenger, He called them to believe in Muhammad and the Qur'an, and reminded them of the covenant that had been taken from them. Among them were those who affirmed the Prophet (ﷺ) and followed him, and among them were those who disbelieved.

His saying: "wa man yakfur billahi wa malaikatihi wa kutubihi wa rusulihi wa al-yawmi al-akhiri" (and whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day): that is, in any of these, "faqad dalla" (has certainly strayed) from the right course, "dalalan ba'idan" (a far-off straying). He mentioned the Messenger earlier in reference to the Book that was sent down upon him, and mentioned the messengers here in reference to the Books in general, so the mention of messengers in general is appropriate. The angels are placed before the messengers because they are the intermediaries between Allah and His messengers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: "ya ayyuha alladhina amanu kunu qawwamina" (O you who believe, be steadfast upholders of justice) through the end of the verse, that he said: Allah commanded the believers to speak the truth, even if against themselves, or their fathers, or their sons; they should not favour the rich for his wealth, nor show mercy to the poor for his poverty. And concerning His saying: "fa-la tattabi'u al-hawa" (do not follow desire), lest you abandon the truth and so transgress; "wa in talwu" (and if you distort), meaning with your tongues in testimony; "aw tu'ridu" (or you turn away) from it.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from him regarding the meaning of the verse, that he said: "Two men sit before the judge, and the judge's twisting and turning away is toward one of the two men against the other."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, al-Baqarah was the first surah revealed, then he followed it with Surat al-Nisa'. He said: A man would have testimony before his cousin or his relatives, so he would twist his tongue with it, or conceal it, because of the hardship he saw in them, until he became wealthy, and then he would settle it when he became wealthy. Then "kunu qawwamina bil-qist" (be steadfast upholders of justice) was revealed through the end of the verse. Ibn Jarir also narrated from him: "wa in talwu aw tu'ridu" means: you twist your tongue away from the truth, and this is evasiveness (al-lajlajah), so you do not establish the testimony in its proper form.

Al-I'rad means: abandonment.

al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Abdullah ibn Salam, Asad and Usayd, the two sons of Ka'b, Tha'labah ibn Qays, Salam the son of 'Abdullah ibn Salam's sister, Salamah his brother's son, and Yamin ibn Yamin came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and your Book, and in Musa and the Torah, and in 'Uzayr, and we disbelieve in what is other than that of the Books and messengers." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rather, believe in Allah and His Messenger Muhammad, and His Book, the Qur'an, and in every Book that came before it." They said: "We will not do so." So "ya ayyuha alladhina amanu amminu billah" (O you who believe, believe in Allah) through the end of the verse was revealed.

The authenticity of this must be examined, for al-Tha'labi, may Allah have mercy on him, is not among the transmitters of narration, and he does not distinguish between the sound and the fabricated.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning this verse, that he said: It refers to the People of the Book. Allah had taken their covenant in the Torah and the Gospel, and they acknowledged against themselves that they would believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). When Allah sent His Messenger, He called them to believe in Muhammad and the Qur'an, and reminded them of the covenant that had been taken from them. Among them were those who affirmed the Prophet (ﷺ) and followed him, and among them were those who disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 137–141 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, glorified is He, reports about this group, who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief after all of that, that Allah, glorified is He, would not forgive their sins, nor guide them to a path by which they could reach the truth and travel towards goodness. This is because it is extremely unlikely that they would sincerely devote themselves to Allah and believe with a sound faith. This wavering on their part, at one time claiming to be believers and at another time slipping out of faith and returning to what is their habit and condition of persistent disbelief and continual denial, most clearly shows that they are playing with the religion. They have no sound intention and no pure purpose. It has been said: the intended people here are the Jews, for they believed in Musa (Moses), then disbelieved in Uzair (Ezra), then believed in Uzair, then disbelieved in Isa (Jesus), then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: they believed in Musa, then disbelieved in him by worshipping the calf, then believed in him when he returned to them, then disbelieved in Isa, then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning of the verse is that they increased in disbelief and persisted in it, as is apparent from their state. Otherwise, a disbeliever who believes, makes his faith sincere and turns away from disbelief has been guided by Allah to the path that brings forgiveness, and Islam erases what came before it. But since this is extremely unlikely from them, their forgiveness and their guidance to the path of truth is considered unlikely.

His words: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾. Using "good news" for what is purely evil for them is mockery of them, and its explanation has already passed.

His words: ﴿who take the disbelievers as allies﴾ are a description of the hypocrites, or are in the accusative as a term of censure; that is, they make the disbelievers their allies, supporting them in their disbelief and colluding with them in their misguidance.

His words: ﴿instead of the believers﴾ are in the accusative of circumstance; that is, they support the disbelievers, going beyond the guardianship of the believers. ﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾ This question is for rebuke and reproach, and the sentence is parenthetical. His words: ﴿For honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ this sentence gives the reason for the earlier rebuke about seeking honour from the disbelievers. All kinds and instances of honour belong exclusively to Allah, glorified is He, and whatever honour exists alongside Him is from His bounty and favour, as in His words: ﴿Honour belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Al-'Izzah (honour) means dominance; it is said: "'azzahu ya'izzuhu 'izzan," meaning he overpowered him.

﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book﴾. The address is to everyone who has shown faith, whether believer or hypocrite, because whoever shows faith is bound to comply with what Allah has sent down. It has also been said that it is addressed only to the hypocrites, as the severity and rebuke suggest. ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqub read "nazzala" with a fatha on the nun and the zay and with shadda on the zay, and its subject is a pronoun referring back to the name of Allah, the Exalted, in His words: ﴿For honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾. Ḥumayd read it with a light zay, fatha on the zay, and fatha on the nun. The rest read it with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the shadded zay, in the passive voice.

His words: ﴿that when you hear the signs of Allah﴾ are in the accusative place according to the first reading, as the object of "nazzala" (He has sent down), and in the nominative place according to the second reading, as its subject, and in the nominative place according to the third reading, as the substitute for the unnamed agent of the passive verb. Here "anna" is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and the implied construction is: "that when you hear the signs of Allah." Al-Kitab (the Book) is the Qur'an.

His words: ﴿they are disbelieved in and mocked﴾ are two circumstantial clauses; that is, when you hear disbelief in and mockery of the signs of Allah. The hearing is attributed to the signs, and what is meant is the hearing of disbelief and mockery. His words: ﴿then do not sit with them until they engage in a discussion other than that﴾; that is, He has sent down to you in the Book that when you hear disbelief and mockery of the signs of Allah, you must not sit with them as long as they are like that, until they engage in a discussion other than disbelief and mockery of them.

The verse which Allah sent down to them in the Book is His words: ﴿And when you see those who engage in mockery of Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in a discussion other than that﴾ [al-An'am: 68]. A group of those who had entered Islam used to sit with the polytheists and the Jews while they mocked and ridiculed the Qur'an, and so they were forbidden from doing so.

(p. 337) In this verse, by consideration of the general wording, which is what matters rather than the specific occasion of revelation, there is evidence for avoiding every gathering in which its people engage in what implies disparagement and mockery of the legal evidences. This often happens with the captives of taqlid (blind adherence to a school of law), who have replaced the Book and the Sunnah with the opinions of men, and nothing remains in their hands except "our imam of the school said such-and-such," and "such-and-such a follower of his said such-and-such." When they hear someone deriving a ruling on that matter from a Qur'anic verse or a Prophetic hadith, they mock him, pay no attention at all to what he has said, and think that he has come with a dreadful matter and a monstrous affair, and has opposed the doctrine of their imam, whom they regard as a teacher of the sacred law. They have gone so far that they place his opinion, which is corrupt, and his reasoning, which deviates from the path of truth, ahead of Allah, His Book and His Messenger. Surely we belong to Allah and to Him we return. What these schools have done to their adherents! The imams to whom these blind followers ascribe themselves are innocent of their actions, for they have explicitly forbidden taqlid in their writings. We have made this clear in our treatise entitled al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid (The Beneficial Word on the Ruling on Taqlid) and in our work entitled Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab (The Etiquette of the Seeker and the Limit of Desire). O Allah, benefit us by what You have taught us, make us among those who follow the Book and the Sunnah, and keep us far from the opinions of men, which are built on a crumbling precipice. O You who answer those who ask.

His words: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ give the reason for the prohibition; that is, if you do that and do not desist, then you are like them in disbelief. It has been said that this likeness is not in all attributes, but it is an imputation of resemblance based on outward judgment, as in the words of the poet:

"Every companion follows the one he associates with."

This verse is muhkam (clear and unabrogated) according to all the people of knowledge, except what is reported from al-Kalbi, who said that it is mansukh (abrogated) by His words: ﴿And they are not in any way accountable for them, nor are the righteous accountable for them﴾ [al-An'am: 69]. This is rejected, for part of taqwa (God-consciousness) is avoiding the gatherings of those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and mock them.

His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell﴾ give the reason for their being like them in disbelief. It has been said that they are the ones who sit, and those they sit with, according to those who take the address to be directed at the hypocrites. His words: ﴿who wait for you﴾ mean: who await for you whatever new good or evil may happen to you. The relative clause is in the accusative as a description of the hypocrites, or as a substitute for them only, not for the disbelievers, because the waiting mentioned is from the hypocrites and not the disbelievers. It may also be in the accusative as a term of censure.

﴿If there comes to you a victory from Allah, they say: "Were we not with you?"﴾ This sentence and the one after it describe their waiting; that is, if a victory from Allah comes to you by granting you triumph over those among the disbelievers who oppose you, they say to you: ﴿"Were we not with you?"﴾ in outward Islam, in observing its rulings, in lending support, in increasing your numbers. ﴿And if there is a share for the disbelievers﴾ of superiority over you and triumph against you, they say to the disbelievers: ﴿"Did we not gain mastery over you?"﴾; that is, did we not overpower you, defeat you and gain control over you, but we spared you?

It has been said that the meaning is that they said to the disbelievers who had triumphed over the Muslims: "Did we not gain mastery over you, so that the Muslims feared you, and we held them back from you?" The first interpretation is better, for the meaning of istihwadh is domination. It is said: "istahwadha 'ala kadhā," meaning he dominated over it. From this is His words: ﴿Satan has gained mastery over them﴾. It is not correct to say: "Did we not overpower you so that the Muslims feared you?" Rather the meaning is: Did we not overpower you, O company of disbelievers, and gain control over you, then leave you and spare you, until you achieved this victory over the Muslims? ﴿And we protected you from the believers﴾ by weakening and discouraging them from you, until their hearts became too weak to repel you and they were unable to avenge themselves on you. What is meant is that they lean toward whichever of the two groups has the upper hand and victory, and they show them that they were with them against the defeated group. This is the behaviour of the hypocrites, may Allah remove them far away, and the behaviour of whoever follows their example among the people of Islam, in showing each group that they are with it against the other, and in inclining towards whoever has a share of worldly benefit, whether wealth or status. They meet him with flattery, fawning, humility and abasement, and they meet whoever has no share of worldly benefit with harshness, roughness and bad manners, looking down on him and confronting him with every kind of unpleasantness. May Allah make the manners of the people of hypocrisy ugly and remove them far away.

His words: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ refer to what their hearts harbour of hypocrisy and hatred for the truth and its people. On that Day the realities will be unveiled and the hidden intentions will become manifest, even if in this world they protected their blood and safeguarded their property by uttering the word of Islam hypocritically. ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. This applies to the Day of Resurrection if by "way" is meant victory and dominance, or to this world if by it is meant proof.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: All the people of interpretation (ta'wil) said that what is meant is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is weak, because the statement would have no benefit, and its cause is the misconception of those who imagine that the end of the speech refers back to its beginning, namely His words: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and that would make it redundant, since it would be a repetition of the same meaning. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers by which He would wipe out their dominion, remove their traces, and bring their domain to ruin, as the authentic hadith in the Sahih indicates: "And I will not give power over them to an enemy other than themselves, so that he would ravage their domain, even if all those in its regions gathered against them, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive." It has also been said that He, glorified is He, does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers so long as they act by the truth, are not content with falsehood, and do not abandon forbidding evil, as He said: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is extremely precious. It has also been said that Allah does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers by the sacred law; if it occurs, it is contrary to the sacred law.

This is the essence of what the people of knowledge have said about this verse, and it is suitable as evidence for many issues. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved﴾ (the verse), that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah, then disbelieved, and the Christians believed in the Gospel, then disbelieved.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding the verse that he said: These are the Jews who believed in the Torah, then disbelieved, (p. 338) then he mentioned the Christians and said: ﴿then believed, then disbelieved﴾, meaning: we believed in the Gospel, then they disbelieved, ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse that he said: These are the hypocrites who believed twice, then disbelieved twice, then increased in disbelief after that.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: "They persisted in their disbelief until they died."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Abu Wa'il, who said: "A man may speak in a gathering with a word of falsehood in order to make his companions laugh, and so Allah becomes angry with them all." They mentioned this to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "Abu Wa'il has spoken truly. Is this not in the Book of Allah? ﴿So do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than this﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Mujahid, who said: "It was revealed in Surat al-An'am: ﴿until they engage in a conversation other than this﴾, and then the severity was revealed in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that Allah will gather together in Hell the hypocrites from the people of Madinah and the disbelievers from the people of Makkah who engaged in discussion and mocked the Qur'an, all of them together.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿those who wait for you﴾, that he said: "They are the hypocrites who wait for the believers. ﴿If there is a victory for you from Allah﴾: if the Muslims gain booty from their enemy, the hypocrites say, 'Were we not with you?' and they are given a share of the booty like what you take. ﴿And if there is a portion for the disbelievers﴾ which they obtain from the Muslims, the hypocrites say to the disbelievers: ﴿Did we not gain mastery over you?﴾ Did we not make clear to you that we are upon what you are upon? We have been holding them back from you."

Ibn Jarir related, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿Did we not gain mastery over you?﴾, that he said: "We overcame you."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ali that he was asked: "What do you say about this verse, ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾, when they fight us and prevail and kill?" He said: "Come closer, come closer," and then recited: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding the verse that he said: "It refers to the Hereafter." Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from Ibn Abbas. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from Abu Malik as well. Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi regarding "a way" (sabilan) that he said: "A proof (hujjah)."

The relative clause is in the accusative as a description of the hypocrites, or as a substitute for them only, not for the disbelievers, because the waiting mentioned is from the hypocrites and not the disbelievers. It may also be in the accusative as a term of censure.

﴿If there comes to you a victory from Allah, they say: "Were we not with you?"﴾ This sentence and the one after it describe their waiting; that is, if a victory from Allah comes to you by granting you triumph over those among the disbelievers who oppose you, they say to you: ﴿"Were we not with you?"﴾ in outward Islam, in observing its rulings, in lending support, in increasing your numbers. ﴿And if there is a share for the disbelievers﴾ of superiority over you and triumph against you, they say to the disbelievers: ﴿"Did we not gain mastery over you?"﴾; that is, did we not overpower you, defeat you and gain control over you, but we spared you?

It has been said that the meaning is that they said to the disbelievers who had triumphed over the Muslims: "Did we not gain mastery over you, so that the Muslims feared you, and we held them back from you?" The first interpretation is better, for the meaning of istihwadh is domination. It is said: "istahwadha 'ala kadhā," meaning he dominated over it. From this is His words: ﴿Satan has gained mastery over them﴾. It is not correct to say: "Did we not overpower you so that the Muslims feared you?" Rather the meaning is: Did we not overpower you, O company of disbelievers, and gain control over you, then leave you and spare you, until you achieved this victory over the Muslims? ﴿And we protected you from the believers﴾ by weakening and discouraging them from you, until their hearts became too weak to repel you and they were unable to avenge themselves on you. What is meant is that they lean toward whichever of the two groups has the upper hand and victory, and they show them that they were with them against the defeated group. This is the behaviour of the hypocrites, may Allah remove them far away, and the behaviour of whoever follows their example among the people of Islam, in showing each group that they are with it against the other, and in inclining towards whoever has a share of worldly benefit, whether wealth or status. They meet him with flattery, fawning, humility and abasement, and they meet whoever has no share of worldly benefit with harshness, roughness and bad manners, looking down on him and confronting him with every kind of unpleasantness. May Allah make the manners of the people of hypocrisy ugly and remove them far away.

His words: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ refer to what their hearts harbour of hypocrisy and hatred for the truth and its people. On that Day the realities will be unveiled and the hidden intentions will become manifest, even if in this world they protected their blood and safeguarded their property by uttering the word of Islam hypocritically. ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. This applies to the Day of Resurrection if by "way" is meant victory and dominance, or to this world if by it is meant proof.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: All the people of interpretation (ta'wil) said that what is meant is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is weak, because the statement would have no benefit, and its cause is the misconception of those who imagine that the end of the speech refers back to its beginning, namely His words: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and that would make it redundant, since it would be a repetition of the same meaning. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers by which He would wipe out their dominion, remove their traces, and bring their domain to ruin, as the authentic hadith in the Sahih indicates: "And I will not give power over them to an enemy other than themselves, so that he would ravage their domain, even if all those in its regions gathered against them, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive." It has also been said that He, glorified is He, does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers so long as they act by the truth, are not content with falsehood, and do not abandon forbidding evil, as He said: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is extremely precious. It has also been said that Allah does not give the disbelievers a way over the believers by the sacred law; if it occurs, it is contrary to the sacred law.

This is the essence of what the people of knowledge have said about this verse, and it is suitable as evidence for many issues. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved﴾ (the verse), that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah, then disbelieved, and the Christians believed in the Gospel, then disbelieved.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding the verse that he said: These are the Jews who believed in the Torah, then disbelieved, (p. 338) then he mentioned the Christians and said: ﴿then believed, then disbelieved﴾, meaning: we believed in the Gospel, then they disbelieved, ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse that he said: These are the hypocrites who believed twice, then disbelieved twice, then increased in disbelief after that.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾, that he said: "They persisted in their disbelief until they died."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Abu Wa'il, who said: "A man may speak in a gathering with a word of falsehood in order to make his companions laugh, and so Allah becomes angry with them all." They mentioned this to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "Abu Wa'il has spoken truly. Is this not in the Book of Allah? ﴿So do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than this﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Mujahid, who said: "It was revealed in Surat al-An'am: ﴿until they engage in a conversation other than this﴾, and then the severity was revealed in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that Allah will gather together in Hell the hypocrites from the people of Madinah and the disbelievers from the people of Makkah who engaged in discussion and mocked the Qur'an, all of them together.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿those who wait for you﴾, that he said: "They are the hypocrites who wait for the believers. ﴿If there is a victory for you from Allah﴾: if the Muslims gain booty from their enemy, the hypocrites say, 'Were we not with you?' and they are given a share of the booty like what you take. ﴿And if there is a portion for the disbelievers﴾ which they obtain from the Muslims, the hypocrites say to the disbelievers: ﴿Did we not gain mastery over you?﴾ Did we not make clear to you that we are upon what you are upon? We have been holding them back from you."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related a similar report from Abu Malik as well. Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi regarding "a way" (sabilan) that he said: "A proof (hujjah)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 137–141 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, glorified is He, reports about this group, who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief after all of that, that Allah, glorified is He, would not forgive their sins, nor guide them to a path by which they could reach the truth and travel towards goodness. This is because it is extremely unlikely that they would sincerely devote themselves to Allah and believe with a sound faith. This wavering on their part, at one time claiming to be believers and at another time slipping out of faith and returning to what is their habit and condition of persistent disbelief and continual denial, most clearly shows that they are playing with the religion. They have no sound intention and no pure purpose. It has been said: the intended people here are the Jews, for they believed in Musa (Moses), then disbelieved in Uzair (Ezra), then believed in Uzair, then disbelieved in Isa (Jesus), then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: they believed in Musa, then disbelieved in him by worshipping the calf, then believed in him when he returned to them, then disbelieved in Isa, then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning of the verse is that they increased in disbelief and persisted in it, as is apparent from their state. Otherwise, a disbeliever who believes, makes his faith sincere and turns away from disbelief has been guided by Allah to the path that brings forgiveness, and Islam erases what came before it. But since this is extremely unlikely from them, their forgiveness and their guidance to the path of truth is considered unlikely.

His words: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾. Using "good news" for what is purely evil for them is mockery of them, and its explanation has already passed.

His words: ﴿who take the disbelievers as allies﴾ are a description of the hypocrites, or are in the accusative as a term of censure; that is, they make the disbelievers their allies, supporting them in their disbelief and colluding with them in their misguidance.

His words: ﴿instead of the believers﴾ are in the accusative of circumstance; that is, they support the disbelievers, going beyond the guardianship of the believers. ﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾ This question is for rebuke and reproach, and the sentence is parenthetical. His words: ﴿For honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ this sentence gives the reason for the earlier rebuke about seeking honour from the disbelievers. All kinds and instances of honour belong exclusively to Allah, glorified is He, and whatever honour exists alongside Him is from His bounty and favour, as in His words: ﴿Honour belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Al-'Izzah (honour) means dominance; it is said: "'azzahu ya'izzuhu 'izzan," meaning he overpowered him.

﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book﴾. The address is to everyone who has shown faith, whether believer or hypocrite, because whoever shows faith is bound to comply with what Allah has sent down. It has also been said that it is addressed only to the hypocrites, as the severity and rebuke suggest. ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqub read "nazzala" with a fatha on the nun and the zay and with shadda on the zay, and its subject is a pronoun referring back to the name of Allah, the Exalted, in His words: ﴿For honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾. Ḥumayd read it with a light zay, fatha on the zay, and fatha on the nun. The rest read it with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the shadded zay, in the passive voice.

His words: ﴿that when you hear the signs of Allah﴾ are in the accusative place according to the first reading, as the object of "nazzala" (He has sent down), and in the nominative place according to the second reading, as its subject, and in the nominative place according to the third reading, as the substitute for the unnamed agent of the passive verb. Here "anna" is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and the implied construction is: "that when you hear the signs of Allah." Al-Kitab (the Book) is the Qur'an.

When they hear someone deriving a ruling on that matter from a Qur'anic verse or a Prophetic hadith, they mock him, pay no attention at all to what he has said, and think that he has come with a dreadful matter and a monstrous affair, and has opposed the doctrine of their imam, whom they regard as a teacher of the sacred law. They have gone so far that they place his opinion, which is corrupt, and his reasoning, which deviates from the path of truth, ahead of Allah, His Book and His Messenger. Surely we belong to Allah and to Him we return. What these schools have done to their adherents! The imams to whom these blind followers ascribe themselves are innocent of their actions, for they have explicitly forbidden taqlid in their writings. We have made this clear in our treatise entitled al-Qawl al-Mufid fi Hukm al-Taqlid (The Beneficial Word on the Ruling on Taqlid) and in our work entitled Adab al-Talab wa Muntaha al-Arab (The Etiquette of the Seeker and the Limit of Desire). O Allah, benefit us by what You have taught us, make us among those who follow the Book and the Sunnah, and keep us far from the opinions of men, which are built on a crumbling precipice. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 142–147:

His words, ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah﴾: This is an independent statement that includes an explanation of some of the hypocrites' foul deeds and disgraceful conduct. The meaning of *khada* (deception) has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. Their deceiving Allah means that they act like one who deceives: they display faith and conceal disbelief. The meaning of Allah being their deceiver is that He dealt with them as one deals with someone who has deceived him. He left them in the state they were in, outwardly showing Islam in this world, and so He preserved their wealth and their blood by it, and He delayed their punishment until the Hereafter. Thus He repaid their deception with the lowest level of the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: *al-khadi'* is the active participle of *khada'tuhu*, *fa-khada'tuhu*, when you overcome him, and you were more deceptive than him. *Al-kusala* (the lazy), with a *damma* on the *kaf*, is the plural of *kaslan*, and it is also read with a *fatha*. The meaning is that they pray while being lazy and sluggish, not hoping for reward and not fearing punishment. *Al-riya'* is displaying what is good so that people will see it, not for the sake of obeying Allah's command, and its explanation has already been given. *Al-muraa'ah* is the form *mufa'alah*.

His words, ﴿and they do not remember Allah except a little﴾: This is coordinated with (*yuraa'una*, they show off). That is, they do not remember Him, glorified is He, except with a little remembrance, or they do not pray except a little prayer. Describing the remembrance as little is either because of their lack of sincerity, or because it is not accepted, or because it is little in itself, since the one who performs an act of obedience for the purpose of showing off performs it only in gatherings and does not perform it when alone, as the sincere person does. His words, ﴿wavering between that﴾: *Al-mudhabdhab* is one who hesitates between two matters, and *al-dhabdhabah* is agitation. It is said: *dhabdhabahu fa-tadhabdhaba* (he agitated him so he was agitated). From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*Have you not seen that Allah has given you a sovereignty, under which every king trembles and wavers?*

Ibn Jinni said: *al-mudhabdhab* is the restless one who does not remain in one state. These hypocrites hesitate between the believers and the polytheists, neither sincerely holding to faith nor openly declaring disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: The true meaning of *al-mudhabdhab* is one who is pushed away from both sides, that is, he is repelled and driven off, so he does not settle on one side, as one says: "So-and-so is thrown about by the winds." Except that *al-dhabdhabah* contains a repetition that is not in *al-dhabb*, as if the meaning were: whenever he inclines toward one side, he is repelled from it, and so on. The majority read it with a *damma* on the *mim* and *fatha* on both *dhal*s. Ibn Abbas read it with a *kasra* on the second *dhal*. In the codex of Ubayy it is *mutadhabdhibin*. Al-Hasan read it with a *fatha* on the *mim* and both *dhal*s. The accusative of *mudhabdhabin* is either as a circumstantial state (*hal*) or as a dispraise. The reference in His words *bayna dhalika* (between that) is to faith and disbelief. His words, ﴿neither to these nor to those﴾: That is, neither attributed to the believers nor to the disbelievers. The phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, or as a substitute for *mudhabdhabin*, or as an explanation of it. ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray﴾: That is, He forsakes him and deprives him of success. ﴿You will not find for him a way﴾: That is, a path that leads him to the truth.

His words, ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾: That is, do not make them your exclusive associates and intimates whom you befriend in place of your brothers among the believers, as the hypocrites did in their allegiance to the disbelievers. ﴿Do you want to give Allah a clear authority against yourselves?﴾ The interrogation is for reproach and rebuke. That is: Do you want to give Allah a clear proof against you by which He punishes you because of your committing what He has forbidden you, namely allying with the disbelievers? ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾: The Kufans read *al-darki* with a sukun on the *ra'* (p-339), and the others read it with a vowel.

Abu Ali said: They are two dialects, and the plural is *adrak*. It was said that the plural of the vowelled form is *adrak*, like *jamal* and *ajmal*, and the plural of the unvowelled form is *adrukun*, like *fals* and *afluss*. Al-Nahhas said: The vowelled form is more eloquent.

*Al-darak* means a stratum. The Fire has seven levels, and the hypocrite is in the lowest of them, which is the Abyss (*al-Hawiyah*), because of the severity of his disbelief and the abundance of his treacheries. The highest of the levels is Jahannam, then al-Hutamah, then al-Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the highest tier. May Allah protect us from its punishment. ﴿And you will not find for them a helper﴾: One who will rescue them from that level. The Fire has seven levels, and the hypocrite is in the lowest of them, which is the Abyss (*al-Hawiyah*), because of the severity of his disbelief and the abundance of his treacheries. The highest of the levels is Jahannam, then al-Hutamah, then al-Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah. All of them may be called by the name of the highest tier. His words, ﴿with the believers﴾: Al-Farra' said: That is, from among the believers, meaning those from whom hypocrisy never came at all.

Al-Qutaybi said: He turned away from their speech out of anger against them, and said, ﴿then those are with the believers﴾ and did not say, "they are the believers." End of quote. The apparent meaning is that the sense of *ma'a* (with) is significant here, that is: then those are companions of the believers in the rulings of this world and the Hereafter.

The *ya'* of *yu'ti* is omitted in the writing as it is omitted in pronunciation, because it is vowelless and the *lam* after it is vowelless as well. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada regarding His words, ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful...﴾ the verse, that he said: Indeed Allah does not punish one who is grateful or one who is a believer.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 148–149:

He negated love as a metaphor for hatred. The reading of the majority is ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ with the passive form (al-bina' lil-majhul). Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib read ( ﴿except one who has wronged﴾ ) with the active form (al-bina' lil-ma'lum). According to the first reading, the exception is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil, an exception from the same category as what precedes it) with an omitted genitive modifier, meaning: "except the loud utterance of one who has been wronged." It was also said that, according to the first reading as well, the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception from a different category): "but one who has been wronged, he may say: so-and-so wronged me."

The scholars differed over the manner of the open speech of evil that is permitted to one who has been wronged. It was said: it is that he supplicates against the one who wronged him. It was also said: there is no harm in his speaking openly with evil speech against the one who wronged him, by saying: "So-and-so wronged me," or "he is a wrongdoer," or the like. It was also said: its meaning is: "except one who is compelled to speak openly with evil speech, such as disbelief or the like; for him it is permitted, and the verse according to this is about compulsion." Qutrub said likewise, and said: it may be that it is in the sense of a substitution (badal), as if he said: "Allah does not love except one who has been wronged," meaning: He does not love the wrongdoer, but He loves the one wronged. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is permitted for one who has been wronged to speak words that are evil in regard to the aspect of his being wronged. This is supported by the established hadith in the Sahih with the wording: "Procrastination by the wealthy is injustice, which makes his honour and his punishment lawful." As for the second reading, the exception is disconnected: "except one who has wronged in deed or speech, so openly speak evil speech to him," in the sense of forbidding his action and rebuking him.

Some said: the meaning of the statement is: "Allah does not love that anyone speak openly with evil speech. But one who has wronged, he speaks openly with evil out of injustice and aggression, and he is a wrongdoer in that." This is the case of many of the oppressors, for they, along with their oppression, lash out with their tongues against those they have wronged and disparage their honour. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that the meaning is: "except one who has wronged and so said evil; for it is incumbent that they take hold of his hands," and the exception is not from the first clause. ﴿And Allah is ever Hearing, Knowing﴾: this is a warning to the wrongdoer that Allah hears what issues from him and knows it. Then, after He permitted the wronged person to speak openly with evil, He recommended what is preferable and better, so He said:

﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾ (by which you are afflicted), ﴿then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning﴾ toward His servants, ﴿Competent﴾ to take vengeance upon them for what their hands have earned. So follow Him, glorified is He, for He pardons while having the power [to punish]. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Allah does not love the open utterance of evil speech﴾ he said: Allah does not love that anyone supplicate against anyone, except one who has been wronged; for He permitted him to supplicate against the one who wronged him, and to be patient, and that is better for him.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning a man who was a guest of another man in a desert land, and he did not host him; then he mentioned that he did not host him, and did not add more to that. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Isma'il, concerning ﴿Allah does not love the open utterance of evil speech except one who has been wronged﴾ that he said: al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim used to say: this is by inversion (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir), Allah says: "What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful and believe?" ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾, and he used to recite it that way. Then he said: ﴿Allah does not love the open utterance of evil speech﴾, meaning: under all circumstances. Thus he said, and this is close to distorting the meaning of the verse.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tirmidhi related from Aisha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever supplicates against one who has wronged him has taken his revenge." Abu Dawud related something similar from her through another chain. Abu Dawud also related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The two who revile each other, the sin is upon the one who begins, as long as the wronged one does not transgress."

When he finished mentioning the polytheists and the hypocrites, he mentioned the disbelievers among the People of the Book, who are the Jews and the Christians, because they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus, that amounted to disbelief in all the messengers and the revealed books, and disbelief in that is disbelief in Allah. The statement ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ should be understood as meaning that this entailed their disbelief in some of the books and messengers, not that they disbelieved in Allah and all His messengers. The People of the Book did not disbelieve in Allah or in all His messengers, but when they disbelieved in some of them, that amounted to disbelief in Allah and in all the messengers.

The meaning of ﴿And they wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers﴾ is that they disbelieved in the messengers because of their disbelief in some of them, while believing in Allah. This was a differentiation between Allah and His messengers. ﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾: they are the Jews who believed in Moses and disbelieved in Jesus and Muhammad, and likewise the Christians who believed in Jesus and disbelieved in Muhammad. ﴿And they wish to adopt a way between that﴾, i.e., they wish to adopt a religion that is intermediate between belief and disbelief. The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the statement "We believe... and disbelieve...". ﴿Those are the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the complete disbelievers.

His words ﴿truly﴾ (ḥaqqan) are a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning as an emphatic (mu'akkid) for the content of the sentence; that is, "that is true, truly." Alternatively, it is an adjective (ṣifah) modifying the verbal noun of "the disbelievers," meaning "true disbelief." His words ﴿And they do not differentiate between any of them﴾ mean by saying, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others." The preposition bayna (between) is used with aḥad (any one) because aḥad is general, applying to the singular, masculine and feminine, and to the dual and plural of both.

This has already been verified. The demonstrative in His words ﴿those﴾ refers to those who believed in Allah and His messengers and did not differentiate between any of them. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning this verse, who said: "Those are the enemies of Allah, the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah and Moses and disbelieved in the Gospel and Jesus, and the Christians believed in the Gospel and Jesus and disbelieved in the Qur'an and Muhammad. They adopted Judaism and Christianity, which are two innovations that are not from Allah, and they abandoned Islam, which is the religion of Allah with which He sent His messengers." Ibn Jarir also reported, from al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj, something similar.
