Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 153–159 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. They are the Jews. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to ascend to the sky while they watched, and then to bring down to them a written book, which would be a proof of his truthfulness, all at once, as Musa (Moses) had brought the Torah, out of obstinacy on their part. May God curse them. So God, mighty and majestic, informed him that they had already asked Musa a greater question than this one. They said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, that is, visibly. Its meaning has already been explained in al-Baqarah. (جَهْرَةً) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a sight in plain view.

His saying: ﴿then they had asked﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you consider this request from them to be a great one, then they asked Musa for something greater than that. His saying: ﴿the thunderbolt seized them﴾: it is the fire that came down upon them from the sky and destroyed them. The (بِ) in His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ indicates cause, meaning: because of their wrongdoing in their false request, since seeing God visibly is impossible in that state. That does not entail its impossibility on the Day of Resurrection, for the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths have come with that. Whoever uses this verse to argue that seeing God is impossible on the Day of Resurrection has made a clear error.

Then they did not stop at this false request, which arose from them because of their wrongdoing after they had seen the miracles. Rather, they added to it something even worse, which is the worship of the calf. In the speech there is an omission, and the estimated meaning is: then We revived them, and they took the calf.

(al-Bayyinat) means the proofs and evidences, and the miracles of the hand, the staff, the splitting of the sea, and others. ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾, that is, what they had done of obstinacy and worship of the calf. ﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof, which is the signs with which he came. It was called authority (sultan) because whoever brings it overcomes his opponent. Among this is God's command to him, glorified be He, to order them to kill themselves in repentance for their disobedience, for that is part of the authority by which He overpowered them. ﴿And We raised the mountain above them for their covenant﴾, that is, because of their covenant, so that they would give it. For it is related that they refused to accept the law of Musa, so God raised the mountain over them and they accepted it. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking the covenant which was taken from them, which is acting according to what is in the Torah. The lifting of the mountain has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, and likewise the explanation of their entering the gate in prostration. ﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, that is, by taking what you were commanded to leave of the fish in it. This has already been explained. It was also read as (لا تَعْتَدُوا) and (وتَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, emphasized, which is the pact that He took from them in the Torah. It is also said that it is a covenant strengthened by oath, so it was called firm (ghalidh) for that reason.

His saying: ﴿So because of their breaking their covenant﴾: (ما) is redundant for emphasis, or it is indefinite, and their breaking is a substitute for it (badal). The (بِ) is connected to an omitted element, and the estimated meaning is: so because of their breaking their covenant We cursed them. Al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing, up to His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾. He said: so the wrongdoing for which the thunderbolt seized them is explained by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and what follows that.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those who were seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, while those who killed the prophets and slandered Maryam with falsehood came long after Musa, so the thunderbolt did not seize those who slandered Maryam in their entirety. Al-Mahdawi and others said: this is not a valid objection, for it is possible that the address is about them while the intended ones are their forefathers. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, because of their breaking the covenant We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, for this story extends to His saying ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them﴾. Their breaking of the covenant was that He had taken from them that they would make clear the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking their covenant and their doing such and such, God sealed their hearts. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking, they do not believe except a little, and the (فا) in His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is extraneous (muqhimah).

His saying: ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying ﴿and their killing﴾. By ﴿the signs of God﴾ is meant their books which they distorted. By ﴿the prophets﴾ are meant those whom they killed, Yahya (John) and Zakariyya (Zechariah). (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of aghlaf, which means covered with a sheath, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so it does not understand what you say. It is also said that (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of ghilaf, and the meaning is that their hearts are containers for knowledge, so they have no need of any knowledge other than what their hearts have already contained. This is like their saying ﴿our hearts are in coverings﴾. Their purpose in this was to reject the proof of the messengers.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God sealed them over for their disbelief﴾. This sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah): that is, their not accepting the truth is not because their hearts are sheathed according to their intended purpose, but rather by the sealing that God placed upon them. Al-Tab' (sealing) means stamping, and its meaning has already been clarified in al-Baqarah. His saying: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: they are sealed by God because of their disbelief, so they do not believe except with a little faith, or except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him. His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief﴾ is conjoined to their saying. The repetition of the preposition is because a separation occurred between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. This repetition is to indicate that they disbelieved with disbelief after disbelief. It is also said that the intended disbelief here is their disbelief in the Messiah, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it.

His saying: ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾: this is their accusing her of [fornication] with Yusuf the carpenter, who was among the righteous. (Buhtan) is extreme lying which one wonders at. His saying: ﴿and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is among their crimes and sins. For they lied that they killed him, boasted of killing him, and mentioned him with the title of messenger in mockery, since they denied it and did not acknowledge that he was a prophet. What they claimed, that they killed him, is contained in the Injil (Gospel) which explains his description and clarifies his reality. What is in it is a distortion by the Christians, may God curse them. They lied, and God spoke truly in His mighty Book: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾. The clause is in the circumstantial mode (ḥāliyyah), that is: they said that while the state was that they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another. It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾, that is, concerning the matter of Isa. Some of them said: We killed him, and whoever witnessed his being raised to the sky said: We did not kill him. It is also said: the difference among them is that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Isa was crucified in respect of his human nature (nasut), not in respect of his divine nature (hut). And the Melkites said: the killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah in his entirety, both his human and divine natures. They have on this kind of difference a long discourse with no basis. Therefore God said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾, that is, in a hesitation that does not come out into the domain of soundness nor into the domain of falsehood in their belief. Rather, they are hesitant and doubtful in their uncertainty, wandering in their ignorance and bewildered. And ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: (min) is superfluous to emphasize the negation of knowledge, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), that is: but they follow assumption. It is also said that it is a substitute for what precedes it, but the first is preferable.

It should not be said: following assumption contradicts the doubt which God informed about them that they were in; for the doubt intended here is hesitation, as we have mentioned, and assumption is a type of it, and what is intended here is not the inclination of one of the two sides.

His saying: (وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا) [and they did not kill him with certainty]: that is, a certain killing, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; or (certain) as a circumstantial state, meaning: while certain. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (قَتَلُوهُ) refers to Isa. It is also said that it refers to the assumption, and the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, like your saying "I killed him by knowledge" when you know him with complete knowledge.

Abu 'Ubayda said: if the meaning were "they did not kill Isa with certainty," it would have said only "they did not kill him." It is also said the meaning is: (p-342) and they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them. It is also said the meaning is: rather God raised him to Himself with certainty, and this is an error, because (بَلْ) does not govern what precedes it in what comes before it. Ibn al-Anbari permitted putting (يَقِينًا) in the accusative by a hidden verb which is the answer to an oath, and that (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾) would be a new independent sentence. There is no justification for these sayings. The pronouns before (قَتَلُوهُ) and after it refer to Isa. Mentioning certainty here is for the purpose of mocking them, since it indicates their knowledge in general.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him to Himself﴾ is a refutation of them and an affirmation of what is correct. The mention of his raising, peace be upon him, has already been made in Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. By the People of the Book are meant the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: there is no one of the People of the Book but that, by God, he will surely believe in him before his death. The pronoun in (بِهِ) refers to Isa, and the pronoun in (مَوْتِهِ) refers to what the speech indicates, which is the word "one" (aḥad) that is implied, or the "Book-follower" (kitābiyy) indicated by "People of the Book." In this there is evidence that no Jew or Christian dies without having believed in the Messiah. It is also said: both pronouns refer to Isa, and the meaning is: Isa will not die until every person of the Book in his age believes in him. It is also said: the first pronoun refers to God, and it is said: to Muhammad. Ibn Jarir chose that both pronouns refer to Isa, and a group of the early generations (salaf) held it, and it is the apparent meaning. The intended belief is belief in him at his descent at the end of time, as the mass-transmitted hadiths have reported. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾, Isa, a witness over the People of the Book, bearing witness against the Jews for denying him, and against the Christians for exaggerating about him, to the point that they said he is the son of God.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: "Some Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Musa brought the tablets from God, so bring us the tablets from God so that we may believe you. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from the sky﴾ up to ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: "The Jews and the Christians said to Muhammad (ﷺ): We will not pledge allegiance to you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from God addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God, and addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾," the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, he said: "They, when they see Him, have seen Him. They only said 'plainly, show us God'. He said: it is brought forward and delayed."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We raised the mountain above them﴾, he said: "It was a mountain they were at the base of, and God raised it and made it above them as if it were a canopy. He said: you shall certainly take My command, or I will drop it upon you. They said: We will take it. So God held it back from them."

He came out to them from a spring in the house, and his head was dripping water. He said: 'Among you is one who will disbelieve in me twelve times after having believed in me.' Then he said: 'Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed in my place and will be with me in my rank?' Many of them restricted it by saying that whoever reaches him at his descent to the earth will believe in him. The reports about the descent of ʿIsa are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), as we have clarified in a separate work containing what has been transmitted concerning the awaited one (al-Muntazar), the Dajjal, and the Masih.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 153–159 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. They are the Jews. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to ascend to the sky while they watched, and then to bring down to them a written book, which would be a proof of his truthfulness, all at once, as Musa (Moses) had brought the Torah, out of obstinacy on their part. May God curse them. So God, mighty and majestic, informed him that they had already asked Musa a greater question than this one. They said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, that is, visibly. Its meaning has already been explained in al-Baqarah. (جَهْرَةً) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a sight in plain view.

His saying: ﴿then they had asked﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you consider this request from them to be a great one, then they asked Musa for something greater than that. His saying: ﴿the thunderbolt seized them﴾: it is the fire that came down upon them from the sky and destroyed them. The (بِ) in His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ indicates cause, meaning: because of their wrongdoing in their false request, since seeing God visibly is impossible in that state. That does not entail its impossibility on the Day of Resurrection, for the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths have come with that. Whoever uses this verse to argue that seeing God is impossible on the Day of Resurrection has made a clear error.

Then they did not stop at this false request, which arose from them because of their wrongdoing after they had seen the miracles. Rather, they added to it something even worse, which is the worship of the calf. In the speech there is an omission, and the estimated meaning is: then We revived them, and they took the calf.

(al-Bayyinat) means the proofs and evidences, and the miracles of the hand, the staff, the splitting of the sea, and others. ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾, that is, what they had done of obstinacy and worship of the calf. ﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof, which is the signs with which he came. It was called authority (sultan) because whoever brings it overcomes his opponent. Among this is God's command to him, glorified be He, to order them to kill themselves in repentance for their disobedience, for that is part of the authority by which He overpowered them. ﴿And We raised the mountain above them for their covenant﴾, that is, because of their covenant, so that they would give it. For it is related that they refused to accept the law of Musa, so God raised the mountain over them and they accepted it. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking the covenant which was taken from them, which is acting according to what is in the Torah. The lifting of the mountain has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, and likewise the explanation of their entering the gate in prostration. ﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, that is, by taking what you were commanded to leave of the fish in it. This has already been explained. It was also read as (لا تَعْتَدُوا) and (وتَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, emphasized, which is the pact that He took from them in the Torah. It is also said that it is a covenant strengthened by oath, so it was called firm (ghalidh) for that reason.

His saying: ﴿So because of their breaking their covenant﴾: (ما) is redundant for emphasis, or it is indefinite, and their breaking is a substitute for it (badal). The (بِ) is connected to an omitted element, and the estimated meaning is: so because of their breaking their covenant We cursed them. Al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing, up to His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾. He said: so the wrongdoing for which the thunderbolt seized them is explained by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and what follows that.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those who were seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, while those who killed the prophets and slandered Maryam with falsehood came long after Musa, so the thunderbolt did not seize those who slandered Maryam in their entirety. Al-Mahdawi and others said: this is not a valid objection, for it is possible that the address is about them while the intended ones are their forefathers. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, because of their breaking the covenant We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, for this story extends to His saying ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them﴾. Their breaking of the covenant was that He had taken from them that they would make clear the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking their covenant and their doing such and such, God sealed their hearts. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking, they do not believe except a little, and the (فا) in His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is extraneous (muqhimah).

His saying: ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying ﴿and their killing﴾. By ﴿the signs of God﴾ is meant their books which they distorted. By ﴿the prophets﴾ are meant those whom they killed, Yahya (John) and Zakariyya (Zechariah). (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of aghlaf, which means covered with a sheath, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so it does not understand what you say. It is also said that (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of ghilaf, and the meaning is that their hearts are containers for knowledge, so they have no need of any knowledge other than what their hearts have already contained. This is like their saying ﴿our hearts are in coverings﴾. Their purpose in this was to reject the proof of the messengers.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God sealed them over for their disbelief﴾. This sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah): that is, their not accepting the truth is not because their hearts are sheathed according to their intended purpose, but rather by the sealing that God placed upon them. Al-Tab' (sealing) means stamping, and its meaning has already been clarified in al-Baqarah. His saying: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: they are sealed by God because of their disbelief, so they do not believe except with a little faith, or except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him. His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief﴾ is conjoined to their saying. The repetition of the preposition is because a separation occurred between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. This repetition is to indicate that they disbelieved with disbelief after disbelief. It is also said that the intended disbelief here is their disbelief in the Messiah, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it.

His saying: ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾: this is their accusing her of [fornication] with Yusuf the carpenter, who was among the righteous. (Buhtan) is extreme lying which one wonders at. His saying: ﴿and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is among their crimes and sins. For they lied that they killed him, boasted of killing him, and mentioned him with the title of messenger in mockery, since they denied it and did not acknowledge that he was a prophet. What they claimed, that they killed him, is contained in the Injil (Gospel) which explains his description and clarifies his reality. What is in it is a distortion by the Christians, may God curse them. They lied, and God spoke truly in His mighty Book: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾. The clause is in the circumstantial mode (ḥāliyyah), that is: they said that while the state was that they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another. It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾, that is, concerning the matter of Isa. Some of them said: We killed him, and whoever witnessed his being raised to the sky said: We did not kill him. It is also said: the difference among them is that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Isa was crucified in respect of his human nature (nasut), not in respect of his divine nature (hut). And the Melkites said: the killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah in his entirety, both his human and divine natures. They have on this kind of difference a long discourse with no basis. Therefore God said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾, that is, in a hesitation that does not come out into the domain of soundness nor into the domain of falsehood in their belief. Rather, they are hesitant and doubtful in their uncertainty, wandering in their ignorance and bewildered. And ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: (min) is superfluous to emphasize the negation of knowledge, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), that is: but they follow assumption. It is also said that it is a substitute for what precedes it, but the first is preferable.

It should not be said: following assumption contradicts the doubt which God informed about them that they were in; for the doubt intended here is hesitation, as we have mentioned, and assumption is a type of it, and what is intended here is not the inclination of one of the two sides.

His saying: (وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا) [and they did not kill him with certainty]: that is, a certain killing, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; or (certain) as a circumstantial state, meaning: while certain. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (قَتَلُوهُ) refers to Isa. It is also said that it refers to the assumption, and the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, like your saying "I killed him by knowledge" when you know him with complete knowledge.

Abu 'Ubayda said: if the meaning were "they did not kill Isa with certainty," it would have said only "they did not kill him." It is also said the meaning is: (p-342) and they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them. It is also said the meaning is: rather God raised him to Himself with certainty, and this is an error, because (بَلْ) does not govern what precedes it in what comes before it. Ibn al-Anbari permitted putting (يَقِينًا) in the accusative by a hidden verb which is the answer to an oath, and that (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾) would be a new independent sentence. There is no justification for these sayings. The pronouns before (قَتَلُوهُ) and after it refer to Isa. Mentioning certainty here is for the purpose of mocking them, since it indicates their knowledge in general.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him to Himself﴾ is a refutation of them and an affirmation of what is correct. The mention of his raising, peace be upon him, has already been made in Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. By the People of the Book are meant the Jews and the Christians. This has already been explained. It was also read as (لا تَعْتَدُوا) and (وتَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, emphasized, which is the pact that He took from them in the Torah. It is also said that it is a covenant strengthened by oath, so it was called firm (ghalidh) for that reason.

His saying: ﴿So because of their breaking their covenant﴾: (ما) is redundant for emphasis, or it is indefinite, and their breaking is a substitute for it (badal). The (بِ) is connected to an omitted element, and the estimated meaning is: so because of their breaking their covenant We cursed them. Al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing, up to His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾. He said: so the wrongdoing for which the thunderbolt seized them is explained by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and what follows that.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those who were seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, while those who killed the prophets and slandered Maryam with falsehood came long after Musa, so the thunderbolt did not seize those who slandered Maryam in their entirety. Al-Mahdawi and others said: this is not a valid objection, for it is possible that the address is about them while the intended ones are their forefathers. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, because of their breaking the covenant We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, for this story extends to His saying ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them﴾. Their breaking of the covenant was that He had taken from them that they would make clear the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking their covenant and their doing such and such, God sealed their hearts. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking, they do not believe except a little, and the (فا) in His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is extraneous (muqhimah).

His saying: ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying ﴿and their killing﴾. By ﴿the signs of God﴾ is meant their books which they distorted. By ﴿the prophets﴾ are meant those whom they killed, Yahya (John) and Zakariyya (Zechariah). (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of aghlaf, which means covered with a sheath, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so it does not understand what you say. It is also said that (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of ghilaf, and the meaning is that their hearts are containers for knowledge, so they have no need of any knowledge other than what their hearts have already contained. This is like their saying ﴿our hearts are in coverings﴾. Their purpose in this was to reject the proof of the messengers.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God sealed them over for their disbelief﴾. This sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah): that is, their not accepting the truth is not because their hearts are sheathed according to their intended purpose, but rather by the sealing that God placed upon them. Al-Tab' (sealing) means stamping, and its meaning has already been clarified in al-Baqarah. His saying: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: they are sealed by God because of their disbelief, so they do not believe except with a little faith, or except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him. His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief﴾ is conjoined to their saying. The repetition of the preposition is because a separation occurred between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. This repetition is to indicate that they disbelieved with disbelief after disbelief. It is also said that the intended disbelief here is their disbelief in the Messiah, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it.

His saying: ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾: this is their accusing her of [fornication] with Yusuf the carpenter, who was among the righteous. (Buhtan) is extreme lying which one wonders at. His saying: ﴿and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is among their crimes and sins. For they lied that they killed him, boasted of killing him, and mentioned him with the title of messenger in mockery, since they denied it and did not acknowledge that he was a prophet. What they claimed, that they killed him, is contained in the Injil (Gospel) which explains his description and clarifies his reality. What is in it is a distortion by the Christians, may God curse them. They lied, and God spoke truly in His mighty Book: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾. The clause is in the circumstantial mode (ḥāliyyah), that is: they said that while the state was that they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another. It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾, that is, concerning the matter of Isa. Some of them said: We killed him, and whoever witnessed his being raised to the sky said: We did not kill him. It is also said: the difference among them is that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Isa was crucified in respect of his human nature (nasut), not in respect of his divine nature (hut). And the Melkites said: the killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah in his entirety, both his human and divine natures. They have on this kind of difference a long discourse with no basis. Therefore God said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾, that is, in a hesitation that does not come out into the domain of soundness nor into the domain of falsehood in their belief. Rather, they are hesitant and doubtful in their uncertainty, wandering in their ignorance and bewildered. And ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: (min) is superfluous to emphasize the negation of knowledge, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), that is: but they follow assumption. It is also said that it is a substitute for what precedes it, but the first is preferable.

It should not be said: following assumption contradicts the doubt which God informed about them that they were in; for the doubt intended here is hesitation, as we have mentioned, and assumption is a type of it, and what is intended here is not the inclination of one of the two sides.

His saying: (وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا) [and they did not kill him with certainty]: that is, a certain killing, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; or (certain) as a circumstantial state, meaning: while certain. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (قَتَلُوهُ) refers to Isa. It is also said that it refers to the assumption, and the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, like your saying "I killed him by knowledge" when you know him with complete knowledge.

Abu 'Ubayda said: if the meaning were "they did not kill Isa with certainty," it would have said only "they did not kill him." It is also said the meaning is: (p-342) and they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them. It is also said the meaning is: rather God raised him to Himself with certainty, and this is an error, because (بَلْ) does not govern what precedes it in what comes before it. Ibn al-Anbari permitted putting (يَقِينًا) in the accusative by a hidden verb which is the answer to an oath, and that (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾) would be a new independent sentence. There is no justification for these sayings. The pronouns before (قَتَلُوهُ) and after it refer to Isa. Mentioning certainty here is for the purpose of mocking them, since it indicates their knowledge in general.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him to Himself﴾ is a refutation of them and an affirmation of what is correct. The mention of his raising, peace be upon him, has already been made in Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. By the People of the Book are meant the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: there is no one of the People of the Book but that, by God, he will surely believe in him before his death. The pronoun in (بِهِ) refers to Isa, and the pronoun in (مَوْتِهِ) refers to what the speech indicates, which is the word "one" (aḥad) that is implied, or the "Book-follower" (kitābiyy) indicated by "People of the Book." In this there is evidence that no Jew or Christian dies without having believed in the Messiah. It is also said: both pronouns refer to Isa, and the meaning is: Isa will not die until every person of the Book in his age believes in him. It is also said: the first pronoun refers to God, and it is said: to Muhammad. Ibn Jarir chose that both pronouns refer to Isa, and a group of the early generations (salaf) held it, and it is the apparent meaning. The intended belief is belief in him at his descent at the end of time, as the mass-transmitted hadiths have reported. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾, Isa, a witness over the People of the Book, bearing witness against the Jews for denying him, and against the Christians for exaggerating about him, to the point that they said he is the son of God.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: "Some Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Musa brought the tablets from God, so bring us the tablets from God so that we may believe you. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from the sky﴾ up to ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: "The Jews and the Christians said to Muhammad (ﷺ): We will not pledge allegiance to you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from God addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God, and addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾," the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, he said: "They, when they see Him, have seen Him. They only said 'plainly, show us God'. He said: it is brought forward and delayed."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We raised the mountain above them﴾, he said: "It was a mountain they were at the base of, and God raised it and made it above them as if it were a canopy. He said: you shall certainly take My command, or I will drop it upon you. They said: We will take it. So God held it back from them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, that he said: "They accused her of fornication."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When Allah intended to raise ʿIsa (Jesus) to the heaven, he went out to his companions, and in the house were twelve men from among the Hawariyyun (the disciples). He came out to them from a spring in the house, and his head was dripping water. He said: 'Among you is one who will disbelieve in me twelve times after having believed in me.' Then he said: 'Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed in my place and will be with me in my rank?' A young man from the youngest of them stood up, and he said to him: 'Sit down.' Then he repeated it to them, and the young man stood up and said: 'Me.' He said: 'You are that one.' So the likeness of ʿIsa was cast upon him, and ʿIsa was raised from an opening in the house to the heaven." He said: "The Jews came in search, and they seized the one with his likeness, killed him, and then crucified him. Some of them disbelieved in him twelve times after having believed in him, and they split into three sects. One sect said: 'Allah was among us as He willed, then He ascended to the heaven.' These are the Yaʿqubiyya. Another sect said: 'The son of Allah was among us as He willed, then Allah raised him to Himself.' These are the Nasturiyya. And another sect said: 'ʿAbd Allah and His Messenger was among us.' These are the Muslims. Then the two disbelieving sects joined forces against the Muslim sect and killed them. Islam remained effaced until Allah sent Muhammad, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾ [al-Saff: 14], meaning: the group that believed in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿and a group disbelieved﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿so We supported those who believed﴾ in the time of ʿIsa, by making Muhammad's religion prevail over the religion of the disbelievers."

Ibn Kathir, after citing it with this wording from Ibn Abi Hatim, said: "Ahmad ibn Sinan related to us, Abu Muʿawiya related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and so he mentioned it." He said: "This is a sound chain up to Ibn ʿAbbas." Ibn Kathir was correct, for all of these are men of the Sahih (of the authentic collections). al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Abu Kurayb, from Abu Muʿawiya, with similar wording.

His story (peace be upon him) has been related through various routes with different wordings. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it from Wahb ibn Munabbih in a form close to what is in the Gospel, and Ibn al-Mundhir likewise related it from him.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾, that he said: "They did not kill their supposition with certainty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir related the same from Ibn Juwaybir and al-Suddi as well.

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾, that he said: "It is the coming out of ʿIsa son of Mary." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from several routes from him concerning the verse that he said: "Before the death of ʿIsa." They also related from him that he said: "Before the death of the Jew." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "People from the People of the Book will reach ʿIsa when he is raised; they will surely believe in him."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "No Jew dies ever until he believes in ʿIsa." It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "What if he falls from the top of a house?" He said: "He will speak of it in the air." It was said: "What if one of them has his neck struck?" He said: "His tongue will stammer with it." Something similar has been related from him through several routes, and a number of the Successors (Tabiʿun) held it, and many of the Successors and those after them went to the view that the meaning is "before the death of ʿIsa," as related from Ibn ʿAbbas earlier. Many of them restricted it by saying that whoever reaches him at his descent to the earth will believe in him. The reports about the descent of ʿIsa are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), as we have clarified in a separate work containing what has been transmitted concerning the awaited one (al-Muntazar), the Dajjal, and the Masih.

His saying: ﴿then they had asked﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you consider this request from them to be a great one, then they asked Musa for something greater than that. The (بِ) in His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ indicates cause, meaning: because of their wrongdoing in their false request, since seeing God visibly is impossible in that state. That does not entail its impossibility on the Day of Resurrection, for the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths have come with that. Whoever uses this verse to argue that seeing God is impossible on the Day of Resurrection has made a clear error.

Then they did not stop at this false request, which arose from them because of their wrongdoing after they had seen the miracles. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾," the verse.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We raised the mountain above them﴾, he said: "It was a mountain they were at the base of, and God raised it and made it above them as if it were a canopy. He said: you shall certainly take My command, or I will drop it upon you. They said: We will take it. So God held it back from them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, that he said: "They accused her of fornication."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When Allah intended to raise ʿIsa (Jesus) to the heaven, he went out to his companions, and in the house were twelve men from among the Hawariyyun (the disciples). He came out to them from a spring in the house, and his head was dripping water. He said: 'Among you is one who will disbelieve in me twelve times after having believed in me.' Then he said: 'Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed in my place and will be with me in my rank?' A young man from the youngest of them stood up, and he said to him: 'Sit down.' Then he repeated it to them, and the young man stood up and said: 'Me.' He said: 'You are that one.' So the likeness of ʿIsa was cast upon him, and ʿIsa was raised from an opening in the house to the heaven." He said: "The Jews came in search, and they seized the one with his likeness, killed him, and then crucified him. Some of them disbelieved in him twelve times after having believed in him, and they split into three sects. One sect said: 'Allah was among us as He willed, then He ascended to the heaven.' These are the Yaʿqubiyya. Another sect said: 'The son of Allah was among us as He willed, then Allah raised him to Himself.' These are the Nasturiyya. And another sect said: 'ʿAbd Allah and His Messenger was among us.' These are the Muslims. Then the two disbelieving sects joined forces against the Muslim sect and killed them. He said: "This is a sound chain up to Ibn ʿAbbas." al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾, that he said: "It is the coming out of ʿIsa son of Mary." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "People from the People of the Book will reach ʿIsa when he is raised; they will surely believe in him."

He said: "He will speak of it in the air." It was said: "What if one of them has his neck struck?" He said: "His tongue will stammer with it." Something similar has been related from him through several routes, and a number of the Successors (Tabiʿun) held it, and many of the Successors and those after them went to the view that the meaning is "before the death of ʿIsa," as related from Ibn ʿAbbas earlier. Many of them restricted it by saying that whoever reaches him at his descent to the earth will believe in him. The reports about the descent of ʿIsa are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), as we have clarified in a separate work containing what has been transmitted concerning the awaited one (al-Muntazar), the Dajjal, and the Masih.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 153–159 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. They are the Jews. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to ascend to the sky while they watched, and then to bring down to them a written book, which would be a proof of his truthfulness, all at once, as Musa (Moses) had brought the Torah, out of obstinacy on their part. May God curse them. So God, mighty and majestic, informed him that they had already asked Musa a greater question than this one. They said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, that is, visibly. Its meaning has already been explained in al-Baqarah. (جَهْرَةً) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a sight in plain view.

His saying: ﴿then they had asked﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you consider this request from them to be a great one, then they asked Musa for something greater than that. His saying: ﴿the thunderbolt seized them﴾: it is the fire that came down upon them from the sky and destroyed them. The (بِ) in His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ indicates cause, meaning: because of their wrongdoing in their false request, since seeing God visibly is impossible in that state. That does not entail its impossibility on the Day of Resurrection, for the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths have come with that. Whoever uses this verse to argue that seeing God is impossible on the Day of Resurrection has made a clear error.

Then they did not stop at this false request, which arose from them because of their wrongdoing after they had seen the miracles. Rather, they added to it something even worse, which is the worship of the calf. In the speech there is an omission, and the estimated meaning is: then We revived them, and they took the calf.

(al-Bayyinat) means the proofs and evidences, and the miracles of the hand, the staff, the splitting of the sea, and others. ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾, that is, what they had done of obstinacy and worship of the calf. ﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof, which is the signs with which he came. It was called authority (sultan) because whoever brings it overcomes his opponent. Among this is God's command to him, glorified be He, to order them to kill themselves in repentance for their disobedience, for that is part of the authority by which He overpowered them. ﴿And We raised the mountain above them for their covenant﴾, that is, because of their covenant, so that they would give it. For it is related that they refused to accept the law of Musa, so God raised the mountain over them and they accepted it. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking the covenant which was taken from them, which is acting according to what is in the Torah. The lifting of the mountain has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, and likewise the explanation of their entering the gate in prostration. ﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, that is, by taking what you were commanded to leave of the fish in it. This has already been explained. It was also read as (لا تَعْتَدُوا) and (وتَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, emphasized, which is the pact that He took from them in the Torah. It is also said that it is a covenant strengthened by oath, so it was called firm (ghalidh) for that reason.

His saying: ﴿So because of their breaking their covenant﴾: (ما) is redundant for emphasis, or it is indefinite, and their breaking is a substitute for it (badal). The (بِ) is connected to an omitted element, and the estimated meaning is: so because of their breaking their covenant We cursed them. Al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing, up to His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾. He said: so the wrongdoing for which the thunderbolt seized them is explained by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and what follows that.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those who were seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, while those who killed the prophets and slandered Maryam with falsehood came long after Musa, so the thunderbolt did not seize those who slandered Maryam in their entirety. Al-Mahdawi and others said: this is not a valid objection, for it is possible that the address is about them while the intended ones are their forefathers. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, because of their breaking the covenant We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, for this story extends to His saying ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them﴾. Their breaking of the covenant was that He had taken from them that they would make clear the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking their covenant and their doing such and such, God sealed their hearts. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking, they do not believe except a little, and the (فا) in His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is extraneous (muqhimah).

His saying: ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying ﴿and their killing﴾. By ﴿the signs of God﴾ is meant their books which they distorted. By ﴿the prophets﴾ are meant those whom they killed, Yahya (John) and Zakariyya (Zechariah). (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of aghlaf, which means covered with a sheath, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so it does not understand what you say. It is also said that (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of ghilaf, and the meaning is that their hearts are containers for knowledge, so they have no need of any knowledge other than what their hearts have already contained. This is like their saying ﴿our hearts are in coverings﴾. Their purpose in this was to reject the proof of the messengers.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God sealed them over for their disbelief﴾. This sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah): that is, their not accepting the truth is not because their hearts are sheathed according to their intended purpose, but rather by the sealing that God placed upon them. Al-Tab' (sealing) means stamping, and its meaning has already been clarified in al-Baqarah. His saying: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: they are sealed by God because of their disbelief, so they do not believe except with a little faith, or except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him. His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief﴾ is conjoined to their saying. The repetition of the preposition is because a separation occurred between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. This repetition is to indicate that they disbelieved with disbelief after disbelief. It is also said that the intended disbelief here is their disbelief in the Messiah, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it.

His saying: ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾: this is their accusing her of [fornication] with Yusuf the carpenter, who was among the righteous. (Buhtan) is extreme lying which one wonders at. His saying: ﴿and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is among their crimes and sins. For they lied that they killed him, boasted of killing him, and mentioned him with the title of messenger in mockery, since they denied it and did not acknowledge that he was a prophet. What they claimed, that they killed him, is contained in the Injil (Gospel) which explains his description and clarifies his reality. What is in it is a distortion by the Christians, may God curse them. They lied, and God spoke truly in His mighty Book: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾. The clause is in the circumstantial mode (ḥāliyyah), that is: they said that while the state was that they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another. It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾, that is, concerning the matter of Isa. Some of them said: We killed him, and whoever witnessed his being raised to the sky said: We did not kill him. It is also said: the difference among them is that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Isa was crucified in respect of his human nature (nasut), not in respect of his divine nature (hut). And the Melkites said: the killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah in his entirety, both his human and divine natures. They have on this kind of difference a long discourse with no basis. Therefore God said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾, that is, in a hesitation that does not come out into the domain of soundness nor into the domain of falsehood in their belief. Rather, they are hesitant and doubtful in their uncertainty, wandering in their ignorance and bewildered. And ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: (min) is superfluous to emphasize the negation of knowledge, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), that is: but they follow assumption. It is also said that it is a substitute for what precedes it, but the first is preferable.

It should not be said: following assumption contradicts the doubt which God informed about them that they were in; for the doubt intended here is hesitation, as we have mentioned, and assumption is a type of it, and what is intended here is not the inclination of one of the two sides.

His saying: (وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا) [and they did not kill him with certainty]: that is, a certain killing, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; or (certain) as a circumstantial state, meaning: while certain. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (قَتَلُوهُ) refers to Isa. It is also said that it refers to the assumption, and the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, like your saying "I killed him by knowledge" when you know him with complete knowledge.

Abu 'Ubayda said: if the meaning were "they did not kill Isa with certainty," it would have said only "they did not kill him." It is also said the meaning is: (p-342) and they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them. It is also said the meaning is: rather God raised him to Himself with certainty, and this is an error, because (بَلْ) does not govern what precedes it in what comes before it. Ibn al-Anbari permitted putting (يَقِينًا) in the accusative by a hidden verb which is the answer to an oath, and that (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾) would be a new independent sentence. There is no justification for these sayings. The pronouns before (قَتَلُوهُ) and after it refer to Isa. Mentioning certainty here is for the purpose of mocking them, since it indicates their knowledge in general.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him to Himself﴾ is a refutation of them and an affirmation of what is correct. The mention of his raising, peace be upon him, has already been made in Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. By the People of the Book are meant the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: there is no one of the People of the Book but that, by God, he will surely believe in him before his death. The pronoun in (بِهِ) refers to Isa, and the pronoun in (مَوْتِهِ) refers to what the speech indicates, which is the word "one" (aḥad) that is implied, or the "Book-follower" (kitābiyy) indicated by "People of the Book." In this there is evidence that no Jew or Christian dies without having believed in the Messiah. It is also said: both pronouns refer to Isa, and the meaning is: Isa will not die until every person of the Book in his age believes in him. It is also said: the first pronoun refers to God, and it is said: to Muhammad. Ibn Jarir chose that both pronouns refer to Isa, and a group of the early generations (salaf) held it, and it is the apparent meaning. The intended belief is belief in him at his descent at the end of time, as the mass-transmitted hadiths have reported. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾, Isa, a witness over the People of the Book, bearing witness against the Jews for denying him, and against the Christians for exaggerating about him, to the point that they said he is the son of God.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: "Some Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Musa brought the tablets from God, so bring us the tablets from God so that we may believe you. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from the sky﴾ up to ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: "The Jews and the Christians said to Muhammad (ﷺ): We will not pledge allegiance to you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from God addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God, and addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾," the verse.

His saying: ﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying ﴿and their killing﴾. By ﴿the signs of God﴾ is meant their books which they distorted. By ﴿the prophets﴾ are meant those whom they killed, Yahya (John) and Zakariyya (Zechariah). (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of aghlaf, which means covered with a sheath, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so it does not understand what you say. It is also said that (غُلْفٌ) is the plural of ghilaf, and the meaning is that their hearts are containers for knowledge, so they have no need of any knowledge other than what their hearts have already contained. This is like their saying ﴿our hearts are in coverings﴾. Their purpose in this was to reject the proof of the messengers.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God sealed them over for their disbelief﴾. This sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah): that is, their not accepting the truth is not because their hearts are sheathed according to their intended purpose, but rather by the sealing that God placed upon them. Al-Tab' (sealing) means stamping, and its meaning has already been clarified in al-Baqarah. His saying: ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾, that is: they are sealed by God because of their disbelief, so they do not believe except with a little faith, or except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him. His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief﴾ is conjoined to their saying. The repetition of the preposition is because a separation occurred between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. This repetition is to indicate that they disbelieved with disbelief after disbelief. It is also said that the intended disbelief here is their disbelief in the Messiah, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it.

His saying: ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾: this is their accusing her of [fornication] with Yusuf the carpenter, who was among the righteous. (Buhtan) is extreme lying which one wonders at. His saying: ﴿and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of God﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is among their crimes and sins. For they lied that they killed him, boasted of killing him, and mentioned him with the title of messenger in mockery, since they denied it and did not acknowledge that he was a prophet. What they claimed, that they killed him, is contained in the Injil (Gospel) which explains his description and clarifies his reality. What is in it is a distortion by the Christians, may God curse them. They lied, and God spoke truly in His mighty Book: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾. The clause is in the circumstantial mode (ḥāliyyah), that is: they said that while the state was that they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another. It is also said: they did not know his person, and they killed the one they killed while they were in doubt about him. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾, that is, concerning the matter of Isa. Some of them said: We killed him, and whoever witnessed his being raised to the sky said: We did not kill him. It is also said: the difference among them is that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Isa was crucified in respect of his human nature (nasut), not in respect of his divine nature (hut). And the Melkites said: the killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah in his entirety, both his human and divine natures. They have on this kind of difference a long discourse with no basis. Therefore God said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾, that is, in a hesitation that does not come out into the domain of soundness nor into the domain of falsehood in their belief. Rather, they are hesitant and doubtful in their uncertainty, wandering in their ignorance and bewildered. And ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾: (min) is superfluous to emphasize the negation of knowledge, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), that is: but they follow assumption. It is also said that it is a substitute for what precedes it, but the first is preferable.

It should not be said: following assumption contradicts the doubt which God informed about them that they were in; for the doubt intended here is hesitation, as we have mentioned, and assumption is a type of it, and what is intended here is not the inclination of one of the two sides.

His saying: (وما قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا) [and they did not kill him with certainty]: that is, a certain killing, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; or (certain) as a circumstantial state, meaning: while certain. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (قَتَلُوهُ) refers to Isa. It is also said that it refers to the assumption, and the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, like your saying "I killed him by knowledge" when you know him with complete knowledge.

Abu 'Ubayda said: if the meaning were "they did not kill Isa with certainty," it would have said only "they did not kill him." It is also said the meaning is: (p-342) and they did not kill the one who was made to appear to them. It is also said the meaning is: rather God raised him to Himself with certainty, and this is an error, because (بَلْ) does not govern what precedes it in what comes before it. Ibn al-Anbari permitted putting (يَقِينًا) in the accusative by a hidden verb which is the answer to an oath, and that (﴿بَلْ رَفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إلَيْهِ﴾) would be a new independent sentence. There is no justification for these sayings. The pronouns before (قَتَلُوهُ) and after it refer to Isa. Mentioning certainty here is for the purpose of mocking them, since it indicates their knowledge in general.

His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him to Himself﴾ is a refutation of them and an affirmation of what is correct. The mention of his raising, peace be upon him, has already been made in Al 'Imran.

His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾. By the People of the Book are meant the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: there is no one of the People of the Book but that, by God, he will surely believe in him before his death. The pronoun in (بِهِ) refers to Isa, and the pronoun in (مَوْتِهِ) refers to what the speech indicates, which is the word "one" (aḥad) that is implied, or the "Book-follower" (kitābiyy) indicated by "People of the Book." In this there is evidence that no Jew or Christian dies without having believed in the Messiah. It is also said: both pronouns refer to Isa, and the meaning is: Isa will not die until every person of the Book in his age believes in him. It is also said: the first pronoun refers to God, and it is said: to Muhammad. Ibn Jarir chose that both pronouns refer to Isa, and a group of the early generations (salaf) held it, and it is the apparent meaning. The intended belief is belief in him at his descent at the end of time, as the mass-transmitted hadiths have reported. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾, Isa, a witness over the People of the Book, bearing witness against the Jews for denying him, and against the Christians for exaggerating about him, to the point that they said he is the son of God.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: "Some Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: Musa brought the tablets from God, so bring us the tablets from God so that we may believe you. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from the sky﴾ up to ﴿and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: "The Jews and the Christians said to Muhammad (ﷺ): We will not pledge allegiance to you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from God addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God, and addressed to so-and-so that you are the messenger of God. So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾," the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, he said: "They, when they see Him, have seen Him. They only said 'plainly, show us God'. He said: it is brought forward and delayed."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And We raised the mountain above them﴾, he said: "It was a mountain they were at the base of, and God raised it and made it above them as if it were a canopy. He said: you shall certainly take My command, or I will drop it upon you. They said: We will take it. So God held it back from them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾, that he said: "They accused her of fornication."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When Allah intended to raise ʿIsa (Jesus) to the heaven, he went out to his companions, and in the house were twelve men from among the Hawariyyun (the disciples). He came out to them from a spring in the house, and his head was dripping water. He said: 'Among you is one who will disbelieve in me twelve times after having believed in me.' Then he said: 'Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed in my place and will be with me in my rank?' A young man from the youngest of them stood up, and he said to him: 'Sit down.' Then he repeated it to them, and the young man stood up and said: 'Me.' He said: 'You are that one.' So the likeness of ʿIsa was cast upon him, and ʿIsa was raised from an opening in the house to the heaven." He said: "The Jews came in search, and they seized the one with his likeness, killed him, and then crucified him. Some of them disbelieved in him twelve times after having believed in him, and they split into three sects. One sect said: 'Allah was among us as He willed, then He ascended to the heaven.' These are the Yaʿqubiyya. Another sect said: 'The son of Allah was among us as He willed, then Allah raised him to Himself.' These are the Nasturiyya. And another sect said: 'ʿAbd Allah and His Messenger was among us.' These are the Muslims. Then the two disbelieving sects joined forces against the Muslim sect and killed them. Islam remained effaced until Allah sent Muhammad, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾ [al-Saff: 14], meaning: the group that believed in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿and a group disbelieved﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿so We supported those who believed﴾ in the time of ʿIsa, by making Muhammad's religion prevail over the religion of the disbelievers."

Ibn Kathir, after citing it with this wording from Ibn Abi Hatim, said: "Ahmad ibn Sinan related to us, Abu Muʿawiya related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and so he mentioned it." He said: "This is a sound chain up to Ibn ʿAbbas." Ibn Kathir was correct, for all of these are men of the Sahih (of the authentic collections). al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Abu Kurayb, from Abu Muʿawiya, with similar wording.

His story (peace be upon him) has been related through various routes with different wordings. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it from Wahb ibn Munabbih in a form close to what is in the Gospel, and Ibn al-Mundhir likewise related it from him.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾, that he said: "They did not kill their supposition with certainty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir related the same from Ibn Juwaybir and al-Suddi as well.

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾, that he said: "It is the coming out of ʿIsa son of Mary." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from several routes from him concerning the verse that he said: "Before the death of ʿIsa." They also related from him that he said: "Before the death of the Jew." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "People from the People of the Book will reach ʿIsa when he is raised; they will surely believe in him."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "No Jew dies ever until he believes in ʿIsa." It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "What if he falls from the top of a house?" He said: "He will speak of it in the air." It was said: "What if one of them has his neck struck?" He said: "His tongue will stammer with it." Something similar has been related from him through several routes, and a number of the Successors (Tabiʿun) held it, and many of the Successors and those after them went to the view that the meaning is "before the death of ʿIsa," as related from Ibn ʿAbbas earlier. Many of them restricted it by saying that whoever reaches him at his descent to the earth will believe in him. The reports about the descent of ʿIsa are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), as we have clarified in a separate work containing what has been transmitted concerning the awaited one (al-Muntazar), the Dajjal, and the Masih.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verses 153–159 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. They are the Jews. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to ascend to the sky while they watched, and then to bring down to them a written book, which would be a proof of his truthfulness, all at once, as Musa (Moses) had brought the Torah, out of obstinacy on their part. May God curse them. So God, mighty and majestic, informed him that they had already asked Musa a greater question than this one. They said: ﴿Show us God plainly﴾, that is, visibly. Its meaning has already been explained in al-Baqarah. (جَهْرَةً) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a sight in plain view.

His saying: ﴿then they had asked﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you consider this request from them to be a great one, then they asked Musa for something greater than that. His saying: ﴿the thunderbolt seized them﴾: it is the fire that came down upon them from the sky and destroyed them. The (بِ) in His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ indicates cause, meaning: because of their wrongdoing in their false request, since seeing God visibly is impossible in that state. That does not entail its impossibility on the Day of Resurrection, for the mass-transmitted (mutawatir) hadiths have come with that. Whoever uses this verse to argue that seeing God is impossible on the Day of Resurrection has made a clear error.

Then they did not stop at this false request, which arose from them because of their wrongdoing after they had seen the miracles. Rather, they added to it something even worse, which is the worship of the calf. In the speech there is an omission, and the estimated meaning is: then We revived them, and they took the calf.

(al-Bayyinat) means the proofs and evidences, and the miracles of the hand, the staff, the splitting of the sea, and others. ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾, that is, what they had done of obstinacy and worship of the calf. ﴿And We gave Musa a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof, which is the signs with which he came. It was called authority (sultan) because whoever brings it overcomes his opponent. Among this is God's command to him, glorified be He, to order them to kill themselves in repentance for their disobedience, for that is part of the authority by which He overpowered them. ﴿And We raised the mountain above them for their covenant﴾, that is, because of their covenant, so that they would give it. For it is related that they refused to accept the law of Musa, so God raised the mountain over them and they accepted it. It is also said that the meaning is: because of their breaking the covenant which was taken from them, which is acting according to what is in the Torah. The lifting of the mountain has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, and likewise the explanation of their entering the gate in prostration. ﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, that is, by taking what you were commanded to leave of the fish in it. This has already been explained. It was also read as (لا تَعْتَدُوا) and (وتَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, emphasized, which is the pact that He took from them in the Torah. It is also said that it is a covenant strengthened by oath, so it was called firm (ghalidh) for that reason.

His saying: ﴿So because of their breaking their covenant﴾: (ما) is redundant for emphasis, or it is indefinite, and their breaking is a substitute for it (badal). The (بِ) is connected to an omitted element, and the estimated meaning is: so because of their breaking their covenant We cursed them. Al-Kisa'i said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing, up to His saying ﴿so because of their breaking their covenant﴾. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others rejected this, because those who were seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Musa, while those who killed the prophets and slandered Maryam with falsehood came long after Musa, so the thunderbolt did not seize those who slandered Maryam in their entirety.
