These are the Yaʿqubiyya. Another sect said: 'The son of Allah was among us as He willed, then Allah raised him to Himself.' These are the Nasturiyya. And another sect said: 'ʿAbd Allah and His Messenger was among us.' These are the Muslims. Then the two disbelieving sects joined forces against the Muslim sect and killed them. Islam remained effaced until Allah sent Muhammad, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾ [al-Saff: 14], meaning: the group that believed in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿and a group disbelieved﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved in the time of ʿIsa, ﴿so We supported those who believed﴾ in the time of ʿIsa, by making Muhammad's religion prevail over the religion of the disbelievers."

Ibn Kathir, after citing it with this wording from Ibn Abi Hatim, said: "Ahmad ibn Sinan related to us, Abu Muʿawiya related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and so he mentioned it." He said: "This is a sound chain up to Ibn ʿAbbas." Ibn Kathir was correct, for all of these are men of the Sahih (of the authentic collections). al-Nasa'i also related it from the hadith of Abu Kurayb, from Abu Muʿawiya, with similar wording.

His story (peace be upon him) has been related through various routes with different wordings. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it from Wahb ibn Munabbih in a form close to what is in the Gospel, and Ibn al-Mundhir likewise related it from him.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾, that he said: "They did not kill their supposition with certainty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir related the same from Ibn Juwaybir and al-Suddi as well.

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾, that he said: "It is the coming out of ʿIsa son of Mary." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from several routes from him concerning the verse that he said: "Before the death of ʿIsa." They also related from him that he said: "Before the death of the Jew." Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "People from the People of the Book will reach ʿIsa when he is raised; they will surely believe in him."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "No Jew dies ever until he believes in ʿIsa." It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "What if he falls from the top of a house?" He said: "He will speak of it in the air." It was said: "What if one of them has his neck struck?" He said: "His tongue will stammer with it." Something similar has been related from him through several routes, and a number of the Successors (Tabiʿun) held it, and many of the Successors and those after them went to the view that the meaning is "before the death of ʿIsa," as related from Ibn ʿAbbas earlier. Many of them restricted it by saying that whoever reaches him at his descent to the earth will believe in him. The reports about the descent of ʿIsa are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), as we have clarified in a separate work containing what has been transmitted concerning the awaited one (al-Muntazar), the Dajjal, and the Masih.

The particle bāʾ in His saying (fa-bi-ẓulmin) [فَبِظُلْمٍ] denotes causation, and the indefiniteness and tanwīn indicate magnitude. The meaning is: "Because of a great wrong, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, not because of anything else, as they claimed that these had been forbidden to those before them." Al-Zajjaj said: this is a substitution (badal) for His saying (fa-bi-mā naqḍihim) [فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ] (An-Nisa 155, Al-Ma'idah 13). The good things mentioned are what Allah, glorified is He, specified in His saying: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾, and so on.

(And because of) their hindering themselves and others from the way of Allah, which is following Muhammad (ﷺ), and their distorting (the Scripture), killing the prophets, and the well-known sins that proceeded from them. His saying (kathīran) [كَثِيرًا] ("many") is an object of the verb mentioned, meaning: "because they hindered many people," or it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a great hindering."

﴿And their taking usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾: that is, their dealing in usury among themselves and their consuming it, though it was forbidden to them. ﴿And their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾, such as bribery and the illicit gain (suḥt) they used to take. His saying: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾ is an exception (istidrāk) from His saying: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾, or from ﴿those who were Jews﴾. This is because the Jews denied and said: "These things were prohibited originally, and you make them lawful." So (the verse) "But those firmly grounded in knowledge" was revealed. The rāsikh (firmly grounded) is one who goes deep in the knowledge of the Book and is established in it; al-rusūkh means firmness. The discussion of it has already passed in Āl ʿImrān. The intended ones are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and those like them.

Al-rāsikhūn (those firmly grounded) is the subject (mubtada'), and yu'minūna (they believe) is its predicate. Al-mu'minūn (the believers) is conjoined to al-rāsikhūn. The believers are intended either as those among the People of the Book who believed, or as the Emigrants and the Helpers, or as all of them. His saying: (wal-muqīmīna al-ṣalāh) [وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاةَ] (and those who establish prayer) was recited by al-Ḥasan, Mālik ibn Dīnār, and a group as (wal-muqīmūna al-ṣalāh) [وَالْمُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ], in the nominative, as a conjunction to what precedes it. Likewise it is in the codex of Ibn Masʿūd. Scholars differed about the reason for its accusative form in the reading of the majority, and gave several opinions.

The first: the view of Sībawayh that it is in the accusative as an expression of praise, meaning: "I mean those who establish prayer." Sībawayh said: "This is a chapter on what is put in the accusative for honor, and among it is (wal-muqīmīna al-ṣalāh)." He recited:

Every people obeyed the command of its leader, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of its misguided one.

The spearers, who have not yet speared anyone, and the sayers, to whoever asks, "A house—we will leave it."

And he recited:

Let my people not be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels,

Those who descend upon every battlefield, and those who are good at tying the knots of the loincloths.

Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is the most correct of what has been said about al-muqīmīn." Al-Kisāʾī and al-Khalīl said: it is conjoined to His saying (bi-mā unzila ilayka) [بِما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ] (in what was revealed to you). Al-Akhfash said: this is far-fetched, because the meaning would then be: "and they believe in those who establish prayer." Al-Mubarrad (Muhammad ibn Yazid) explained it by saying that al-muqīmīn here are the angels, so the meaning becomes: "they believe in what was revealed to you, and in what was revealed before you, and in the angels." He preferred this.

It has been related that the accusative for praise is far-fetched, because praise comes only after the predicate is complete, and the predicate of al-rāsikhūn is His saying: ﴿Those—We will give them a great reward﴾. It has also been said that al-muqīmīn is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying (minhum) [مِنهم] ("among them"), but in this there is conjoining to a pronoun without repeating the preposition. It is related from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about al-muqīmīn in this verse, and about His saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians﴾ (Ta-Ha 63), and about His saying (wal-ṣābiʾūn) [وَالصَّابِئُونَ] ("and the Sabians") (Al-Ma'idah 69), so she said: "O nephew, the scribes made mistakes." Abu ʿUbayd reported it from her in his Fadāʾil, and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir (also reported it).

Abān ibn ʿUthmān said: "The scribe was dictating to me, and he wrote, ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them and the believers﴾, then he said, 'What shall I write?' He was told: 'Write (wal-muqīmīna al-ṣalāh).' From that this occurred." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from him. Al-Qushayrī said: "This is false, because those who collected the Book were examples in the language, so this should not be suspected of them." It may be answered regarding al-Qushayrī that it is related from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he finished the codex and it was brought to him, he said: "I see in it some error (laḥn) which the Arabs will correct with their tongues." Ibn Abī Dāwūd reported it from him through several chains. Many imams of grammar and exegesis preferred the view of Sībawayh, while Ibn Jarir al-Ṭabarī and al-Qaffāl preferred the view of al-Khalīl and al-Kisāʾī. According to the view of Sībawayh, the clause (in between) is a parenthetical insertion between the subject and predicate, according to those who say the predicate of al-rāsikhūn is His saying ﴿those—We will give them﴾, or between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, if we make the predicate of al-rāsikhūn "yu'minūn," and make His saying (wal-mu'tūna al-zakāh) [وَالْمُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ] ("and those who give zakat") a conjunction to (al-mu'minūn) and not to... According to Sībawayh, al-mu'tūna al-zakāh is in the nominative, by beginning (ibtidāʾ), or by an omitted subject, meaning: "they are those who give zakat."

His saying: ﴿And the believers in Allah and the Last Day﴾ refers to the believers among the People of the Book. They are first described as firmly grounded in knowledge, then as believing in the Books of Allah, and that they establish prayer, give zakat, and believe in Allah and the Last Day. It has also been said that they are the believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, as has passed, and that they combine all these attributes. The reference in His saying: ﴿Those—We will give them a great reward﴾ is to al-rāsikhūn and what is conjoined to them.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. The meaning is that the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the matter of those prophets before him, so why do you ask of him what no one among the contemporaries of the messengers asked? Revelation (waḥy) is information conveyed in concealment. It is said: "He was revealed to with speech, a revelation (waḥy)," and (awḥā yūḥī īḥāʾan) is also used. He specified Noah because he was the first prophet to whom laws were revealed, and it has been said other than this.

The kāf in His saying (kamā) [كَما] is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a revelation like Our revelation to Noah," or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "We revealed to you this revelation in a state of being likened to Our revelation to Noah." His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾ is conjoined to ﴿We revealed to Noah﴾, ﴿and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes (al-asbāṭ)﴾, who are the sons of Jacob as has passed, ﴿and Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾. He singled these out for mention after their inclusion in the word "prophets," as an honor for them, like His saying: ﴿His angels, His messengers, and Gabriel﴾. Jesus is placed before Job and those after him, even though they lived in a time before his, in refutation of the Jews who disbelieved in him. Also, the waw here is only for general conjunction.

His saying: ﴿And We gave David a Zabur﴾ is conjoined to (awḥaynā) ("We revealed"). The Zabur is the Book of David. Al-Qurṭubī said: "It consists of one hundred and fifty surahs, in which there is no ruling, no lawful, and no unlawful, but only wisdoms and admonitions." I (al-Shawkānī) say: it consists of one hundred and fifty mazāmīr (psalms), and a mazmūr is a section containing words of David, in which he seeks refuge in Allah from his adversaries, supplicates Allah against them, and asks Him for victory, and sometimes it contains admonitions. He used to say this mostly in the synagogue, and with his speaking he used some instruments that produce pleasant tunes, as is stated clearly in many of those psalms. The zubur (plural of zabūr) means writing, and al-zabūr in the sense of al-mazbūr ("the written"), like al-rasūl (the messenger) in the sense of al-marsūl, al-ḥalūb, and al-rakūb.

Ḥamzah recited (zubūran) [زُبُورًا] with a ḍammah on the zāy, as a plural of zubur, like fals and fulūs. Al-zubur means al-mazbūr, and the original meaning of the word is securing; it is said: "a well that is mazbūrah," meaning "walled with stones." The Book was called Zabūr because of the strength of its bond.

His saying: (wa-rusulan) [وَرُسُلًا] is in the accusative by a deleted verb indicated by (awḥaynā), meaning: "And We sent messengers ﴿about whom We have told you before﴾." It has also been said it is in the accusative by a verb indicated by (qaṣaṣnāhum) ("We have told you about them"), meaning: "and We told about messengers." Similar to it is what Sībawayh recited:

I have become one who does not carry a weapon, nor can I hold the camel's halter if it bolts,

And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

meaning: "and I fear the wolf." Ubayy recited (rusulun) [رُسُلٌ] in the nominative, meaning: "and among them are messengers." The meaning of (min qablu) ("before") is that He related it to him before this surah, or before this day. It has been said that when Allah mentioned in His Book some names of His prophets and did not mention the names of others, the Jews said: "Muhammad mentioned the prophets and did not mention Moses," so this was revealed: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾ (An-Nisa 164). The majority recited the noble name in the nominative, meaning that Allah is the One who spoke to Moses. Al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited the noble name in the accusative, meaning that Moses is the one who spoke to Allah, glorified is He. (Taklīman) [تَكْلِيمًا] is an emphatic verbal noun. The purpose of the emphasis is to remove the suspicion that the speaking is figurative. As al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs call whatever reaches a human being speech by any means. It has also been said: what is not emphasized by a verbal noun, but when it is emphasized, it is only the real speech.

Al-Naḥḥās said: the grammarians agreed that when you emphasize the verb with a verbal noun, it is not figurative.

His saying: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners﴾ is a substitution (badal) for the first (rusulan), or it is in the accusative by a deleted verb, meaning: "and We sent," or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, with (rusulan) serving as a preparation for what follows, or it is in the accusative for praise, meaning: "bringers of good news to the people of obedience and warners to the people of disobedience."

His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ means: an excuse by which they would plead, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses?"﴾ (Ta-Ha 134). The excuse is called an argument (ḥujjah), although no servant has any argument against Allah, to alert that this excuse is accepted by Him, out of His bounty and mercy. The meaning of His saying "after the messengers" is after the sending of the messengers. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: no one can overpower Him, ﴿Wise﴾ in His acts, among which is the sending of messengers.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid regarding ﴿And their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾ that he said: "Themselves and others from the truth." Ibn Isḥāq reported in al-Dalāʾil from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding His saying: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Usayd ibn Shuʿbah, and Thaʿlabah ibn Shuʿbah, when they left the Jews and embraced Islam."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil reported from him that some Jews said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that Allah revealed anything to a human after Moses," so Allah revealed (Indeed, We have revealed to you) to the end of the verse. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, al-Ḥākim, and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how many are the prophets?' He said: 'One hundred and twenty-four thousand.' I said: 'How many of them are messengers?' He said: 'Three hundred and thirteen, a great number.'" Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from Abu Umamah, marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet), except that he said: "and the messengers were three hundred and fifteen."

Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ḥākim reported with a weak chain from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among my brothers among the prophets who passed before me were eight thousand prophets, then came Jesus, then I came after him.'" Al-Ḥākim reported something similar from Anas with a weak chain.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one is more jealous than Allah; for this reason He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden. No one loves praise more than Allah; for this reason He praised Himself. No one loves excuses more than Allah; for this reason He sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners.'"

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾ is conjoined to ﴿We revealed to Noah﴾, ﴿and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes (al-asbāṭ)﴾, who are the sons of Jacob as has passed, ﴿and Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾. He singled these out for mention after their inclusion in the word "prophets," as an honor for them, like His saying: ﴿His angels, His messengers, and Gabriel﴾. I (al-Shawkānī) say: it consists of one hundred and fifty mazāmīr (psalms), and a mazmūr is a section containing words of David, in which he seeks refuge in Allah from his adversaries, supplicates Allah against them, and asks Him for victory, and sometimes it contains admonitions. He used to say this mostly in the synagogue, and with his speaking he used some instruments that produce pleasant tunes, as is stated clearly in many of those psalms. The zubur (plural of zabūr) means writing, and al-zabūr in the sense of al-mazbūr ("the written"), like al-rasūl (the messenger) in the sense of al-marsūl, al-ḥalūb, and al-rakūb.

It has also been said it is in the accusative by a verb indicated by (qaṣaṣnāhum) ("We have told you about them"), meaning: "and We told about messengers." Similar to it is what Sībawayh recited:

I have become one who does not carry a weapon, nor can I hold the camel's halter if it bolts,

And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

meaning: "and I fear the wolf." Ubayy recited (rusulun) [رُسُلٌ] in the nominative, meaning: "and among them are messengers." Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ḥākim reported with a weak chain from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among my brothers among the prophets who passed before me were eight thousand prophets, then came Jesus, then I came after him.'" Al-Ḥākim reported something similar from Anas with a weak chain.

The good things mentioned are what Allah, glorified is He, specified in His saying: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾, and so on.

(And because of) their hindering themselves and others from the way of Allah, which is following Muhammad (ﷺ), and their distorting (the Scripture), killing the prophets, and the well-known sins that proceeded from them. His saying (kathīran) [كَثِيرًا] ("many") is an object of the verb mentioned, meaning: "because they hindered many people," or it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a great hindering."

The intended ones are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and those like them.

Every people obeyed the command of its leader, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of its misguided one.

The spearers, who have not yet speared anyone, and the sayers, to whoever asks, "A house—we will leave it."

And he recited:

Let my people not be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels,

Those who descend upon every battlefield, and those who are good at tying the knots of the loincloths.

Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is the most correct of what has been said about al-muqīmīn." He preferred this.

Abu ʿUbayd reported it from her in his Fadāʾil, and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir (also reported it).

It may be answered regarding al-Qushayrī that it is related from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he finished the codex and it was brought to him, he said: "I see in it some error (laḥn) which the Arabs will correct with their tongues." Many imams of grammar and exegesis preferred the view of Sībawayh, while Ibn Jarir al-Ṭabarī and al-Qaffāl preferred the view of al-Khalīl and al-Kisāʾī. According to Sībawayh, al-mu'tūna al-zakāh is in the nominative, by beginning (ibtidāʾ), or by an omitted subject, meaning: "they are those who give zakat."

And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from Abu Umamah, marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet), except that he said: "and the messengers were three hundred and fifteen."

Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ḥākim reported with a weak chain from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among my brothers among the prophets who passed before me were eight thousand prophets, then came Jesus, then I came after him.'" Al-Ḥākim reported something similar from Anas with a weak chain.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one is more jealous than Allah; for this reason He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden. The good things mentioned are what Allah, glorified is He, specified in His saying: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾, and so on.

(And because of) their hindering themselves and others from the way of Allah, which is following Muhammad (ﷺ), and their distorting (the Scripture), killing the prophets, and the well-known sins that proceeded from them. His saying (kathīran) [كَثِيرًا] ("many") is an object of the verb mentioned, meaning: "because they hindered many people," or it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a great hindering."

﴿And their taking usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾: that is, their dealing in usury among themselves and their consuming it, though it was forbidden to them. ﴿And their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾, such as bribery and the illicit gain (suḥt) they used to take. This is because the Jews denied and said: "These things were prohibited originally, and you make them lawful." So (the verse) "But those firmly grounded in knowledge" was revealed. The rāsikh (firmly grounded) is one who goes deep in the knowledge of the Book and is established in it; al-rusūkh means firmness. The discussion of it has already passed in Āl ʿImrān. The intended ones are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and those like them.

Every people obeyed the command of its leader, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of its misguided one.

The spearers, who have not yet speared anyone, and the sayers, to whoever asks, "A house—we will leave it."

And he recited:

Let my people not be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels,

Those who descend upon every battlefield, and those who are good at tying the knots of the loincloths.

Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is the most correct of what has been said about al-muqīmīn." (And because of) their hindering themselves and others from the way of Allah, which is following Muhammad (ﷺ), and their distorting (the Scripture), killing the prophets, and the well-known sins that proceeded from them. His saying (kathīran) [كَثِيرًا] ("many") is an object of the verb mentioned, meaning: "because they hindered many people," or it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a great hindering."

﴿And their taking usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾: that is, their dealing in usury among themselves and their consuming it, though it was forbidden to them. ﴿And their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾, such as bribery and the illicit gain (suḥt) they used to take. His saying: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾ is an exception (istidrāk) from His saying: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾, or from ﴿those who were Jews﴾. This is because the Jews denied and said: "These things were prohibited originally, and you make them lawful." So (the verse) "But those firmly grounded in knowledge" was revealed. The rāsikh (firmly grounded) is one who goes deep in the knowledge of the Book and is established in it; al-rusūkh means firmness. The discussion of it has already passed in Āl ʿImrān. The intended ones are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and those like them.

His saying: (wal-muqīmīna al-ṣalāh) [وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاةَ] (and those who establish prayer) was recited by al-Ḥasan, Mālik ibn Dīnār, and a group as (wal-muqīmūna al-ṣalāh) [وَالْمُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ], in the nominative, as a conjunction to what precedes it. Every people obeyed the command of its leader, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of its misguided one.

The spearers, who have not yet speared anyone, and the sayers, to whoever asks, "A house—we will leave it."

And he recited:

Let my people not be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels,

Those who descend upon every battlefield, and those who are good at tying the knots of the loincloths.

Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is the most correct of what has been said about al-muqīmīn." He preferred this.

Abu ʿUbayd reported it from her in his Fadāʾil, and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir (also reported it).

And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

meaning: "and I fear the wolf." Ubayy recited (rusulun) [رُسُلٌ] in the nominative, meaning: "and among them are messengers." Al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited the noble name in the accusative, meaning that Moses is the one who spoke to Allah, glorified is He. (Taklīman) [تَكْلِيمًا] is an emphatic verbal noun. His saying: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners﴾ is a substitution (badal) for the first (rusulan), or it is in the accusative by a deleted verb, meaning: "and We sent," or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, with (rusulan) serving as a preparation for what follows, or it is in the accusative for praise, meaning: "bringers of good news to the people of obedience and warners to the people of disobedience."

His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ means: an excuse by which they would plead, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses?"﴾ (Ta-Ha 134). The excuse is called an argument (ḥujjah), although no servant has any argument against Allah, to alert that this excuse is accepted by Him, out of His bounty and mercy. The meaning of His saying "after the messengers" is after the sending of the messengers. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: no one can overpower Him, ﴿Wise﴾ in His acts, among which is the sending of messengers.

He said: 'One hundred and twenty-four thousand.' I said: 'How many of them are messengers?' He said: 'Three hundred and thirteen, a great number.'" Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from Abu Umamah, marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet), except that he said: "and the messengers were three hundred and fifteen."

Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ḥākim reported with a weak chain from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among my brothers among the prophets who passed before me were eight thousand prophets, then came Jesus, then I came after him.'" Al-Ḥākim reported something similar from Anas with a weak chain.

His saying: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners﴾ is a substitution (badal) for the first (rusulan), or it is in the accusative by a deleted verb, meaning: "and We sent," or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, with (rusulan) serving as a preparation for what follows, or it is in the accusative for praise, meaning: "bringers of good news to the people of obedience and warners to the people of disobedience."

His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ means: an excuse by which they would plead, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses?"﴾ (Ta-Ha 134). The excuse is called an argument (ḥujjah), although no servant has any argument against Allah, to alert that this excuse is accepted by Him, out of His bounty and mercy. The meaning of His saying "after the messengers" is after the sending of the messengers. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: no one can overpower Him, ﴿Wise﴾ in His acts, among which is the sending of messengers.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid regarding ﴿And their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾ that he said: "Themselves and others from the truth." Ibn Isḥāq reported in al-Dalāʾil from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding His saying: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them﴾ that he said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Usayd ibn Shuʿbah, and Thaʿlabah ibn Shuʿbah, when they left the Jews and embraced Islam."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil reported from him that some Jews said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that Allah revealed anything to a human after Moses," so Allah revealed (Indeed, We have revealed to you) to the end of the verse. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, al-Ḥākim, and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how many are the prophets?' He said: 'One hundred and twenty-four thousand.' I said: 'How many of them are messengers?' He said: 'Three hundred and thirteen, a great number.'" Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported something similar from Abu Umamah, marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet), except that he said: "and the messengers were three hundred and fifteen."

Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ḥākim reported with a weak chain from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among my brothers among the prophets who passed before me were eight thousand prophets, then came Jesus, then I came after him.'" Al-Ḥākim reported something similar from Anas with a weak chain.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one is more jealous than Allah; for this reason He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden. No one loves praise more than Allah; for this reason He praised Himself. No one loves excuses more than Allah; for this reason He sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners.'"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 4, verses 167–171**

(p-345) His words: ﴿But God bears witness﴾. The noble name (Allah) is the subject (mubtada', grammatical subject) and the verb is its predicate (khabar). With the nun of *innallah* doubled (*lakinna*), the word is in the accusative as the noun of *lakin* (but). The contrast (istidrak) refers to an omitted element that is implied, as if they had said: "We do not testify to this for you, O Muhammad," meaning the revelation and prophethood. So it was revealed: ﴿But God bears witness﴾.

His words: (and the angels bear witness) is a clause conjoined to the first clause, or a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject). Likewise his words: (He has sent it down with His knowledge) is a circumstantial clause, meaning: accompanied by His knowledge, which no one else possesses, of your fitness for what God has chosen you for, namely prophethood, and of the Qur'an He sent down to you. ﴿And God suffices as a witness﴾, meaning: God suffices as a witness, and the *ba'* (bi-) is superfluous. The witness of God, glorified is He, is what He produces of miracles that indicate the truth of prophethood, for the existence of these miracles is a testimony to the Prophet (ﷺ) of the truth of what he reported of this and other matters. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ in everything that must be believed, or in this specific matter, which is what is at issue here, ﴿and avert [others] from the way of God﴾, which is the religion of Islam, by denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: "We do not find his description in our book, and prophethood is only among the descendants of Aaron and David," and by saying: "The law of Moses is not abrogated." ﴿They have certainly strayed far astray﴾ from the truth by what they did, for although they disbelieved, they also prevented others from the truth.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ by denying [the truth], ﴿and wrong﴾ others by barring them from the way; or they wronged Muhammad by concealing his prophethood; or they wronged themselves by their disbelief. All these meanings may be intended. ﴿God will never forgive them﴾ if they persist in their disbelief and die as disbelievers, ﴿nor will He guide them to a path except the path of Hell﴾, because they committed what necessitates that by their bad choice and extreme wretchedness, and they denied the clear and obstinately opposed the manifest. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾, meaning: He will admit them to Hell, abiding in it; this is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah).

His words: (forever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). It serves to rule out the possibility that "abiding" here means a long stay. (And that is) meaning: their eternal dwelling in Hell, or the withholding of forgiveness from them and their being guided along with abiding in Hell, ﴿is ever easy for God﴾, because nothing is difficult for Him, glorified is He. ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. ﴿So believe, [it is] better for you﴾. The grammarians differed over the case of *khayran* (better): Sibawayh and al-Khalil said it is governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Intend or bring about what is better for you." Al-Farra' said it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "Believe a belief that is better for you." Abu Ubayda and al-Kisa'i held that it is the predicate of an implied *kana* (was), meaning: "Believe, and belief will be better for you." The strongest of these opinions is the third, then the first, then the second, though it has some weakness. ﴿And if you disbelieve﴾, meaning: if you persist in your disbelief, ﴿then indeed, to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of His creatures, and you are among them. He who owns you and them is able to recompense you for your evil deeds. So in this sentence there is a warning to them, together with a clarification of the way of proof and the removal of the veil from the evidence, in a manner that obliges them to acceptance and submission, because they acknowledge that God is their Creator: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 87].

His words: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion﴾. Ghuluww (excess) is going beyond the limit. From it comes *ghala as-si'r* (prices rose), and *ghala ar-rajulu fi al-amr* (the man went to excess in the matter). And *ghala bil-jariyah lahmuha wa 'azmuha* (the girl's flesh and bones grew) when she quickly reached youth and surpassed her peers.

The meaning of the verse is a prohibition to them against excess at times and laxity at other times. Of excess is the excess of the Christians regarding Jesus, to the point that they made him a lord. Of laxity is the excess of the Jews regarding him, peace be upon him, to the point that they claimed he was born of other than rightful lineage. How fine is the saying of the poet:

*"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate; both extremes of the matter are blameworthy."*

﴿And do not say about God except the truth﴾, which is what He described Himself with and what His messengers described Him with. Do not say falsehood, like the saying of the Jews, "Uzair is the son of God," and the saying of the Christians, "The Messiah is the son of God." ﴿The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God﴾. "The Messiah" is the subject, "Jesus" is an apposition (badal) to it, "son of Mary" is an adjective of Jesus, and "messenger of God" is the predicate. It is also permissible that "Jesus son of Mary" be an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), and the sentence is then an explanation of the prohibition. The discussion of the Messiah has already been presented in Al 'Imran.

His words: (and His word) is conjoined to "messenger of God." And ﴿which He bestowed upon Mary﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: he was by His word "Be," and he was, a human being without a father. It was said that "His word" means God's glad tiding to Mary and His message to her through Gabriel, by His saying: ﴿When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God gives you good tidings of a word from Him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45]. It was also said that "word" here means "sign," as in ﴿and she confirmed the words of her Lord﴾ [at-Tahrim: 12], and His saying: ﴿Were the sea ink for the words of God, it would be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27].

His words: (and a spirit from Him). That is, He sent Gabriel, who blew into Mary's garment, and she conceived by God's permission. This attribution is one of honor, although all spirits are from His creation. It was also said: whoever manifests wondrous things is called a spirit and is attributed to God, so it is said: "This is a spirit from God," meaning: from His creation, just as it is said of a blessing that it is from God. It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "from His creation," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 13], meaning: from His creation. It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "a mercy from Him." It was said: it means "a proof from Him," and Jesus was a proof and argument against his people. His words: (from Him) is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of "spirit," meaning: existing from Him. The spirit is attributed to Him, glorified is He, even though it came by Gabriel's blowing, because He, exalted is He, is the one who commanded Gabriel to blow.

﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, meaning: believe that He, glorified is He, is one God who did not beget and was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal; and believe that His messengers are truthful, conveying from God what He commanded them to convey. Do not deny them, and do not go to excess regarding them, making some of them gods.

His words: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾. "Three" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, "Do not say: our gods are three." Al-Farra' and Abu Ubayd said: meaning, "Do not say: they are three," like His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: meaning, "Do not say: He is the third of three," so the subject and the attribute were omitted. The Christians, despite the diversity of their sects, agree on the Trinity. By "three" they mean the three hypostases (aqanim), so they make Him, glorified is He, one substance with three hypostases. By hypostases they mean the hypostasis of existence, the hypostasis of life, and the hypostasis of knowledge. Sometimes they express the hypostases as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, meaning by the Father existence, by the Spirit life, and by the Son the Messiah. It was also said that the three gods are: God, glorified and exalted is He; Mary; and the Messiah.

The Christians have become deeply confused over this, and we have found in the four Gospels, which they call by the name "Injil" (Gospel), great divergence concerning Jesus. Sometimes he is described as "son of man," sometimes as "son of God," and sometimes as "son of the Lord." This is an obvious contradiction and a trifling with religion.

The truth is what God has told us in the Qur'an. Whatever contradicts it in the Torah (Tawrat), the Gospel, or the Psalms (Zabur) is from the alteration of the alterers and the manipulation of the manipulators. Among the most astonishing things we have seen is that each of the four Gospels is attributed to one of Jesus's companions, and the substance of all of them is that each of these four recounted the biography of Jesus from the time God sent him until the time He raised him to Himself, and recounted what happened to him of miracles and disputes with the Jews and others. Their wording differs but their meanings agree, and one may add to another according to what memory and precision require. They mention what Jesus said and what was said to him, but there is nothing in them of the speech of God, glorified is He, and God did not send down to Jesus a book from Him. Rather, Jesus, peace be upon him, argued against them by what was in the Torah and mentioned that he had not come with anything that contradicted it. Likewise the Psalms, for from beginning to end it is the speech of David, peace be upon him. God's speech is more truthful and His book is more right. He has informed us that the Gospel is His book, which He sent down to His servant and messenger Jesus son of Mary, and that the Psalms are His book, which He gave to David and sent down to him.

His words: ﴿Desist, [it is] better for you﴾, meaning: desist from the Trinity. The accusative of "better" here has the three possibilities mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿So believe, [it is] better for you﴾.

﴿God is but one God﴾, having no partner, no consort, and no offspring. ﴿Glory be to Him, [exalted above] having a son﴾, meaning: I glorify Him by declaring Him far above having a son. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾. Whatever you have made a partner or a son for Him is part of that, and the owned, created being cannot be a partner or a son. ﴿And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾: creatures entrust their affairs to Him, while they possess neither harm nor benefit for themselves.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* have related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A group of Jews entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to them: 'I swear by God, I know that you know that I am the Messenger of God.' They said: 'We do not know that.' So God revealed: ﴿But God bears witness﴾, the verse."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* related from Abu Musa that an-Najashi said to Ja'far: "What does your companion say about the son of Mary?" He said: "He says about him what God said: he is the spirit of God and His word; He brought him forth from the chaste virgin whom no human had touched." Then [an-Najashi] took a stick from the ground and lifted it, and said: "O assembly of priests and monks, these [people] do not exceed what you say about the son of Mary by the weight of this." Al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* also related it from Ibn Mas'ud with a longer version than this.

al-Bukhari related from Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not exalt me as the Christians exalted Jesus son of Mary; I am only a servant, so say: 'the servant of God and His messenger.'"

*"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate; both extremes of the matter are blameworthy."*

﴿And do not say about God except the truth﴾, which is what He described Himself with and what His messengers described Him with. Do not say falsehood, like the saying of the Jews, "Uzair is the son of God," and the saying of the Christians, "The Messiah is the son of God." ﴿The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was only a messenger of God﴾. "The Messiah" is the subject, "Jesus" is an apposition (badal) to it, "son of Mary" is an adjective of Jesus, and "messenger of God" is the predicate. It is also permissible that "Jesus son of Mary" be an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), and the sentence is then an explanation of the prohibition. The discussion of the Messiah has already been presented in Al 'Imran.

His words: (and His word) is conjoined to "messenger of God." And ﴿which He bestowed upon Mary﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: he was by His word "Be," and he was, a human being without a father. It was said that "His word" means God's glad tiding to Mary and His message to her through Gabriel, by His saying: ﴿When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God gives you good tidings of a word from Him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45]. It was also said that "word" here means "sign," as in ﴿and she confirmed the words of her Lord﴾ [at-Tahrim: 12], and His saying: ﴿Were the sea ink for the words of God, it would be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27].

His words: (and a spirit from Him). That is, He sent Gabriel, who blew into Mary's garment, and she conceived by God's permission. This attribution is one of honor, although all spirits are from His creation. It was also said: whoever manifests wondrous things is called a spirit and is attributed to God, so it is said: "This is a spirit from God," meaning: from His creation, just as it is said of a blessing that it is from God. It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "from His creation," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 13], meaning: from His creation. It was also said: "a spirit from Him" means "a mercy from Him." It was said: it means "a proof from Him," and Jesus was a proof and argument against his people. His words: (from Him) is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of "spirit," meaning: existing from Him. The spirit is attributed to Him, glorified is He, even though it came by Gabriel's blowing, because He, exalted is He, is the one who commanded Gabriel to blow.

﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, meaning: believe that He, glorified is He, is one God who did not beget and was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal; and believe that His messengers are truthful, conveying from God what He commanded them to convey. Do not deny them, and do not go to excess regarding them, making some of them gods.

His words: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾. "Three" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, "Do not say: our gods are three." Al-Farra' and Abu Ubayd said: meaning, "Do not say: they are three," like His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: meaning, "Do not say: He is the third of three," so the subject and the attribute were omitted. The Christians, despite the diversity of their sects, agree on the Trinity. By "three" they mean the three hypostases (aqanim), so they make Him, glorified is He, one substance with three hypostases. By hypostases they mean the hypostasis of existence, the hypostasis of life, and the hypostasis of knowledge. Sometimes they express the hypostases as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, meaning by the Father existence, by the Spirit life, and by the Son the Messiah. It was also said that the three gods are: God, glorified and exalted is He; Mary; and the Messiah.

The Christians have become deeply confused over this, and we have found in the four Gospels, which they call by the name "Injil" (Gospel), great divergence concerning Jesus. Sometimes he is described as "son of man," sometimes as "son of God," and sometimes as "son of the Lord." This is an obvious contradiction and a trifling with religion.

The truth is what God has told us in the Qur'an. Whatever contradicts it in the Torah (Tawrat), the Gospel, or the Psalms (Zabur) is from the alteration of the alterers and the manipulation of the manipulators. Among the most astonishing things we have seen is that each of the four Gospels is attributed to one of Jesus's companions, and the substance of all of them is that each of these four recounted the biography of Jesus from the time God sent him until the time He raised him to Himself, and recounted what happened to him of miracles and disputes with the Jews and others. Their wording differs but their meanings agree, and one may add to another according to what memory and precision require. They mention what Jesus said and what was said to him, but there is nothing in them of the speech of God, glorified is He, and God did not send down to Jesus a book from Him. Rather, Jesus, peace be upon him, argued against them by what was in the Torah and mentioned that he had not come with anything that contradicted it. Likewise the Psalms, for from beginning to end it is the speech of David, peace be upon him. God's speech is more truthful and His book is more right. He has informed us that the Gospel is His book, which He sent down to His servant and messenger Jesus son of Mary, and that the Psalms are His book, which He gave to David and sent down to him.

His words: ﴿Desist, [it is] better for you﴾, meaning: desist from the Trinity. The accusative of "better" here has the three possibilities mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿So believe, [it is] better for you﴾.

﴿God is but one God﴾, having no partner, no consort, and no offspring. ﴿Glory be to Him, [exalted above] having a son﴾, meaning: I glorify Him by declaring Him far above having a son. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾. Whatever you have made a partner or a son for Him is part of that, and the owned, created being cannot be a partner or a son. ﴿And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾: creatures entrust their affairs to Him, while they possess neither harm nor benefit for themselves.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* have related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A group of Jews entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to them: 'I swear by God, I know that you know that I am the Messenger of God.' They said: 'We do not know that.' So God revealed: ﴿But God bears witness﴾, the verse."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* related from Abu Musa that an-Najashi said to Ja'far: "What does your companion say about the son of Mary?" He said: "He says about him what God said: he is the spirit of God and His word; He brought him forth from the chaste virgin whom no human had touched." Then [an-Najashi] took a stick from the ground and lifted it, and said: "O assembly of priests and monks, these [people] do not exceed what you say about the son of Mary by the weight of this." Al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* also related it from Ibn Mas'ud with a longer version than this.

al-Bukhari related from Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not exalt me as the Christians exalted Jesus son of Mary; I am only a servant, so say: 'the servant of God and His messenger.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 4, verse 172–175:

The root of yastankif (يَسْتَنْكِفُ) is n-k-f, and the other letters are additional. It is said: nakaftu min al-shay'i, istankaftu minhu, and ankaftuhu; i.e., I purified him from what is disdained. Al-Zajjaj said: istankafa means anifa (to be too proud), derived from nakaftu al-dam'a (I wiped away the tears) when I removed them with your finger from your cheeks. It was also said that it comes from al-nakaf, which is a defect; it is said: "ma 'alayhi fi hadha al-amr nakafun wa la wakafun," i.e., there is no fault in it. The meaning of the first is: he will not be too proud to worship, nor will he deem himself exempt from it. The meaning of the second is: he will not find fault with worship, nor will he withdraw from it. ﴿Nor the angels brought near﴾ is a conjunction with al-Masih; i.e., nor will the angels brought near be too proud to be servants of Allah. Those who argue for the superiority of the angels over the prophets have used this as evidence, and the author of al-Kashshaf established the manner of the proof with what neither fattens nor satisfies hunger, and claimed that good taste (al-dhawq) judges accordingly. How excellent is Arabic taste when it is mixed with love of a school of thought and tainted with the blemishes of rigidity, it is thus. Everyone who understands the language of the Arabs knows that whoever says "the imam is not too proud for this statement, nor the follower," or "neither the great nor the small," or "neither the noble nor the lowly," then this indicates that the conjoined is greater in standing than the thing it is conjoined to. In any case, how wretched is occupation with this question, how little its benefit, and how far it is from being a centre among the legal and religious centres or a bridge among the bridges! ﴿And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant﴾ i.e., he is too proud out of arrogance and considers himself above worship. ﴿Then He will gather them all to Himself﴾ the one who disdains and others, and He will recompense each according to his deeds.

He omitted mention of the one who does not disdain here because the opening of the speech indicates it, and because the gathering is for both groups. ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full﴾ without any part of them being lost (p-347) ﴿And as for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment﴾ because of their disdain and arrogance. ﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any protector﴾ who will befriend them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who will support them.

His statement: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord﴾ by what He sent down to you of His books, and by the one He sent to you of His messengers, and the miracles which He established for them. Al-burhan is that by which the sought-after matter is proven. ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ which is the Qur'an, and He named it light because one is guided by it out of the darkness of misguidance.

﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him﴾ i.e., to Allah. It was also said: to the light mentioned. ﴿He will admit them into mercy from Him﴾ by which He shows them mercy, ﴿and bounty﴾ which He bestows upon them, ﴿and guide them to Himself﴾ i.e., to carrying out what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade; or to Him, glorified and exalted be He, in terms of their destination to His reward and His bounty, ﴿on a straight path﴾ i.e., a road they travel to Him, straight without crookedness, which is adherence to the religion of Islam and abandoning other religions. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the pronoun in His statement "ilayhi" refers to the name of Allah mentioned earlier. It was also said: it refers to the Qur'an; it was said: to the mercy and bounty, because both carry the meaning of reward. The accusative of "siratan" is because it is a second object of the verb mentioned; it was also said: it is in the accusative of circumstance.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ﴿The Messiah will not disdain﴾ will not be arrogant. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Isma'ili in his Mu'jam transmitted with a weak chain from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, regarding His statement ﴿so He will pay them their rewards and increase them from His bounty﴾: 'Their rewards: He will admit them to Paradise, and He will increase them from His bounty by intercession for whoever deserved the Fire among those who did them kindness in the world.'"

Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir, saying: Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of Baqiyya, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd Allah al-Kindi, from al-A'mash, from Shaqiq, from Ibn Mas'ud, and mentioned it, and said: this chain is not established; but if it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud as a statement of his own (mawquf), then it is good. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada regarding ﴿there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof﴾ that it means a clear evidence, ﴿and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ he said: this is the Qur'an. Both of them also transmitted from Mujahid that he said: burhan is proof (hujja). Both of them also transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding His statement ﴿and held fast to Him﴾ that he said: the Qur'an.

Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir, saying: Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of Baqiyya, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd Allah al-Kindi, from al-A'mash, from Shaqiq, from Ibn Mas'ud, and mentioned it, and said: this chain is not established; but if it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud as a statement of his own (mawquf), then it is good. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada regarding ﴿there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof﴾ that it means a clear evidence, ﴿and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ he said: this is the Qur'an. Both of them also transmitted from Mujahid that he said: burhan is proof (hujja). Both of them also transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding His statement ﴿and held fast to Him﴾ that he said: the Qur'an.

The commentary has already discussed *al-kalala* (the deceased who leaves neither ascendant nor descendant) at the beginning of this surah, and the questioner intended by His words "they ask you" will be mentioned later. His words, ﴿If a man dies﴾, mean: if a man dies, as was mentioned in His words, ﴿And if a woman fears﴾ [an-Nisa: 128].

His words, ﴿and he has no child﴾, are either a description of *imru'* (a man) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*). There is no objection to it being a circumstantial clause. The word *walad* (child) applies to both male and female. He mentioned only the absence of a child here, although the absence of a child is a condition of *kalala*, relying on its being evident. It has been said: the meaning of *walad* here is the son, which is one of the two meanings of a homonym, because a daughter does not exclude a sister. His words, ﴿and he has a sister﴾, are conjoined to His words, ﴿he has no child﴾.

The sister intended here is the full sister or the paternal sister, not the maternal sister, because her prescribed share is one-sixth, as was mentioned earlier. The majority of scholars among the Companions, the Successors and those after them have held that full or paternal sisters are *'asaba* (residuary heirs) for the daughters, even if there is no brother with them.

Ibn 'Abbas held that and, Dawud al-Zahiri and a group also held it, and they said: there is no inheritance for a full or paternal sister alongside a daughter. They argued from the apparent wording of this verse, since it made the absence of a child, which includes male and female, a condition for the sister's inheritance. This argument would be sound if the Sunnah did not contain what proves the sister's inheritance alongside a daughter. That is what is established in the Sahih: that Mu'adh judged, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning a daughter and a sister, and gave the daughter one half and the sister one half. It is also established in the Sahih that "the Prophet (ﷺ) judged concerning a daughter, a son's daughter and a sister, giving the daughter one half, the son's daughter one sixth, and the sister the remainder." Thus this Sunnah requires interpreting *walad* as the son, not the daughter.

His words, ﴿and he inherits from her﴾, mean: the man inherits from her, i.e., he inherits from the sister, ﴿if she has no child﴾, a male child, if by his inheriting from her is meant his taking all that she left. If what is meant is that his inheritance from her is established in general, whether as a whole or in part, then it is correct to interpret *walad* as including male and female. He (glorified be He) limited this verse to the negation of a child, although the father excludes the brother just as a male child does, because the purpose here is to state the brother's rights only in the presence of a child. As for his exclusion by the father, it has been made clear by the Sunnah, as is established in the Sahih from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give the prescribed shares to their owners, and what remains goes to the nearest male relative." The father has a better claim than the brother.

His words, ﴿if there are two﴾, mean: if those who inherit through siblingship are two. The grammatical agreement (feminine and dual) is with the preceding conditional clause, and likewise the plural in His words, ﴿and if they are siblings﴾, is according to the sense of the report. ﴿For the two of them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, if the man has no child, as has passed. Whatever is above two sisters receives two-thirds all the more so.

﴿And if they are siblings﴾, i.e., those who inherit through siblingship, ﴿men and women﴾, i.e., mixed, males and females, ﴿then for the male is the like of the portion of two females﴾ among them, as residuaries (*ta'sib*).

﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾, i.e., He makes clear to you the ruling on *kalala* and the rest of the rulings, lest you go astray. This is how al-Qurtubi related it from the Basrans.

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "so that you do not go astray," and al-Farra' and other Kufans agreed with him. ﴿And Allah, of all things﴾ among the things of which these rulings mentioned are part, ﴿is Knowing﴾, i.e., abundantly knowledgeable.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me while I was ill and not in my senses. He performed ablution, then poured (water) over me, and I regained my senses. I said: 'Indeed, only a *kalala* inherits from me; so how is the inheritance?' Then the verse of the prescribed shares was revealed."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Hatim related it from him with the wording: "It was revealed concerning me, ﴿They ask you. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning *kalala*﴾."

Ibn Rahawayh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Umar that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How is *kalala* inherited?" So Allah revealed, ﴿They ask you. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning *kalala*﴾, the verse.

Malik, Muslim, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Umar, who said: "I did not ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about anything more than I asked him about *kalala*, until he struck my chest with his finger and said: 'Does not the verse of summer, which is at the end of Surat an-Nisa, suffice you?'"

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about *kalala*. He said: 'The verse of summer suffices you.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Umar, who said: "There are three things I wished the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had laid down for us a definite rule about, to which we could refer: the grandfather, *kalala*, and some aspects of usury."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "The last surah to be revealed in its entirety was Bara'ah, and the last verse to be revealed was the closing of Surat an-Nisa: ﴿They ask you. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning *kalala*﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Sirin, who said: "When Umar ibn al-Khattab recited ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾, he would say: 'O Allah, whoever You made *kalala* clear to, but You did not make it clear to me...'"

We have already clarified the discussion of *kalala* at the beginning of this surah, with its disagreements, evidences and preferences, so we will not repeat it.

Here ends the first part of this blessed commentary, named *Fath al-Qadir*, which combines the two disciplines of transmission (*riwaya*) and understanding (*dirayah*) in the science of tafsir, by the pen of its author, who hopes from his Lord (glorified be He) that He help him to complete it, benefit by it whomever He wills of His servants, and make it a treasure for him when he comes to the Abode of the Hereafter: Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Shawkani, may Allah forgive them both. The conclusion of this point was on the Great Festival, the blessed Day of Sacrifice, in the year 1224 after the Prophetic Hijrah, praising Allah, and invoking blessings and peace upon His Messenger and beloved Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, and upon his family and companions.

End. Praise be to Him: completed by listening, and praise be to Allah, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah of the year 1232.

Yahya ibn 'Ali al-Shawkani.
